Key facts · Date · 6 April 1948 — first industrial policy of independent India · Presented by · Dr. Syama Prasad Mookerjee , first Industry (& Supply) Minister · Where · Constituent Assembly (Legislative) — no Lok Sabha yet · Main aim · Promote the public sector ; declared India a mixed economy · Categories · Four · Mookerjee → मुखड़ा : he gave India's industry its first face (मुखड़ा). Patel = first Home Minister; Mahalanobis was never a minister — he was a planner. · The four categories — remember S·B·I·O · Category · Count · What it meant · S · Strategic — exclusive Central monopoly · 3 · Arms & ammunition, atomic energy, railway transport · B · Basic — new units only by the State · 6 · Coal, iron & steel, aircraft, shipbuilding, telephone/telegraph/wireless equipment, mineral oils. Existing private units could continue (reviewed after 10 years) but could not expand freely · I · Important — regulated by government · 18 · Private allowed but centrally regulated: sugar, cement, heavy chemicals, cotton & woollen textiles, etc. · O · Others · rest · Open to private enterprise, individuals, cooperatives · “SBI-O” and 3 × 6 = 18. Strategic 3, Basic 6, Important 18 (3 × 6), then Others. Read it like the bank: SBI + O. · The lecture first said 'six' strategic, then corrected itself to three. Strategic = 3 (arms & ammunition, atomic energy, railways). The six are the basic industries. · Nehru was Prime Minister from 15 August 1947 , not from 1952. What began in 1952 was the first elected Lok Sabha . Until then the Constituent Assembly also worked as the provisional Parliament — which is why the 1948 resolution was placed there. · Why so anti-private? Memories of the East India Company (a trader that became ruler), socialist ideals (DPSP Art. 39(b)–(c): prevent concentration of wealth) and the wish to protect small artisans. The lecture's image: the government behaved like an over-caring parent until 1990. · IPR 1948: 6 April 1948, S.P. Mookerjee, Constituent Assembly. · Four categories SBI-O: Strategic 3 (central monopoly), Basic 6 (new units by State), Important 18 (regulated), Others. · Made India a mixed economy; main aim = promote public sector.

Key facts · Date · 30 April 1956 · Nickname · Economic Constitution of India · Linked plan · 2nd Five Year Plan (1956–61, Mahalanobis model) · Central theme · State control of the 'commanding heights' — public sector to lead heavy and basic industry · Classification · Three schedules — A, B, C · Also said · Support small & cottage industries; reduce regional disparities; fair treatment of labour · Schedules A · B · C · Schedule · Count · Rule · A · 17 · Exclusive responsibility of the State (the old 3 strategic grew to 17) · B · 12 · Progressively State-owned; private sector may supplement (the old 6 basic doubled to 12) · C · rest · Left to private initiative, under licensing (old 18 + Others merged) · “17-12-बाकी” and the growth story: 3 → 17 , 6 → 12 (doubled), 18 + others → C . Two schedules for government, one for private — the state holds the steering wheel. · Decode the economics English. 'State control of the commanding heights of the economy' simply means the government took the top seat in every key decision. That is the 1956 answer. 'Import-led growth', 'consumer goods', 'full privatisation' — all traps. · 1956 was the basis of the 2nd Plan, not the 3rd. In the 'NOT associated' PYQ, 'formed the basis of the Third Five Year Plan' was the odd one out. (Note: the 1956 text did mention reducing regional disparities and helping small industry — but in 'key feature' questions the three-schedule classification is the best answer.) · Licence Raj (लाइसेंस राज) · Meaning · Private firms needed government licences to start, expand, change product or import machines · Law · Industries (Development & Regulation) Act, 1951 · Became densest · After IPR 1956 · Effects · Entry barriers, hindered expansion, inefficiency, red-tapism, corruption · Ended · Largely by NIP 1991 · Freight Equalisation Policy · Introduced · 1952 · Abolished · 1993 · Idea · Minerals (coal, iron) cost the same to transport anywhere in India — to balance industrial growth · Result · Mineral-rich east (Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha, Bengal) lost its natural advantage; industry clustered in the west (Gujarat, Maharashtra) · Why heavy industry? Poverty goes when jobs come; jobs come from industry. The lecture's logic: the government wanted big industry but did not trust Tata/Birla to lead it — so the State took Schedule A and B itself. · IPR 1956: 30 April 1956, 'Economic Constitution', basis of 2nd Plan. · Three schedules: A 17 (State only), B 12 (State leads, private supplements), C rest. · Commanding heights = State control; Licence Raj densest after 1956. · Freight Equalisation 1952–1993 hurt the mineral-rich east.

The control years · 1969 · MRTP Act — Monopolies & Restrictive Trade Practices (in force 1 June 1970); 14 banks nationalised (19 July) · 1973 · FERA — Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (replaced the 1947 Act); Industrial Policy Statement 1973 (joint sector) · 1977 · Industrial Policy Statement — George Fernandes, Janata govt (23 Dec) · 1978 · District Industries Centres begin (1 May 1978) · 1980 · Industrial Policy Statement (23 July); 6 more banks nationalised (15 April) · MRTP Act 1969 · Aim · Stop concentration of economic power and monopolies · How · Big firms (assets above a limit: ₹20 crore in 1969, ₹100 crore from 1985) needed approval to set up or expand · 1991 · Asset threshold removed · Replaced by · Competition Act 2002 (CCI set up 2003); MRTP repealed 2009 · MRTP threshold was ₹20 crore (later ₹100 crore), not ₹500 crore as one lecture said. And MRTP did not need '75 licences' — that was classroom exaggeration for the paperwork maze. · FERA → FEMA · FERA · 1973 (in force 1974); tightly controlled foreign exchange; violation = criminal offence · FEMA · Foreign Exchange Management Act 1999 (in force 1 June 2000); violation = civil offence · Trick · R = Regulation = Rigid; M = Management = Mild · FERA is 1973, not 1971. One lecture said 'FERA 1971 became FEMA 1999' — the year is 1973. Also, MRTP (1969) and FERA (1973) were separate Acts; the 1980 statement did not create them. · Industrial Policy Statement 1977 · By · George Fernandes , Industry Minister, Janata government · Core idea · Decentralisation — take industry to villages and small towns; rural and urban growth together · Small units · Priority to small-scale, cottage and tiny units (tiny sector defined); SSI reserved list raised from ~180 to 500+ items · New body · District Industries Centre (DIC) — single window per district for loans, raw material, training, marketing · Big houses · Restrictions on large business houses tightened · Decentralisation is not disinvestment. One lecture called 1977's decentralisation 'disinvestment' (selling government shares). Disinvestment began in 1991–92 . In 1977, decentralisation meant spreading small industries to districts. · “77 = गांव की ओर” : 1977 took industry to the village — tiny units + DIC. “80 = अच्छा करो” : 1980 tried to make the public sector efficient. · Industrial Policy Statement 1980 · Mood · First softening: competition, modernisation, selective liberalisation ; automatic capacity expansion allowed · Objectives · Optimum use of installed capacity · higher productivity · employment · correct regional imbalance ('nucleus plants') · agro-based industry · promote export-oriented and import-substitution industries · consumer protection against high prices and bad quality · economic federalism · Public sector · Revive its efficiency · NOT an objective · Permitting maximum FDI — that is 1991 · The 1980 PYQ confused even the teacher. Official objectives include promoting export-oriented industries and consumer protection — so those are NOT the odd ones out. The option that does not fit 1980 is 'permitting maximum foreign direct investment' . · US/China vs India on monopoly. The goal — stop wealth piling up with a few — was the same everywhere. The US and China answered with more competitors ; India answered by capping the big firms . The lecture's point: capping killed growth; competition would have grown it. · MRTP 1969 (threshold ₹20 cr → ₹100 cr 1985 → removed 1991) → Competition Act 2002 → repealed 2009. · FERA 1973 (criminal) → FEMA 1999 (civil). · 1977: George Fernandes, decentralisation, tiny units, DIC (1978). · 1980: efficiency of PSUs, selective liberalisation; max FDI is NOT a 1980 objective.

Key facts · Date · 24 July 1991 (same day as the Union Budget) · Trigger · Balance of payments crisis 1990–91 (reserves for ~2 weeks of imports; gold pledged) · Prime Minister · P.V. Narasimha Rao (also held Industry) · Finance Minister · Manmohan Singh · Pillars · L iberalisation · P rivatisation · G lobalisation · Status · Still India's last full industrial policy · What 1991 changed · Area · Change · De-licensing · Compulsory licensing abolished except a short list (18 then; now 4 : cigars & cigarettes, electronic aerospace & defence equipment, industrial explosives, hazardous chemicals) · De-reservation · Public-sector-only list cut from 17 to 8 · FDI · Automatic approval up to 51% in 34 high-priority industries — first time foreigners could hold majority · Technology · Automatic approval for foreign technology agreements · MRTP · Asset threshold removed; no prior approval for big firms · Disinvestment · Sale of part of government's stake in PSUs (from 1991–92) · Trade · Tariffs cut, quantitative restrictions and import licensing phased out · Public-sector reserved list · 1956 · 17 (Schedule A) · 1991 · 8 · 2001 · 3 — defence, atomic energy, railway transport · Today · 2 — atomic energy and railway operations · Dec 2025 · SHANTI Act lets private firms build and run nuclear power plants; sensitive fuel-cycle work stays with government · Numbers the lectures got wrong. 1991 reserved 8 industries (one lecture said 5 'core areas'). FDI up to 51% was in 34 high-priority industries (one lecture said 47). Also, 1991 is the latest industrial policy — the '2002, 2011, 2022 policies' in one lecture were other documents (2011 was the National Manufacturing Policy). · “1991 = undo button.” Whatever 1950–1990 did, 1991 reversed: licence → de-licence; reserved → de-reserved; FERA → (FEMA 1999); MRTP → (Competition Act 2002); closed → FDI. L because licences broke firms, P because PSUs were inefficient, G because we needed money and competition. · Nationalisation is NOT a pillar of 1991. Nationalisation (making companies government-owned) was 1969 and 1980 for banks. Options mixing 'nationalisation' into LPG are wrong. · 1991 → 8th Plan. The 8th Plan (1992–97) was the first plan after LPG and moved India to indicative planning — the government points the direction, the market does the running. · NIP 24 July 1991: BoP crisis; PM Narasimha Rao, FM Manmohan Singh; LPG. · Licensing now only 4 industries; reserved list 17 → 8 → 3 → 2 (atomic energy, railways). · 51% FDI automatic in 34 industries; MRTP threshold removed; disinvestment begins. · Nationalisation ≠ LPG.

iprplans.h: 1991 से पहले बनाम बाद · PYQ पैटर्न
iprplans.x: Two phases in one table · 1947–1990 · After 1991 · Role of state · Over-caring parent; public sector dominant · Regulator and facilitator · Trade strategy · Inward-looking , import substitution, high tariffs · Outward-looking; tariffs cut, QRs removed · Private sector · Licence Raj, MRTP, FERA · De-licensed, competition law, FEMA · Foreign capital · Very limited · FDI welcomed (51% → up to 100% in many sectors) · Result · Protected market → inefficiency, low innovation · Competition → efficiency · Match the period, then the tone. Any 1947–90 question: answer contains inward-looking, import substitution, protection of domestic industry, entry barriers, inefficiency . Any post-1991 question: reduced tariffs, removed licensing, removed quantitative restrictions, prudential norms . · Why public sector got the lead (1947–90) · Correct reason · A tool to achieve social goals , balanced regional development and control of strategic industries · Wrong reasons · 'Public sector was inherently more efficient' · 'private sector had enough capital and technology' · 'no demand for industrial goods' · Banking reforms · Bank nationalisation · 14 banks on 19 July 1969; 6 banks on 15 April 1980 · Narasimham Committee I · 1991 — financial system reforms · Narasimham Committee II · 1998 — banking sector reforms; merge and consolidate strong public sector banks · Prudential norms · Capital adequacy — CRAR = Capital to Risk-weighted Assets Ratio (Basel norms) · Assertion–reason on trade reforms. 'Trade reforms removed quantitative restrictions on imports and exports' ✓. 'Trade reforms increased import licensing to support domestic manufacturers' ✗ — increasing licences is the pre-1991 habit. · The lecture's parenting analogy. A child never allowed to fall never learns to stand. 1947–90 India held its industry's hand so tightly that it never learned to compete — and 1991 finally let go. · 1947–90: inward-looking, import substitution, protection → inefficiency. · Post-1991: tariffs cut, licensing and QRs removed, prudential norms (CRAR). · Public sector's lead: social goals, balanced regional development, strategic control. · Banks nationalised 1969 (14) and 1980 (6); Narasimham I 1991, II 1998 (merge & consolidate).

Singh, Chandra Shekhar governments) and the BoP crisis · Then · 8th Plan started in 1992 after LPG reforms · Rajiv Gandhi was not PM in 1990–92. Narasimha Rao · Human resource development ; first after LPG; indicative planning · 5.6% → 6.8% · 9th · 1997–2002 · A.B. Vajpayee · Growth with social justice and equality · 6.5% → 5.4% · 10th · 2002–07 · Vajpayee → Manmohan Singh · 8% growth; double per-capita income in 10 years · 8.0% → 7.6% · 11th · 2007–12 · Manmohan Singh · Towards faster and more inclusive growth · 9.0% → ~8% · 12th · 2012–17 · Manmohan Singh → Narendra Modi · Faster, more inclusive and sustainable growth · 8.0% (last plan) · 11 → 12 just adds a word. 11th = faster + inclusive. 12th = faster + inclusive + sustainable . 9th = social justice + equality (नौ = न्याय). · Match-type PYQ trap: 'Faster and more inclusive growth' = 11th ; 'Faster, more inclusive and sustainable growth' = 12th . folkdances.x: India has roughly 250 folk dances worth knowing, about eight per state. SSC asks them in four shapes: (1) which state (by far the most common), (2) which community or tribe performs it, (3) what it depicts or when it is danced (war, harvest, wedding, a deity), and (4) statement questions (CGL 2024–25 asked these on Jhora, Dangi, Kalbelia, Ghoomar, Tamasha, Jhumair and Dumhal). The lecture's rule: learn the state first; details come second. · The name often gives the state away. Kunitha → Karnataka (Dollu, Suggi Kunitha). Cholom → Manipur (Pung, Dhol Cholom). Lam → Mizoram (Khuallam, Chheih Lam, Tlanglam, Sarlamkai; lam = dance in Mizo). Chham → the Tibetan-Buddhist belt (Ladakh, HP, Sikkim, Arunachal). -attam / -kali / -koothu → Kerala or Tamil Nadu (a double 't' is the clue). Nacha / Nach → Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Bihar (Danda Nacha, Raut Nacha, Launda Nach). Nati / Natti → Himachal (Barada Nati is the Uttarakhand exception). · The eight classical dances (Sangeet Natak Akademi) · Classical dance · State · Hook · Bharatanatyam · Tamil Nadu · Oldest; temple dance of Thanjavur · Kathak · Uttar Pradesh · Katha = story; Lucknow, Jaipur, Banaras gharanas · Kathakali · Kerala · Green faces, huge headgear · Mohiniattam · Kerala · Mohini = enchantress; lasya · Kuchipudi · Andhra Pradesh · Village Kuchipudi; Bhamakalapam · Odissi · Odisha · Tribhanga; Gotipua and Mahari are its roots · Manipuri · Manipur · Ras Leela; Jagoi · Sattriya · Assam · Sankardeva's sattras · Classical vs folk. If a question asks for a folk dance of Punjab and the options are Kuchipudi, Yakshagana, Mohiniattam and Bhangra, eliminate the three classical/theatre forms of the south. The Ministry of Culture also counts Chhau as classical (nine in all), but SSC keys follow the Akademi's eight. · Indian dance forms on UNESCO's Intangible Heritage list · Element · State · Year · Koodiyattam · Kerala · Proclaimed 2001 (inscribed 2008) · Ramlila · Uttar Pradesh · Proclaimed 2005 (inscribed 2008) · Baul songs · West Bengal · Proclaimed 2005 (inscribed 2008) · Ramman · Uttarakhand (Chamoli) · 2009 · Chhau · Odisha, Jharkhand, West Bengal · 2010 · Kalbelia · Rajasthan · 2010 · Mudiyettu · Kerala · 2010 · Sankirtana · Manipur · 2013 · Garba · Gujarat · 2023 · Dance forms on UNESCO's list, year by year · India's dance and theatre forms on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Ghoomar is not on it. · Ghoomar is NOT on the UNESCO list. A CGL statement said 'Ghoomar and Kalbelia are both UNESCO-listed' — only Kalbelia (2010) is. From Rajasthan, only Kalbelia; from Gujarat, only Garba (2023). · Sort by theme when the name rings no bell. Dances fall into a few families: war/martial, harvest/sowing, weddings, unmarried girls, festivals, a deity, and animal mimicry. Revise → Themes groups them this way. If a question says 'depicts victory in war', you only have to scan the martial list. · Dance ↔ festival. Many dances are asked through the festival they belong to: Ponung at Solung, Popir at Mopin, Bagurumba at Bwisagu, Chu Faat at Pang Lhabsol, Wangala and Nongkrem are both festival and dance, Karma at Karma Puja, Garba at Navratri. If you finished the Festivals workbook, half of this is already known. · Statement questions. Extreme words — only, exclusively, solo, women alone — are usually false. That is how two 2024 CGL statements were built: 'Dangi is a solo narrative dance' (false: it is a group dance) and 'women alone perform the Mardani variant of Jhumair' (false). · Learn the state first. · Kunitha → Karnataka; Cholom → Manipur; Lam → Mizoram; Chham → Buddhist Himalaya; -attam/-kali → Kerala/TN. · 8 classical: Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kathakali, Mohiniattam, Kuchipudi, Odissi, Manipuri, Sattriya. · UNESCO: Chhau & Kalbelia & Mudiyettu 2010, Garba 2023; Ghoomar is not listed.

Veeranatyam (Andhra) and Perini Shivatandavam (Telangana) are both warrior dances offered to Shiva. Veera = brave, Andhra; Perini = Kakatiya kings of Warangal, Telangana. · AP: Veeranatyam (Veeramusti), Lambadi, Dhimsa (Araku), Kolattam, Bhamakalapam (Siddhendra Yogi), Burrakatha, Butta Bommalu, Dappu, Vilasini Natyam. · Telangana: Gussadi (Raj Gond, Adilabad), Mathuri, Perini (Kakatiya), Bonalu (Mahakali). · Pongal is TN, not Telangana.

Bardo → border → masks to keep evil out. Wancho → 'want Oreo' → Oriah festival. Popir → 'पापी' (evil spirits chased) + 'गला' → Galo . Ponung → 'फ़ोन पे अच्छी फ़सल' → harvest, Adi. · Popir vs Ponung. Both were asked as 'which state' (answer Arunachal), but the tribes differ: Popir = Galo (Mopin), Ponung = Adi (Solung). Lecture 1 mixed Ozele into the Galo list; leave it out. · Monpa owns three: Aji Lamu, Lion & Peacock, and the Yak dance — all Buddhist, all around Tawang. Masks + Buddhism in Arunachal → Monpa or Sherdukpen. · Rikham Pada Nyishi; Aji Lamu, Lion & Peacock, Yak Monpa; Wancho (Oriah); Buiya Digaru Mishmi. · Adi: Ponung (women, Solung), Pasi Kongki, Tapu. Galo: Popir (Mopin). · Chalo Loku Nocte; Bardo Chham Sherdukpen (12 zodiac masks).

“ अली (Ali-Ai-Ligang) भोर (Bhortal) में देव (Deodhani) के पास गया — मैथ्स में अंक (Ankiya Naat) दिला देना, इस पाली (Ojapali) में झूम (Jhumur) के नाचूंगा।” The second lecture adds: “ बगल (Bagurumba) की बहू (Bihu) भोर (Bhortal) में उठती है” — and BB : Bagurumba = Bodo. · Assam · Dance · Who / what · Remember · Bihu · Assamese · Bohag Bihu (April); women in mekhela chador ; dhol & pepa · Bagurumba · Bodo women · 'Butterfly dance'; Bwisagu; dress dokhona & aronai · Sattriya · — · Classical; Srimanta Sankardeva · Ankiya Naat · — · One-act Vaishnavite play by Sankardeva · Bhortal · Satriya community, Barpeta · Cymbal (bhortal) dance by Narahari Burha Bhakat · Ojapali · — · Semi-dramatic narrative chorus; the Oja leads, the Palis follow · Deodhani · — · Trance dance to snake goddess Manasa · Ali-Ai-Ligang · Mising · Sowing festival in Falgun; Gumrag dance · Jhumur · Tea tribes · Tea-garden workers; also West Bengal · Current affairs: on 17 January 2026 , more than 10,000 Bodo artists danced Bagurumba together at the Sarusajai stadium in Guwahati ( Bagurumba Dwhou ), with Prime Minister Modi present — billed as a record-setting performance. · Sattriya (dance) vs Satriya (community). Sattriya is the classical dance founded by Sankardeva. appointments.h: नियुक्ति के प्रश्न कैसे आते हैं
appointments.x: Appointments are pure facts, so there's little to understand and a lot to remember. SSC asks them in four shapes: (1) who has been appointed as… (most common), (2) which number (26th CEC, 53rd CJI), (3) first woman / first from a country , and (4) the static part behind the post — the Article, the Act, the tenure, who appoints and who removes. The lecture's advice: when you read a name, ask which Part and Article is this body in, what is the tenure, and can the person be reappointed? · Three kinds of bodies — know which is which · Type · Made by · Examples · Constitutional · Named in the Constitution · ECI (Art 324), UPSC (315), CAG (148), Finance Commission (280), AG (76), Advocate General (165), NCSC (338), NCST (338A), NCBC (338B) · Statutory · An Act of Parliament · CIC (RTI Act 2005), NHRC (PHRA 1993), NCW (1990 Act), CVC (CVC Act 2003), NGT (NGT Act 2010), SEBI (1992), Lokpal (2013) · Executive / extra-constitutional · A government (cabinet) resolution · NITI Aayog (2015), Planning Commission (1950), Law Commission, CBI (powers from DSPE Act 1946) · Ask “कौन बनाया?” If the Constitution made it → constitutional. If Parliament passed an Act → statutory. If the cabinet just decided → executive. NITI Aayog, Law Commission and CBI are the three favourite traps — none is constitutional, none is statutory. · Which number? — the most-asked ordinals · Post · Holder · Number · Chief Election Commissioner · Gyanesh Kumar · 26th · RBI Governor · Sanjay Malhotra · 26th · Chief Justice of India · Justice Surya Kant · 53rd · Vice-President · C.P. space.h: अंतरिक्ष की भाषा — पेलोड से रोवर तक
space.x: Every space question uses a small set of words. Learn them once and the long Steno/CGL statement questions become easy to read. A space mission is a complete plan to solve one problem from space — e.g. 'photograph flooded Delhi every hour'. The lecture called its example Mission Aankh : put a camera in the sky. · The building blocks of a mission · Word · What it is · Mission Aankh example · Payload · The main item the mission exists for · The camera / sensor · Satellite bus · Support platform: solar panels, battery, antenna, thermal control, small thrusters, computer · Keeps the camera powered, cool and pointed at Delhi · Spacecraft · Payload + satellite bus together · The whole flying machine · Launch vehicle / rocket · Carries the spacecraft to the right height and path — a 'space taxi' · PSLV, GSLV, LVM3 · Ground segment · Control centre, big antennas and computers on Earth · ISRO's control room that commands and receives images · P + B = S. P ayload + B us = S pacecraft. The rocket is only the bus-to-school; the student (spacecraft) writes the exam. Rocket ≠ satellite. · Spacecraft by job — the spy-movie analogy · Type · What it does · Indian / world example · Orbiter · Circles the body and watches from outside · Chandrayaan-2 orbiter, Mangalyaan · Lander · Lands and works from one spot (soil, temperature, surroundings) · Vikram (Chandrayaan-3) · Rover · Comes out of the lander and moves around · Pragyan; NASA's Curiosity, Perseverance · Flyby · Passes close at high speed, collects data, does not enter orbit · Voyager, Pioneer 10 · Atmospheric probe · Plunges into an atmosphere to measure gases, pressure, temperature · Galileo probe at Jupiter · Crew capsule / module · Pressurised cabin with oxygen, temperature control, safety, re-entry system · Gaganyaan crew module, Orion · Space observatory · A telescope 'lab' placed above clouds and pollution · AstroSat, Hubble, JWST · A satellite is anything that keeps going round another body. Once a spacecraft lands (Vikram on the Moon) it is no longer a satellite — it is just a spacecraft/lander. So: every artificial satellite is a spacecraft, but not every spacecraft is a satellite. · Why doesn't a satellite fall? Not because there is no gravity — gravity is exactly what holds it. The satellite is thrown sideways so fast that while it falls, the round Earth curves away beneath it. It is in continuous free fall . Forward motion + gravity = orbit. No engine has to run; in space there is no friction to slow it (Newton's first law). · Two speeds to remember · Orbital velocity (LEO) · ≈ 7.8 km/s ≈ 28,000 km/h — goes round Earth in ~90 min · Escape velocity (Earth) · 11.2 km/s — leave Earth's gravity for the Moon/Mars · GEO satellite speed · ≈ 3.07 km/s — slower because it is farther out · Rule · Lower orbit → higher speed → shorter period · पहलवान rule. Near a strong wrestler (low orbit, strong gravity) you must run very fast; far away (high orbit) you can stroll past. So low orbit = fast, high orbit = slow. · Rover needs a lander. Chandrayaan-3 = propulsion module (carrier) + Vikram (lander) + Pragyan (rover). Chandrayaan-2 had an orbiter instead of a propulsion module — the orbiter still works. · Payload + bus = spacecraft; rocket only carries it. · Orbiter watches, lander sits, rover moves, flyby passes, probe dives in. · Satellite stays up by continuous free fall; LEO 7.8 km/s, escape 11.2 km/s.

space.t: Orbits: LEO, MEO, GEO, SSO & Lagrange points
space.x: Orbits by height · Orbit · Height · Used for · LEO — Low Earth Orbit · 160–2,000 km · Earth observation (sharp images), ISS (~400 km), Gaganyaan (~400 km), Hubble (~540 km), Starlink-type constellations · MEO — Medium Earth Orbit · Between LEO and GEO (~20,000 km) · Navigation — GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou · GEO — Geostationary · 35,786 km above the equator · Communication, TV broadcast, weather (INSAT, GSAT) · Camera distance rule. Want sharp detail (crop, flood, rooftop)? Stand close → LEO. Want a rough road map? Middle → MEO. Want the whole cloud system or a fixed relay mirror? Stand far → GEO. · Orbits by shape, tilt and timing · Orbit · Key idea · Geosynchronous (GSO) · Period = one sidereal day (~23 h 56 min). Can be tilted or elliptical, so it traces a figure-8 in the sky · Geostationary (GEO) · A special GSO: circular + zero inclination (over the equator) + same direction as Earth's spin → looks fixed · GTO — Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit · Elliptical 'parking-to-GEO' orbit; rockets drop satellites here, satellites raise themselves to GEO · Polar orbit · Passes over both poles; Earth turns beneath it, so it scans the whole globe strip by strip · Sun-synchronous (SSO) · Near-polar; crosses a given place at the same local solar time every day — same shadows, so images can be compared · HEO — Highly Elliptical · Very elongated; spends long time over one high-latitude region · Equatorial orbit · Orbit in the plane of the equator · Every geostationary orbit is geosynchronous, but not every geosynchronous orbit is geostationary. A GSO that is tilted or elliptical repeats every 24 h but wanders north–south. Only circular + equatorial + prograde makes it 'stationary'. · Orbit vocabulary · Apogee / Perigee · Farthest / nearest point of an orbit around Earth (P = Paas = Perigee) · Aphelion / Perihelion · Farthest / nearest point around the Sun · Prograde / Retrograde · Same / opposite direction as Earth's rotation (west→east is prograde) · Inclination · Tilt of the orbit plane from the equator · ISS · ~400 km, 51.6° inclination, ~90 min per orbit, ~28,000 km/h, ~16 orbits a day · Lagrange points are five spots where the pull of two big bodies (Sun–Earth or Earth–Moon) plus orbital motion balance, so a small spacecraft can stay in step with them using very little fuel. Gravity is not zero there — net force just matches what the orbit needs. They are also called libration points . · The Sun–Earth Lagrange points · Point · Where · Use · L1 · Between Sun and Earth, ~1.5 million km from Earth · Uninterrupted view of the Sun — Aditya-L1 , SOHO · L2 · Behind Earth, ~1.5 million km away · Deep-space viewing with Sun, Earth, Moon behind — JWST , Gaia · L3 · Opposite side of the Sun · Not used · L4, L5 · 60° ahead / behind Earth on its orbit; form equilateral triangles with Sun and Earth · Only stable points; Trojan asteroids gather here · L1 looks at the Sun, L2 looks away. L1–L2 distance ≈ 3 million km; L2–L3 ≈ 300 million km (asked in CHSL Mains). L1, L2, L3 are unstable — spacecraft keep doing small burns; L4 & L5 are stable. · Orbit → job → satellite name. GEO: INSAT, GSAT, CMS-03. SSO/polar: Cartosat, Resourcesat, EOS, NISAR (747 km). L1: Aditya. LEO: XPoSat, AstroSat (650 km), ISS, Gaganyaan. · LEO <2,000 km (imaging, ISS); MEO ~20,000 km (GPS); GEO 35,786 km (communication, weather). · GEO = GSO + circular + equatorial; SSO = same local time each pass. · L1 Aditya, L2 JWST; L4/L5 the only stable points.

A balloon flies forward when air rushes out behind. A rocket does the same with hot gas: momentum thrown backward pushes the rocket forward — Newton's third law (conservation of momentum). It does not need air to push against, so it works in vacuum. The push is called thrust . · Burning needs oxygen, and space has none. So a rocket carries its own oxidiser along with the fuel ; fuel + oxidiser = propellant . · Propellant types · Type · Fuel + oxidiser · Strength · Weakness · Solid · Pre-mixed grain · Huge thrust, simple, good for lift-off & strap-on boosters · Cannot throttle, stop or restart · Liquid (storable) · e.g. UDMH + N₂O₄ in separate tanks (Vikas engine) · Throttle, shut down, restart — good for manoeuvring · More complex · Cryogenic · Liquid hydrogen (−253 °C) + liquid oxygen (−183 °C) · Highest energy per kg · Super-cold storage; heat and cold side by side · Semi-cryogenic · Refined kerosene (RP-1) + liquid oxygen · Only LOX needs cooling; kerosene is dense and cheap · Kerosene leaves soot (coking) — bad for reuse · Methalox · Liquid methane + liquid oxygen · Clean burn — good for reusable engines · Methane also needs cooling (−162 °C) · 'Semi-cryogenic' does NOT mean half solid, half liquid. It means only the oxidiser (LOX) is cryogenic; the fuel is kerosene at room temperature. Cryogenic = LH₂ + LOX. Semi-cryo = kerosene + LOX. Methalox = methane + LOX. · Fuel family ladder: Hydrogen (cryo, cleanest, hardest) → Kerosene (semi-cryo, sooty like a lantern chimney) → Methane (methalox, clean and reusable). The oxidiser is LOX in all three — the fuel is what changes. · Staging. Carrying empty tanks is like climbing a hill with empty steel tiffins. So a rocket drops each stage when its fuel is spent; the lighter rocket speeds up. Strap-on boosters give extra lift-off thrust. Dropping expensive stages is costly — hence reusable rockets. · Indian engines & stages · Vikas · Liquid engine (UDMH + N₂O₄) — PSLV 2nd stage, GSLV/LVM3 core · CE-7.5 · Indigenous cryogenic engine of GSLV Mk II upper stage (CUS); first success GSLV-D5, Jan 2014 · CE-20 / C25 stage · LVM3's cryogenic upper stage (C25 ≈ 25 t propellant); C32 is the upgraded version · S200 · Solid strap-on booster of LVM3 · SCE-200 · Semi-cryogenic (kerosene–LOX) engine under development · Scramjet · Air-breathing: no compressor fans; very high forward speed compresses incoming air, oxygen from air burns hydrogen. ISRO test 28 Aug 2016 · Mach number · Speed ÷ speed of sound. 1 supersonic, >5 hypersonic · Fuel choice explains ISRO's roadmap. GSLV/LVM3 use hydrogen-cryo upper stages; NGLV moves to methalox for reusable boosters (clean burn), with spark torch igniters for repeated restarts (Lesson 7). · Rocket = Newton's third law; carries its own oxidiser. · Solid = thrust, no restart; liquid = control; cryo = LH₂+LOX; semi-cryo = kerosene+LOX; methalox = methane+LOX. · Stages are dropped to shed dead weight; Vikas liquid, CE-20 cryo, S200 solid.

space.h: भारत की अंतरिक्ष यात्रा — इनकोस्पार से राकेश शर्मा तक
space.x: After the USSR launched Sputnik-1 (4 Oct 1957) , the USA answered by setting up NASA (1958) . In India, Dr Vikram Sarabhai — father of the Indian space programme — convinced Nehru that space technology could reach farmers, teachers and fishermen far away. India first had to learn what space was: hence a research committee before any agency. · Timeline · 1962 · INCOSPAR (Indian National Committee for Space Research) under the Department of Atomic Energy ; set up by Vikram Sarabhai with Homi Bhabha's support · 21 Nov 1963 · First sounding rocket Nike-Apache (US-made) from Thumba (TERLS), Kerala — near the magnetic equator · 1967 · Experimental Satellite Communication Earth Station, Ahmedabad , to train engineers · 15 Aug 1969 · ISRO formed, superseding INCOSPAR · 1972 · Space Commission and Department of Space set up; ISRO brought under DoS (Sept 1972). DoS reports directly to the Prime Minister · 1975–76 · SITE — Satellite Instructional Television Experiment using NASA's ATS-6, TV lessons to ~2,400 villages · 19 Apr 1975 · Aryabhata , first Indian satellite — built in India, launched from Kapustin Yar (USSR) on a Soviet rocket; project led by U.R. Rao · 1977–79 · STEP — Satellite Telecommunication Experiments Project with the P&T department using the Franco-German Symphonie satellite · 1979 & 1981 · Bhaskara-I & II — first Indian experimental remote-sensing satellites (launched by USSR) · 10 Aug 1979 · SLV-3 first flight fails; Prof Satish Dhawan takes the blame publicly · 18 Jul 1980 · SLV-3 puts Rohini RS-1 in orbit from Sriharikota — first Indian satellite on an Indian rocket; project director APJ Abdul Kalam · 1981 · APPLE (Ariane Passenger PayLoad Experiment) — first indigenous experimental communication satellite, launched on Europe's Ariane · 1983 · INSAT-1B — first operational INSAT (1A of 1982 failed): communication + TV + weather on one satellite · 1984 · Rakesh Sharma (IAF) — first Indian in space, Soviet Soyuz T-11 , to Salyut-7 · The very first rocket from Thumba was American. One lecture said the first two rockets came from Russia (M-100) and France (Centaure). Those came later; 21 Nov 1963 was the US-built Nike-Apache . Also: INCOSPAR (1962) is not ISRO — ISRO is 1969. · 62-63-69-72-75-80: समिति (committee) → रॉकेट (Thumba) → ISRO → विभाग (DoS) → उपग्रह (Aryabhata) → अपना रॉकेट (SLV-3 + Rohini). 'Committee, rocket, organisation, department, satellite, own rocket.' · Aryabhata was Indian-made but not Indian-launched. First Indian satellite on an Indian rocket = Rohini RS-1 (1980, SLV-3) . Rohini Technology Payload (RTP) flew on the failed 1979 SLV-3. · People to know · Vikram Sarabhai · Father of Indian space programme; VSSC named after him; Space Applications Centre idea · Homi J. Bhabha · Father of the nuclear programme; INCOSPAR sat under his DAE · Satish Dhawan · ISRO chairman 1972–84; Sriharikota launch centre named after him · U.R. Rao · Led Aryabhata; URSC Bengaluru named after him · APJ Abdul Kalam · SLV-3 project director; 'Missile Man' · Rakesh Sharma · 1984, Soyuz T-11; 'Saare Jahan Se Achha' · Shubhanshu Shukla · 2025, first Indian on the ISS (Axiom-4) · V. Narayanan · Current ISRO Chairman (from 14 Jan 2025) · Failure → fix → retry runs through the whole story: SLV-3 (1979 fail, 1980 success), INSAT-1A → 1B, PSLV-D1 (1993 fail) → D2 (1994 success), Chandrayaan-2 lander → Chandrayaan-3. · 1962 INCOSPAR (DAE) → 1963 Nike-Apache, Thumba → 1969 ISRO → 1972 DoS & Space Commission. · Aryabhata 19 Apr 1975 (USSR launch); Rohini RS-1 on SLV-3, 18 Jul 1980. · SITE 1975 (ATS-6), STEP (Symphonie), APPLE 1981 (Ariane), INSAT-1B 1983, Rakesh Sharma 1984.

space.t: ISRO centres & how space is governed
space.x: Build a mission 'Kheti & Baadh' (farm and flood watch) and each ISRO centre does one job: the camera, the satellite around it, the rocket, the engine, the engine test, the launch, then the data. · Which centre does what · Centre · Place · Job · SAC — Space Applications Centre · Ahmedabad · Payloads (cameras, sensors, transponders) · URSC — U.R. space.t: India's rockets: SLV-3 to LVM3 and SSLV
space.x: The launch-vehicle family · Vehicle · Stages · Lift-off mass · Payload · Notes · SLV-3 · 4, all solid · 17 t · 40 kg to LEO · First Indian rocket; Rohini 1980; retired 1983 · ASLV · 5, all solid (strap-ons counted) · ~40 t · 150 kg to 400 km LEO · First success ASLV-D3, 1992 · PSLV · 4: Solid–Liquid–Solid–Liquid · 230 t (CA) – 320 t (XL) · ~1,750 kg SSO; ~1,425 kg sub-GTO · 'Workhorse'; first success PSLV-D2, 15 Oct 1994 (IRS-P2); variants CA, DL, QL, XL · GSLV Mk II · 3: Solid–Liquid (Vikas)–Cryogenic · ~420 t · ~2,250 kg GTO · Indigenous cryo stage since GSLV-D5 (2014) · LVM3 (GSLV Mk III) · 3: S200 boosters, L110 core, C25 cryo · ~640 t · 4,000 kg GTO; 8,000 kg LEO · 'Bahubali' / 'Fat Boy'; heaviest Indian rocket · SSLV · 3 solid + liquid VTM (Velocity Trimming Module) · ~120 t · 500 kg to LEO; ~300 kg SSO · Launch-on-demand, low cost; 34 m tall, 2 m wide · HLVM3 · Human-rated LVM3 · — · Gaganyaan crew module to ~400 km · Crew escape system added · Stage count 4-5-4-3-3-3: SLV-3 four, ASLV five, PSLV four, GSLV three, LVM3 three, SSLV three (+VTM). space.h: पुनः प्रयोज्य रॉकेट और निजी क्षेत्र
space.x: Throwing away a rocket after every flight is like buying a new bus for every Lucknow–Delhi trip. A Reusable Launch Vehicle (RLV) recovers parts to fly again and cut recurring cost. Two kinds of recovery: the winged top stage lands horizontally on a runway like a plane; the booster lands vertically on its tail like SpaceX's Falcon 9. · ISRO's reusable-tech trail · 23 May 2016 · RLV-TD HEX — winged demonstrator flown to ~Mach 5 on an HS9 solid booster from Sriharikota, splashed into the Bay of Bengal · 28 Aug 2016 · First experimental scramjet engine test (Advanced Technology Vehicle), Sriharikota · 2 Apr 2023 · RLV-LEX-01 — autonomous runway landing, Chitradurga (Karnataka); dropped from a Chinook helicopter · 22 Mar 2024 · RLV-LEX-02 — 'Pushpak' released 4.5 km up, 4 km away; corrected cross-range and landed itself · 23 Jun 2024 · RLV-LEX-03 — third and final landing test under tougher wind and dispersion · LEX = Landing EXperiment, Pushpak = the plane. Ramayana's flying chariot lands on a runway. LEX tests the top stage; booster recovery comes with NGLV. · Next Generation Launch Vehicle (NGLV) · Approved · Sept 2024, ₹8,240 crore · Payload · Up to ~30 t to LEO (expendable), ~10 t to GTO — about 3× LVM3 · Cost · About 1.5× LVM3 · Design · Three stages, partially reusable first stage; ISRO now plans LOX–methane engines · Timeline · First flight targeted early 2030s; needs Sriharikota's third launch pad · Spark torch igniter · Gives reliable ignition and many restarts — essential to bring a booster back · NGLV's fuel changed. The older plan (in one lecture) used semi-cryogenic kerosene boosters; recent PYQs (CGL 2025) state LOX–methane was chosen for clean burn and reuse. If a question offers methalox for NGLV, pick it. · Private rockets · Company · What · Fact to remember · Skyroot Aerospace (Hyderabad) · Vikram-S , 18 Nov 2022, mission 'Prarambh' · India's first private rocket (suborbital) · Skyroot Aerospace · Vikram-1 , 18 Jul 2026, mission ' Aagaman ' · India's first private orbital rocket; 500 km LEO; stages Kalam-1200, Kalam-250, Kalam-100 (solid) + Raman liquid stage. India = 3rd country with private orbital launch after USA & China · Agnikul Cosmos (IIT-Madras incubated) · Agnibaan SOrTeD , 30 May 2024 · From Agnikul's own pad Dhanush ; engine Agnilet — world's first single-piece 3D-printed semi-cryogenic engine · Space Zone India + Martin Group · RHUMI-1 , Aug 2024 · India's first reusable hybrid rocket (Tamil Nadu) · Vikram-S was Skyroot's, not Agnikul's. The Steno lecture marked Agnikul for 'first private rocket Vikram-S'. The rocket is named after Vikram Sarabhai and built by Skyroot ; Agnikul's rocket is Agnibaan . Also, Agnilet is semi-cryogenic , not cryogenic. · Skyroot = Vikram + Kalam (rocket named after Sarabhai, motors after Kalam). Agnikul = Agni-everything : Agnibaan rocket, Agnilet engine, Dhanush pad. · Reuse needs three things together: clean fuel (methalox, no soot), restartable ignition (spark torch igniter) and autonomous landing (LEX series). That is why all three show up in recent PYQs. · RLV-TD 2016 → LEX-01 (2023) → LEX-02 & 03 (2024, Pushpak, Chitradurga). · NGLV: ₹8,240 cr, ~30 t LEO, 3× LVM3 at 1.5× cost, methalox, reusable. · Skyroot: Vikram-S (2022), Vikram-1 'Aagaman' (18 Jul 2026, first private orbital). Agnikul: Agnibaan, Agnilet, Dhanush.

space.t: Satellites by job: communication, imaging, navigation
space.x: Satellite families · Family · Job · Orbit · Examples · INSAT · 'Bahubali' — communication, TV, weather, disaster warning, search & rescue · GEO · INSAT-1B (1983); INSAT-3D/3DR/3DS = weather only · GSAT / CMS · Pure communication, high-throughput broadband · GEO · GSAT-7 'Rukmini' (Navy, 2013), GSAT-20/N2 (Ka-band), CMS-03 · IRS → EOS · Remote sensing / Earth observation · SSO / polar · IRS-1A (1988), Cartosat (mapping), Resourcesat, Oceansat, RISAT (radar), EOS series · NavIC (IRNSS) · Regional navigation · GEO + inclined GSO · IRNSS-1A (2013) …, NVS-01 (2023), NVS-02 (2025) · IDRSS · Data relay — LEO spacecraft talk to ground in near real time via a high relay satellite · GEO · For Gaganyaan & LEO satellites · 3D = Weather. INSAT is the Bahubali that does everything; the moment you see '3D', '3DR' or '3DS' after it, that Bahubali has been given only weather duty. · Why does navigation need at least four satellites? One satellite tells you only your distance (a circle of possible positions). Two circles cross at two points; three pin one point. The fourth corrects your phone clock against the satellites' atomic clocks — a tiny time error is a big position error. That is why atomic-clock failures crippled NavIC (by March 2026 only a few satellites gave full service) and why NVS replacements matter. · NavIC · Full name · Navigation with Indian Constellation (earlier IRNSS) · Design · 7 satellites: 3 GEO + 4 inclined geosynchronous · Coverage · India plus ~1,500 km beyond its boundary · Second generation · NVS-01 (May 2023, GSLV-F12, first Indian atomic clock); NVS-02 (29 Jan 2025, GSLV-F15) stuck in transfer orbit — oxidiser valve did not open; NVS-03 on GSLV-F18 due Oct 2026 · GAGAN · GPS-Aided GEO Augmented Navigation — ISRO + Airports Authority of India; for aircraft landing; operational 2015 · Remote sensing = learning about the ground without touching it. Passive sensors read reflected sunlight (no data at night/clouds). Active sensors send their own signal — Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) works day, night and through clouds (RISAT, EOS-04, NISAR). Data goes to NRSC, Hyderabad ; the public sees it on Bhuvan ; weather data on MOSDAC ; archives on Bhoonidhi . · NISAR — NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar · Item · Fact · Launch · 30 Jul 2025, GSLV-F16 , Sriharikota (GSLV Mk II) · Mass · ~2,393 kg · Orbit · Sun-synchronous, 747 km , ~100 min period; revisits each spot every 12 days · Radars · L-band (NASA) ~24 cm wavelength; S-band (ISRO) ~9–10 cm · Antenna · 12 m mesh reflector on a 9 m boom · Firsts · First dual-frequency radar Earth-observation satellite; first ISRO–NASA hardware partnership · Phases · Commissioning ~90 days after launch; science phase from Nov 2025 · NISAR's S-band is not 12 cm. Higher frequency = shorter wavelength: L-band 1.25 GHz ≈ 24 cm, S-band 3.2 GHz ≈ 9.4 cm. What matters for the exam: L from NASA, S from ISRO . · Name tells job: Carto-sat = cartography (maps); Resource-sat = resources; Ocean-sat = ocean colour, fish zones; RI-SAT = Radar Imaging; EMISAT = electronic intelligence; HysIS = hyperspectral; Anvesha (EOS-N1) = hyperspectral surveillance. · INSAT = all-rounder; INSAT-3D/3DR/3DS = weather; GSAT/CMS = communication; IRS/EOS = imaging; NavIC = navigation; IDRSS = relay. · Navigation needs 3 satellites for position + 1 for clock; NavIC 7 satellites, 1,500 km beyond India. · NISAR: GSLV-F16, 30 Jul 2025, 747 km SSO, 12-day revisit, L-band NASA, S-band ISRO.

mensuration2d.x: Hidden inside every 2D question. Tier 1 rarely asks a pure conversion, but CHSL/MTS and CGL often hide a hectare → m² step inside a fencing or cultivation cost question. Tier 2 expects you to pick the right π in one glance. · Perimeter is the length of the boundary (unit: m, cm). Area is the surface enclosed (unit: m², cm²). Fencing, wire, rope, border, boundary → perimeter. Painting, carpeting, tiling, ploughing, levelling → area. · Unit ladder (learn the squares!) · Length · 1 m = 100 cm, 1 km = 1000 m · Square the factor for area · Area: m² → cm² · 1 m² = 100 × 100 = 10,000 cm² · Not 100! · Area: cm² → mm² · 1 cm² = 100 mm² · 10 mm × 10 mm · Are · 1 are = 100 m² · A 10 m × 10 m plot · Hectare · 1 ha = 100 are = 10,000 m² · A 100 m × 100 m plot · Square km · 1 km² = 100 ha = 10 6 m² · 1000 m × 1000 m · Cost · Cost = (area or perimeter) × rate · Rate per m² → area; rate per m → perimeter · Perimeter vs area · Area: the surface inside (m²). · Perimeter: the boundary length (m). · Why 1 m² = 10,000 cm² · Each small square drawn is 10 cm × 10 cm = 100 cm². There are 100 of them → 10,000 cm². · Which π to use? · π = 22/7 · When r, d or the answer is a multiple of 7 · r = 7, 14, 21, 3.5, 10.5 … · π = 3.14 · When r is 10, 5, 20 … or the question says 3.14 · Area of r = 10 → 314 · Leave as π · When options contain π · Never convert if options have π · Useful numbers · 2π × 7 = 44, π × 7² = 154 · 2π × 21 = 132, π × 21² = 1386 · SSC CHSL 2018 · 7 Mar S1 · 24.64 ha = 24.64 × 10,000 = 2,46,400 m² · πr² = 2,46,400 → r² = 2,46,400 × 7/22 = 78,400 → r = 280 m · Boundary = 2πr = 2 × 22/7 × 280 = 1760 m · Cost = 1760 × 5.40 = ₹9,504 · ₹9,504 · Rope/boundary → perimeter; cost per metre. Convert hectare first. · Area = 10,000/12 m² · 3x × 4x = 12x² = 10,000/12 → x² = 10,000/144 → x = 100/12 · Breadth = 3x = 300/12 = 25 m · 25 m · 12x² = 10,000/12 → x = 100/12: square roots are easy when you keep it as a fraction. · Square the scale. If every length is multiplied by k, the perimeter becomes k times and the area k² times. Doubling the side of a square → 4 × area. Use this before any formula. · Remember the 7-family: r = 7 → C = 44, A = 154; r = 14 → C = 88, A = 616; r = 21 → C = 132, A = 1386; r = 3.5 → C = 22, A = 38.5. · 1 m² is NOT 100 cm². Area units convert by the square of the length factor: 1 m² = 10,000 cm², 1 hectare = 10,000 m² (not 1,000). · Scaling (k → k²) is the base of L11 (percentage change in area). The 22/7 habits are used in every circle lesson (L5–L7, L10). · Perimeter = boundary (m); area = surface (m²) · 1 m² = 10,000 cm²; 1 are = 100 m²; 1 ha = 10,000 m²; 1 km² = 100 ha · Lengths × k → area × k² · π = 22/7 for multiples of 7; keep π if options have π
