One question nearly every shift: who founded which organisation, in which year, in which city , and their newspaper or slogan. Learn the table, not the story. · In the 1800s, educated Indians looked hard at their own society. They saw evils like sati (burning a widow on her husband's pyre), child marriage, the ban on widows remarrying, and untouchability. They formed societies to reform things from within. The table looks long, but it sorts easily into four groups. 1. The Bengal pioneers came first. Raja Ram Mohan Roy , the father of the Indian Renaissance, founded the Brahmo Samaj (1828) and helped end sati. Vidyasagar won the right of widows to remarry. 2. The revivalists looked back to old roots: Dayanand Saraswati's Arya Samaj (Back to the Vedas), the Theosophists with Annie Besant, and Vivekananda's Ramakrishna Mission. 3. Voices against caste : Jyotiba Phule's Satyashodhak Samaj in Pune, Sree Narayana Guru in Kerala, Periyar, and Ambedkar. 4. Muslim and Sikh reform : Sir Syed Ahmad Khan's Aligarh movement for modern education, the Deoband school, and the Singh Sabha. Next, tie each group to a city: Brahmo to Calcutta, Prarthana to Bombay, Satyashodhak to Pune, Ramakrishna to Belur. Finally, note that many campaigns ended in a law: sati banned in 1829, widow remarriage allowed in 1856, the Age of Consent Act in 1891. Expect one question on who started which newspaper and one on an education commission or press law, with its year and Viceroy . Pairs like Al-Hilal–Azad , Comrade–Mohammad Ali , Hunter Commission–Ripon and Metcalfe–liberator of the press come back again and again. · When the East India Company first ruled Bengal, there was no newspaper at all. In 1780 an Irishman, James Augustus Hicky , printed Hicky's Bengal Gazette in Calcutta. He mocked Company officials, and in 1782 his press was seized. From the very start, the rulers feared the printed word. Indians soon learned to use this weapon. Raja Ram Mohan Roy wrote papers in Bengali and Persian; later Amrita Bazar Patrika , The Hindu and Tilak's Kesari carried news of famine, unfair taxes and the Congress to every town. The British answered with laws. Lord Lytton's Vernacular Press Act (1878) gagged Indian-language papers, so Amrita Bazar Patrika switched to English almost overnight to escape it. New press laws in 1908 and 1910 were aimed at the angry Swadeshi papers. Schooling followed a similar path. At first the Company backed Persian and Sanskrit learning. Then Macaulay's Minute (1835) made English the language of higher education, and Wood's Despatch (1854) led to the first three universities in 1857. The result surprised the rulers: English-educated Indians read about liberty and democracy, and used that same English to demand freedom. · Newspaper ↔ founder ↔ year · Paper · Founder / editor · Year · language · note · Hicky's Bengal Gazette · James Augustus Hicky · 1780 · English · Calcutta — India's first newspaper (also called the Calcutta General Advertiser ) · Sambad Kaumudi · Raja Ram Mohan Roy · 1821 · Bengali · Mirat-ul-Akhbar · Raja Ram Mohan Roy · 1822 · Persian ; closed in protest against the press regulation of 1823 · Bombay Samachar · Fardunjee Marzban · 1822 · Gujarati ; still published — among the oldest newspapers in Asia · Amrita Bazar Patrika · Sisir Kumar Ghosh & Motilal Ghosh · 1868 · began in Bengali ; turned English in 1878 to escape the Vernacular Press Act · The Hindu · G. Guaranteed: the 1885 founding details, the Surat split, the Partition of Bengal and Swadeshi, Lucknow Pact, Home Rule League — with years and presidents. · By the 1880s, educated Indians wanted a voice in how they were ruled. In 1885 a retired British officer, A. O. Hume , helped them found the Indian National Congress in Bombay. Its early leaders, the Moderates, like Dadabhai Naoroji and Gokhale, were polite and patient. They sent petitions and made speeches asking for reforms within British rule. Naoroji also showed how British rule drained India's wealth. Many younger Indians grew tired of asking politely. The anger burst out in 1905, when Lord Curzon split Bengal in two. Bengal answered with Swadeshi (use Indian goods) and boycott of British goods, the first mass movement. The Extremists, Lal-Bal-Pal, led by Bal Gangadhar Tilak , demanded Swaraj (self-rule) as a birthright. The two camps clashed, and in 1907 the Congress split at Surat. Meanwhile the Muslim League was founded in 1906, and in 1909 the British gave Muslims separate electorates. The protests worked: the partition was cancelled in 1911. In 1916 the Moderates and Extremists reunited, and the Congress and the League signed the Lucknow Pact . Tilak and Annie Besant started Home Rule Leagues. The most asked single stretch in all of History. Fix the four movements in order with their years , why each ended, and the three Round Table Conferences. · Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi spent about twenty years in South Africa, where he developed satyagraha: fighting injustice through peaceful refusal and a readiness to suffer. He returned to India in 1915. First he tried it on local problems: indigo farmers at Champaran (1917), mill workers in Ahmedabad and peasants of Kheda (1918). He won, and became a leader of ordinary people. In 1919 the Rowlatt Act let the British jail people without trial. At Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar, General Dyer fired on an unarmed crowd. Gandhi then launched the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920): give up titles, leave British schools and courts, boycott foreign cloth. When a crowd killed policemen at Chauri Chaura in 1922, he called it off, because the struggle had to stay non-violent. In 1928 the all-British Simon Commission was met with Go back Simon. In 1929, at Lahore, the Congress demanded Purna Swaraj (complete independence). In 1930 Gandhi walked to Dandi and made salt, breaking a British law and starting Civil Disobedience. The Gandhi-Irwin Pact paused it, and Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference in London. histmodern.t: Women & lesser-known heroes of the freedom struggle
histmodern.h: स्वतंत्रता संग्राम की महिलाएँ एवं गुमनाम नायक
histmodern.x: SSC now asks about lesser-known heroes — 'Kanaklata Barua belonged to which state?', 'who led the Rampa rebellion?', 'who founded the Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company?'. Match each name to a place and one deed . · History books often remember a few big names, but the freedom struggle was fought in every corner of India — by queens, poets, students and tribal chiefs. Long before 1857, Rani Velu Nachiyar of Sivaganga won back her kingdom from the Company in 1780 with Hyder Ali's help, and Rani Chennamma of Kittur took up the sword in 1824 when the British refused to accept her adopted son. In the hills, the Company's roads, taxes and forest rules angered tribes who had lived freely for centuries. Tirot Sing of the Khasis, Tilka Manjhi near Bhagalpur and Alluri Sitarama Raju in the Rampa hills fought back with bows and guns. Most were captured or killed, but their courage lived on in local songs. Under Gandhi, women came out in thousands. Usha Mehta ran a secret radio in 1942; Matangini Hazra , aged 73, and Kanaklata Barua , just 17, were shot while carrying the tricolour. In the south, V. O. Chidambaram Pillai even started an Indian shipping company to break the British hold on the sea trade. Their stories show that freedom was won by ordinary people as much as by famous leaders. · Women of the struggle · Name · Region · Remember her for · Rani Velu Nachiyar · Sivaganga (Tamil Nadu) · Fought the Company and regained her kingdom in 1780 with Hyder Ali 's help; Bhagat Singh, Azad, the Kakori and Lahore conspiracy cases, Bose and the INA, Quit India, and the 1946–47 plans — expect at least one, often two. · Not everyone believed peaceful protest alone would win freedom. From the early 1900s young revolutionaries chose bombs and guns. In Bengal, groups like the Anushilan Samiti formed, and Khudiram Bose was hanged at 18. Abroad, Indians formed the Ghadar Party in San Francisco. In 1925 Ramprasad Bismil's group robbed a train at Kakori. Then Bhagat Singh , Chandra Shekhar Azad and their comrades shot the officer Saunders to avenge Lala Lajpat Rai, and threw bombs in the Assembly to be heard. Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru were hanged in 1931. During the Second World War, Britain wanted India's help but would not promise freedom. Gandhi answered with Quit India on 8 August 1942: Do or Die. Leaders were jailed at once, but people set up parallel governments in places like Ballia and Satara. Abroad, Subhas Chandra Bose led the Indian National Army to fight the British. After the war, the INA trials and the navy mutiny of 1946 showed Britain it could no longer rely on Indian soldiers. Plans like the Cabinet Mission failed to keep India united, and violence grew. The Acts from 1773 to 1947 — "which Act introduced X" is a standing question. Add the three land revenue settlements and the Drain Theory. · The British ruled India through a chain of laws passed in London. Each Act gave the government a little more shape and, slowly, gave Indians a little more space. First Parliament reined in the Company: the Regulating Act of 1773 created a Governor-General of Bengal, and the 1833 Act made him Governor-General of India. After 1857, the 1858 Act handed India to the Crown. Then Indians were let in step by step: nominated members (1861), indirect elections (1892), separate electorates (1909), dyarchy (shared power) in the provinces (1919), and provincial autonomy under the 1935 Act , the main source of India's Constitution. The other half of this lesson is money. To collect land tax, the British used three systems. In Bengal, Cornwallis's Permanent Settlement fixed the tax forever and made zamindars the owners. In Madras and Bombay, the Ryotwari system dealt directly with the farmer. In the north-west, the Mahalwari system dealt with the whole village. Heavy taxes, forced cash crops like indigo and the ruin of handicrafts made people poor; Naoroji called this the drain of wealth. Peasants and tribal people rose again and again, from the Santhals to Birsa Munda's Ulgulan. histmodern.x: Post-1947 history is now a regular SSC topic: how Junagadh, Hyderabad and Kashmir joined , the year each state was formed , and the members of the States Reorganisation Commission . It overlaps with Polity questions. · On 15 August 1947 India was free, but it was not yet one country on the map. Besides the British provinces there were over 560 princely states , big and small, and the British had told them they could join India, join Pakistan or try to stay independent. A broken map would have meant a weak nation. Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel , the Home Minister, and his secretary V. P. Menon took on the job. They asked each ruler to sign an Instrument of Accession , handing over only defence, external affairs and communications. Using persuasion, pensions and, when needed, pressure, they brought nearly every state in by 15 August. Only three held out: Junagadh joined after a plebiscite in 1948, Hyderabad after the army's Operation Polo , and Kashmir when Maharaja Hari Singh signed in October 1947 as raiders attacked. Next came the question of language. People wanted states where their own language was spoken. When Potti Sriramulu died fasting for a Telugu state in 1952, Andhra was created in 1953. The Fazl Ali Commission then studied the whole map, and the States Reorganisation Act of 1956 made language the main basis of our states. · Integrating the princely states · States Ministry · Set up in July 1947 — minister Sardar Patel , secretary V. artculture.x: A guaranteed 1–2 marks. Only two things matter: dance ↔ state and exponent ↔ dance ; then gharanas and instruments. · Indian classical dance and music grew over many centuries in temples and royal courts. The oldest guide to both is the Natyashastra of Bharata Muni, which describes the nine rasas (moods) a performance should create. Today eight dances are officially classical. What the exam really asks is which dance belongs to which state, and who its famous dancers are. So build a mental map of India. Start in the south: Tamil Nadu has Bharatanatyam , the oldest; Kerala has two, Kathakali (men, heavy make-up) and Mohiniyattam (women); Andhra Pradesh has Kuchipudi. Move up the east coast to Odisha for Odissi, then to the north-east: Manipur for Manipuri, and Assam for Sattriya, the newest, added in 2000. Finally go to Uttar Pradesh for Kathak , the only one shaped by the Mughal court. Three dances carry their place in their name: Odissi, Manipuri and Kuchipudi. Music splits north and south in the same way. Hindustani music in the north grew with Persian contact, with forms like khayal and instruments like sitar and tabla. Carnatic music in the south stayed closer to the old Sanskrit tradition, with its trinity of composers led by Tyagaraja. For musicians, learn one instrument per famous name. · Eight classical dances · Dance · State · Famous exponents · note · Bharatanatyam · Tamil Nadu · Rukmini Devi Arundale, Balasaraswati, Yamini Krishnamurthy, Padma Subrahmanyam. The style table is the whole chapter. · India's buildings tell the story of its religions and rulers. The earliest great monuments were Buddhist. Ashoka began the stupa at Sanchi , a solid dome built over relics. Monks also cut prayer halls and living rooms out of hillsides. These caves run from Barabar in Bihar, the oldest, to Ajanta , famous for its paintings, and Ellora , where Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves stand side by side. Later, Hindu temples were built in stone, and three regional styles grew. The north built Nagara temples with a curved tower, like Khajuraho and Konark. The south built Dravida temples with a pyramid-shaped tower, tall gateways and walls, like Brihadeshwara at Thanjavur. The Deccan, in between, mixed the two in the Vesara style, seen at Pattadakal and Belur. From the Delhi Sultanate on, Islamic builders brought the true arch and dome, along with stone inlay, jali screens and garden tombs. This tradition runs from the Qutub Minar to its peak in the Taj Mahal. Finally the British built in Gothic and Indo-Saracenic styles, and Lutyens and Baker designed New Delhi. The intangible list (Garba, Durga Puja, Kumbh, Yoga) is asked just as often. · UNESCO keeps a World Heritage List of places so valuable that they belong to all humanity. Each place is put in one of three boxes: cultural (made by people — temples, forts, cities), natural (forests, mountains, wildlife) or mixed (both at once). As of the 2026 session, India has 45 sites : 37 cultural, 7 natural and 1 mixed — Sarnath became the 45th on 25 July 2026. The story starts in 1983 with four: two cave sites in Maharashtra ( Ajanta, Ellora ) and two Mughal monuments in Agra ( Agra Fort, Taj Mahal ). The seven natural sites are easy to picture as a journey — rhinos and wild buffalo in Assam (Kaziranga, Manas), birds in Rajasthan (Keoladeo), tigers in the mangroves of Bengal (Sundarbans), the high Himalaya (Nanda Devi, Great Himalayan NP) and the long Western Ghats . The one mixed site is Khangchendzonga in Sikkim. There is a second list for things you cannot touch — songs, dances, festivals and crafts. This is the intangible cultural heritage list. India has 15 elements on it up to Garba of Gujarat (2023) . The folk-painting table below is the money table. · Long before galleries existed, Indians painted on walls, cloth and paper to tell stories of gods and heroes and to mark festivals. Each region kept its own style, made with local materials. That is why exam questions ask which painting belongs to which state. This lesson also covers court painting, folk theatre, puppets and crafts, so do not read it as one long list. Sort it into four boxes. Box 1: folk paintings, by region. East: Madhubani (Bihar), Pattachitra (Odisha), Kalighat (Bengal). West: Warli (Maharashtra), Phad (Rajasthan). Centre: Gond (Madhya Pradesh). South: Kalamkari (Andhra Pradesh), Cheriyal (Telangana). Mountains: Thangka (Sikkim and Ladakh). Box 2: court painting, by ruler. The Mughal school began under Humayun, grew under Akbar and peaked under Jahangir . Rajasthani and Pahari schools grew in the courts of Rajasthan and the hills, and the Bengal School of Abanindranath Tagore brought a national style. Box 3: theatre and puppets, by state : Nautanki in Uttar Pradesh, Tamasha in Maharashtra, Yakshagana in Karnataka, Kathputli string puppets in Rajasthan. Box 4: crafts and textiles, by town : Banarasi silk, Chikankari from Lucknow, Patola from Patan. SSC asks book ↔ author almost every shift, and since 2024 the classical languages count (now 11 ) is a favourite. Add the Eighth Schedule number ( 22 ) and the first Jnanpith , and this lesson is pure recall marks. · Think of Indian literature as three shelves in a library. The top shelf is Sanskrit . It begins with the grammarians — Panini wrote the rules, Patanjali explained them. Then come the playwrights: Bhasa (the oldest), Shudraka , Kalidasa , Vishakhadatta and Bhavabhuti . Next to them sit the long poems: Bharavi and Magha both took their stories from the Mahabharata. At the end are Jayadeva , the singer of Radha and Krishna, and Kalhana , the historian of Kashmir. The middle shelf is Persian and Urdu . Amir Khusrau wrote for the Delhi Sultans, Mirza Ghalib for the last Mughal, and Muhammad Iqbal gave us Saare Jahan Se Achha . The bottom shelf is modern : Bankim Chandra (Vande Mataram), Tagore (two national anthems — India's and Bangladesh's), Premchand (Godaan) and the Tamil poet Subramania Bharati . Beside the shelves is a box of scripts : Brahmi , the mother script, runs left to right; Kharosthi alone runs right to left . worldhist.t: The ancient world to the Age of Discovery
worldhist.h: प्राचीन विश्व से खोज-यात्राओं के युग तक
worldhist.x: An occasional one-mark question: which river ↔ which civilisation , Alexander and Porus , Magna Carta 1215 , Martin Luther 1517 or who discovered what . Learn the dates in the timeline and you are covered. · The first cities grew up beside big rivers, because rivers gave water, fertile mud and an easy road for trade. In Mesopotamia ('land between the rivers' — the Tigris and Euphrates, today's Iraq) people pressed wedge-shaped cuneiform marks into clay, and King Hammurabi of Babylon carved one of the first written law codes. Egypt grew along the Nile , wrote in picture-signs called hieroglyphics and built the pyramids . China began on the Huang He , and India on the Indus . Next came Greece , a land of small city-states. Athens tried democracy , and three teachers followed one another: Socrates → Plato → Aristotle . Aristotle taught Alexander , who reached India in 326 BCE and fought Porus on the Jhelum. Then Rome rose: Julius Caesar was a general, and Augustus became the first emperor. Jump to Europe after 1200: Magna Carta (1215) limited the king; Constantinople fell to the Turks ( 1453 ); the Renaissance and the printing press spread new ideas; Luther challenged the Church ( 1517 ); and sailors went looking for a sea route to India — Columbus found America instead (1492), Vasco da Gama reached Calicut (1498). · River-valley civilisations · Civilisation · River · Writing · Famous for · Mesopotamia (Sumer, Babylon) — Iraq · Tigris and Euphrates · Cuneiform (wedge marks on clay) · Code of Hammurabi (c. 1750 BCE); Magellan died on the way — the voyage was finished by Elcano . Julius Caesar was never emperor ; Augustus was the first. The Hydaspes is the Jhelum , but the river where Alexander's army stopped is the Beas . Cuneiform = Mesopotamia , hieroglyphics = Egypt . Magna Carta is 1215 (King John), not the 1689 Bill of Rights. · Mesopotamia grew on the Tigris and Euphrates with cuneiform writing and Hammurabi's code; Egypt on the Nile with hieroglyphics and pyramids; China on the Huang He. · Socrates taught Plato, Plato taught Aristotle, and Aristotle taught Alexander, who defeated Porus on the Hydaspes (Jhelum) in 326 BCE and turned back at the Beas. · Julius Caesar was killed in 44 BCE and Augustus became the first Roman emperor in 27 BCE; the Prophet's Hijra to Medina in 622 CE begins the Islamic calendar. · Magna Carta came in 1215, Constantinople fell in 1453, Gutenberg built his press around 1440, and Martin Luther posted his Ninety-five Theses in 1517. · Dias rounded the Cape in 1488, Columbus reached America in 1492, Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498, Cabral reached Brazil in 1500, and Magellan's voyage of 1519 to 1522 was the first round the world.

Usually one question — most often the French Revolution's slogan/date, the Russian Revolution's year and leader, or a World War treaty. Dates and "who said what" are enough. · Indian history did not happen alone, and the exam asks about a few big world events. Start with the revolutions, which share one idea: people, not kings alone, should decide how they are ruled. In England (1688) Parliament became supreme. In America (1776) colonists refused taxes without a say and declared independence. In France (1789) people stormed the Bastille under the slogan Liberty, Equality, Fraternity. In Russia (1917) the Tsar fell and Lenin's Bolsheviks took power. Meanwhile the Industrial Revolution in England brought machines and factories. In 1914 an assassination at Sarajevo set off the First World War . It ended in 1918, and the Treaty of Versailles punished Germany hard. The League of Nations was set up to keep the peace, but it failed. Germany's anger at Versailles helped Hitler rise. In 1939 Germany invaded Poland, and the Second World War began. The USA joined after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in 1941. The war ended in 1945, after atom bombs fell on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. To stop another such war, the United Nations was set up in 1945, with India among its founding members. This is a pure-marks lesson: SSC loves "who was called X", "who wrote Y", "who gave the slogan Z". Nothing to understand — only to recall. Read it last before the exam. · This lesson has no story of its own. It collects who-is-who facts from every other lesson: travellers, titles, slogans and books. The best way to learn it is to hang each item on a story you already know. Travellers : put them on the line of kings. Megasthenes comes to Chandragupta Maurya, Fa-Hien to Chandragupta II, Hiuen Tsang to Harsha, Al-Beruni with Mahmud of Ghazni, Ibn Battuta to Muhammad bin Tughlaq, Domingo Paes to Krishnadeva Raya, and Englishmen like Thomas Roe to Jahangir. If you can say the kings in order, the travellers follow. Titles : group them by era. Older ones: Indian Napoleon (Samudragupta), Parrot of India (Amir Khusrau), Tiger of Mysore (Tipu). Freedom-era ones: Grand Old Man (Naoroji), Lokmanya (Tilak), Netaji (Bose), Sardar (Patel). Slogans : link each to its movement. Swaraj is my birthright goes with Tilak and the Extremists, Do or Die with Gandhi and Quit India, Give me blood with Bose and the INA. Books : pair each writer with his age, from Kautilya's Arthashastra and Abul Fazl's Ain-i-Akbari to Gandhi's Hind Swaraj. computer.x: Every paper opens the computer section with one or two easy marks from here: generation ↔ technology , father of the computer , ENIAC/UNIVAC full forms , and analog vs digital vs hybrid examples. Every paper opens computer awareness with 1 to 3 easy questions from here: the full form of ENIAC, who designed a machine, which generation used integrated circuits, which computer type suits weather forecasting, or which part sits on the motherboard. RRB NTPC asks history and "brain of the computer" questions very often. These are free marks if you remember names, dates and the motherboard parts. · A computer is an electronic machine that takes in data, works on it by following a list of instructions, and gives back a result. Think of a kitchen : raw vegetables go in ( input ), the cook chops and fries them following a recipe ( processing ), and a finished dish comes out ( output ). The fridge where food waits is storage . This Input–Process–Output cycle is the heart of every computer, from a phone to a supercomputer. The machine has no brain of its own. It is fast, accurate and never gets tired, but it only does what the recipe (the program ) says. Feed it wrong data and you get wrong answers: Garbage In, Garbage Out . Almost every paper asks a full form (CPU, ALU, CU, BIOS, POST, SMPS, USB, HDMI, VGA), what the ALU or CU does , cold vs warm booting , or which port connects what . The CPU is the most asked single topic in computer awareness. Expect questions like "which is NOT part of the CPU", "MAR stands for", "which register holds the address of the next instruction", "which bus decides maximum memory", "which port sends one bit at a time" and "which port carries HD audio and video". SSC CGL Tier-II asked MAR twice (2023) and RRB NTPC asks "brain of the computer" again and again. · Open a desktop cabinet and you find a big green board, the motherboard . Think of it as a city . The CPU (Central Processing Unit) is the town hall where every decision is made. Inside it, the Control Unit is the manager giving orders, the ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit) is the clerk who adds, subtracts and compares, and the registers are the tiny trays on the clerk's desk holding what is being worked on right now. Roads called buses carry traffic: the data bus carries the goods, the address bus carries the house numbers, and the control bus carries the traffic signals. The SMPS is the power station turning wall AC into the DC the parts need. When you press the power button, a small program in ROM called the BIOS wakes up, checks that everything is present (the POST ), and then loads the operating system. This is booting . The holes at the back, called ports , are the city gates where keyboards, screens and cables enter. · The CPU · CPU · Central Processing Unit. "Which of these is an input device", "which device reads answer sheets", "which reads cheques", "which key is a toggle key", "who invented the mouse" and "which device is both input and output" are asked in almost every CHSL, MTS, NTPC and Group D paper. SSC CGL Tier-II 2023 asked OCR directly. These are among the easiest marks in the whole subject. · A computer cannot see, hear or speak by itself. It needs input devices to receive information from us and output devices to show results back. Think of a post office : the letter box where you drop letters is input, the sorting room inside is the CPU, and the postman who delivers to your door is output. The keyboard and mouse are the everyday letter boxes. Special readers do special jobs: a bank's machine reads the magnetic numbers printed at the bottom of every cheque ( MICR ), an exam centre's machine reads the darkened circles on answer sheets ( OMR ), and a shop counter reads barcodes. On the output side, a monitor gives a temporary picture called soft copy , while a printer gives paper called hard copy . Some printers hit the paper like a typewriter ( impact ); others spray ink or use a laser without touching it ( non-impact ). A touch screen does both jobs at once: you give input by touching the same glass that shows output. · Hardware and software · Hardware · Physical, tangible parts you can see and touch: keyboard, mouse, monitor, CPU. · Software · Programs; intangible, you can see them on screen but cannot touch them: MS-Office, Windows. · Computer · A combination of hardware and software; both need each other. · Statement check · "All components are either hardware or software" = correct. computer.x: Asked in nearly every paper: which memory is volatile (RAM), 1 nibble = ? bits , largest/smallest unit , ROM types (PROM, EPROM, EEPROM) , SRAM vs DRAM , and fastest memory (registers, then cache). Memory is asked in almost every computer section: "which memory is volatile", "which RAM needs refreshing", "which memory communicates directly with the CPU", "where is firmware stored", "fastest memory" and "EPROM is erased by". SSC CGL Tier-II asked cache in 2022 and 2023 and DRAM refresh in 2024; RRB NTPC 2025 asked ROM and RAM. Learn the speed order and the ROM family well. · Imagine a library with a student studying at a desk. The student is the CPU. The few papers held in hand are the registers : tiny but instant. The open books on the desk are the cache : small, very quick to reach. The bookshelf beside the desk is RAM : bigger, a little slower. The library's store room is secondary storage such as the hard disk: huge, but you must fetch a book to the desk before reading it. When the library closes (power goes off), the desk and shelf are cleared. That is why RAM is volatile : it forgets everything without power. The rule book printed into the wall never changes; that is ROM , which keeps its contents and holds the start-up instructions. All memory is counted in bits (a single 0 or 1). Four bits make a nibble , eight bits make a byte , and from there sizes grow by 1024 each step: KB, MB, GB, TB and beyond. · Memory as hardware · RAM · Hardware chip (yes). · ROM · Hardware chip (yes). · Cache · Hardware: L2 and L3 chips (older boards) and L1 inside the CPU with no separate hardware. · Virtual memory (VM) · NOT separate hardware; it is space reserved on the hard disk. · Registers · NOT separate hardware chips; they are inside the CPU. · Primary memory · RAM and ROM; also called main memory or internal memory. · Secondary memory · Also called auxiliary memory: tape, disks, optical discs, pen drive, memory card, SSD. · Volatile memory · Loses data when power goes: RAM and cache. · Non-volatile memory · Keeps data without power: ROM, flash, tape, disks, CD, DVD, BD, pen drive, memory card, SSD. · Memory units · Unit · Equals · Note · Bit · Binary digit — 0 or 1 · Smallest unit of data · Nibble · 4 bits · Half a byte · Byte · 8 bits · Stores one character (ASCII) · Kilobyte (KB) · 1024 bytes · 2^10 bytes · Megabyte (MB) · 1024 KB · 2^20 = 1,048,576 bytes · Gigabyte (GB) · 1024 MB · 2^30 bytes · Terabyte (TB) · 1024 GB · 2^40 bytes · Petabyte (PB) · 1024 TB · 2^50 bytes · Exabyte (EB) · 1024 PB · 2^60 bytes · Zettabyte (ZB) · 1024 EB · 2^70 bytes · Yottabyte (YB) · 1024 ZB · 2^80 bytes — largest unit in the usual exam list · Binary vs decimal counting · Binary (computer memory) · 1 KB = 1024 bytes (2^10) · Decimal (disk makers, SI) · 1 kB = 1000 bytes · IEC names for binary · KiB, MiB, GiB (kibibyte, mebibyte, gibibyte) · 1 byte · 8 bits · 1 KB in bits · 8 × 1024 = 8192 bits · 1 MB in bytes · 1,048,576 bytes · Word · Number of bits a CPU handles at once — 32-bit, 64-bit · Newer SI prefixes (2022) · ronna (R) and quetta (Q) beyond yotta — exams still treat YB as the largest · RAM · RAM · Random Access Memory: main memory, internal, volatile, primary. · Also called · RWM (Read Write Memory) [exam favourite]. · Structure · A grid of memory cells; each cell has a unique address, like a house number; each cell stores one bit. · Access · Random read and random write. · Job · Holds running programs and data temporarily; the CPU reads and writes it directly. More RAM = better speed and capability. · DRAM · Dynamic RAM: must be refreshed again and again (refreshing memory); made of capacitors and transistors; cheaper and slower; used in normal computers. Refreshing recharges the capacitors that store the bits. · SRAM · Static RAM: no refreshing; made of flip-flops and transistors; costly and faster; used in special systems like Air Traffic Control and the stock exchange (BSE), and as cache. · SDRAM · Synchronous DRAM. Today's computers use DDR5-SDRAM. · DDR generations · SDR (Single Data Rate) moves data once per clock; DDR (Double Data Rate) moves data twice per clock; DDR2, DDR3, DDR4, DDR5 each move more data per clock. "signals per clock pulse" as 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 for DDR to DDR5. · ROM family · ROM · Read Only Memory: primary, non-volatile. Used to store software that does not need updates (firmware). · Masked ROM (M-ROM) · Written once at the factory; property WORM = Write Once Read Many. · BIOS · Basic Input Output System: the boot-up program stored in ROM; the first program that runs. · Booting · Starting the computer; cold booting = start, warm/hot booting = restart. · Shadowing · Copying BIOS from ROM to RAM so it runs faster (BIOS shadow = ROM to RAM). · PROM · Programmable ROM: blank chip, programmed once by the user, cannot be erased. · EPROM · Erasable Programmable ROM: blank, erased by Ultra-Violet (UV) rays. · EEPROM · Electrically Erasable Programmable ROM: erased electrically, byte by byte (slow: 8 times for 8 bits). · Flash EEPROM (flash memory) · Electrically erasable block by block (sector), so faster than EEPROM; non-volatile. Used in pen drives (USBFD), memory cards and SSDs. · Firmware · A program permanently written on a hardware chip; stored in ROM. · Cache memory · Caching · Like hoarding: keeping a copy of what you will need soon. · Cache · Small, very fast memory between the CPU and RAM; holds copies (duplicate values) of frequently used RAM data and instructions. · Cache hit · The CPU finds the needed data in the cache. · Position · Closest memory to the CPU after registers; "middle memory" between CPU and RAM. · Levels · L1 (inside CPU, fastest, smallest) → L2 → L3 → DRAM → hard disk. · Access time · Time a memory takes to give data to the CPU. By default its size is about equal to RAM and can go up to 3 times RAM. · Swapping / paging · Moving pages between RAM and virtual memory (page replacement). · Registers · Store data inside the CPU; minimum access time of all memories. · Memory speed order · Rank · Memory · Note · 1 (fastest) · Registers · Inside CPU · 2 · L1 cache · Inside CPU · 3 · L2 cache · — · 4 · L3 cache · — · 5 · SRAM · — · 6 · DRAM (main memory) · — · 7 · ROM / EEPROM / flash (pen drive, memory card, SSD) · — · 8 · Hard disk · Magnetic · 9 · Optical disc (CD/DVD/BD) · — · 10 (slowest) · Magnetic tape · Sequential access · Primary vs secondary and virtual memory · Primary memory · RAM, ROM, cache — directly accessed by the CPU; also called main or internal memory · Secondary memory · HDD, SSD, CD, pen drive — NOT directly accessed; data is first loaded into RAM; also called auxiliary memory · Registers · Inside the CPU itself — fastest of all · Cache · High-speed buffer between CPU and RAM; stores frequently used data · Virtual memory · Part of the hard disk/SSD used as if it were extra RAM (page file / swap) · Buffer · Temporary area that holds data while it moves between devices · Volatile · RAM, cache, registers — lose data without power · Non-volatile · ROM, flash, HDD, SSD, CD/DVD — keep data without power · Which answer for "fastest memory"? Read the options. If registers are in the options, registers are the fastest. If registers are not there and cache is, cache is the fastest. If neither is there, RAM beats ROM, hard disk and DVD. Two such questions with different answers for exactly this reason. · How the CPU reads a file on the hard disk. the CPU never reads secondary memory directly. The file is first copied from the hard disk into RAM; the CPU then reads it from RAM (often through the cache). This is why RAM size affects speed: if RAM is too small, the computer keeps swapping data with virtual memory on the slow hard disk. · Why DRAM needs refreshing. each DRAM bit is a tiny capacitor that slowly leaks its charge. The memory controller re-reads and re-writes (recharges) every cell thousands of times a second. SRAM uses flip-flops that hold their state while power is on, so it needs no refresh. · Two's complement. flip every bit (1's complement) and add 1. For 4-bit 1000: flip → 0111, add 1 → 1000. In 8 bits, -1 = 11111111. · Comparing sizes. convert to one unit. 3500 KB is about 3.4 MB, which is smaller than 2 GB. 2350 bytes is bigger than 2 KB (2048 bytes). 25 KB is much smaller than 100 MB. · ROM family by eraser — P-E-EE : P ROM = Pen (ink, once only), E PROM = Eraser of light (UV), EE PROM = Electric Eraser. Units — K M G T P E Z Y : K ing M ohan G ot T en P apayas, E ach Z esty and Y ellow. DRAM = "Dynamic = Daily refresh"; SRAM = "Static = Stays, no refresh, Super fast, Super costly". Every paper has at least one question here: "1 TB = ?", "nibble = ?", "biggest unit", "hard disk is which storage", "which is not an optical disc", "ASCII full form/bits", "binary of a number" or "smallest storage unit on a disk". SSC CGL Tier-II 2022 asked magnetic tape statements word-for-word from these notes, CHSL asked hard disk and optical discs, and NTPC asks bits and cells. · RAM forgets everything when the power goes off, so a computer needs a place to keep files for years. That place is secondary storage . Think of it as the cupboards and lockers of a house, as opposed to the kitchen table (RAM) where you work. Some cupboards are magnetic : a hard disk stores data as tiny magnetised spots on spinning metal plates, and a tape stores it along a long ribbon that must be wound to the right place, like an old cassette. Some are optical : CDs, DVDs and Blu-ray discs are read by a laser beam. The newest are flash : pen drives, memory cards and SSDs keep data in chips with no moving parts, so they are fast and shock-proof. Finally, cloud storage is like renting a locker in a bank far away: your files live on someone else's servers and you reach them over the internet. Because any cupboard can break, wise people keep copies called back-ups . · Ways of storing data · Magnetism · Magnetic memory: magnetic tape, hard disk, floppy disk. · Optical (laser light) · CD, DVD, Blu-ray Disc (BD/BRD). · Electrical · RAM, ROM, cache, USB flash drive (pen drive), memory card, SSD. · Primary storage · RAM, ROM. · Secondary / auxiliary storage · Tape, hard disk, floppy, CD, DVD, BD, pen drive, memory card, SSD. So it counts using only two digits: the binary system. We humans count with ten digits (0 to 9), the decimal system, probably because we have ten fingers. Think of a row of light bulbs . In decimal, each place is worth ten times the place to its right (1, 10, 100). In binary, each bulb is worth double the one to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Switch on the bulbs worth 8 and 2 and you are showing 10. Long binary strings are hard to read, so programmers group them: three bits make one octal digit and four bits make one hexadecimal digit (0–9 and A–F). Letters are stored as numbers too. A code table such as ASCII or Unicode says which number means 'A' and which means 'क'. NTPC asks compiler questions often, and SSC asks open-source and freeware examples. · Think of a computer as a restaurant . The stove, fridge and tables you can touch are the hardware . The recipes and the rules for running the place are the software — you cannot touch them, but nothing gets cooked without them. A few instructions are painted permanently on the kitchen wall so the staff know how to switch everything on in the morning; that is firmware , like the BIOS stored in a ROM chip. The manager of the restaurant is the operating system (Windows, Linux, Android). It decides which order is cooked first, which cook uses which stove and where the ingredients are kept. Software that keeps the machine itself running is system software ; software that does your job, such as typing a letter in MS Word, is application software . The kitchen staff understand only one language: 0s and 1s . Programmers write in friendlier languages, so a translator is needed. computer.x: Operating systems give 1 to 3 questions per paper: "which is not an OS", "first OS written in C", "single-user OS", "kernel/shell", "multiprocessing vs multitasking", "real-time OS example", Windows features like Recycle Bin, Control Panel and File Explorer, and Windows shortcuts. SSC CGL Tier-II 2022-2023 asked Control Panel, Alt + Enter and File Explorer's View tab; CHSL Tier-II 2023 asked Recycle Bin. · Think of a big hotel. The guests (users) want food, rooms and laundry. They do not go into the kitchen or the boiler room themselves; they talk to the reception. The reception passes every request to the right department and makes sure no two guests get the same room. The operating system (ऑपरेटिंग सिस्टम) is that reception: it stands between you and the hardware (its primary job) and gives a platform on which applications run (its secondary job). Behind the reception is the hotel manager who actually controls the staff, rooms and money but never meets guests. That manager is the kernel (कर्नेल): the core of the OS that controls hardware. The receptionist who takes your words and passes them on is the shell, which turns your commands into something the kernel understands. Old hotels made you write requests on a slip in a fixed format: that is a Character User Interface (CUI), like MS-DOS where you type commands. Modern hotels let you just point at pictures on a menu: that is a Graphical User Interface (GUI), like Windows, where you click icons. A hotel can also work in different styles: serve one batch of similar guests at a time (batch OS), give each guest a fixed few minutes in turn (multitasking/time-sharing), use many receptionists at once (multiprocessing), or promise a reply in a fixed time no matter what (real-time OS, like a parachute or aircraft system). · Operating system basics · Operating system (OS) · System software that works as an intermediary between the user and the hardware (primary function) and provides a platform for application software (secondary function). · Layers · Computer user <→ application software (MS-Office) <→ operating system (Windows) <→ hardware. · Functions · Process (CPU) management, memory management, file management, device (I/O) management, security, booting, user interface, resource allocation. · Not functions of OS · Translating high-level language into machine language (that is a compiler's job); data classification; input of data itself. · Location · The OS is stored on the hard disk (HDD) and loaded into RAM at booting. · Kernel · Core of the OS; controls all hardware and software but does not interact with users directly; does memory and file management. SSC CGL Tier-II 2024 asked the .exe extension. Learning this lesson as a list gives quick marks. · Imagine a big wardrobe full of boxes. Each box has a label on the end saying what is inside: "shirts", "shoes", "documents". A file extension (फ़ाइल एक्सटेंशन) is that label at the end of a file name, after the dot: report.docx, photo.jpg, song.mp3. The computer reads the label to know which program should open the file. The wardrobe itself has a filing method: which shelf, which row, where the next free space is. That method is the file system (फ़ाइल सिस्टम), a part of the operating system that manages all files. Windows uses NTFS; old DOS used FAT. Computer people love short forms. Instead of saying "Basic Input Output System" they say BIOS; instead of "Portable Document Format" they say PDF. The single most-asked area of the computer section: every SSC and RRB paper has 1–3 shortcut questions. Examiners love keys that do different jobs in Word, Excel and the browser (Ctrl+D, Ctrl+H, F5, F7, F12). · A keyboard shortcut is like speed dial on a phone. You could open the contacts list, scroll and tap a name — or you could press one button. In the same way you can click Edit and then Copy with the mouse, or simply press Ctrl+C . Most shortcuts are built from modifier keys held down — Ctrl, Alt, Shift and the Windows logo key — plus one letter or function key. Hold the modifier, tap the second key, then let go. Many letters are easy to guess: Ctrl+ P for Print, Ctrl+ S for Save, Ctrl+ F for Find, Ctrl+ N for New. Remember one important rule: a shortcut belongs to the program that is active . Ctrl+D in Word opens the Font box, in Excel it fills a cell downwards, and in Chrome it bookmarks the page. So always read the question carefully — 'in MS Word', 'in Excel', 'in a web browser' — before picking the answer. CGL Tier-II asked the cell, A10, MATCH and column width; CHSL asked Ctrl + D, Shift + F11 and Alt + I + R. · MS Excel is a spreadsheet — think of a huge attendance register drawn as a grid. The whole register is a workbook (one file); each page in it is a worksheet ; each little box is a cell . Columns go across with letters (A, B, C…) and rows go down with numbers (1, 2, 3…), so every box has an address such as B3 — column B, row 3, like a seat number in a cinema. The magic of Excel is the formula . Type =B3+C3 in a cell and Excel adds those two boxes; change either number and the answer updates by itself. Ready-made formulas are called functions : SUM adds, AVERAGE finds the mean, MAX picks the largest. When you copy a formula down, Excel shifts the addresses automatically (a relative reference ). If you want one address to stay fixed — say a tax rate in one cell — you pin it with dollar signs, $B$1 (an absolute reference ). PowerPoint gives 1 or 2 questions in SSC Tier-II computer modules and CHSL Tier-I: "F5 / Shift + F5", "Esc ends a slide show", "Ctrl + M new slide", "transition vs animation", "slide master", "which view shows only text", "slide sorter", "9 layouts", "placeholders". SSC CGL Tier-II 2024 asked how to exit a slide show; CHSL 2024 asked moving between slides with the keyboard. · PowerPoint is a set of digital flash cards for a talk. Each card is a slide ; the whole pack is a presentation saved as a .pptx file. A layout decides where the title and text boxes sit on one slide; a theme gives every slide the same colours and fonts; and the Slide Master is the master card — change it once and every slide changes. Movement comes in two kinds. A transition is the effect as you move from one slide to the next, like turning a page. An animation moves something inside a slide — a bullet flying in, a picture fading out. Press F5 to start the show from the first slide, or Shift+F5 to start from the slide you are on. MS Access is a different tool: a database , like a well-kept office register. Data sits in tables ; a query asks a question, a form is a neat screen for typing data in, and a report prints the results. Every record is identified by a unique primary key , like a roll number. · PowerPoint basics · Type of software · Presentation software by Microsoft · File extensions · .pptx (2007 onwards); .ppt older; .ppsx opens directly as a show; .potx template; .pptm macro-enabled · Slide · One page of a presentation · Layout · Arrangement of placeholders on a slide (Title Slide, Title and Content, Two Content, Blank …) · Placeholder · Dotted box that holds title, text, picture or chart · Theme / Design · Matching colours, fonts and background for all slides (Design tab) · Slide Master · Controls the design and layout of every slide (View → Slide Master) · Transition · Effect while moving from one slide to the next (Transitions tab) · Animation · Effect on text or objects within a slide: Entrance, Emphasis, Exit, Motion Paths (Animations tab) · Speaker notes · Notes for the presenter, typed under the slide; not shown to the audience · Presenter View · Presenter sees notes and next slide while the audience sees only the slide · Rehearse Timings · Records how long each slide is shown · Hide Slide · Slide stays in the file but is skipped during the show · Default slide size · Widescreen 16:9 (PowerPoint 2013 onwards); 4:3 earlier · MS-PowerPoint · Presentation program (part of MS-Office / Microsoft 365). · File · Presentation file; default name Presentation1; extension .ppt (till 2003), .pptx (2007 onwards); .pot = design template; .pps = slide show; .pptm = macro-enabled. · File name length · Up to 225 characters manually. · Slide layouts · 9: Title Slide, Title and Content, Title Only, Two Content, Section Header, Blank, Content with Caption, Picture with Caption, Comparison. · Default layout · Title Slide (introduces the topic and sets the tone). · New presentation · Ctrl + N. 1–2 questions in most CGL and CHSL papers: primary vs foreign key , record = row, field = column , the objects of MS Access (table, query, form, report), DDL vs DML commands in SQL, and the full forms DBMS, RDBMS, SQL . · Think of a school office register. Each page is about one thing — students, fees or marks. That page is a table . Each line is one student: a record (row). Each column heading — Roll No, Name, Class — is a field . Two students can share a name, but never a roll number. That unique column is the primary key . On the fees page, the clerk writes only the roll number to show whose fee it is; that roll number on another page is a foreign key , and it links the two pages. A DBMS (Database Management System) is the clerk who keeps the register: it stores data once, lets many people use it, and stops wrong entries. MS Access is the DBMS inside MS Office. You ask it questions with a query , type data into a neat form , and print a report . SSC CGL Tier-II asked the browser, Gmail Compose, email meaning and the Trash folder; NTPC asked URL and Tim Berners-Lee twice. · Think of the internet as the road network of the whole world: millions of computers joined by cables, towers and satellites. The World Wide Web is only one kind of traffic on those roads, just as buses are only one kind of vehicle. Email, video calls and file transfer also travel on the same internet but are not the web. The web is a giant library of pages joined by hyperlinks . Every page has an address called a URL , like a postal address. Computers, however, only understand number addresses (IP addresses), so a helper called DNS works like a phone directory: you give it a name such as google.com and it returns the number. To read pages you need a browser (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari) – the reading glasses. To find pages whose address you do not know you use a search engine (Google, Bing) – the library catalogue. The company that gives you the connection, like a water-pipe supplier, is your ISP . · What the internet is · Internet · Network of networks; also called the information highway and the "web" (trap/jaal). Email questions focus on CC vs BCC , the folders (Drafts, Outbox, Spam) and the inventor Ray Tomlinson . Banking questions ask the full forms and differences of NEFT, RTGS, IMPS, UPI and safe-payment habits (OTP, PIN). · E-mail is a post office that works in seconds. Your e-mail address is your letter box: the part before @ is your name on the box, the part after it is the post office (the mail server) that keeps the box, as in ravi@gmail.com. When you write a letter you can put people in the To line (the main readers), in CC (a copy for information, everyone can see it) or in BCC (a hidden copy – other readers never learn this person got it). Unfinished letters wait in Drafts ; letters still leaving sit in the Outbox ; letters already gone appear in Sent ; junk lands in Spam . E-banking is the same idea for money. Instead of standing in a bank queue, you move money with net banking, a mobile app or UPI . CGL 2023 and 2024 asked the switch twice; CHSL asked topology and IP bits. · A network is simply two or more computers joined so they can share files, printers and the internet – like houses in a colony joined by lanes so neighbours can share things. Size gives the name: a PAN is around one person (phone to earphones by Bluetooth), a LAN covers a room or building, a MAN covers a city, and a WAN spans countries – the internet is the biggest WAN. The topology is the shape of the lanes: one long road (bus), everyone connected to a central chowk (star), a circle (ring) or every house joined to every other (mesh). Devices act like traffic staff: a hub shouts every message to everyone, a switch delivers it only to the right house, a router chooses the route between colonies (networks), and a modem converts the computer's digital signal for the telephone or cable line. The SSC syllabus names network and information security threats and preventive measures . Expect the difference between virus, worm and Trojan , attacks like phishing and DDoS , and what a firewall or encryption does. Security questions now come in every SSC Tier-II computer module: "malware disguised as legitimate software", "phishing", "worm vs virus", "ransomware", "firewall type", "what is a cookie", "first virus". SSC CGL Tier-II 2022 asked Trojan, CHSL Tier-II 2023 asked packet-filtering firewall, and CHSL 2021 asked phishing and virus. Expect 2 to 4 marks from here. · Think of your computer as a house. Malware means any harmful software that gets inside. A virus hides inside a genuine file and spreads only when that file is opened, like a germ on a shared towel. A worm crawls from house to house by itself through the network. A Trojan horse arrives as a gift – a free game – with thieves hidden inside. Ransomware locks your cupboards and asks for money for the key. Spyware and keyloggers are hidden cameras recording what you do and type. Criminals also simply trick people. Phishing is a fake e-mail from 'your bank' asking for your password; the same trick by phone call is vishing and by SMS is smishing . Protection works in layers like locks, guards and alarms: a firewall is the gatekeeper checking traffic, antivirus is the guard who catches known intruders, encryption turns data into secret code, and two-factor authentication asks for a second key such as an OTP. Asked more and more in CGL, CHSL and NTPC: which section of the IT Act deals with what (66 hacking, 66C identity theft, 66D cheating by personation, 66E privacy, 66F cyber terrorism, 67 obscene material), when the Act came , CERT-In , the helpline 1930 , and the dates of Digital India, Aadhaar, UPI and DigiLocker . · Laws for the street were written long before computers. When people began signing contracts by e-mail and stealing money with a click, India needed new rules. So Parliament passed the Information Technology Act, 2000 . It did two big things: it made electronic records and digital signatures legal , like paper and ink, and it made cyber crimes punishable . In 2008 the Act was amended to catch newer crimes: identity theft, cheating by pretending to be someone online, taking private pictures, and cyber terrorism (Section 66F, punishable with life imprisonment). One section, 66A , which punished "offensive" messages, was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015 for hurting free speech. Laws need guards. CERT-In is the national fire brigade for cyber attacks. A citizen who is cheated online calls 1930 or reports on cybercrime.gov.in . Artificial Intelligence means making machines do things that need human-like thinking, such as recognising faces or answering questions. Machine learning is AI that learns from examples instead of fixed rules – the way a child learns what a dog looks like after seeing many dogs. Generative AI creates new text, pictures or music; chatbots are one example. Cloud computing is renting computing power over the internet like taking a taxi instead of buying a car: you can rent ready software (SaaS), a platform to build on (PaaS) or bare infrastructure (IaaS). The Internet of Things connects everyday objects – fans, meters, watches – to the internet. A blockchain is a record book copied on thousands of computers so no single person can secretly change it; Bitcoin was built on it. chemistry.x: Easy marks that come round every year: sublimation examples (camphor, naphthalene, dry ice), which state diffuses fastest , latent heat , the fourth and fifth states (plasma, Bose–Einstein condensate) and evaporation causes cooling . · Everything around you — the water you drink, the air you breathe, the chair you sit on — is matter : anything that has mass and takes up space. Matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving and that pull on each other. Picture a crowded school assembly . When everyone stands in neat rows holding hands, that is a solid : fixed shape, particles only shiver in place. When the bell rings and children walk around the ground but stay close, that is a liquid : it flows and takes the shape of its container but keeps its volume. When school is over and everyone runs off in every direction, that is a gas : no fixed shape or volume, and particles far apart. Heat gives particles energy to break free (melting, boiling); taking heat away lets them settle down again (condensing, freezing). Some solids skip the liquid stage and turn straight into gas — that is sublimation , which is why mothballs slowly vanish in your cupboard. · Three common states compared · Property · Solid · Liquid · Gas · Shape · Fixed · Takes the container's shape · No fixed shape · Volume · Fixed · Fixed · Fills the whole container · Space between particles · Least · More · Most · Force of attraction · Strongest · Weaker · Weakest · Compressibility · Almost none · Very little · Highly compressible (hence LPG, CNG cylinders) · Diffusion · Slowest · Faster · Fastest (smell of incense spreads) · Changes of state · Change · From → to · Name of the point / example · Melting / fusion · Solid → liquid · Melting point; Expect one question on which separation method suits which mixture (chromatography for dyes, fractional distillation for air or crude oil, centrifugation for cream), and one on compound vs mixture or true solution, colloid, suspension . · Think of a kitchen . Salt and sugar each have a fixed make-up — they are pure substances . Mix salt into water and you get salt water : you can taste both, change how much salt you add, and get the salt back by boiling off the water. That is a mixture . Now think of water itself. It is made of hydrogen and oxygen, but it is nothing like either — hydrogen burns, oxygen helps burning, yet water puts fire out. When elements join chemically in a fixed ratio and get brand-new properties, you have a compound . An element is the simplest pure substance, made of only one kind of atom — like gold, oxygen or carbon. Almost every shift has one: who discovered the electron / proton / neutron / nucleus , isotopes vs isobars , electronic configuration (2, 8, 8…), valency , or the charge and mass of sub-atomic particles . · About 2,500 years ago the Indian sage Maharishi Kanad said matter is made of tiny indivisible particles he called parmanu . In 1808 John Dalton made this a science: atoms are tiny, cannot be split, and atoms of one element are all alike. Then the cracks appeared. In 1897 J. J. Thomson found tiny negative particles — electrons — and pictured the atom as a plum pudding (or a watermelon): a ball of positive charge with electrons stuck in it like seeds. In 1911 Ernest Rutherford fired alpha particles at a very thin gold foil. Most went straight through, but a few bounced right back — as if a bullet had hit a tiny steel ball hidden in cotton wool. The atom, he said, is mostly empty space with a tiny, heavy, positive nucleus at the centre. Niels Bohr (1913) then said electrons move in fixed shells or energy levels (K, L, M, N) and do not lose energy while there. Finally, James Chadwick (1932) found the neutron , the uncharged particle in the nucleus. That completed today's picture: protons and neutrons in the nucleus, electrons in shells around it. · The three sub-atomic particles · Particle · Symbol · Charge · Relative mass · Where · Discovered by · Electron · e⁻ · −1 (−1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) · 1/1836 of a proton (about 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) · Shells around the nucleus · J. A sure topic: who made which table (Döbereiner's triads, Newlands' octaves, Mendeleev, Moseley), periods and groups , trends (atomic size, metallic character, electronegativity) and the families — alkali metals, halogens, noble gases. · By the 1860s about 63 elements were known and chemists wanted to arrange them like books in a library. Döbereiner grouped them in threes ( triads ), Newlands noticed every eighth element was like the first, like the notes of music ( law of octaves ). In 1869 the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev arranged elements by atomic mass and boldly left gaps for elements not yet found — and even predicted their properties. When gallium and germanium were discovered and matched his guesses, the world was convinced. He is called the father of the periodic table . One problem remained: a few elements sat in the wrong order by mass. In 1913 Henry Moseley showed the real key is the atomic number . Today's modern periodic table lists 118 elements by atomic number in 7 periods (rows) and 18 groups (columns). Elements in one group behave alike because they have the same number of outer electrons — like members of one family. · How the table grew · 1817–1829 · Döbereiner's triads — e.g. Li, Na, K; the middle mass is about the average of the other two · 1864 · Newlands' law of octaves — every 8th element like the 1st (worked only up to calcium) · 1869 · Mendeleev's periodic law — properties repeat with atomic mass; Look for ionic vs covalent examples, the hydrogen bond (why ice floats, why water boils high), Avogadro's number , molar mass , 22.4 L at STP , and simple number of atoms / molecules calculations. · Atoms want what noble gases already have: a full outer shell of eight electrons (the octet ). They get it in two main ways. Giving and taking : sodium has one spare electron and chlorine needs one. Sodium hands it over, becomes Na⁺, chlorine becomes Cl⁻, and the opposite charges hold them tight — an ionic (electrovalent) bond , like a shopkeeper and a buyer exchanging money. Ionic compounds are hard crystals with high melting points that conduct electricity when melted or dissolved. Sharing : two chlorine atoms each need one electron, so they share a pair — a covalent bond , like two friends sharing an umbrella. Covalent substances (water, methane, sugar) usually melt and boil low and do not conduct. Chemists count atoms in moles , just as a shop counts bananas in dozens. Papers like to name a reaction and ask its type (combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement, redox), ask whether it is exothermic or endothermic , or ask about rusting, rancidity and catalysts . · Light a matchstick, leave a cut apple out, put an iron nail in the rain, or let milk turn to curd — in each case new substances form. That is a chemical change . Melting ice or tearing paper only changes shape or state; that is a physical change , and nothing new is made. You can usually spot a chemical reaction by a sign: a colour change (the cut apple goes brown), a gas bubbling out, a solid (precipitate) forming in a liquid, a change in temperature , or light . Chemists write reactions as equations , like a recipe: what goes in (reactants) on the left, what comes out (products) on the right. Because atoms are never made or lost (Lavoisier's law), the number of each kind of atom must be the same on both sides — that is balancing the equation. · Types of reactions · Type · Pattern · Example · Combination · A + B → AB · CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ (quicklime + water = slaked lime, lots of heat); One of the most asked chapters: which acid is in which food (vinegar, lemon, tamarind, curd, ant sting), the pH of blood, stomach and common things, indicator colours , aqua regia , and what to put on an ant or bee sting . · Taste a lemon: it is sour — that is an acid . Touch soap between wet fingers: it feels slippery and tastes bitter — that is a base . Bases that dissolve in water are called alkalis . Acids and bases are like two teams. An acid gives H⁺ ions in water; a base gives OH⁻ ions . When they meet, H⁺ and OH⁻ join to make water, and the rest of the two teams makes a salt . That is neutralisation — and it is why an antacid (a base) calms a burning stomach (too much hydrochloric acid). To measure how acidic something is we use the pH scale , from 0 to 14, given by the Danish chemist S. P. L. Sørensen . pH 7 is neutral (pure water). Below 7 is acidic — the lower, the stronger. Above 7 is basic. Each step is ten times stronger than the next. Asked often: the reactivity series , exceptions (mercury is liquid, sodium is soft, graphite conducts, iodine shines), which metal is kept in kerosene , galvanisation , amphoteric oxides and the most malleable / best conducting metal. · Think of the jewellery shop and the gas station. Metals — gold, silver, copper, iron — are shiny, can be beaten into sheets ( malleable ), drawn into wires ( ductile ), ring when struck ( sonorous ) and carry heat and electricity. Non-metals — oxygen, carbon, sulphur, chlorine — are mostly dull, brittle if solid, and poor conductors. But chemistry loves exceptions, and so do examiners: mercury is a liquid metal, sodium and potassium are so soft you can cut them with a knife, diamond (a non-metal) is the hardest natural substance, graphite (a non-metal) conducts electricity, and iodine is a non-metal with a shine. Metals also differ in how eagerly they react. Potassium and sodium catch fire in water, so they are stored under kerosene ; gold and platinum hardly react at all, which is why old gold coins still shine. Ranking them gives the reactivity series — the key to which metal pushes out which. · Metals vs non-metals · Property · Metals · Non-metals · State · Solid (except mercury) · Solid, liquid (bromine) or gas · Lustre · Shiny · Dull (except iodine, graphite, diamond) · Malleability / ductility · Yes — gold is the most malleable and ductile · No — brittle · Conductivity · Good conductors (silver best, then copper); chemistry.x: Pure recall and very frequent: baking soda, washing soda, bleaching powder, plaster of Paris, gypsum — their formulas and uses — plus the vitriols , laughing gas , marsh gas , lunar caustic and quicklime vs slaked lime . · Every kitchen and hospital in India uses a few chemicals by their everyday names. The baking soda in dhokla and the washing soda in the dhobi's tub are both sodium compounds, but they are not the same. The plaster on a broken arm and the chalk on a blackboard both come from calcium. Many of these come from one simple starting point: common salt . Pass electricity through salty water (brine) — the chlor-alkali process — and you get caustic soda , chlorine and hydrogen . Chlorine plus slaked lime gives bleaching powder . Salt with ammonia and CO₂ gives baking soda , and heating that gives washing soda . Learn this lesson as a table of pairs — common name ↔ formula ↔ one use — and you have some of the easiest marks in the paper. Steady favourites: ore ↔ metal pairs (bauxite, haematite, galena, cinnabar, cassiterite, zinc blende), froth flotation , roasting vs calcination , blast furnace , and the composition of alloys (brass, bronze, German silver, solder, stainless steel). · Metals rarely lie around pure. Most are locked in rocks as compounds — oxides, sulphides, carbonates. A rock that holds a metal is a mineral ; a mineral from which the metal can be taken out cheaply is an ore . So every ore is a mineral, but not every mineral is an ore. Getting the metal out is metallurgy , and it runs like a factory line. First concentrate the ore — wash away earth and rock (gangue), or froth it up with pine oil so sulphide particles float. Then roast sulphide ores in air, or calcine carbonate ores with little air, to get an oxide. Then reduce the oxide: with carbon (coke) for middle metals like iron and zinc, or with electricity for very reactive ones like sodium and aluminium. Finally refine it to make it pure. Pure metals are often too soft or rust too easily, so we mix them into alloys : copper plus zinc gives golden brass , iron plus chromium and nickel gives rust-free stainless steel , and 22-carat jewellery is gold hardened with a little copper or silver. · Metals and their ores · Metal · Main ores · Formula / note · Aluminium · Bauxite; Always one or two questions: allotropes of carbon (diamond, graphite, fullerene, graphene), alkane / alkene / alkyne formulas, functional groups (formalin, acetone, ethanol), which gas ripens fruit , and who made urea first . · Carbon is the Lego brick of life. It has four hands (valency 4) and loves holding hands with other carbon atoms in long chains, branches and rings — this is called catenation . That is why carbon forms more compounds than any other element: millions of them, from the sugar in your tea to the DNA in your cells. Pure carbon itself comes in different outfits called allotropes . In diamond every carbon holds four others in a rigid 3-D net — the hardest natural substance. In graphite each carbon holds only three, forming flat sheets that slide over each other — soft, slippery, and it conducts electricity (your 'pencil lead'). In 1985 a football-shaped molecule of 60 carbons, buckminsterfullerene , was found, and in 2004 a single sheet of graphite, graphene , was peeled off with sticky tape. Chemists once believed living things had a special 'vital force' needed to make organic compounds. In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made urea in a flask from an inorganic salt — and modern organic chemistry was born. · Allotropes of carbon · Allotrope · Structure · Properties · Uses · Diamond · Each C bonded to 4 others in a 3-D tetrahedral network · Hardest natural substance; Expect: monomer of PVC / Teflon / polythene , first fully synthetic fibre (nylon), artificial silk (rayon), thermoplastic vs thermosetting (bakelite, melamine), and vulcanisation of rubber. · Think of a pearl necklace . Each pearl is a small molecule, a monomer ; string thousands of them together and you get one giant molecule — a polymer ('poly' = many, 'mer' = parts). Nature makes them all the time: cotton and wood are cellulose , rice and potato are starch , hair and silk are proteins , and rubber comes from the milky latex of the rubber tree. In the 20th century chemists learned to make their own. In 1907 Leo Baekeland made bakelite , the first fully synthetic plastic. In 1935 Wallace Carothers at DuPont made nylon , the first fully synthetic fibre — strong enough for parachutes and ropes. Then came polythene bags, PVC pipes, Teflon pans and polyester shirts. Plastics are of two kinds. Thermoplastics soften on heating and can be remoulded, like wax (polythene, PVC). Thermosetting plastics set hard once and never soften again, like a boiled egg (bakelite, melamine) — perfect for switches and plates. The catch: most plastics do not rot, which is why single-use plastic was banned in India in 2022. · Common synthetic polymers · Polymer · Monomer(s) · Uses · Polythene (polyethylene) · Ethene (ethylene) · Carry bags, bottles, toys, pipes · PVC (polyvinyl chloride) · Vinyl chloride · Pipes, raincoats, wire insulation, flooring · Teflon (PTFE) · Tetrafluoroethylene · Non-stick cookware coating · Polystyrene · Styrene · Thermocol (packing, disposable cups) · Nylon-6,6 · Hexamethylenediamine + adipic acid · Ropes, parachutes, tents, toothbrush bristles, stockings · Polyester (terylene, dacron, PET) · Ethylene glycol + terephthalic acid · Clothes (terrycot, terrywool blends), PET bottles · Acrylic (orlon, PAN) · Acrylonitrile · Artificial wool — sweaters, blankets · Bakelite · Phenol + formaldehyde · Electrical switches, handles of pans (thermosetting) · Melamine · Melamine + formaldehyde · Crockery, floor tiles; Regular questions: main gas in LPG / CNG / biogas , the smell in LPG , highest calorific value , the hottest zone of a flame , types of coal , octane number , and which fire extinguisher for an electrical fire . · A fire needs three friends at once — the fire triangle : fuel to burn, oxygen to help it burn, and enough heat to reach the fuel's ignition temperature . Take away any one and the fire dies. That is all a fire extinguisher does: water cools, a CO₂ blanket cuts off oxygen, and turning off the gas removes the fuel. Fuels are judged by their calorific value — how much heat a kilogram gives. Hydrogen tops the list but is hard to store safely; LPG and CNG are clean and high; wood and cow-dung cakes are low and smoky. A good fuel burns at a steady rate, is cheap, easy to carry and leaves little pollution. Look closely at a candle flame and you will see three zones: a dark inner zone of unburnt wax vapour, a bright yellow middle zone where burning is incomplete, and a faint blue outer zone where burning is complete — and that is the hottest part, the one a goldsmith blows on to melt gold. · Calorific values (approximate, kJ/kg) · Fuel · Calorific value · Hydrogen · About 150,000 (highest) · LPG · About 55,000 · Methane / CNG · About 50,000 · Petrol, kerosene, diesel · About 45,000 · Biogas · About 35,000–40,000 · Coal · About 25,000–33,000 · Wood · About 17,000–22,000 · Cow-dung cake · About 6,000–8,000 · Gaseous fuels · Fuel · Main components · Note · LPG (liquefied petroleum gas) · Butane (mainly) and propane · Odourless; Now and then: Boyle's / Charles's law in one line, why soda fizzes (Henry's law), why fish struggle in warm water , osmosis (raisins, pickles, RO filters) and water as the universal solvent . · Squeeze a closed syringe and the trapped air pushes back harder — less space, more pressure. That is Boyle's law . Warm a balloon in the sun and it swells — more heat, more volume. That is Charles's law . Gases behave this simply because their particles are far apart and bounce around freely. A solution is a mixture where one thing (the solute , like sugar) spreads evenly through another (the solvent , like water). Water dissolves so many things that it is called the universal solvent . Gases dissolve too. A soft drink is bottled with CO₂ under high pressure; open it, the pressure drops, and the gas fizzes out — Henry's law . Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen than cold water, which is why fish gasp in warm ponds. And when a raisin soaks in water it swells, because water moves through its skin from the weaker to the stronger solution — osmosis . · Gas laws · Law · Statement · Formula / everyday sign · Boyle's law (1662) · At constant temperature, volume is inversely proportional to pressure · PV = constant; Popular in every exam: the gas behind the Bhopal tragedy (methyl isocyanate), ozone-depleting CFCs and the Montreal Protocol , greenhouse gases , acid rain and the Taj Mahal , smog , and diseases like Minamata (mercury) and Itai-itai (cadmium). · The air is a blanket. A little carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour in it trap the Earth's heat and keep us warm — the natural greenhouse effect . Burning coal and petrol has thickened that blanket, and the planet is warming. High above, 15–35 km up in the stratosphere , a thin layer of ozone (O₃) acts as sunscreen, absorbing harmful ultraviolet rays. In the 1980s scientists found a 'hole' in it over Antarctica, punched by chlorine from CFCs — the gases in old fridges, ACs and spray cans. The world signed the Montreal Protocol (1987) to phase them out, and the ozone layer is slowly healing. Smoke from factories carries sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides ; in clouds they become sulphuric and nitric acid and fall as acid rain , eating into marble — the Taj Mahal's 'marble cancer'. Expect: who discovered hydrogen / oxygen / nitrogen , uses of noble gases (argon in bulbs, neon in signs, helium in balloons), hard and soft water , heavy water , and the colour and smell of gases . · In 1766 Henry Cavendish collected a gas that burned with a pop and called it 'inflammable air'; Lavoisier later named it hydrogen — 'water-maker' — because burning it gives water. A few years later Joseph Priestley (and Carl Scheele before him) made a gas in which a candle burned brilliantly: oxygen . Water seems simple, but it is not always pure. Rainwater that trickles through rocks picks up calcium and magnesium salts and becomes hard — soap will not lather in it and kettles get scaly. If the salts are bicarbonates, boiling removes them ( temporary hardness ); if they are chlorides or sulphates, you need washing soda or an ion-exchange softener ( permanent hardness ). Then there are the quiet noble gases . They hardly react, which is exactly why we use them: argon fills bulbs so the filament does not burn, neon glows red-orange in signs, and helium — light and non-flammable — lifts balloons and helps deep-sea divers breathe. · Gases and their discoverers · Gas · Discovered by · Key uses / facts · Hydrogen · Henry Cavendish, 1766 (named by Lavoisier) · Lightest gas; chemistry.t: Radioactivity, nuclear energy and famous chemists
chemistry.h: रेडियोधर्मिता, नाभिकीय ऊर्जा और प्रसिद्ध रसायनज्ञ
chemistry.x: Regulars: who discovered radioactivity (Becquerel), alpha, beta, gamma — which is most penetrating, half-life sums, fission vs fusion , parts of a reactor , India's nuclear firsts (Apsara, Tarapur, Pokhran), and Nobel prizes in chemistry . · In 1896 Henri Becquerel left uranium salt on a wrapped photographic plate in a drawer. When he developed it, the plate was fogged — the uranium was giving out invisible rays all by itself. Marie and Pierre Curie chased these rays, named the effect radioactivity , and discovered two new elements, polonium and radium . Marie Curie remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences — Physics (1903) and Chemistry (1911). A radioactive nucleus is unstable, like an overloaded shelf. It throws out alpha particles (helium nuclei — stopped by paper), beta particles (fast electrons — stopped by aluminium), or gamma rays (light-like waves — need thick lead or concrete). The time for half of a sample to decay is its half-life . Split a heavy nucleus like uranium-235 with a neutron and it releases huge energy plus more neutrons — fission , the chain reaction inside nuclear power plants and the atom bomb. Squeeze light nuclei like hydrogen together and they join — fusion , which powers the Sun and the hydrogen bomb. From the ancient period the favourites are Arthashastra, Indica, Ashtadhyayi, Kalidasa's plays, Harshacharita, Rajatarangini, Mricchakatika, Mudrarakshasa and the Tamil epics . · Think of ancient India as a library with three shelves . The first shelf holds the epics and grammar : Valmiki's Ramayana, Vyasa's Mahabharata and Panini's Ashtadhyayi. The second holds courts and kings : Chanakya's Arthashastra for Chandragupta Maurya, Kalidasa's plays in the Gupta court, and Banabhatta's biography of Harsha. The third holds science : Aryabhata's mathematics, Charaka's medicine and Sushruta's surgery. Foreign visitors left notes too — Megasthenes (Greek, Mauryan court), Fa-Hien and Hiuen Tsang (Chinese Buddhist pilgrims). Down south, Tamil poets wrote the Tirukkural and the twin epics Silappatikaram and Manimekalai . · Books and authors · Book · Author · Note · Arthashastra · Kautilya (Chanakya) · A treatise on statecraft and economy from the Mauryan age. · Indica · Megasthenes · Greek ambassador of Seleucus at the court of Chandragupta Maurya. · Ashtadhyayi · Panini · The classic grammar of Sanskrit, in eight chapters. · Yoga Sutras · Patanjali · The foundational text of yoga; The Mughal emperors kept memoirs — Babur's Baburnama and Jahangir's Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri — and hired court historians : Abul Fazl for Akbar, Abdul Hamid Lahori for Shah Jahan. Babur's daughter Gulbadan Begum wrote her brother Humayun's life — one of the few histories by a woman. Travellers watched from outside: Al-Biruni came with Mahmud of Ghazni, Ibn Battuta served Muhammad bin Tughlaq, and Bernier saw Shah Jahan's court. Meanwhile the Bhakti poets wrote for the people in their own tongues — Tulsidas, Surdas, Kabir — and Jayasi wrote the Padmavat. · Books and authors · Book · Author · Note · Baburnama (Tuzuk-i-Baburi) · Babur · Memoirs of the founder of the Mughal empire, in Chagatai Turkish. · Humayun-nama · Gulbadan Begum · Babur's daughter wrote the life of her brother Humayun. · Akbarnama · Abul Fazl · Official history of Akbar's reign;
