Classic pairs keep coming back: Das Kapital, Wealth of Nations, Origin of Species, The Prince, The Republic, Social Contract, Animal Farm, War and Peace, Hamlet, A Brief History of Time, The Alchemist . · Some books changed how the world thinks. Plato's Republic and Aristotle's Politics began political philosophy; Machiavelli 's The Prince taught rulers to be practical; Rousseau 's Social Contract inspired the French Revolution. In economics, Adam Smith argued for free markets in The Wealth of Nations (1776), Karl Marx answered with Das Kapital, and Keynes rescued the 1930s with his General Theory. Darwin 's Origin of Species (1859) changed biology. And then the great stories — Homer's Iliad, Shakespeare's plays, Tolstoy's War and Peace, Dickens's Oliver Twist, Orwell's Animal Farm — and modern favourites like The Alchemist and Harry Potter. · Books and authors · Book · Author · Note · Hamlet · William Shakespeare · Also Macbeth, Othello, King Lear, Romeo and Juliet, The Merchant of Venice. · War and Peace · Leo Tolstoy · Also Anna Karenina. · Crime and Punishment · Fyodor Dostoevsky · Les Misérables · Victor Hugo · Oliver Twist · Charles Dickens · Also A Tale of Two Cities, David Copperfield. · Animal Farm · George Orwell · Also Nineteen Eighty-Four; Orwell was born in Motihari, Bihar. · Iliad · Homer · Also the Odyssey. · The Divine Comedy · Dante Alighieri · Don Quixote · Miguel de Cervantes · Paradise Lost · John Milton · Faust · Johann Wolfgang von Goethe · Pride and Prejudice · Jane Austen · The Adventures of Tom Sawyer · Mark Twain · The Old Man and the Sea · Ernest Hemingway · Pulitzer 1953. · Das Kapital · Karl Marx · With Engels he also wrote The Communist Manifesto (1848). · The Wealth of Nations · Adam Smith · 1776 — Smith is the father of economics. · On the Origin of Species · Charles Darwin · 1859 — natural selection. · The Prince · Niccolò Machiavelli · The Republic · Plato · Politics · Aristotle · The Social Contract · Jean-Jacques Rousseau · Utopia · Thomas More · One Hundred Years of Solitude · Gabriel García Márquez · Harry Potter series · J. days.x: Asked often: National Science Day (Raman effect), National Voters' Day , National Technology Day (Pokhran-II), Constitution Day , National Handloom Day , Hindi Diwas , Panchayati Raj Day and the new National Space Day . · Other national days remember an event . On 28 February 1928 C. V. Raman announced his discovery — so that is National Science Day . On 11 May 1998 India tested nuclear weapons at Pokhran — National Technology Day . On 7 August 1905 the Swadeshi movement began — National Handloom Day . On 23 August 2023 Chandrayaan-3 touched down on the Moon — National Space Day . The Constitution gives two: it was adopted on 26 November 1949 (Constitution Day) and came into force on 26 January 1950 (Republic Day). Regulars: Army Day (15 Jan), Air Force Day (8 Oct), Navy Day (4 Dec), Armed Forces Flag Day (7 Dec), Kargil Vijay Diwas (26 Jul) and Vijay Diwas (16 Dec). · Each service has its own birthday-like day. The Army celebrates 15 January, when General K. M. Cariappa took over from the last British commander in 1949. The Air Force was set up on 8 October 1932. The Navy marks 4 December, when Indian missile boats struck Karachi in 1971 (Operation Trident). Two victories are remembered: 16 December 1971, when Pakistan's army surrendered in Dhaka and Bangladesh was born, and 26 July 1999, when the Kargil heights were won back. On 7 December every citizen can donate on Armed Forces Flag Day. · Days and dates · Day · Date · Why this date · Armed Forces Veterans' Day · 14 January · Field Marshal K. M. defence.x: Expect: Supreme Commander (the President), the Chief of Defence Staff , mottos of the three services, and where the IMA, NDA and other academies are. · India's armed forces have three services — the Army , the Navy and the Air Force — under the Ministry of Defence. Their Supreme Commander is the President of India . Since 1 January 2020 a Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) heads the Department of Military Affairs and works for jointness among the three; the first CDS was General Bipin Rawat . Each service has a Sanskrit or English motto: the Army's 'Service Before Self', the Navy's 'Sham No Varunah' and the Air Force's 'Nabhah Sparsham Deeptam' from the Gita. Learn them as a map: the Army's Northern command watches J&K from Udhampur; the Eastern Army and Navy commands sit in Kolkata and Visakhapatnam; the Air Force's Eastern command is up in Shillong. In war : Param Vir Chakra, Maha Vir Chakra, Vir Chakra. In peace : Ashoka Chakra, Kirti Chakra, Shaurya Chakra. Which force guards which border (BSF, ITBP, SSB, Assam Rifles), the oldest (Assam Rifles) and largest (CRPF) forces, the 'Black Cats' (NSG), and raising years are asked again and again. · Behind the Army stand the Central Armed Police Forces under the Home Ministry. Learn them by the border they guard: the BSF faces Pakistan and Bangladesh, the ITBP the Himalayan border with China, the SSB the open borders with Nepal and Bhutan, and the Assam Rifles — India's oldest force, raised in 1835 — the Myanmar border. P. J. Abdul Kalam . It gave five missiles — remember “PATNA” : P rithvi (surface-to-surface), A gni (long-range ballistic), T rishul (short-range air defence), N ag (anti-tank), A kash (surface-to-air). Then came BrahMos with Russia — named after the Brahmaputra and the Moskva — one of the fastest cruise missiles. At sea, INS Vikrant (2022) is India's first home-built aircraft carrier, and INS Arihant its first nuclear-powered missile submarine. Operation names are favourites — old ones ( Polo, Vijay, Meghdoot, Blue Star, Cactus ) and new ones ( Ganga, Kaveri, Ajay, Dost , and Operation Sindoor of May 2025). · Every big operation gets a code name. In 1948 Operation Polo brought Hyderabad into India; in 1961 Operation Vijay freed Goa. In 1984 Meghdoot took the Siachen glacier, and in 1988 Cactus saved the Maldives government from a coup. Recent operations are often rescue missions , named after rivers or friendship: Ganga brought students home from Ukraine (2022), Kaveri from Sudan and Ajay from Israel (2023), Dost helped quake-hit Turkey. In May 2025, after the Pahalgam terror attack, Operation Sindoor struck terror camps in Pakistan and PoK. · Operations · Operation · What it was · Note · Operation Polo · Integration of Hyderabad State, 1948 · Also called 'police action'. · Operation Vijay (1961) · Liberation of Goa from Portugal · Kargil 1999 was also named Operation Vijay. · Operation Trident · Attack on Karachi harbour, 1971 · Remembered on Navy Day (4 December). · Operation Meghdoot · Securing the Siachen Glacier, 1984 · Operation Blue Star · Golden Temple, Amritsar, 1984 · Operation Pawan · Indian Peace Keeping Force in Sri Lanka, 1987 · Operation Cactus · Foiling a coup in the Maldives, 1988 · Operation Shakti · Pokhran-II nuclear tests, 1998 · The 1974 test was 'Smiling Buddha'. · Operation Safed Sagar · Air Force operations in the Kargil war, 1999 · Operation Parakram · Military build-up after the 2001 Parliament attack · Operation Black Tornado · NSG operation in the 26/11 Mumbai attacks, 2008 · Operation Rahat · Evacuation from war-torn Yemen, 2015 · Operation Maitri · Relief after the Nepal earthquake, 2015 · Operation Samudra Setu · Navy bringing Indians home in the COVID-19 pandemic, 2020 · Operation Ganga · Evacuation of Indians from Ukraine, 2022 · Operation Dost · Earthquake relief in Turkey and Syria, 2023 · Operation Kaveri · Evacuation from Sudan, 2023 · Operation Ajay · Evacuation from Israel, 2023 · Operation Brahma · Earthquake relief in Myanmar, 2025 · Operation Sindoor · Strikes on terror camps in Pakistan and PoK, May 2025 · Launched after the Pahalgam terror attack of April 2025. · Operation Sindhu · Evacuation of Indians from Iran, June 2025 · River rescues — “Ganga flew from Ukraine, Kaveri from Sudan, Sindhu from Iran” . defence.x: The commonest defence question: 'Exercise X is held between India and which country?' Top picks: Yudh Abhyas (USA), Mitra Shakti (Sri Lanka), Surya Kiran (Nepal), Sampriti (Bangladesh), Nomadic Elephant (Mongolia), Garuda Shakti (Indonesia), Dharma Guardian (Japan). · Exercise names often hide a clue to the partner. Nomadic Elephant — the nomads of Mongolia. Surya Kiran — the sun rising over Nepal's Himalaya. Dharma Guardian — Japan's Buddhist heritage. Harimau means 'tiger' in Malay (Malaysia). Dustlik means 'friendship' in Uzbek. Sampriti (harmony) with neighbour Bangladesh. defence.t: Multilateral exercises and the latest editions
defence.x: Asked often: Malabar (the Quad navies), MILAN (India-hosted), RIMPAC , Red Flag , Pitch Black , Tarang Shakti (India's first multinational air exercise) and where the latest edition of an exercise was held. · Some exercises bring many countries together. Malabar started in 1992 between India and the US and now includes all four Quad navies (with Japan and Australia). India hosts MILAN at Visakhapatnam, and in 2024 held Tarang Shakti , its first multinational air exercise. The US hosts RIMPAC near Hawaii and Red Flag in Alaska and Nevada; Australia hosts Pitch Black . Current-affairs questions ask about the latest edition — its number, venue and month. awards.x: Very frequent: the first three recipients (1954), firsts (first woman, first posthumous, first foreigner, youngest), the 2024 five , and facts about the award itself (peepal leaf, no money, at most three a year). · The Bharat Ratna , India's highest civilian honour, was instituted on 2 January 1954 . The first three went that year to C. Rajagopalachari , S. Radhakrishnan and C. V. Raman . It is shaped like a peepal leaf with a sun on it, carries no money , and is normally limited to three a year — though five were announced in 2024. Its 'firsts' are favourites: Lal Bahadur Shastri (first posthumous, 1966), Indira Gandhi (first woman, 1971), Mother Teresa (first naturalised citizen, 1980), Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan (first non-Indian, 1987), Sachin Tendulkar (youngest and first sportsperson, 2014). As of 2026 there are 53 recipients; none were named in 2025. · About the award · Instituted · 2 January 1954 · Design · A bronze peepal leaf with the sun and 'Bharat Ratna' in Devanagari · Money · None — only a sanad (certificate) and the medallion · How many a year · Normally at most three (five in 2024) · Who recommends · The Prime Minister, to the President · Posthumous · Allowed since 1955; first posthumous award 1966 (Shastri) · Total (as of 2026) · 53 recipients; the 2024 awardees are the latest · Recipients to remember · Recipient · Year · Note · C. Asked in current affairs every year: the Padma Vibhushan recipients of the year, the total number of awards, and basic facts — three tiers, announced on the eve of Republic Day . · Below the Bharat Ratna come the three Padma awards, also started in 1954: Padma Vibhushan (exceptional service), Padma Bhushan (high order) and Padma Shri (distinguished service). They are announced every year on the eve of Republic Day and presented by the President at Rashtrapati Bhavan in March–April. For 2026 the President approved 131 awards — 5 Padma Vibhushan, 13 Padma Bhushan and 113 Padma Shri. The five Vibhushans went to actor Dharmendra (posthumous), jurist K. T. Thomas , violinist N. Rajam , writer P. Narayanan and former Kerala CM V. S. awards.t: Literary awards — India and the world
awards.x: Regulars: Jnanpith (first winner, first woman, latest winners), Sahitya Akademi (24 languages), Saraswati Samman and Vyas Samman (K. K. Birla Foundation), the Booker and Pulitzer with their Indian winners. · India's top literary prize, the Jnanpith , is given by the Bharatiya Jnanpith trust. The first went to Malayalam poet G. Sankara Kurup in 1965; the first woman was Bengali novelist Ashapoorna Devi ; Amitav Ghosh became the first English writer to win it in 2018. Recent winners: Gulzar and Jagadguru Rambhadracharya (2023), and Hindi writer Vinod Kumar Shukla (2024). The Sahitya Akademi honours one book a year in each of 24 languages. The K. K. Birla Foundation gives the Saraswati Samman (any Indian language) and the Vyas Samman (Hindi). awards.x: Always asked: Indian Nobel laureates with field and year (Tagore 1913, Raman 1930, Khorana 1968, Mother Teresa 1979, Chandrasekhar 1983, Sen 1998, Satyarthi 2014, Banerjee 2019) and basic Nobel facts (1901, Alfred Nobel, Oslo for Peace). · Alfred Nobel, the inventor of dynamite, left his fortune to reward those who did the most good for humanity. The first prizes were given in 1901 in five fields — Physics, Chemistry, Medicine, Literature and Peace; Economics was added in 1969 . All are handed out on 10 December , Nobel's death anniversary — Peace in Oslo , the rest in Stockholm . India's story begins with Rabindranath Tagore , the first Asian laureate, in 1913, and C. V. Raman , the first Asian scientist to win, in 1930. parks.t: Protected areas: laws, types and projects
parks.h: संरक्षित क्षेत्र: क़ानून, प्रकार और परियोजनाएँ
parks.x: Asked again and again: the year of each Act and Project (Wildlife Act 1972, Project Tiger 1973, Project Elephant 1992), national park vs sanctuary , India's first national park (Hailey/Corbett, 1936) and the counts of each kind. · Indian wildlife law begins with the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 . It lets states declare two main kinds of protected area. A national park is the strictest: no grazing, no private rights, and its boundary can be changed only by the state legislature. A wildlife sanctuary is looser: some human activity is allowed if it doesn't harm wildlife. In 2002 the Act added conservation reserves and community reserves . Big species got their own missions: Project Tiger (1973), crocodiles (1975), Project Elephant (1992), snow leopards (2009), dolphins (2020) and Project Cheetah (2022). Always asked: Project Tiger 1973 , the number of tiger reserves (58) and the newest ones, the largest (Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam) and smallest (Bor), and the state with the most tigers (Madhya Pradesh). · In 1973 India had fewer than 2,000 tigers left. Project Tiger began on 1 April 1973 at Jim Corbett with nine reserves. In 2005 the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) was set up to run it. Know the 18 biosphere reserves with their states, the first (Nilgiri, 1986), the largest (Great Rann of Kutch) and smallest (Dibru-Saikhowa), and the 13 in UNESCO's list — the newest, Cold Desert , joined in September 2025. · A biosphere reserve protects a whole landscape and the people living in it. It has three rings: a strictly protected core , a buffer for research and education, and a transition zone where villages and farms carry on. The idea comes from UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere (MAB) programme, started in 1971 . India's first was Nilgiri (1986), spread over Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka. Today there are 18 , the last being Panna (2011). 13 are in UNESCO's World Network — Cold Desert in Himachal Pradesh became the 13th in September 2025. parks.t: Animals and where to find them
parks.x: A favourite question type: “Which park is famous for X?” Learn one park per animal — rhino–Kaziranga, lion–Gir, sangai–Keibul Lamjao, hangul–Dachigam, barasingha–Kanha, Nilgiri tahr–Eravikulam, Olive Ridley–Gahirmatha. · Many of India's rarest animals survive in just one place. The Asiatic lion lives wild only in Gir . The sangai deer dances on the floating meadows of Keibul Lamjao . The hangul , Kashmir's only red deer, clings on in Dachigam . In Kanha , rangers saved the barasingha from fewer than 70 animals. Some come home after long journeys: Olive Ridley turtles return to Gahirmatha beach every winter, and cheetahs — extinct in India since 1952 — were brought from Namibia to Kuno in 2022. environment.t: Ecology: key terms and who coined them
environment.h: पारिस्थितिकी: मुख्य शब्द और उनके जनक
environment.x: SSC asks the meaning of ecological terms (niche, ecotone, biome, ecosystem), who coined them (Haeckel — ecology, Tansley — ecosystem) and the type of interaction in an example (lichen = mutualism, Cuscuta = parasitism). · In 1866 the German biologist Ernst Haeckel gave a name to the study of living things and their homes: ecology , from the Greek oikos , house. In 1935 A. G. Tansley joined the living and the non-living into one working unit and called it the ecosystem . Inside it, every species has an address — its habitat — and a job — its niche . Living things also deal with each other. In a lichen , an alga and a fungus both gain ( mutualism ). An orchid sits on a mango tree without harming it ( commensalism ). Cuscuta sucks food from its host ( parasitism ). Where two ecosystems meet, as in a mangrove, we get an ecotone , often richer in species — the edge effect . · Ecological terms · Term · Meaning · Note · Ecology · Study of living things and their surroundings · The word comes from Greek 'oikos' (house). · Habitat · The place where an organism naturally lives · Ecological niche · The role a species plays in its community · Its 'profession', not its 'address'. · Population · All the individuals of one species in an area · Community · All the populations of different species living together in an area · Ecosystem · Living things and their non-living surroundings working as one unit · The basic functional unit of ecology. · Biome · A large region with its own typical climate, plants and animals · Tundra, taiga, desert, rainforest. · Biosphere · The part of the Earth where life exists · Land, water and lower air together. · Ecotone · A transition zone between two ecosystems · Example: a mangrove between land and sea. · Edge effect · More kinds of species found in a transition zone · Carrying capacity · The largest population an environment can support · Ecological succession · The gradual change of a community over time to a stable climax · Starts with pioneer species such as lichens. · Who coined the term · Term / idea · Given by · Note · Ecology · Ernst Haeckel · German biologist, 1866. · Ecosystem · A. G. Tansley · British ecologist, 1935. · Biosphere · Eduard Suess · Austrian geologist, 1875. · Biodiversity · Walter G. Rosen · Coined in 1985; made popular by E. O. Interactions by signs: ++ mutualism, +0 commensalism, +− parasitism/predation, −0 amensalism, −− competition . · Habitat ≠ niche : habitat is where it lives, niche is what it does. Tansley (1935). · Habitat is where a species lives; niche is the role it plays. · An ecotone is a transition zone between two ecosystems; it often shows the edge effect. · Lichen and Rhizobium-legume are mutualism; orchid on a tree is commensalism; Cuscuta is parasitism. · Biodiversity was coined by Walter Rosen (1985); biodiversity hotspot by Norman Myers (1988).

Asked every year: the 10% law (Lindeman), producers vs consumers vs decomposers , which pyramid is always upright (energy) and which can be inverted (biomass in the sea, numbers in a parasitic chain). · All energy in an ecosystem starts with the Sun . Green plants — the producers — catch it in photosynthesis. A grasshopper eats the grass ( primary consumer ), a frog eats the grasshopper ( secondary consumer ), a snake eats the frog, and an eagle eats the snake. Each step is a trophic level . When anything dies, decomposers — bacteria and fungi — return its nutrients to the soil. At each step only about 10% of the energy passes on; the rest is lost as heat. This is Lindeman's ten per cent law (1942). So food chains are short (usually 4–5 links) and the pyramid of energy is always upright . Energy flows one way ; nutrients go round in cycles . Many food chains linked together make a food web . · Who plays which role · Organism · Role · Note · grass · Producer (first trophic level) · Green plants make their own food — they are autotrophs. · phytoplankton in a pond · Producer (first trophic level) · a grasshopper eating grass · Primary consumer (herbivore) · a deer · Primary consumer (herbivore) · a frog that eats grasshoppers · Secondary consumer · a snake that eats frogs · Tertiary consumer · an eagle at the end of the chain · Top (apex) consumer · bacteria and fungi · Decomposers · They break dead matter into simple nutrients. · an earthworm feeding on dead leaves · Detritivore · a vulture eating a dead animal · Scavenger · Shapes of ecological pyramids · Pyramid · Shape · Why · Pyramid of energy (any ecosystem) · Upright — it can never be inverted · Energy is lost at every step, so it always narrows upward. · Pyramid of numbers in a grassland · Upright · Lots of grass, fewer grasshoppers, fewer frogs. · Pyramid of biomass in a sea or pond · Inverted · A small mass of fast-growing phytoplankton feeds a larger mass of zooplankton and fish. · Pyramid of numbers in a parasitic food chain · Inverted · One host carries many parasites. · Pyramid of numbers for a tree, its insects and birds · Spindle-shaped · One tree, many insects, fewer birds. · Food chain facts · Grazing food chain · Starts with green plants: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle · Detritus food chain · Starts with dead matter: dead leaves → earthworm → bird · Energy flow · One way (unidirectional) — Sun → producers → consumers · Ten per cent law · About 10% of energy passes to the next level (Lindeman, 1942) · Most productive ecosystems · Tropical rainforests on land; estuaries and coral reefs in water · Gross vs net primary productivity · NPP = GPP minus what plants use in respiration · Standing crop · The living mass present at a trophic level at one time · “Energy Never turns upside down” — the pyramid of E nergy is never inverted. “Sea Biomass Stands on its head” — the biomass pyramid in the sea is inverted. · Decomposers are not a trophic level in the pyramid; they work at every level. A tree pyramid of numbers is spindle-shaped (one tree, many insects), and a parasitic one is inverted . Energy is not recycled — only nutrients are. · Producers (green plants) are the first trophic level; herbivores are primary consumers. · Bacteria and fungi are decomposers; earthworms are detritivores. · Only about 10% of energy passes from one level to the next (Lindeman's law, 1942). · The pyramid of energy is always upright; biomass in the sea and numbers in a parasitic chain can be inverted. · Energy flows one way; nutrients move in cycles.

environment.x: Favourites: which bacterium does what in the nitrogen cycle (Rhizobium, Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter, Pseudomonas), the composition of air , and the names of grasslands (Pampas — Argentina, Veld — South Africa, Downs — Australia). · Matter on Earth is never used up — it goes round in biogeochemical cycles . Air is 78% nitrogen , but plants cannot use it directly. Rhizobium in the root nodules of peas and beans, Azotobacter in soil and cyanobacteria in paddy fields fix it into ammonia. Nitrosomonas turns ammonia into nitrite, Nitrobacter turns nitrite into nitrate, and Pseudomonas sends nitrogen back to the air. The phosphorus cycle has no gas stage — it is a sedimentary cycle. Climate decides the great biomes . The tropical rainforest holds the most species; the taiga (coniferous forest) is the largest land biome; the tundra has frozen ground (permafrost) and mosses. environment.x: Asked again and again: India's four hotspots , the number of hotspots in the world (36) , in-situ vs ex-situ conservation, the IUCN Red List categories and IUCN's headquarters ( Gland, Switzerland ). · Biodiversity — the variety of life — works at three levels: genetic , species and ecosystem diversity. India has only about 2.4% of the world's land but about 7–8% of its recorded species, which makes it one of the 17 megadiverse countries . In 1988 Norman Myers named the richest but most threatened regions hotspots : a hotspot needs at least 1,500 endemic plant species and must have lost at least 70% of its original habitat. The world has 36 ; India touches four — the Himalaya , Indo-Burma , the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka , and Sundaland (Nicobar Islands). We protect species in two ways. In-situ means in their home — national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves and sacred groves . Ex-situ means outside it — zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks and cryopreservation. Everyday air pollution is quieter but larger. Vehicles give out carbon monoxide , which grabs haemoglobin and starves the body of oxygen. Coal burning gives sulphur dioxide ; with nitrogen oxides it makes acid rain , which corrodes marble — the 'marble cancer' of the Taj Mahal. Smoke plus fog makes smog . The old London smog (1952) was sulphur smoke on cold mornings; the photochemical smog of Los Angeles forms when sunlight acts on exhaust gases and makes ozone and PAN . environment.x: The commonest pollution questions: Minamata → mercury , Itai-itai → cadmium , blue baby → nitrates , fluorosis → fluoride , and the meaning of BOD , eutrophication and biomagnification . Noise is measured in decibels . · In the 1950s, a factory at Minamata in Japan poured mercury waste into the bay. Fish soaked it up, people ate the fish, and a nerve disease spread — Minamata disease . Downstream from a mine on Japan's Jinzu river, cadmium made bones so brittle that patients cried 'itai-itai' — 'it hurts, it hurts'. Poisons like these and the pesticide DDT grow more concentrated at every step up the food chain: biomagnification . When fertiliser and detergent run into a lake, the extra nitrates and phosphates feed huge algal blooms . When the algae die, bacteria use up the oxygen and fish die — eutrophication . The oxygen used by microbes to break down waste is the BOD : clean water has a BOD below about 5 ppm; sewage is far higher. Noise, too, is pollution, measured in decibels ; India's rules set the lowest limit for silence zones around hospitals and schools. · Pollution diseases · Disease · Caused by · Note · Minamata disease · Mercury · First seen at Minamata Bay, Japan (1956), from fish eaten by people. · Itai-itai disease · Cadmium · Japan; environment.x: Most-asked: which gases are greenhouse gases , the main source of methane (paddy, cattle), CFCs destroy ozone , ozone is measured in Dobson units , the ozone layer is in the stratosphere , and World Ozone Day is 16 September . · Sunlight warms the Earth, and the Earth sends heat back out. Greenhouse gases — water vapour, carbon dioxide , methane , nitrous oxide and fluorinated gases — trap part of that heat, like the glass of a greenhouse. Without them Earth would be frozen; with too much of them it overheats. Since 1850 burning fossil fuels has pushed CO₂ from about 280 ppm to over 420 ppm , and the world is now about 1.1–1.3 °C warmer. 2024 was the hottest year on record and the first calendar year above 1.5 °C. High above, in the stratosphere , a thin layer of ozone (O₃) blocks harmful ultraviolet rays. In 1985 British scientists found a hole in it over Antarctica , caused mainly by CFCs , whose chlorine destroys ozone. The world answered with the Montreal Protocol (1987), and the layer is now slowly healing. · Greenhouse gases and their sources · Gas · Main source · Note · Carbon dioxide · Burning coal, oil and gas, and cutting forests · The biggest human-made greenhouse gas. · Methane · Paddy fields, cattle and wetlands · Also called marsh gas; Twenty years later the Earth Summit at Rio de Janeiro (1992) produced three big treaties: the climate convention ( UNFCCC ), the biodiversity convention ( CBD ) and, two years later, the desertification convention ( UNCCD , 1994). environment.t: India: green laws, missions, movements and environmentalists
environment.h: भारत: पर्यावरण क़ानून, मिशन, आंदोलन और पर्यावरणविद्
environment.x: Asked very often: Chipko (1973, Uttarakhand, Sunderlal Bahuguna) , Appiko (Karnataka) , Narmada Bachao (Medha Patkar) , NGT (2010) , the eight NAPCC missions and Mission LiFE . · India's green story is older than its laws. In 1730 , at Khejarli near Jodhpur, Amrita Devi Bishnoi and 363 Bishnois died hugging khejri trees to stop the king's axemen. Two and a half centuries later, in 1973 , villagers in Chamoli (now Uttarakhand) again hugged trees — the Chipko movement , organised by Chandi Prasad Bhatt and carried across India by Sunderlal Bahuguna . Karnataka's Appiko (1983) copied it, Kerala's scientists and poets saved Silent Valley , and Medha Patkar led the Narmada Bachao Andolan against big dams. The law followed: the Water Act (1974) created the Central Pollution Control Board , the Air Act came in 1981 and the Environment (Protection) Act in 1986. In 2008 India released its National Action Plan on Climate Change with eight missions , and in 2010 set up the National Green Tribunal to hear green cases quickly. In 2022 India launched Mission LiFE — 'Lifestyle for Environment' — and in 2023 the Green Credit Programme . · India's green milestones · Law / step · Year · Note · Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act · 1974 · India's first pollution law; bodies.t: The Article map: which body, which Article
bodies.h: किस निकाय का कौन सा अनुच्छेद
bodies.x: The single commonest question: “Body X is under which Article?” — Election Commission 324 , Finance Commission 280 , CAG 148 , Attorney General 76 , UPSC 315 , NCSC 338 , GST Council 279A . Next come the amendments that created bodies and the first holder of each post. · A constitutional body is one the Constitution itself creates — its Article names it, and only a constitutional amendment can abolish it. The Election Commission, UPSC, Finance Commission and CAG were there from 26 January 1950. Others were added later by amendments: the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities (7th, 1956), the NCST (89th, 2003), the GST Council (101st, 2016) and the NCBC (102nd, 2018). A statutory body is made by an ordinary Act of Parliament (NHRC, CVC, Lokpal), and an executive body is made by a simple government order (NITI Aayog, CBI). Parts 2 and 3 deal with those. Here, learn the Article numbers as pairs — they are asked in almost every SSC shift. · Body → Article · Body · Article · Note · Election Commission of India · Article 324 · Part XV (Elections), Articles 324–329. · Union Public Service Commission · Article 315 · Articles 315–323 cover the UPSC and the State PSCs. · Finance Commission · Article 280 · Set up by the President every five years. · Comptroller and Auditor General · Article 148 · Articles 148–151 cover the CAG. · Attorney General for India · Article 76 · India's highest law officer. · Advocate General of a state · Article 165 · The state's highest law officer. · National Commission for Scheduled Castes · Article 338 · National Commission for Scheduled Tribes · Article 338A · Added by the 89th Amendment, 2003. · National Commission for Backward Classes · Article 338B · Added by the 102nd Amendment, 2018. · GST Council · Article 279A · Added by the 101st Amendment, 2016. · Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities · Article 350B · Added by the 7th Amendment, 1956. · Inter-State Council · Article 263 · Set up in 1990 on the Sarkaria Commission's advice. · State Election Commission · Article 243K · Holds panchayat elections (municipal ones under Article 243ZA). · State Finance Commission · Article 243I · Reviews the finances of panchayats; Asked again and again: Article 324 , the composition (CEC + 2 Election Commissioners), tenure (6 years or age 65), removal of the CEC (like a Supreme Court judge), the first CEC (Sukumar Sen) and that the ECI does not hold panchayat or municipal elections. · The Election Commission was set up on 25 January 1950 — the day before the Constitution came into force — and that date is now National Voters' Day . Under Article 324 it superintends, directs and controls elections to Parliament , the state legislatures and the offices of the President and Vice-President . Panchayat and municipal polls belong to the State Election Commissions . For most of its life the ECI had only one member. It became a three-member body permanently in 1993 — the same year T. N. Seshan brought in voter ID cards. Since the 2023 Act , the President appoints the CEC and ECs on the advice of a panel of the Prime Minister , the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha and a Union Cabinet Minister named by the PM. · Election Commission at a glance · Article · 324 (Part XV, Articles 324–329) · Composition · Chief Election Commissioner + 2 Election Commissioners (since 1993) · Appointed by · The President, on a selection panel's advice (PM, Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha, a Cabinet Minister) — 2023 Act · Term · 6 years or age 65, whichever is earlier · Removal of the CEC · Like a Supreme Court judge — special majority in both Houses · Removal of an EC · By the President, only on the CEC's recommendation · Decisions · By majority when members differ · Does not conduct · Panchayat and municipal elections (State Election Commissions) · Holder as of 2025–26 (not quizzed) · Gyanesh Kumar became CEC in February 2025 — check before the exam · Election milestones · Event · Year · Note · Election Commission set up (25 January) · 1950 · 25 January is now National Voters' Day. · First general elections · 1951–52 · Under CEC Sukumar Sen. · EVMs first used (Paravur, Kerala) · 1982 · In a single assembly seat. · Commission first made multi-member (briefly) · 1989 · Went back to one member in 1990. · Commission made permanently multi-member (CEC + 2 ECs) · 1993 · From 1 October 1993. · EVMs used in every Lok Sabha seat · 2004 · First National Voters' Day · 2011 · Held every year on 25 January. · NOTA added to the ballot (Supreme Court order) · 2013 · PUCL case, September 2013. · New law on choosing the CEC and ECs · 2023 · The Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act. · “6–65, Judge-like” : CEC serves 6 years or to 65 and goes only the way a Supreme Court judge goes. bodies.t: UPSC and State Public Service Commissions
bodies.h: संघ और राज्य लोक सेवा आयोग
bodies.x: Asked: Articles 315–323 , who appoints (President for UPSC, Governor for State PSC), who removes (the President in both cases), the term (6 years or 65 for UPSC, 62 for State PSC) and to whom they report . · Recruiting civil servants on merit began with the Public Service Commission of 1926 , set up on the Lee Commission 's advice with Sir Ross Barker as chairman. The 1935 Act made it the Federal PSC, and in 1950 it became the Union Public Service Commission under Article 315 . The President appoints its chairman and members, and decides how many there are. Every state has its own State PSC , whose members the Governor appoints — but only the President can remove them. Two or more states can share a Joint State PSC , made by a law of Parliament, with members appointed by the President. The UPSC sends its yearly report to the President ; a State PSC to the Governor (Article 323). · Articles 315–323 · Article · Deals with · Note · Article 315 · Public Service Commissions for the Union and the states · Article 316 · Appointment and term of members · Article 317 · Removal and suspension of members · Article 318 · Conditions of service and staff · Article 319 · Bar on holding office after ceasing to be a member · Article 320 · Functions of the Public Service Commissions · Article 321 · Power to extend their functions · Article 322 · Expenses of the Public Service Commissions · Article 323 · Reports of the Public Service Commissions · UPSC vs State PSC · UPSC · State PSC · Appointed by · The President · The Governor · Removed by · The President · The President (not the Governor) · Term · 6 years or age 65 · 6 years or age 62 · Resignation goes to · The President · The Governor · Annual report goes to · The President · The Governor · After leaving · Chairman: no further government job · Chairman may become UPSC chairman or member · “Governor hires, President fires” — for State PSC members. And 65 vs 62 : the Union is the bigger number. · The Governor appoints State PSC members but cannot remove them — only the President can, after a Supreme Court inquiry for misbehaviour. A Joint State PSC is statutory (made by Parliament), not constitutional. · Articles 315–323 cover the UPSC and State PSCs; Article 320 lists their functions. · UPSC members: appointed by the President; 6 years or age 65. · State PSC members: appointed by the Governor; 6 years or age 62; removed only by the President. · Reports: UPSC to the President, State PSC to the Governor (Article 323). · The first Public Service Commission (1926) followed the Lee Commission; Sir Ross Barker was chairman.

bodies.x: Asked: Finance Commission Article 280 and its chairmen (1st K. C. Neogy, 15th N. K. Singh, 16th Arvind Panagariya); CAG Article 148 , term (6 years or 65), removal like an SC judge , reports ( Article 151 ); GST Council Article 279A , chaired by the Union Finance Minister . · Three bodies guard India's money. The Finance Commission (Article 280) is set up by the President every five years with a chairman and four members . It recommends how the taxes the Centre collects are shared with the states. The 15th (N. K. Singh) gave the states 41% ; the 16th (Arvind Panagariya, set up 31 December 2023) covers 2026–31 . Its advice is not binding; the report is laid before Parliament (Article 281). The Comptroller and Auditor General (Articles 148–151) audits every rupee spent from the Consolidated Funds. Appointed by the President by warrant for 6 years or till 65 , the CAG can be removed only like a Supreme Court judge , and cannot take any government job afterwards. The GST Council (Article 279A, 101st Amendment, 2016) is chaired by the Union Finance Minister , with every state's finance minister as a member. · The three money bodies · Finance Commission · Article 280 · chairman + 4 members · set up by the President every 5 years · advisory · CAG · Articles 148–151 · single person · 6 years or 65 · salary equal to a Supreme Court judge · CAG reports · Union accounts → President → Parliament; state accounts → Governor → state legislature · CAG and Parliament · Called the 'friend, philosopher and guide' of the Public Accounts Committee · GST Council · Article 279A · chaired by the Union Finance Minister · state finance ministers are members · GST Council voting · Decisions need 3/4 of weighted votes — Centre 1/3, all states together 2/3 · Holders as of 2025–26 (not quizzed) · CAG K. Asked: Article 76 (Attorney General) and Article 165 (Advocate General), who appoints them, their qualification (fit to be an SC / HC judge), no fixed term , the right to speak but not vote (Articles 88 and 177) and the first AG (M. C. Setalvad). · The Attorney General for India (Article 76) is the Union government's chief lawyer. The President appoints a person qualified to be a Supreme Court judge , and the AG holds office during the pleasure of the President — the Constitution fixes no term. The AG can speak in both Houses of Parliament and their committees but cannot vote (Article 88), and has the right of audience in every court in India. The first AG was M. C. Setalvad . Each state has an Advocate General (Article 165), appointed by the Governor from people qualified to be High Court judges , holding office at the Governor's pleasure. The 65th Amendment (1990) made it a multi-member commission, and the 89th Amendment (2003) split it: the NCSC (338) and the NCST (338A) have worked separately since 2004 . Each has a chairperson, a vice-chairperson and three members appointed by the President by warrant, and each reports to the President. The NCBC began as a statutory body in 1993 after the Indra Sawhney judgment and became constitutional through the 102nd Amendment (2018) — Article 338B. The Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities (350B, 7th Amendment, 1956) is appointed by the President and reports to him. bodies.x: Asked: the Act and year (NHRC 1993, CIC 2005 via RTI, CVC Act 2003, Lokpal Act 2013), the selection panels , the tenure (NHRC 3 yrs/70, CVC 4 yrs/65, Lokpal 5 yrs/70) and that all four are statutory , not constitutional. · In 1962 the Santhanam Committee looked at corruption; its advice gave India the CVC (by resolution, 1964 ) and the CBI (1963). The CVC became statutory with the CVC Act, 2003 : a Central Vigilance Commissioner and up to two Vigilance Commissioners, chosen by the PM, the Home Minister and the Leader of the Opposition, for 4 years or till 65 . The word Lokpal (coined by L. M. Singhvi, 1963) became law only with the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 ; the first Lokpal, Pinaki Chandra Ghose , came in 2019 . The Lokpal has a chairperson and up to 8 members , half of them judicial. The NHRC was set up on 12 October 1993 under the Protection of Human Rights Act ; its first chairperson was former CJI Ranganath Misra . Since the 2019 amendment its members serve 3 years or till 70 , and a retired Supreme Court judge (not only a former CJI) can head it. The Central Information Commission came from the RTI Act, 2005 : a Chief Information Commissioner and up to 10 Information Commissioners; the first CIC was Wajahat Habibullah . · The four watchdogs · NHRC · Chairperson + 5 full-time members (+ heads of national commissions as deemed members) · 3 years or 70 · CVC · Central Vigilance Commissioner + up to 2 Vigilance Commissioners · 4 years or 65 · reports to the President · Lokpal · Chairperson + up to 8 members (half judicial) · 5 years or 70 · can inquire into the PM, with safeguards · CIC · Chief Information Commissioner + up to 10 Information Commissioners · term set by the Centre since 2019 (3 years by the 2019 rules) · Removal (all four) · By the President, after a Supreme Court inquiry where misbehaviour is alleged · Lokayukta · The state-level Lokpal — set up by each state's own law; Maharashtra was first (1971) · Which Act? · Body · Created under · Note · National Human Rights Commission · Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 · State Human Rights Commissions come from the same Act. · Central Vigilance Commission · Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003 · It existed from 1964 by resolution; statutory since 2003. · Lokpal · Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 · Came into force in January 2014. · Central Information Commission · Right to Information Act, 2005 · State Information Commissions come from the same Act. · Central Bureau of Investigation (its powers) · Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946 · The CBI itself was set up by a resolution in 1963. · Milestones · Event · Year · Note · Santhanam Committee on corruption set up · 1962 · Led to the CVC and the CBI. · The word 'Lokpal' coined by L. Asked: the Act and year (NCW 1990, NCM 1992, SEBI 1992, TRAI 1997, IRDA 1999, Competition 2002, Disaster Management 2005, FSS 2006, NGT 2010, PFRDA 2013), headquarters (SEBI Mumbai, IRDAI Hyderabad) and what each regulates . · Parliament creates a statutory body whenever a field needs a referee. Markets got SEBI (set up 1988, statutory by the SEBI Act 1992, HQ Mumbai). Telecom got TRAI (1997), insurance IRDAI (1999, Hyderabad), competition the CCI (Competition Act 2002, replacing the MRTP Commission), food FSSAI (2006 Act) and pensions PFRDA (2013 Act, runs the NPS). The RBI itself is statutory too — RBI Act, 1934. Social justice got commissions: the National Commission for Women (Act 1990, set up 31 January 1992, first chairperson Jayanti Patnaik), the National Commission for Minorities (Act 1992) and the NCPCR for children (Act 2005). Nature got the National Green Tribunal (2010) — principal bench in New Delhi , zonal benches at Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata and Chennai — and disasters the NDMA (Disaster Management Act 2005), chaired by the Prime Minister . · Act → year · Act · Year · Note · National Commission for Women Act · 1990 · The NCW was set up on 31 January 1992. · National Commission for Minorities Act · 1992 · SEBI Act · 1992 · SEBI began in 1988 as a non-statutory body. · TRAI Act · 1997 · IRDA Act · 1999 · Followed the Malhotra Committee. · Competition Act (CCI) · 2002 · CCI replaced the MRTP Commission. · Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act (NCPCR) · 2005 · NCPCR set up in 2007. · Disaster Management Act (NDMA) · 2005 · Food Safety and Standards Act (FSSAI) · 2006 · FSSAI set up in 2008. · National Investigation Agency Act · 2008 · Passed after the 26/11 Mumbai attacks. · National Green Tribunal Act · 2010 · NGT set up on 18 October 2010. · PFRDA Act · 2013 · PFRDA had worked by government order since 2003. · Reserve Bank of India Act · 1934 · RBI began on 1 April 1935. · Headquarters · Body · Headquarters · Note · SEBI · Mumbai · Reserve Bank of India · Mumbai · IRDAI · Hyderabad · Moved from Delhi in 2001. · TRAI · New Delhi · Competition Commission of India · New Delhi · FSSAI · New Delhi · Under the Ministry of Health. · PFRDA · New Delhi · National Green Tribunal (principal bench) · New Delhi · Zonal benches: Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata, Chennai. · Who looks after what? bodies.x: The classic trap: “Which of these is NOT a constitutional / statutory body?” Remember the three executive bodies — NITI Aayog (2015), CBI (1963) and the National Development Council (1952) — and that the old Planning Commission (1950) was executive too. · Sort every body into three boxes. Constitutional : an Article creates it (EC, UPSC, FC, CAG, GST Council, NCSC/NCST/NCBC). Statutory : an Act of Parliament creates it (NHRC, CVC, Lokpal, CIC, NCW, NCM, NGT, NDMA, NIA, SEBI, the Zonal Councils). Executive (non-constitutional, non-statutory): a simple government resolution creates it. The Planning Commission was born by a Cabinet resolution on 15 March 1950 ; the NDC by another in 1952 . The CBI was set up by a Home Ministry resolution on 1 April 1963 — it uses powers from the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946 , but no Act created it. On 1 January 2015 the NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) replaced the Planning Commission, again by a Cabinet resolution. The PM chairs NITI Aayog; its first Vice-Chairperson was Arvind Panagariya . · Which kind of body? · Body · Kind · Basis · Election Commission · Constitutional body · Article 324. · Union Public Service Commission · Constitutional body · Article 315. · Finance Commission · Constitutional body · Article 280. · Comptroller and Auditor General · Constitutional body · Article 148. · GST Council · Constitutional body · Article 279A. · National Commission for Scheduled Castes · Constitutional body · Article 338. · National Commission for Backward Classes (today) · Constitutional body · Article 338B since 2018. · Inter-State Council · Constitutional body · Provided for in Article 263; set up by Presidential order in 1990. · National Human Rights Commission · Statutory body · Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. · Central Vigilance Commission · Statutory body · CVC Act, 2003. · Lokpal · Statutory body · Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013. · Central Information Commission · Statutory body · RTI Act, 2005. · National Commission for Women · Statutory body · NCW Act, 1990. · National Commission for Minorities · Statutory body · NCM Act, 1992. · National Green Tribunal · Statutory body · NGT Act, 2010. · National Disaster Management Authority · Statutory body · Disaster Management Act, 2005. · National Investigation Agency · Statutory body · NIA Act, 2008. · Zonal Councils · Statutory body · States Reorganisation Act, 1956. · NITI Aayog · Executive body (neither constitutional nor statutory) · Cabinet resolution, 1 January 2015. · Central Bureau of Investigation · Executive body (neither constitutional nor statutory) · Home Ministry resolution, 1963; powers from the DSPE Act, 1946. · National Development Council · Executive body (neither constitutional nor statutory) · Executive resolution, 1952. · Planning Commission (1950–2014) · Executive body (neither constitutional nor statutory) · Cabinet resolution, 1950. · When were they set up? bodies.x: Statement questions mix these up: “6 years or 65” (CEC, CAG, UPSC), 62 for State PSC, “removed like an SC judge” (CEC, CAG), “removed by the President after an SC inquiry” (UPSC, NHRC, CVC) and the number of members in each body. · Put the bodies side by side and three patterns appear. The posts that must be most independent — the CEC and the CAG — can be removed only like a Supreme Court judge , by a special majority in both Houses. The commission members — UPSC, State PSC, NHRC, CVC, Lokpal — are removed by the President , usually after a Supreme Court inquiry into misbehaviour. The law officers — AG and Advocate General — simply serve at the pleasure of the President or Governor. Terms follow a similar logic: 6 years for the constitutional heavyweights (with an age cap of 65 , or 62 for State PSCs), and shorter terms with a higher age cap ( 70 ) for the judge-led commissions — Lokpal 5 years, NHRC 3 years. · Tenure · Post · Term · Note · Chief Election Commissioner · 6 years or age 65 · Election Commissioners: the same. · Comptroller and Auditor General · 6 years or age 65 · UPSC chairman and members · 6 years or age 65 · State PSC chairman and members · 6 years or age 62 · Lokpal chairperson and members · 5 years or age 70 · NHRC chairperson and members · 3 years or age 70 · Cut from 5 years in 2019. · Central Vigilance Commissioner · 4 years or age 65 · Attorney General for India · No fixed term (President's pleasure) · Advocate General: the Governor's pleasure. · CBI Director · At least 2 years (extendable up to 5) · Extensions allowed since 2021. · How removed · Post · Removal · Note · Chief Election Commissioner · Like a Supreme Court judge (special majority in both Houses) · Comptroller and Auditor General · Like a Supreme Court judge (special majority in both Houses) · An Election Commissioner · By the President on the CEC's recommendation · UPSC member · By the President after a Supreme Court inquiry · For misbehaviour; music.x: Asked often: “Tabla / ghatam / shehnai belongs to which category?” — the four classes of the Natya Shastra : Tata (string), Sushira (wind), Avanaddha (skin drum) and Ghana (solid). · About two thousand years ago Bharata Muni wrote the Natya Shastra , a book on drama, dance and music. It sorts every instrument by what vibrates . If a string vibrates, it is tata vadya — sitar, veena, sarod, violin, even the santoor. If air vibrates, it is sushira vadya — flute, shehnai, nadaswaram. If a stretched skin vibrates, it is avanaddha vadya — tabla, mridangam, dholak. If the solid body itself rings when struck, it is ghana vadya — ghatam, manjira, jaltarang. The modern Western system (Hornbostel–Sachs) uses the same four ideas: chordophone, aerophone, membranophone, idiophone. · Instrument → class · Instrument · Class · Note · Sitar · Tata (string) · Plucked; music.t: String maestros: sitar, sarod, santoor, violin
music.x: Among the commonest GK questions in SSC: “X is associated with which instrument?” Ravi Shankar–sitar, Amjad Ali Khan–sarod, Shivkumar Sharma–santoor and L. Subramaniam–violin come up again and again. · In 1918 Allauddin Khan settled in the little town of Maihar (Madhya Pradesh). His pupils changed Indian music: his son Ali Akbar Khan (sarod), his daughter Annapurna Devi (surbahar) and Ravi Shankar (sitar), who later taught the Beatle George Harrison and made the sitar famous worldwide. Ravi Shankar's great rival on the sitar was Vilayat Khan . Other strings have their own heroes. Amjad Ali Khan is the 'Sarod Samrat'. Shivkumar Sharma took the Kashmiri santoor to concert halls. Ram Narayan made the sarangi a solo instrument. L. Subramaniam and N. Rajam play the violin , and Vishwa Mohan Bhatt invented the Mohan veena . · String maestros · Maestro · Instrument · Remember · Ravi Shankar · Sitar · Taught George Harrison; Bharat Ratna 1999. · Vilayat Khan · Sitar · Imdadkhani (Etawah) gharana. · Nikhil Banerjee · Sitar · Maihar gharana. · Anoushka Shankar · Sitar · Daughter of Ravi Shankar. · Shahid Parvez · Sitar · Amjad Ali Khan · Sarod · Called 'Sarod Samrat'; Senia-Bangash gharana. · Ali Akbar Khan · Sarod · Son of Allauddin Khan; Maihar gharana. · Allauddin Khan · Sarod · Founder of the Maihar gharana; guru of Ravi Shankar. · Buddhadev Dasgupta · Sarod · Shivkumar Sharma · Santoor · Brought the Kashmiri santoor to the classical stage. · Bhajan Sopori · Santoor · From Kashmir — the 'Saint of the Santoor'. · Rahul Sharma · Santoor · Son of Shivkumar Sharma. · Tarun Bhattacharya · Santoor · L. Carnatic names also appear: Palghat Mani Iyer (mridangam), Vikku Vinayakram (ghatam), Kadri Gopalnath (saxophone). · On the night of 15 August 1947 , Bismillah Khan of Varanasi played the shehnai at the Red Fort to welcome freedom. He took a wedding instrument to the concert stage and got the Bharat Ratna in 2001 . Pannalal Ghosh did the same for the bamboo flute , and Hariprasad Chaurasia made it loved everywhere. For rhythm, Alla Rakha and his son Zakir Hussain made the tabla a world instrument; Zakir won three Grammys in one night in 2024 and died in December 2024. music.x: Regular questions: the Carnatic trinity (Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar, Syama Sastri), the father of Carnatic music (Purandara Dasa), Tansen and his guru Swami Haridas , and Amir Khusrau (Tuti-e-Hind). · Indian classical music grew from one root but split into two branches. In the north, Hindustani music met Persian and Sufi ideas at the Sultanate and Mughal courts. Amir Khusrau (13th–14th century) created the qawwali and tarana ; Tansen , pupil of Swami Haridas , sang Dhrupad at Akbar's court. Much later V. N. Bhatkhande sorted the ragas into ten thaats , and V. D. Paluskar opened a music school for ordinary people in 1901 . In the south, Carnatic music stayed close to temples and devotion. Purandara Dasa is its father. Around 1800 three composers, all born in Tiruvarur , gave it its classic songs: Tyagaraja , Muthuswami Dikshitar and Syama Sastri — the Trinity . · Who's who of classical music · Known as / for · Person · Note · Father of Carnatic music · Purandara Dasa · 16th century, Vijayanagara; Asked as “Pandit Jasraj / Bhimsen Joshi / Kishori Amonkar belonged to which gharana?” Remember Kirana (Bhimsen Joshi, Gangubai Hangal), Mewati (Jasraj), Jaipur-Atrauli (Kishori Amonkar), Patiala (Bade Ghulam Ali Khan) and Gwalior (the oldest khayal gharana). · A gharana ('household') is a family or school of music. Its style passes from guru to shishya, often from father to son, and carries the name of a town. The Gwalior gharana is the oldest khayal school. The Kirana gharana, from Kairana in Uttar Pradesh, gave us Bhimsen Joshi and Gangubai Hangal . Kishori Amonkar sang in the Jaipur-Atrauli style founded by Alladiya Khan; Pandit Jasraj led the Mewati gharana; Bade Ghulam Ali Khan was the star of Patiala . Instrumentalists have gharanas too: Maihar (Ravi Shankar), Imdadkhani (Vilayat Khan), and the tabla gharanas of Punjab and Benares . · Musicians and their gharanas · Musician · Gharana · Note · Bhimsen Joshi · Kirana · Bharat Ratna; famous for 'Mile Sur Mera Tumhara'. · Gangubai Hangal · Kirana · From Hubballi-Dharwad, Karnataka. · Abdul Karim Khan · Kirana · Founder of the Kirana gharana. · Prabha Atre · Kirana · Kishori Amonkar · Jaipur-Atrauli · Daughter of Mogubai Kurdikar. · Alladiya Khan · Jaipur-Atrauli · Founder of the Jaipur-Atrauli gharana. · Mallikarjun Mansur · Jaipur-Atrauli · Pandit Jasraj · Mewati · A minor planet is named after him. · Bade Ghulam Ali Khan · Patiala · Faiyaz Khan · Agra · Rashid Khan · Rampur-Sahaswan · Amir Khan · Indore · Founder of the Indore gharana. · Haddu Khan and Hassu Khan · Gwalior · Gwalior is the oldest khayal gharana. · Girija Devi · Benares · 'Queen of thumri'. · Ravi Shankar, Ali Akbar Khan, Annapurna Devi · Maihar · All pupils of Allauddin Khan. · Vilayat Khan · Imdadkhani (Etawah) · Alla Rakha (tabla) · Punjab · The Dagar family (Dhrupad) · Dagar vani · “Bhim and Ganga live in Kirana” (Bhimsen Joshi, Gangubai Hangal). “Jas–Mew” : Jasraj–Mewati. “Kishori goes to Jaipur” . · The Kirana gharana is named after Kairana in UP, though its stars came from Karnataka and Maharashtra. music.t: Ragas, their times, and musical terms
music.h: राग, उनका समय और संगीत शब्दावली
music.x: Asked: the time or season of a raga (Bhairav — morning, Yaman — evening, Malhar — rain, Deepak — fire), and the meaning of terms — raga, tala, alap, thaat, melakarta, shruti — and of forms like Dhrupad, khayal, thumri, qawwali . · A raga is not just a tune; it is a set of notes with rules and a mood. Hindustani tradition gives each raga a time of day : Bhairav greets the dawn, Bhimpalasi fills the afternoon, Marwa belongs to sunset, Yaman to the evening and Darbari Kanada to late night. Some belong to seasons : Malhar to the monsoon, Basant to spring. Legends grew around them: Tansen is said to have lit lamps by singing Raga Deepak and brought rain with Megh Malhar . Rhythm is counted in a tala — a cycle of beats whose first beat is sam . A recital opens slowly with the alap and ends fast with the jhala . · Ragas and their time · Raga · Time / season · Note · Bhairav · Early morning (dawn) · Sung at sunrise. · Ahir Bhairav · Early morning (dawn) · Todi · Late morning · Bhimpalasi · Afternoon · Multani · Afternoon · Marwa · Sunset (dusk) · Puriya Dhanashri · Sunset (dusk) · Yaman · Evening (early night) · One of the first ragas a student learns. · Bhupali · Evening (early night) · Darbari Kanada · Late night · Credited to Tansen. · Malkauns · Late night · Miyan ki Malhar · Monsoon (rain) · Credited to Tansen; Asked: the style of a singer (Hindustani, Carnatic, ghazal, folk), their nicknames ('Nightingale of India', 'Mallika-e-Ghazal') and their firsts — M. S. Subbulakshmi first musician with the Bharat Ratna, first Indian musician to sing at the UN (1966). · Indian singing has many voices. In the Hindustani world, Bhimsen Joshi and Gangubai Hangal carried the Kirana style, Kishori Amonkar the Jaipur-Atrauli style and Pandit Jasraj the Mewati style. In the south, M. S. Subbulakshmi sang at the United Nations in 1966 , won the Ramon Magsaysay Award (1974) and became the first musician to get the Bharat Ratna (1998) . Beyond classical music, Begum Akhtar became the queen of ghazal , Lata Mangeshkar sang for Indian films for seven decades, Bhupen Hazarika carried Assamese folk songs to the world, and Teejan Bai sings the Mahabharata in the Pandavani style of Chhattisgarh. · Singers and their style · Singer · Style · Remember · Bhimsen Joshi · Hindustani classical · Kirana gharana; Bharat Ratna (announced 2008, given 2009). · Kishori Amonkar · Hindustani classical · Jaipur-Atrauli gharana. · Pandit Jasraj · Hindustani classical · Mewati gharana. · Gangubai Hangal · Hindustani classical · Kirana gharana. · Kumar Gandharva · Hindustani classical · Lived in Dewas, MP; mixed folk tunes into classical music. · Girija Devi · Hindustani classical · 'Queen of thumri', Benares gharana. · Bade Ghulam Ali Khan · Hindustani classical · Patiala gharana. · M. Asked: “Pena / Ravanahatha / Tumbi / Pepa is a folk instrument of which state?” Learn the pairs — Pena–Manipur, Ravanahatha–Rajasthan, Tumbi–Punjab, Pepa–Assam, Chenda–Kerala, Thavil–Tamil Nadu. · Every region has its own sound. In the Thar desert of Rajasthan , Manganiyar singers play the kamaicha and the ancient ravanahatha , with the twang of the morchang . In Punjab , the one-string tumbi and the jingling chimta drive bhangra songs. In Assam , the buffalo-horn pepa and bamboo gogona announce Bihu; in Manipur , the bowed pena and the pung drum lead the dance. In Kerala , temple festivals thunder with the chenda , edakka and timila ; Tamil Nadu temples ring with the nadaswaram and thavil . Goa made the clay-pot ghumot its heritage instrument, and the Bauls of Bengal wander with their ektara . · Folk instruments and their states · Instrument · State / UT · Remember · Ravanahatha · Rajasthan · An ancient bowed fiddle, linked in legend with Ravana. · Kamaicha · Rajasthan · Bowed; played by the Manganiyars of the Thar. · Morchang · Rajasthan · Metal jaw harp. · Bhapang · Rajasthan · Plucked drum-string of the Mewat (Alwar) region. · Tumbi · Punjab · One-string instrument of bhangra songs. · Chimta · Punjab · Long tongs with jingles. · Pena · Manipur · A one-string bowed fiddle. · Pung · Manipur · Drum played in the Pung Cholom dance. · Chenda · Kerala · Played in temple festivals and Kathakali. · Edakka · Kerala · Hourglass drum of temple music. · Mizhavu · Kerala · Big copper drum of Koodiyattam. · Timila · Kerala · Hourglass drum of the Panchavadyam. · Thavil · Tamil Nadu · Barrel drum played with the nadaswaram. · Nadaswaram · Tamil Nadu · Temple wind instrument. · Yazh · Tamil Nadu · Ancient Tamil harp of the Sangam age. · Pepa · Assam · Buffalo-horn pipe of Bihu. · Gogona · Assam · Bamboo jaw harp of Bihu. · Rabab · Jammu and Kashmir · Plucked; used in Kashmiri folk and Sufiana music. · Tumbaknari · Jammu and Kashmir · Clay goblet drum. · Hudka · Uttarakhand · Hourglass drum of Jagar songs. · Dhol-Damau · Uttarakhand · Pair of drums of the Garhwal and Kumaon hills. · Tuntuna · Maharashtra · One-string instrument of devotional and folk singers. · Sundari · Maharashtra · A small shehnai-like pipe from Solapur. · Ghumot · Goa · Earthen pot drum; declared Goa's heritage instrument. · Mardala · Odisha · Barrel drum of Odissi music and dance. · Ektara (Baul singers) · West Bengal · Baul singers carry it. · “Pena–Pung–Manipur” (three Ps and an M). “Pepa Plays at Bihu” — Assam. “Tumbi Thumps in Punjab” . “Ravana's fiddle in Rajasthan” . · The ravanahatha is named after Ravana but is a Rajasthani folk fiddle, not from Sri Lanka in the exam sense. classical.t: Texts and terms of classical dance
classical.h: शास्त्रीय नृत्य के ग्रंथ और शब्द
classical.x: Asked again and again: who wrote the Natya Shastra (Bharata Muni), the Abhinaya Darpana (Nandikeshvara), the meaning of mudra , nritta / nritya / natya , and tandava vs lasya . · Every Indian classical dance traces itself to one book: the Natya Shastra of Bharata Muni , written roughly 2,000 years ago. It covers drama, dance and music, and was so respected it was called the fifth Veda . Later, Nandikeshvara wrote the Abhinaya Darpana ('mirror of gesture'), still the handbook of hand gestures for Bharatanatyam dancers. These texts split dance into three: nritta (pure rhythm), nritya (expression with meaning) and natya (drama). Expression — abhinaya — comes through the body, voice, costume and inner feeling, and its goal is rasa , the mood the audience tastes. Dance itself has two moods: Shiva's vigorous tandava and Parvati's graceful lasya . · Classical dance in numbers (as of 2026) · Recognised by the Sangeet Natak Akademi · 8 — Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kathakali, Kuchipudi, Odissi, Manipuri, Mohiniyattam, Sattriya · Ministry of Culture's list · 9 — the eight plus Chhau · Newest addition (SNA) · Sattriya, in 2000 · Kinds of abhinaya · 4 — angika, vachika, aharya, sattvika · Rasas · 8 in the Natya Shastra; two-hand gestures are samyukta. · Abhinaya · The art of expression — conveying meaning to the audience · Natya Shastra gives four kinds: angika, vachika, aharya and sattvika. · Angika abhinaya · Expression through the body, limbs and gestures · Vachika abhinaya · Expression through speech, song and recitation · Aharya abhinaya · Expression through costume, make-up and jewellery · Kathakali's make-up is the best-known aharya. · Sattvika abhinaya · Expression of inner feelings — tears, trembling, sweat · Rasa · The emotional flavour the audience enjoys · The Natya Shastra lists eight; shanta (peace) was added later as the ninth. · Bhava · The emotion or mood shown by the performer · Bhava produces rasa. · Bols · Spoken rhythmic syllables recited before or during footwork · Typical of Kathak. · Texts and their authors · Text · Author · Note · Natya Shastra · Bharata Muni · The oldest Indian text on drama, dance and music; called the 'fifth Veda'. · Abhinaya Darpana · Nandikeshvara · 'The Mirror of Gesture' — the main handbook of mudras for Bharatanatyam. · Sangita Ratnakara · Sarangadeva · 13th-century text on music and dance. · Gita Govinda · Jayadeva · 12th-century poem of Radha and Krishna; T andava = T hunder (Shiva); L asya = L ovely (Parvati). · The Natya Shastra is by Bharata , not Bharavi or Bhasa. The Abhinaya Darpana is by Nandikeshvara , not Bharata. A mudra is a hand gesture; bhava is the emotion shown and rasa the mood felt. · The Natya Shastra by Bharata Muni is the root text of Indian dance, drama and music — the 'fifth Veda'. · The Abhinaya Darpana by Nandikeshvara is the main handbook of mudras. · Nritta is pure dance, nritya is expressive dance, natya is dance-drama. · Tandava is vigorous (Shiva); lasya is graceful (Parvati). · The Sangeet Natak Akademi recognises 8 classical dances; the Ministry of Culture lists 9 with Chhau.

classical.t: The eight classical dances and their states
classical.h: आठ शास्त्रीय नृत्य और उनके राज्य
classical.x: The single commonest question: “X is a classical dance of which state?” Also asked: which dance is the newest (Sattriya, 2000), which state has two (Kerala), and which dance grew out of Sadir or the Gotipua boys. · Picture a map of India with eight lights. In the south, Tamil Nadu gives Bharatanatyam , Andhra Pradesh gives Kuchipudi , and Kerala gives two — the dance-drama Kathakali and the gentle Mohiniyattam . In the north, Kathak of Uttar Pradesh is the only classical dance, born from storytellers and polished in the Mughal and Lucknow courts. In the east, Odissi (Odisha) is carved on the walls of Konark, Manipuri (Manipur) dances Krishna's Ras Lila, and Sattriya (Assam), created by the saint Sankaradeva in the 15th century, became the eighth in 2000 . SSC loves a feature → dance question: tribhanga (Odissi), tarangam on a brass plate (Kuchipudi), chakkars (Kathak), green make-up (Kathakali), Ras Lila (Manipuri), monasteries of Majuli (Sattriya). · Each dance has a signature you can spot in a second. An Odissi dancer stands in the tribhanga , bent in three places like a temple statue. A Bharatanatyam dancer sinks into araimandi , knees out. A Kuchipudi dancer balances on the rim of a brass plate . A Kathak dancer whirls in chakkars while ankle bells ring out the tatkar . Kerala's Kathakali actors wear green faces and giant crowns, and tell epics all night to the chenda drum. Mohiniyattam sways like palm trees in a white-and-gold saree. Manipuri dancers wear no ankle bells and a stiff round skirt, and Sattriya was danced for centuries only by monks in Assam's sattras. · Music behind each dance · Carnatic music · Bharatanatyam, Kuchipudi, Mohiniyattam · Sopana style (Kerala) · Kathakali — with chenda, maddalam, chengila and elathalam · Hindustani music · Kathak — tabla, pakhawaj, sarangi · Odissi music · Odissi — mardala drum; classical.h: दक्षिण के शास्त्रीय नृत्यों के नर्तक
classical.x: Every SSC shift seems to have one: “X is an exponent of which dance?” The south's big names — Rukmini Devi Arundale and Padma Subrahmanyam (Bharatanatyam), Vempati Chinna Satyam and Raja–Radha Reddy (Kuchipudi), Kalamandalam Kalyanikutty Amma (Mohiniyattam). · In the 1930s Sadir , the dance of temple women, was looked down on. Rukmini Devi Arundale , from a respected Brahmin family, learned it, staged it in 1935 and founded Kalakshetra in Chennai in 1936 — Bharatanatyam became respectable across India. T. Balasaraswati , from the hereditary tradition, kept its older soul alive. Later stars include Padma Subrahmanyam , Alarmel Valli , Leela Samson and the actress Vyjayanthimala . In Andhra, Vempati Chinna Satyam turned village Kuchipudi into a solo concert art, and Raja and Radha Reddy took it abroad. In Kerala, the poet Vallathol 's Kalamandalam trained Kathakali greats like Kalamandalam Krishnan Nair , Ramankutty Nair and Gopi , and Kalyanikutty Amma rebuilt Mohiniyattam. · Dancer ↔ dance (south) · Dancer · Dance · Note · Rukmini Devi Arundale · Bharatanatyam · Founded Kalakshetra (1936); first woman nominated to the Rajya Sabha (1952). · T. classical.x: The most-asked names in the whole topic: Birju Maharaj and Sitara Devi (Kathak), Kelucharan Mohapatra (Odissi), Guru Bipin Singh (Manipuri). Sattriya names like Jatin Goswami now appear often too. · Pandit Birju Maharaj was born into the Lucknow Kathak family of Kalka-Bindadin; his uncles Shambhu and Lachhu Maharaj were masters too. He choreographed for films like Devdas and Bajirao Mastani and won the Padma Vibhushan in 1986. Sitara Devi danced with such energy that Tagore called her 'Nritya Samragini' . Later came Kumudini Lakhia , Shovana Narayan and Uma Sharma . In Odisha, Kelucharan Mohapatra , a former Gotipua boy, rebuilt Odissi in the 1950s with Pankaj Charan Das and Deba Prasad Das ; his students include Sanjukta Panigrahi , Kumkum Mohanty and Protima Bedi . Guru Bipin Singh shaped modern Manipuri with the Jhaveri sisters , and Assam's Jatin Goswami carried Sattriya out of the monasteries. · Dancer ↔ dance (north and east) · Dancer · Dance · Note · Pandit Birju Maharaj · Kathak · Lucknow (Kalka-Bindadin) gharana; classical.t: Gurus, schools and dancers of many styles
classical.x: Asked often: Kalakshetra (Chennai, Rukmini Devi), Kerala Kalamandalam (Vallathol), Darpana (Mrinalini Sarabhai, Ahmedabad), Nrityagram (Protima Bedi). Also the dancers known for two styles — Sonal Mansingh, Yamini Krishnamurthy, Mallika Sarabhai. · Modern classical dance was saved by schools. The poet Vallathol Narayana Menon founded Kerala Kalamandalam in 1930 to rescue Kathakali and Mohiniyattam. Rukmini Devi Arundale started Kalakshetra in Chennai in 1936 . Mrinalini Sarabhai opened Darpana in Ahmedabad in 1949, and the government's Sangeet Natak Akademi (1952) set up the Kathak Kendra in Delhi and the Manipuri Dance Academy in Imphal. Protima Bedi built Nrityagram , a dance village near Bengaluru, in 1990. Some stars mastered more than one style: Sonal Mansingh (Bharatanatyam and Odissi), Yamini Krishnamurthy (Bharatanatyam and Kuchipudi), Mallika Sarabhai (Kuchipudi and Bharatanatyam), and Mrinalini Sarabhai (Bharatanatyam and Kathakali). Uday Shankar blended Indian styles into a new creative dance and is called the father of modern Indian dance. · Dancers of more than one style · Sonal Mansingh · Bharatanatyam and Odissi — Padma Vibhushan 2003; Asked as “The X Dance Festival is held in which state?” The big four: Khajuraho (MP), Konark (Odisha), Mamallapuram (Tamil Nadu), Elephanta (Maharashtra). Modhera (Gujarat) is the usual trap. · India loves to set its classical dancers against old stone. Every February the Khajuraho Dance Festival (since 1975) lights up the Chandela temples of Madhya Pradesh . In early December, the Konark Dance Festival fills the open-air stage beside Odisha's Sun Temple. In Tamil Nadu , Mamallapuram dancers perform before the giant rock carving of Arjuna's Penance, and at Chidambaram the Natyanjali festival honours Nataraja on Maha Shivaratri. On the west coast, the Elephanta Festival is held near Mumbai's cave temples, and Gujarat holds the Modhera Dance Festival at its own Sun Temple each January. Karnataka has Pattadakal and Hampi Utsav ; Kerala has Nishagandhi in Thiruvananthapuram. · Festival ↔ state · Festival · State · Note · Khajuraho Dance Festival · Madhya Pradesh · Every February since 1975, against the Chandela temples. · Konark Dance Festival · Odisha · 1–5 December, in the open-air theatre by the Sun Temple. · Mukteswar Dance Festival · Odisha · Odissi at the Mukteswar temple, Bhubaneswar (January). · Mamallapuram Dance Festival · Tamil Nadu · December–January, with Arjuna's Penance as the backdrop. · Natyanjali Festival · Tamil Nadu · At the Nataraja temple, Chidambaram, around Maha Shivaratri. · Elephanta Festival · Maharashtra · February, at the Elephanta Caves near Mumbai. · Ellora–Ajanta Festival · Maharashtra · Near Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (Aurangabad). · Modhera Dance Festival (Uttarardh Mahotsav) · Gujarat · January, at the Sun Temple of Modhera. · Nishagandhi Dance Festival · Kerala · January, Thiruvananthapuram. · Pattadakal Dance Festival · Karnataka · At the Chalukya temples of Pattadakal. · Hampi Utsav · Karnataka · Also called the Vijaya Utsav. · Rajgir Mahotsav · Bihar · Bhoramdeo Mahotsav · Chhattisgarh · Taj Mahotsav · Uttar Pradesh · February, in Agra — arts, crafts and dance. · Sangai Festival · Manipur · November — named after the state animal, the sangai deer. · Two Sun Temples, two festivals : Konark (Odisha, December) and Modhera (Gujarat, January). “K for Khajuraho, K for Kendra (central) — Madhya Pradesh.” · Mamallapuram is in Tamil Nadu , not Kerala or Karnataka. Questions ask which dancer got the Padma Vibhushan in a year (Birju Maharaj 1986, Sonal Mansingh 2003, Yamini Krishnamurthy 2016, Padma Subrahmanyam 2024, Kumudini Lakhia 2025) and who gives the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award and the Kalidas Samman. · The Sangeet Natak Akademi , India's national academy for music, dance and drama, was set up in 1952 and works under the Ministry of Culture from Rabindra Bhavan, New Delhi. It gives the yearly Akademi Award (Puraskar), its highest honour the Fellowship (Akademi Ratna), and since 2006 the Ustad Bismillah Khan Yuva Puraskar for artists up to 40. The Padma awards also honour dancers. T. Balasaraswati got the Padma Vibhushan in 1977, Birju Maharaj in 1986, Kelucharan Mohapatra in 2000 and Sonal Mansingh in 2003. More recently came Yamini Krishnamurthy (2016), Padma Subrahmanyam and Vyjayanthimala (2024) and Kumudini Lakhia (2025). Madhya Pradesh's Kalidas Samman (since 1980) is another top arts prize. · Sangeet Natak Akademi at a glance · Set up · 1952 (by a government resolution); inaugurated in January 1953 · Headquarters · Rabindra Bhavan, New Delhi · Under · Ministry of Culture · First chairman · Justice P. classical.t: Classical vs folk and tribal dances
classical.h: शास्त्रीय बनाम लोक और जनजातीय नृत्य
classical.x: A favourite trick question: “Which of these is NOT a classical dance?” — Bihu, Yakshagana, Garba, Lavani, Kalbelia are folk. Also: Yakshagana vs Kathakali, Bihu vs Sattriya, Gotipua vs Odissi. · A classical dance follows a written grammar going back to the Natya Shastra , needs years of training under a guru, and is recognised by the Sangeet Natak Akademi . A folk dance belongs to a community — danced at harvests, weddings and festivals by ordinary people, with no textbook. A tribal dance belongs to a tribe's own life and rituals. Many pairs share a state and fool students. Assam has classical Sattriya and folk Bihu . Kerala's Kathakali is classical, but Theyyam is ritual and Karnataka's look-alike Yakshagana is folk theatre. Odisha's boy dancers, the Gotipua , are folk — yet they fed into classical Odissi . Garba, Bhangra, Lavani and Ghoomar are all folk. HQs: Redmond, Cupertino, Mountain View, Seattle . · Many of the world's biggest companies began in garages and dorm rooms. Bill Gates and Paul Allen started Microsoft in 1975; Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak built the first Apple computer in 1976. Two Stanford students, Larry Page and Sergey Brin , launched Google in 1998, while Jeff Bezos sold books online as Amazon from 1994. Mark Zuckerberg started Facebook in his Harvard room in 2004. Indians are in this story too: Sabeer Bhatia co-founded Hotmail (1996) and Vinod Khosla co-founded Sun Microsystems (1982). Raja Ram Mohan Roy founded the Brahmo Sabha in 1828 (later the Brahmo Samaj) and also ran newspapers — Sambad Kaumudi in Bengali and Mirat-ul-Akhbar in Persian. In western India came the Prarthana Samaj (1867), Jyotirao Phule 's Satyashodhak Samaj (1873) and Dayananda Saraswati 's Arya Samaj (1875, Bombay). Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission in 1897 and Gokhale the Servants of India Society in 1905. Politics grew out of these: A. O. Hume helped found the Congress in 1885, the Muslim League came in 1906 at Dhaka, and Tilak and Annie Besant began Home Rule Leagues in 1916. inventions.x: SSC asks “Who invented X?” almost every shift. The favourites: steam engine (Watt) , aeroplane (Wright brothers, 1903) , diesel engine (Rudolf Diesel) , printing press (Gutenberg) , dynamite (Nobel) , sewing machine (Elias Howe) , pneumatic tyre (Dunlop) and jet engine (Frank Whittle) . · The modern world began with power. In 1769 James Watt made the steam engine efficient; soon George Stephenson put it on rails and Robert Fulton on a boat. Then came engines that burn fuel inside: Nikolaus Otto 's four-stroke engine (1876), Karl Benz 's car (1886) and Rudolf Diesel 's engine (1892). Dunlop 's air-filled tyre made rides smooth. In 1903 the Wright brothers flew, and Frank Whittle 's jet engine and Igor Sikorsky 's helicopter followed. Small things changed daily life too. Gutenberg printed books with movable type (about 1440). Elias Howe made the sewing machine, Biro the ballpoint pen, Walter Hunt the safety pin, Gillette the safety razor. Alfred Nobel invented dynamite — and left his fortune for the Nobel Prizes. · Machines and transport · Invention · Inventor · Note · steam engine (with a separate condenser) · James Watt · 1769 patent. Thomas Newcomen built an earlier steam engine (1712); Watt made it efficient. The unit of power, the watt, is named after him. · railway steam locomotive 'Rocket' · George Stephenson · 1829, with his son Robert. Called the 'Father of Railways'. (Richard Trevithick ran an earlier locomotive in 1804.) · aeroplane · Wright brothers · Orville and Wilbur Wright made the first powered, controlled flight on 17 December 1903 at Kitty Hawk, USA. · petrol motor car · Karl Benz · Patented in 1886 in Germany. · diesel engine · Rudolf Diesel · Patented in 1892 (Germany); ignites fuel by compression, with no spark plug. · four-stroke petrol engine · Nikolaus Otto · 1876, Germany — the 'Otto cycle'. · motorcycle · Gottlieb Daimler · 1885, with Wilhelm Maybach. · pedal bicycle · Kirkpatrick Macmillan · Around 1839, Scotland. Very common: telephone (Bell) , radio (Marconi) , television (Baird) , electric bulb and phonograph (Edison) , battery (Volta) , WWW (Tim Berners-Lee) , father of the computer (Babbage) . Indian names asked often: Sabeer Bhatia (Hotmail), Ajay Bhatt (USB), Vinod Dham (Pentium), N. S. Kapany (fibre optics). · In 1800 Volta stacked metal discs to make the first battery; in 1831 Faraday turned motion into electricity with a dynamo. Wires soon carried words: Morse 's telegraph (1844), Bell 's telephone (1876). Edison gave us the phonograph (1877) and a long-lasting bulb (1879). Marconi sent signals with no wires at all, and Baird showed television in 1926. The transistor (1947) and the chip (1958) made electronics small. Babbage had dreamed of a computer a century earlier. Cerf and Kahn wrote TCP/IP (1974), Ray Tomlinson sent the first network email with '@' (1971), and Tim Berners-Lee built the World Wide Web (1989). Indians in the story: Sabeer Bhatia (Hotmail), Ajay Bhatt (USB) and Vinod Dham (Pentium). · Communication, electricity and computing · Invention · Inventor · Note · telephone · Alexander Graham Bell · Patented in 1876, USA. · electric telegraph and its code · Samuel Morse · First long-distance message in 1844: 'What hath God wrought'. · radio (wireless telegraphy) · Guglielmo Marconi · 1895–96, Italy; Nobel Prize 1909.
