inventions.x: Top questions: who discovered the electron (Thomson) , proton/nucleus (Rutherford) , neutron (Chadwick) , X-rays (Röntgen) , radioactivity (Becquerel) , radium (the Curies) ; who made the periodic table (Mendeleev) ; who found oxygen (Priestley) and hydrogen (Cavendish) . · In 1895 Röntgen saw a screen glow across his lab — X-rays . A year later Becquerel found uranium giving off rays by itself ( radioactivity ), and the Curies found radium and polonium. Then the atom was opened up: Thomson found the electron (1897), Rutherford the nucleus (1911) and the proton, Chadwick the neutron (1932). Planck and Einstein rebuilt physics with quantum theory and relativity. Chemistry had its own hunters. Cavendish found hydrogen, Daniel Rutherford nitrogen, Priestley oxygen. Dalton said all matter is atoms, and Mendeleev arranged the elements in a table in 1869. Looking up, Copernicus put the Sun at the centre, Galileo saw Jupiter's moons and Hubble found the universe is expanding. · Physics and space · Discovery · Discovered by · Note · electron · J. J. inventions.t: Discoveries in biology: cells, blood and genes
inventions.h: जीव विज्ञान की खोजें: कोशिका, रक्त और जीन
inventions.x: Asked again and again: cell (Robert Hooke, 1665) , nucleus (Robert Brown) , blood groups (Landsteiner) , blood circulation (Harvey) , DNA double helix (Watson and Crick) , laws of inheritance (Mendel) and evolution (Darwin) . · In 1665 Robert Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork and saw tiny boxes — he called them cells . Leeuwenhoek saw living bacteria in a drop of water, Robert Brown found the nucleus, and Schleiden and Schwann said every living thing is made of cells. Earlier, William Harvey had shown that the heart pumps blood round the body. In 1900–01 Karl Landsteiner found the A, B and O blood groups, which made safe transfusions possible. How do children resemble parents? Gregor Mendel , a monk, found the answer with pea plants (1866). Darwin explained how species change by natural selection (1859). In 1953 Watson and Crick , using Rosalind Franklin 's X-ray photographs, showed DNA is a double helix . · Discoveries in biology · Discovery · Discovered by · Note · cell (in cork) · Robert Hooke · 1665, in his book Micrographia. · cell nucleus · Robert Brown · 1831, in orchid cells. · cell theory · Schleiden and Schwann · 1838–39: all living things are made of cells. · bacteria and protozoa (first seen) · Antonie van Leeuwenhoek · 1670s, with his own microscopes. · circulation of blood · William Harvey · 1628, England. · ABO blood groups · Karl Landsteiner · 1900–01; Favourites: smallpox vaccine (Jenner) , rabies vaccine (Pasteur) , polio vaccines (Salk, Sabin) , penicillin (Fleming, 1928) , insulin (Banting and Best) , TB bacterium (Koch) , malaria in mosquitoes (Ronald Ross) — and which vitamin's lack causes which disease . · In 1796 Edward Jenner noticed milkmaids who caught cowpox never got smallpox — the first vaccine . Louis Pasteur proved germs cause disease and made the rabies vaccine (1885); Robert Koch found the germs of TB and cholera. In Secunderabad, Ronald Ross showed mosquitoes carry malaria (1897). In 1928 Alexander Fleming saw mould killing bacteria on a dish — penicillin , the first antibiotic. Banting and Best found insulin (1921), saving diabetics. Casimir Funk gave the name 'vitamine' (1912) to food factors whose lack causes disease: scurvy (C), rickets (D), night blindness (A), beriberi (B1). Medicine's firsts followed — a heart transplant (1967), a test-tube baby (1978), a cloned sheep (1996). · Vaccines, medicines and germs · Discovery · Discovered by · Note · smallpox vaccine · Edward Jenner · 1796, using cowpox — the first vaccine. · rabies vaccine · Louis Pasteur · 1885. inventions.t: Laws and principles, and who gave them
inventions.h: नियम और सिद्धांत तथा उनके प्रतिपादक
inventions.x: SSC often describes a law and asks who gave it: Newton (motion, gravitation), Archimedes (buoyancy), Pascal (fluid pressure), Boyle and Charles (gases), Ohm (current), Faraday (induction), Bernoulli (flow), Heisenberg (uncertainty). · Many laws came from one sharp idea. Archimedes saw the water rise in his bath and shouted 'Eureka!' — buoyancy. Galileo said all bodies fall alike; Kepler showed planets move in ellipses; Newton joined it all with three laws of motion and gravity (1687). Pascal explained hydraulic lifts, Boyle and Charles the behaviour of gases, and Bernoulli why a fast flow means low pressure. Electricity got its rules from Coulomb (force between charges), Ohm (V = IR), Faraday (induction) and Lenz . In the 20th century, Einstein gave E = mc², Heisenberg the uncertainty principle and Pauli the exclusion principle. · Laws and principles · Law / principle · Given by · Note · Three laws of motion and universal gravitation · Isaac Newton · Principia, 1687. · Planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus · Johannes Kepler · Three laws, 1609–1619. · A body in a fluid loses weight equal to the Two questions come every year: “X is the SI unit of what?” and “What is the SI unit of Y?” . Watch the electrical and magnetic ones — tesla, weber, henry, farad, siemens — and the radiation ones — becquerel, gray, sievert . · Science honours its heroes by naming units after them. Newton gives force, Joule energy, Watt power and Pascal pressure. Electricity is a hall of fame: Ampère (current), Volta (voltage), Ohm (resistance), Coulomb (charge), Faraday (the farad, capacitance), Henry (inductance) and Siemens (conductance). Magnetism has Tesla and Weber ; waves have Hertz ; temperature has Kelvin . Radiation has three: Becquerel (how radioactive a source is), Gray (dose absorbed) and Sievert (effect on the body). Note: unit names are written in small letters (newton), symbols in capitals (N). · SI units named after scientists · Unit · Measures · Named after · newton · Force · Isaac Newton. 1 N = 1 kg·m/s². · joule · Work or energy · James Prescott Joule. · watt · Power · James Watt. 1 W = 1 joule per second. · pascal · Pressure · Blaise Pascal. 1 Pa = 1 N/m². · ampere · Electric current · André-Marie Ampère — one of the seven SI base units. · volt · Potential difference · Alessandro Volta. · ohm · Electrical resistance · Georg Ohm; symbol Ω. · coulomb · Electric charge · Charles-Augustin de Coulomb. · hertz · Frequency · Heinrich Hertz; 1 Hz = one cycle per second. · kelvin · Thermodynamic temperature · Lord Kelvin — an SI base unit; 0 K is absolute zero (−273.15 °C). · tesla · Magnetic flux density · Nikola Tesla. · weber · Magnetic flux · Wilhelm Weber. · henry · Inductance · Joseph Henry. · farad · Capacitance · Michael Faraday. · siemens · Electrical conductance · Werner von Siemens — the old name was 'mho'. · becquerel · Radioactivity (activity) · Henri Becquerel. · gray · Absorbed dose of radiation · Louis Harold Gray. · sievert · Equivalent dose of radiation · Rolf Sievert. · The seven SI base units · Length · metre (m) · Mass · kilogram (kg) · Time · second (s) · Electric current · ampere (A) · Temperature · kelvin (K) · Amount of substance · mole (mol) · Luminous intensity · candela (cd) · Magnetism pair — “Weber is the Whole flux, Tesla is per square metre” (1 T = 1 Wb/m²). inventions.t: Scientific instruments and what they measure
inventions.x: One of the commonest GK questions: “A hygrometer measures …?” Learn the pairs: barometer–air pressure , hygrometer–humidity , seismograph–earthquakes , anemometer–wind speed , lactometer–milk , hydrometer–density of liquids , sphygmomanometer–blood pressure , fathometer–sea depth . · Think of a weather station: a barometer reads air pressure, a hygrometer humidity, an anemometer wind speed and a rain gauge rainfall. On a ship, a fathometer sends sound down to find the depth, and a sextant finds the Sun's angle. In a plane, the altimeter shows height; in a car, the speedometer shows speed and the odometer distance. A doctor uses a stethoscope , a sphygmomanometer for blood pressure and an audiometer for hearing. A dairy checks milk with a lactometer ; a steel plant reads furnace heat with a pyrometer ; a seismic station records quakes on a seismograph . In a lab, the ammeter reads current and the voltmeter voltage. · Instruments and what they measure · Instrument · Measures · Note · Barometer · Atmospheric pressure · A sudden fall warns of a storm. · Hygrometer · Relative humidity · Seismograph · Earthquake waves · Its record is a seismogram. · Anemometer · Wind speed · Ammeter · Electric current · Connected in series. · Voltmeter · Potential difference · Connected in parallel. · Galvanometer · Presence and direction of a small current · Lactometer · Purity (density) of milk · Hydrometer · Relative density of liquids · Odometer · Distance travelled by a vehicle · Speedometer · Speed of a vehicle · Altimeter · Height above sea level · Used in aircraft. · Manometer · Pressure of gases · Pyrometer · Very high temperatures · For furnaces — even from a distance. · Sphygmomanometer · Blood pressure · Tachometer · Rotational speed (rpm) of an engine · Audiometer · Sharpness of hearing · Fathometer (echo sounder) · Depth of the sea · Uses sound echoes (sonar). · Rain gauge (udometer) · Rainfall · Calorimeter · Quantity of heat · Geiger counter · Radioactive radiation · Sextant · Angle of the Sun or a star above the horizon · Used in navigation. · Crescograph · Growth of plants · Invented by J. Asked in nearly every exam season: Raman effect (1928, Nobel 1930) , J. C. Bose and the crescograph , S. N. Bose and bosons , Ramanujan and 1729 , Bhabha (nuclear) , Sarabhai (space) , Kalam (missiles) , Khorana (genetic code) , Chandrasekhar limit . Also the days named after them. · In Kolkata in 1928, C. V. Raman showed that light changes colour slightly when scattered by molecules — the Raman effect , India's first science Nobel (1930). In the same city J. C. Bose proved plants respond to stimuli with his crescograph , and S. N. Bose wrote the statistics that gave the world the word ' boson '. Ramanujan , with almost no formal training, filled notebooks with formulas that still amaze mathematicians. Meghnad Saha explained the light of stars. After 1947, Homi Bhabha built India's atomic programme and Vikram Sarabhai its space programme; Kalam turned rockets into the SLV-3 and Agni. Abroad, Khorana cracked the genetic code, Chandrasekhar found the mass limit of white dwarfs, and Venki Ramakrishnan mapped the ribosome. · Indian scientists and their work · Scientist · Known for · Note · C. inventions.t: Ancient Indian science and 'father of' titles
inventions.x: Two kinds of questions: scholar → book (Aryabhata – Aryabhatiya, Sushruta – Sushruta Samhita, Charaka – Charaka Samhita, Bhaskara – Lilavati) and “Who is called the father of …?” (medicine – Hippocrates, surgery – Sushruta, genetics – Mendel, computer – Babbage). · Long before modern labs, Indian scholars wrote science in Sanskrit verse. Aryabhata (born 476 CE) said in the Aryabhatiya that the Earth turns on its axis and gave π as 3.1416. Brahmagupta wrote rules for zero; Bhaskaracharya 's Lilavati taught arithmetic through puzzles. Varahamihira wrote on astronomy. In medicine, Charaka wrote the Charaka Samhita and Sushruta described over 300 operations, even nose repair, in the Sushruta Samhita. Kanada imagined the atom (paramanu). Every field honours a founder with the title 'father'. Medicine has Hippocrates , biology Aristotle , genetics Mendel , chemistry Lavoisier , computers Babbage . Steel flowed from 1912. In 1923 the Mysore state started the iron works at Bhadravati , named after M. Visvesvaraya. Favourites: first cotton mill (Fort Gloster 1818, first successful Mumbai 1854), first jute mill (Rishra 1855), Manchester of India (Ahmedabad), and the leading state for sugarcane (UP), jute (West Bengal) and silk (Karnataka). · Cotton textiles are India's oldest modern industry. A first mill at Fort Gloster near Kolkata (1818) failed. The first successful one was the Bombay Spinning and Weaving Company in Mumbai (1854), started by Cowasji Nanabhai Davar . Ahmedabad got its first mill in 1861 and grew into the “Manchester of India” ; Coimbatore became the Manchester of South India. Jute , the “golden fibre”, has its mills along the Hooghly in West Bengal — the first at Rishra in 1855. Sugar is the next biggest agro-industry; Uttar Pradesh grows the most sugarcane. The star facts: Digboi (Assam, 1901) is India's oldest refinery; Jamnagar (Gujarat, Reliance) is the world's largest refining complex; Mumbai High is the biggest offshore oil field; Sindri is the old fertiliser giant. · Oil was struck at Digboi in Assam in 1889, and its refinery opened in 1901 — India's oldest still working. That is why Assam has four refineries: Digboi, Guwahati (Noonmati, the first public-sector refinery, 1962), Bongaigaon and Numaligarh . Big new oil came from Ankleshwar (Gujarat) and, in 1974, from Mumbai High under the Arabian Sea. Today the biggest refinery is Reliance's Jamnagar complex in Gujarat. The first cement factory came up at Madras (Chennai) in 1904, the first fertiliser plant at Ranipet in 1906, and the big public-sector fertiliser plant at Sindri (Jharkhand) in 1951. The commonest railway question: “The headquarters of X Railway is at …?” — and its reverse. Learn the 17 zones, especially the tricky ones: Hajipur (East Central), Hubballi (South Western), Bilaspur (South East Central), Gorakhpur (North Eastern), Maligaon (NF). · Indian Railways is run by the Railway Board (1905) under the Ministry of Railways. In 1951 the old company railways were merged into zones — Southern, Central and Western came first. Today there are 17 zones , counting the Metro Railway, Kolkata . Kolkata has three headquarters (Eastern, South Eastern, Metro); Mumbai has two (Central at CSMT, Western at Churchgate). Engines and coaches come from its own factories: Chittaranjan (CLW, 1950) for electric engines, Varanasi (BLW, once the Diesel Locomotive Works), ICF Chennai for coaches and Vande Bharat trains, Kapurthala and Raebareli for coaches, and Yelahanka for wheels. · Railway zones and headquarters · Zone · Headquarters · Note · Northern Railway · New Delhi · At Baroda House. · North Eastern Railway · Gorakhpur · Northeast Frontier Railway · Maligaon (Guwahati) · Eastern Railway · Kolkata · At Fairlie Place. · South Eastern Railway · Kolkata · At Garden Reach. · Metro Railway, Kolkata · Kolkata · The only metro run as a zone of Indian Railways. · Central Railway · Mumbai · At Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (CSMT). · Western Railway · Mumbai · At Churchgate. · Southern Railway · Chennai · South Central Railway · Secunderabad · South Western Railway · Hubballi · North Western Railway · Jaipur · West Central Railway · Jabalpur · North Central Railway · Prayagraj · South East Central Railway · Bilaspur · In Chhattisgarh. · East Coast Railway · Bhubaneswar · East Central Railway · Hajipur · The only zonal headquarters in Bihar. · Railway factories · Factory · Place · Note · Integral Coach Factory (ICF) · Chennai · Set up in 1955; industry.x: Always asked: first passenger train — 16 April 1853 , Bori Bunder to Thane (34 km). Then the first electric train (1925) , Kolkata Metro (1984) , Vande Bharat (2019) , the longest platform (Hubballi) and the UNESCO mountain railways . · On 16 April 1853 a train pulled by three engines — Sahib, Sultan and Sindh — ran 34 km from Bori Bunder (Mumbai) to Thane . The east followed in 1854 (Howrah–Hooghly) and the south in 1856. The first electric train ran from Bombay VT to Kurla in 1925 . Kolkata opened India's first metro in 1984 , and in 2024 it ran the first metro under a river , the Hooghly. New trains came fast: the Rajdhani (1969), the Shatabdi (1988), and in 2019 the home-made Vande Bharat Express (New Delhi–Varanasi), built at ICF Chennai. India has 13 major ports (as of 2026). Questions ask the state of a port and its special feature: Kandla/Deendayal (tidal), Kolkata (only riverine), Visakhapatnam (deepest land-locked), Mumbai (natural harbour), and the new Vizhinjam (Kerala) transshipment port. · India's coast is about 7,500 km long. On the east coast stand Kolkata–Haldia (on the Hooghly, the only river port), Paradip , Visakhapatnam , Kamarajar (Ennore) , Chennai and V. O. Chidambaranar (Tuticorin) . On the west coast are Cochin , New Mangalore , Mormugao , Mumbai , Jawaharlal Nehru Port (Nhava Sheva) and Deendayal (Kandla) . Port Blair became the 13th major port in 2010. physgeo.t: The universe and the Solar System
physgeo.x: Asked again and again: the planet records (largest Jupiter, smallest Mercury, hottest Venus, Red Planet Mars, farthest Neptune), which moon belongs to which planet (Ganymede, Titan, Phobos), and Pluto's demotion in 2006. · The universe began with the Big Bang about 13.8 billion years ago. Our Sun is one of billions of stars in the Milky Way , a spiral galaxy. Around the Sun go eight planets : four small rocky ones — Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars — then, beyond the asteroid belt, four giants — Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune . In 2006 the International Astronomical Union (meeting in Prague) made Pluto a dwarf planet . Earth formed about 4.6 billion years ago. physgeo.t: Earth's motions, latitude, longitude, time and eclipses
physgeo.h: पृथ्वी की गतियाँ, अक्षांश-देशांतर, समय और ग्रहण
physgeo.x: Favourites: rotation vs revolution , the solstice and equinox dates , 1° longitude = 4 minutes , IST meridian 82½° E (near Mirzapur), the International Date Line (180°), and when eclipses happen . · The Earth does two things at once. It rotates on its axis from west to east once in about 24 hours — that gives day and night and makes the Sun seem to rise in the east. It also revolves round the Sun in about 365¼ days — the extra quarter day adds up to a leap year every fourth year. Because the axis is tilted 23½° , the Sun's direct rays move between the two tropics, which gives us seasons . Lines of latitude run east–west and measure distance from the Equator; lines of longitude (meridians) run pole to pole and measure time. The Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, so 15° = 1 hour and 1° = 4 minutes . India keeps one time, set by 82½° E : IST = GMT + 5 h 30 min . On the far side of the world the International Date Line (about 180°) is where the date changes. · Earth's motions and time · Rotation · About 24 hours (23 h 56 min against the stars), west to east · Revolution · About 365¼ days — hence a leap year every 4 years · Tilt of the axis · 23½° from the vertical (66½° to the plane of its orbit) · Circle of illumination · The line that divides day from night · Time and longitude · 15° = 1 hour; 1° = 4 minutes · Indian Standard Time · 82½° E (near Mirzapur, UP) — GMT + 5 h 30 min · Arunachal vs Gujarat · About 30° of longitude apart — about 2 hours of Sun time · Crossing the Date Line · Going west (America → Asia): add a day. physgeo.t: Inside the Earth, and its rocks

physgeo.x: Asked every year: which discontinuity lies between which layers (Moho, Gutenberg, Lehmann), SIAL–SIMA–NIFE , the most abundant elements of the crust, and rock types with examples (marble from limestone, slate from shale). · No one has dug deeper than about 12 km, so we know the Earth's inside from earthquake waves . They speed up, slow down and bend at certain depths — these boundaries are called discontinuities . The crust is the thin outer skin; below the Moho is the mantle , the biggest layer; below the Gutenberg line (2,900 km) is the liquid outer core ; below the Lehmann line (5,150 km) is the solid inner core , reaching the centre at about 6,371 km . Rocks come in three families. Igneous rocks (granite, basalt) form when magma cools — they are the 'primary' rocks. Sedimentary rocks (sandstone, limestone, coal) form in layers and are the only ones with fossils. Metamorphic rocks (marble, slate) are older rocks changed by heat and pressure. · Layers in numbers · Radius of the Earth · About 6,371 km · Crust · SIAL (silica + aluminium) on continents; SIMA Common questions: Wegener and continental drift , Pangaea , the Pacific Ring of Fire , P, S and L waves , Richter vs Mercalli , epicentre , and famous volcanoes and their countries (Barren Island is India's only active one). · In 1912 Alfred Wegener said the continents were once joined in one super-continent, Pangaea , which split into Laurasia (north) and Gondwanaland (south). In the 1960s sea-floor spreading and then plate tectonics explained how: the lithosphere is broken into about seven big plates (the largest is the Pacific plate ) that float on the soft asthenosphere. Where plates pull apart new crust forms; where they collide we get trenches, volcanoes and fold mountains like the Himalayas ; where they slide past we get faults like San Andreas . Most earthquakes and volcanoes lie along plate edges, above all round the Pacific — the Ring of Fire , with about three-quarters of the world's active volcanoes. A quake starts at the focus underground; the spot above it is the epicentre . physgeo.x: The usual question: “Which agent makes this landform?” — ox-bow lake and delta (river), U-shaped valley, cirque, moraine and fjord (glacier), barchan and mushroom rock (wind), sea stack and arch (waves), stalactite (underground water). · Inside forces raise the land; outside forces wear it down. Weathering breaks rock in place; erosion carries it away; deposition drops it somewhere new. A river cuts a V-shaped valley and gorges in the mountains, swings in meanders across the plains — leaving ox-bow lakes — and builds a delta at its mouth. A glacier grinds a U-shaped valley , scoops out cirques , and dumps moraines ; when the sea floods a glacial valley it becomes a fjord . In deserts the wind builds crescent barchans , carves mushroom rocks , and carries fine dust far away as loess . On coasts, waves cut cliffs, caves, arches and stacks , and pile sand into beaches and spits . Always asked: the layers in order and what happens in each — weather in the troposphere, ozone in the stratosphere , meteors in the mesosphere, radio waves and the ionosphere in the thermosphere — plus the gases of the air and isolines (isobar, isohyet…). · The air around us is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen , with argon, a little carbon dioxide and water vapour. Going up from the ground: the troposphere (weather, gets colder as you climb), the stratosphere (calm, with the ozone layer that blocks ultraviolet rays), the mesosphere (coldest, meteors burn), the thermosphere (with the ionosphere that bounces radio waves back), and the thin exosphere . The Sun's energy reaching the Earth is called insolation (incoming solar radiation). It is strongest at the Equator, where the rays are nearly vertical. The Earth sends heat back as long-wave terrestrial radiation , and greenhouse gases trap some of it — the greenhouse effect . physgeo.t: Pressure belts, planetary winds and local winds
physgeo.h: दाब पेटियाँ, ग्रहीय पवनें और स्थानीय पवनें
physgeo.x: The most asked bit of climatology: local winds and where they blow (Chinook, Foehn, Sirocco, Mistral, Harmattan, Loo), then the pressure belts , trade winds and westerlies , the Roaring Forties , the Coriolis force and jet streams . · Wind always blows from high pressure to low pressure . The Earth has seven pressure belts: the equatorial low (the calm doldrums ), two subtropical highs near 30° (the horse latitudes ), two subpolar lows near 60°, and two polar highs . Between them blow the planetary winds : trade winds towards the Equator, westerlies towards the poles, and polar easterlies . Because the Earth spins, the Coriolis force bends winds to the right in the northern half and to the left in the southern half (Ferrel's law). Over the open southern oceans the westerlies roar: the Roaring Forties , Furious Fifties and Shrieking Sixties . High up, near the top of the troposphere, race narrow rivers of fast westerly air — the jet streams . Down on the ground, every region has its own local winds : the warm Chinook of the Rockies (the 'snow eater'), the Foehn of the Alps, the dusty Sirocco from the Sahara, the cold Mistral of France, the Harmattan of West Africa (the 'Doctor'), and India's own hot Loo . · More about winds · Coriolis force · Zero at the Equator, greatest at the poles · Buys Ballot's law · Stand with your back to the wind in the northern half — low pressure is on your left · Jet streams · Fast westerly winds 9–12 km up, near the tropopause · Tropical easterly jet · Blows over India in summer and helps the monsoon · Monsoon · Seasonal reversal of winds — from the Arabic 'mausim' (season) · Sea breeze / land breeze · Sea to land by day; Two favourites: what tropical cyclones are called in different regions (hurricane, typhoon, willy-willy) and cloud types (cumulonimbus = thunderstorm). Also: the calm eye , the direction of spin , and types of rainfall . · When moist air rises it cools; at its dew point the water vapour condenses on dust into tiny drops — a cloud . High, wispy cirrus are made of ice; puffy cumulus mean fair weather; flat grey stratus cover the sky; and the giant cumulonimbus brings thunder, lightning and hail. Rain is convectional (hot afternoons at the Equator), orographic (moist wind forced up a mountain — the far side is a dry rain-shadow ), or cyclonic/frontal . A tropical cyclone is a huge low-pressure storm born over warm seas (above about 27 °C). Air spirals in anticlockwise in the northern half and clockwise in the southern half round a calm, cloudless eye . It has different names: hurricane in the Atlantic and Caribbean, typhoon in the China Sea, cyclone in the Indian Ocean, willy-willy in north-west Australia. physgeo.x: Most asked: warm vs cold currents and their ocean (Gulf Stream, Kuroshio, Labrador, Humboldt), spring and neap tides , the Mariana Trench , average salinity (35‰) , and coral reefs and atolls . · About 71% of the Earth is water, most of it in five oceans: the Pacific (largest, deepest), Atlantic , Indian , Southern and Arctic (smallest). From the coast the floor goes down the gentle continental shelf , the steep slope , then the flat abyssal plain , cut by deep trenches — the deepest is the Mariana Trench (Challenger Deep, about 11 km). Sea water has about 35 grams of salt per kilogram (35‰). Tides are caused mainly by the Moon's pull . At new and full moon the Sun and Moon pull together — spring tides ; at the quarter moons they pull at right angles — neap tides . Currents are rivers in the sea: warm ones flow from the Equator towards the poles (Gulf Stream, Kuroshio), cold ones flow towards the Equator (Labrador, Canary, Humboldt). Questions ask for the name of each grassland (Prairies, Pampas, Steppes, Veld, Downs), the Köppen letters (A to E), and the features of each climate — Mediterranean, equatorial, savanna, taiga, tundra. · In 1918 the German scientist Wladimir Köppen sorted the world's climates by temperature and rain into groups with capital letters: A tropical, B dry, C warm temperate, D cold snow-forest, E polar, and later H for highlands. Small letters add detail: f = no dry season, m = monsoon, w = dry winter, s = dry summer. A biome is a large area with its own climate, plants and animals. Near the Equator stand the tropical rainforests (the Amazon's are called selvas ); then the savannas ; then hot deserts near 30°. In the middle latitudes lie temperate grasslands with local names — Prairies, Pampas, Steppes, Veld, Downs . banking.x: Asked again and again: RBI set up on 1 April 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934 , on the Hilton Young Commission 's advice; nationalised on 1 January 1949 ; HQ Mumbai (first Calcutta); first governor Osborne Smith , first Indian governor C. D. Deshmukh ; and its functions . · In 1926 the Hilton Young Commission told the British government that India needed its own central bank. The RBI Act was passed in 1934 , and the Reserve Bank opened on 1 April 1935 in Calcutta — as a private bank owned by shareholders. Its head office moved to Bombay in 1937. After Independence it was nationalised on 1 January 1949 , so it now belongs fully to the Government of India. The RBI prints and issues our currency notes, keeps the government's accounts, acts as the banker's bank and the lender of last resort , guards the forex reserves and regulates banks. Its emblem shows a tiger and a palm tree . The first governor was Sir Osborne Smith ; the first Indian governor was C. D. banking.x: Definitions are the favourite: repo vs reverse repo , CRR vs SLR , MSF , bank rate , OMO , quantitative vs qualitative tools, and the MPC — 6 members, set up in 2016, chaired by the Governor, inflation target 4% ± 2% . · Think of the RBI as the tap that controls money in the economy. When prices rise too fast, it raises the repo rate — the rate at which it lends to banks — so loans become costly and spending slows. It can also raise the CRR (cash banks must keep with the RBI) or sell bonds through open market operations , sucking money out. To push growth, it does the opposite. Banks park spare cash with the RBI at the SDF rate (the floor) and borrow in an emergency at the MSF rate (the ceiling); the repo rate sits in between. Since 2016 the repo rate is decided by a six-member Monetary Policy Committee — three from the RBI, including the Governor who chairs it, and three experts named by the Centre — with the aim of keeping CPI inflation at 4%, within 2–6% . · Policy rates (as of 7 October 2026 — check before your exam) · Repo rate · 5.50% — raised from 5.25% on 7 October 2026 · Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) · 5.25% · Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) and Bank rate · 5.75% · CRR · 3% of NDTL (cut in stages to 3% by late 2025) · SLR · 18% of NDTL · Inflation target · 4% CPI, with a band of 2–6% · The Monetary Policy Committee · Set up · 2016, under Section 45ZB of the RBI Act (added by the Finance Act, 2016) · Members · 6 — the Governor (chair), a Deputy Governor, one RBI officer, and 3 outside experts named by the Centre · Term of outside members · 4 years · Tie · The Governor has a casting (second) vote · Quorum · 4 members · Meetings · At least 4 a year (usually 6) · Recommended by · Urjit Patel Committee (2014) · The tools, defined · What it is · Tool · Note · Rate at which the RBI lends short-term money to banks against government securities · Repo rate · Raised to fight inflation; Frequent: the first bank (Bank of Hindustan, 1770), PNB as the first bank started with Indian capital (Lahore, 1894), Imperial Bank → SBI (1955) , nationalisation of 14 banks in 1969 and 6 in 1980 , and the 2019–20 mergers . · Banking in British India began with the Bank of Hindustan in Calcutta (1770). The three presidency banks — Bengal (1806, as the Bank of Calcutta), Bombay (1840) and Madras (1843) — were merged in 1921 into the Imperial Bank of India . Indians soon started their own banks: Punjab National Bank was founded in Lahore in 1894 with Lala Lajpat Rai among its founders. In 1955 the Imperial Bank became the State Bank of India . On 19 July 1969 PM Indira Gandhi nationalised 14 big banks so that credit would reach farmers and small traders; 6 more followed on 15 April 1980 . Fifty years later the government did the reverse — it merged banks: Vijaya and Dena into Bank of Baroda (2019), and ten banks into four on 1 April 2020 , leaving 12 public sector banks. · The nationalised banks · 1969 (14) · Central Bank of India, Bank of India, Punjab National Bank, Bank of Baroda, United Commercial (UCO) Bank, Canara Bank, Dena Bank, United Bank of India, Syndicate Bank, Allahabad Bank, Indian Bank, Bank of Maharashtra, Indian Overseas Bank, Union Bank of India · 1980 (6) · Andhra Bank, Corporation Bank, New Bank of India, Oriental Bank of Commerce, Punjab & Sind Bank, Vijaya Bank · Public sector banks now · 12 (since 1 April 2020) · Largest bank · State Bank of India · Milestones · Event · Year · Note · Bank of Hindustan — the first bank in India (Calcutta) · 1770 · Set up by Alexander and Co.; Asked often: RRBs (2 October 1975, first Prathama Bank, share 50 : 35 : 15), payment banks (₹2 lakh limit, no loans, Nachiket Mor), small finance banks (75% priority sector) and what makes a bank scheduled . · Not every bank is the same. A scheduled bank is one listed in the Second Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934 ; it can borrow from the RBI and must keep CRR with it. Regional Rural Banks began on 2 October 1975 — the first was Prathama Bank at Moradabad — to lend to small farmers and village workers. Each is owned 50% by the Centre, 35% by a sponsor bank and 15% by the state. Cooperative banks belong to their members. In 2014 the RBI created two new kinds on the Nachiket Mor Committee 's ideas. Payment banks (like India Post Payments Bank) take small deposits — up to ₹2 lakh a customer — and offer payments, but cannot lend. Small finance banks (like AU and Ujjivan) can lend, but must give 75% of their loans to the priority sector. · Numbers to know (as of 2025–26) · RRBs · 28 after the 'One State, One RRB' merger of 1 May 2025 · RRB law · Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976 · Payment bank deposit limit · ₹2 lakh per customer · Small finance bank priority-sector share · 75% of loans · Priority-sector target for commercial banks · 40% of adjusted net bank credit · Minimum capital · Small finance bank ₹200 crore; payment bank ₹100 crore · Which kind of bank? Banks can then use the SARFAESI Act (2002) to seize the security without a court, or take a company to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (2016) . To make banks strong enough to bear such losses, the world follows the Basel III capital rules made at Basel, Switzerland. If a bank fails, the DICGC repays each depositor up to ₹5 lakh (raised from ₹1 lakh in 2020). Our money has its own story. The ₹ symbol , designed by D. Udaya Kumar , was adopted on 15 July 2010 — a blend of Devanagari ‘र’ and Roman ‘R’. On 8 November 2016 the old ₹500 and ₹1000 notes were demonetised, and new notes with Indian heritage motifs followed. agri.t: Cropping seasons: kharif, rabi and zaid
agri.h: फ़सल ऋतुएँ: ख़रीफ़, रबी और ज़ायद
agri.x: The commonest agriculture question: “Which of these is a rabi / kharif crop?” Rice, maize, cotton, soybean, groundnut are kharif ; wheat, barley, gram, mustard are rabi ; watermelon and cucumber are zaid . · India's farm year follows the monsoon. When the rains arrive in June–July , farmers sow the kharif crops — rice, maize, jowar, bajra, cotton, jute, groundnut and soybean — and harvest them in September–October . Kharif comes from an Arabic word for autumn. As the rains end, the rabi crops go in during October–December — wheat, barley, gram, peas and mustard — and are cut in March–April ; winter rain from western disturbances helps them. In the short summer gap ( March–June ) comes zaid : watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables and fodder. · The three seasons · Kharif · Sown June–July with the monsoon; harvested September–October · Rabi · Sown October–December; harvested March–April · Zaid · Between rabi and kharif, roughly March–June · Sesamum (til) · Kharif in the north, rabi in the south · Sugarcane · Not seasonal — takes about a year in the field · Aus, Aman, Boro · The three rice crops of West Bengal (autumn, winter, summer) · Which season is each crop? · Crop · Season · Note · Rice (paddy) · Kharif · Sown with the monsoon (June–July), harvested in autumn. · Maize · Kharif · Also grown as a rabi crop in Bihar. · Jowar · Kharif · Bajra · Kharif · Ragi · Kharif · Cotton · Kharif · Jute · Kharif · Groundnut · Kharif · Mostly a kharif oilseed. · Soybean · Kharif · Arhar (tur) · Kharif · Urad · Kharif · Wheat · Rabi · Sown October–December, harvested March–April. · Barley · Rabi · Gram (chana) · Rabi · India's most important pulse. · Mustard · Rabi · Peas · Rabi · Linseed · Rabi · Masoor (lentil) · Rabi · Watermelon · Zaid · Zaid = the short summer season between rabi and kharif (March–June). · Muskmelon · Zaid · Cucumber · Zaid · Fodder crops (summer) · Zaid · Sugarcane · Perennial (about a year) · Stays in the field for about 10–18 months. · Tea · Perennial (about a year) · A plantation bush plucked for many years. · Hindi name → English name · Hindi name · English name · Note · Gehun · Wheat · Jau · Barley · Makka · Maize · Jowar · Sorghum · Bajra · Pearl millet · Ragi (mandua) · Finger millet · Very rich in calcium. · Kangni · Foxtail millet · Chana · Chickpea (gram) · Arhar (tur) · Pigeon pea · Masoor · Lentil · Moong · Green gram · Urad · Black gram · Sarson · Mustard · Til · Sesame (sesamum) · Alsi · Linseed (flax) · Mungphali · Groundnut · Kapas · Cotton · Ganna · Sugarcane · Kharif = Khet + Rain — monsoon crops. agri.t: Food crops: climate, soil and leading states
agri.h: खाद्य फ़सलें: जलवायु, मिट्टी और अग्रणी राज्य
agri.x: Asked often: the climate a crop needs (rice — over 100 cm rain; wheat — 50–75 cm; cotton — black soil, 210 frost-free days) and the top state (wheat — UP, bajra — Rajasthan, pulses — MP). · Rice is India's main food crop and needs heat (above 25°C), humidity and over 100 cm of rain — or canals in dry Punjab and Haryana. Wheat is the second; it wants a cool growing season and bright sun at ripening, with 50–75 cm of rain. India is the world's second-largest producer of both rice and wheat (after China) and the largest exporter of rice . Millets — jowar, bajra and ragi — are 'coarse grains' that grow in dry, poor soils and are rich in nutrients. India is the world's largest producer of millets and of pulses (also the largest consumer and importer of pulses). Pulses are legumes: their roots fix nitrogen, so they restore soil fertility. · What each crop needs · Crop · Climate and soil · Note · Rice · Above 25°C, high humidity, over 100 cm rain · Grows best in clayey alluvial soil; needs standing water. · Wheat · Cool growing season, bright sun at ripening, 50–75 cm rain · Two zones: the Ganga–Satluj plains and the black-soil Deccan. · Maize · 21–27°C and old alluvial soil · Used as food and fodder. · Bajra · Sandy soils and shallow black soil, very dry · Pulses · Little moisture; they fix nitrogen in the soil · Leguminous — so they are rotated with other crops. · Sugarcane · 21–27°C, 75–100 cm rain, hot and humid · Can grow on many soils; needs heavy manure and labour. · Cotton · Black soil, 210 frost-free days, bright sunshine · The Deccan plateau's black (regur) soil is ideal. · Jute · Flood plains where the soil is renewed every year, high temperature · Called the 'golden fibre'. · Tea · Warm, moist, frost-free; well-drained slopes rich in humus · Needs frequent showers all year and a lot of cheap labour. · Coffee · Hill slopes with shade, warm and wet · Arabica coffee was first grown in the Baba Budan Hills. · Rubber · Over 200 cm rain and above 25°C — moist equatorial climate · Leading state (2023–24 estimates) · Crop · Leading state · Note · Wheat · Uttar Pradesh · UP leads every year; then Madhya Pradesh and Punjab. · Bajra · Rajasthan · Rajasthan grows nearly half of India's bajra. · Jowar · Maharashtra · Ragi · Karnataka · Gram (chana) · Madhya Pradesh · Pulses (all together) · Madhya Pradesh · MP is called the 'pulse bowl'. · Barley · Rajasthan · Soils and crops (see the Indian Geography app for soils) · Alluvial soil · Rice, wheat, sugarcane — the northern plains · Black (regur) soil · Cotton — Deccan plateau; holds moisture · Red soil · Millets, pulses, groundnut · Laterite soil · Tea, coffee, cashew (with manure) · Arid (desert) soil · Bajra, and other crops once irrigated · Rice — leading state · West Bengal in most years, with UP and Punjab close (rankings shift) · Rain ladder: Rubber 200+ → Rice 100+ → Sugarcane 75–100 → Wheat 50–75 . agri.t: Cash and fibre crops: sugarcane, cotton, jute, oilseeds
agri.h: नक़दी और रेशा फ़सलें: गन्ना, कपास, जूट, तिलहन
agri.x: Know the top state for each (sugarcane — UP, cotton — Gujarat, jute — West Bengal, groundnut — Gujarat, mustard — Rajasthan, soybean — MP) and which part of the plant gives each fibre. · Sugarcane is a tropical and subtropical crop; India is the world's second-largest producer after Brazil, and Uttar Pradesh grows the most. It gives sugar, gur and khandsari, and its molasses goes into ethanol. Cotton loves the black soil of the Deccan; Gujarat and Maharashtra lead. Jute , the 'golden fibre', grows in the flood plains of the Ganga–Brahmaputra delta — West Bengal grows over half. Oilseeds cover a large area: groundnut (mostly kharif, Gujarat), mustard (rabi, Rajasthan), soybean (kharif, Madhya Pradesh — the 'Soya State'), sesamum, castor, sunflower and linseed. India still imports much of its edible oil. · Leading state (2023–24 estimates) · Crop · Leading state · Note · Sugarcane · Uttar Pradesh · Then Maharashtra and Karnataka. · Cotton · Gujarat · Maharashtra has the largest cotton area. · Jute · West Bengal · Over half of India's jute; then Bihar and Assam. · Groundnut · Gujarat · Rapeseed and mustard · Rajasthan · Soybean · Madhya Pradesh · MP is called the 'Soya State'. · Castor seed · Gujarat · Raw silk (mulberry) · Karnataka · Where each fibre comes from · Fibre · Comes from · Note · Cotton · Hairs on the seed (inside the boll) · The boll is picked; ginning separates fibre from seed. · Jute · Stem (bast fibre) · Stems are soaked in water — 'retting' — to loosen the fibre. · Coir · Husk of the coconut · Kerala is the centre of the coir industry. · Silk · Cocoon of the silkworm · Rearing silkworms is sericulture. · Wool · Fleece of sheep (and goats) · Pashmina · Undercoat of the Changthangi goat · From Ladakh. · “G-G-C” — Gujarat grows Groundnut, Cotton and Castor. Asked often: tea — Assam, coffee — Karnataka, rubber — Kerala ; black pepper = King of spices, cardamom = Queen of spices ; and the home of Indian coffee — the Baba Budan Hills . · The British brought tea to Assam's hills in the 1830s; today Assam grows over half of India's tea and India is the world's second-largest producer after China. agri.t: Types of farming and shifting cultivation
agri.h: कृषि के प्रकार और स्थानांतरी खेती
agri.x: Two favourites: the local names of shifting cultivation (Jhum — north-east, Podu — Andhra, Bewar — MP, Kuruwa — Jharkhand) and the '-culture' words (sericulture — silk, apiculture — bees, viticulture — grapes). · In shifting cultivation ('slash and burn'), a patch of forest is cut and burnt, crops are grown on the ash for a few years, and when the soil tires the farmers move on and let the forest grow back. It is primitive subsistence farming — grown to feed the family. In India it has many local names; in the north-east it is jhum . Abroad it is milpa (Mexico), roca (Brazil) and ladang (Indonesia). Intensive subsistence farming uses a small plot with heavy labour and inputs. Commercial farming grows crops for sale; plantation farming is its estate form (tea, coffee, rubber). Mixed farming combines crops with livestock. Pure matching questions: revolution → product (white — milk, blue — fish, yellow — oilseeds, round — potato, silver — eggs) and revolution → father (Swaminathan — Green in India, Kurien — White). · In the mid-1960s India faced food shortages. High-yielding wheat seeds bred by Norman Borlaug in Mexico, with fertilisers and irrigation, transformed Punjab, Haryana and western UP. M. S. Swaminathan led the effort in India and is called the father of India's Green Revolution ; IR-8 rice from the Philippines followed. Borlaug won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970. Then came milk. Verghese Kurien built the Amul cooperative at Anand and, as head of the NDDB , ran Operation Flood from 1970 — the White Revolution that made India the world's largest milk producer. Asked: the largest source of irrigation (wells and tube wells), where tank irrigation is common (peninsular India), and project → river (Bhakra — Sutlej, Hirakud — Mahanadi, Sardar Sarovar — Narmada, Tehri — Bhagirathi). · Only part of India's farmland is irrigated; the rest depends on the monsoon. Wells and tube wells are now the largest source — especially in Punjab, Haryana and western UP. Canals come next, from rivers such as the Ganga and Sutlej. Tanks are common in peninsular India (Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana), where hard rock holds little groundwater. The Grand Anicut (Kallanai) on the Kaveri, built by the Chola king Karikala, is among the oldest working water structures in the world. After 1947 Nehru called big dams the 'temples of modern India' . The Damodar Valley project (1948) was the first multipurpose project; Bhakra Nangal on the Sutlej followed. India also has the world's largest population of cattle and buffaloes. The Murrah buffalo of Haryana is the star milk animal; desi cows such as Gir and Sahiwal are being improved under the Rashtriya Gokul Mission (2014). India is the world's second-largest fish producer , and most fish now come from inland farms; Andhra Pradesh is the top fish-producing state. Andhra Pradesh also leads in eggs. states.h: राज्यों का पुनर्गठन — नक्शा कैसे बना
states.x: Asked again and again: the Fazl Ali Commission and the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 ; the year each new state was born (Nagaland 1963, Haryana 1966, Sikkim 1975, the three of 2000, Telangana 2014); which state it was carved from ; and the 2019 and 2020 changes that left India with 28 states and 8 UTs . · In 1947 India was a patchwork of British provinces and more than 500 princely states. People wanted states drawn by language . When Potti Sriramulu died fasting in December 1952, the government gave in: Andhra State was born on 1 October 1953 — the first linguistic state. The States Reorganisation Commission (chair Fazl Ali , members K. M. Panikkar and H. N. Kunzru ) then redrew the whole map. The States Reorganisation Act came into force on 1 November 1956 with 14 states and 6 UTs , and the 7th Amendment ended the old Part A/B/C/D classes. The map kept changing: Bombay State split into Gujarat and Maharashtra (1960), Nagaland (1963), Haryana (1966), Himachal (1971), Manipur, Tripura, Meghalaya (1972), Sikkim (1975), Mizoram, Arunachal, Goa (1987), Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand, Jharkhand (2000) and Telangana (2014). In 2019 the state of Jammu and Kashmir became two UTs, and in 2020 Dadra and Nagar Haveli merged with Daman and Diu . states.x: Most asked: Chandigarh as the shared capital of Punjab and Haryana, Shimla and Dharamshala (Himachal’s two capitals), Rajasthan as the largest state by area, and Punjab as the ‘Land of Five Rivers’. (Delhi, Chandigarh, J&K and Ladakh — the other members of the Northern council — are in the UT lesson.) · Punjab takes its name from five rivers — Sutlej, Beas, Ravi, Chenab and Jhelum. In 1966 its Hindi-speaking south became Haryana , and the new city of Chandigarh , designed by Le Corbusier , became a UT and the capital of both. Himachal Pradesh rose from a UT to a full state on 25 January 1971; it governs from Shimla in summer and declared Dharamshala its winter capital in 2017. Rajasthan , the old Rajputana, is India’s largest state by area (about 10.4% of India). Its capital is the Pink City, Jaipur , but its high court sits at Jodhpur . Uttar Pradesh (capital Lucknow ) is India’s most populous state (Census 2011), sends 80 MPs to the Lok Sabha and touches eight states plus Delhi. In 2000 its hill districts became Uttarakhand — ‘Devbhoomi’, home of the Char Dham and the sources of the Ganga and Yamuna. It runs from Dehradun and named Gairsain its summer capital in 2020. Madhya Pradesh (capital Bhopal ) is the ‘Heart of India’ and the ‘Tiger State’. It was the biggest state until 1 November 2000, when Chhattisgarh — ‘36 forts’, the rice bowl of central India — was carved out, with its capital at Raipur . MP now touches five states: Rajasthan, UP, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra and Gujarat. · Capitals · State · Capital · Note · Uttar Pradesh · Lucknow · The high court is at Prayagraj (Allahabad), with a bench at Lucknow. · Uttarakhand · Dehradun · Winter capital and seat of government. · Uttarakhand (summer) · Gairsain (Bhararisain) · Declared the summer capital in 2020. · Madhya Pradesh · Bhopal · The City of Lakes — the high court is at Jabalpur. · Chhattisgarh · Raipur · Nava Raipur (Atal Nagar) is the new planned capital; the high court is at Bilaspur. · Which state is it? Bengal Presidency once ruled them all; Bihar and Orissa were split off in 1912 (Bihar Diwas, 22 March), and Orissa became its own province on 1 April 1936 — the first drawn by language. In 2011 it became Odisha . Jharkhand , the ‘land of forests’ and coal, was carved from Bihar on 15 November 2000 , Birsa Munda’s birthday, with Ranchi as capital. Kolkata , capital of West Bengal , was the capital of British India until 1911 . West Bengal touches Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan , and its Siliguri Corridor — the ‘Chicken’s Neck’ — is the only land link to the North-East. A favourite: capital of each North-Eastern state (Dispur, Itanagar, Imphal, Shillong, Aizawl, Kohima, Agartala, Gangtok), the nicknames (Abode of Clouds, Land of the Rising Sun), the Seven Sisters and Sikkim, and the years (1963, 1972, 1975, 1987). · Almost the whole North-East was once Assam . Out of it came Nagaland (1963), Meghalaya (1972), and Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh (UTs in 1972, states in 1987). Manipur and Tripura , former princely states, became states in 1972. When Shillong went to Meghalaya, Assam moved its capital to Dispur . These seven are the ‘Seven Sisters’ . Sikkim , a kingdom under the Chogyal, joined India as the 22nd state in 1975 — the ‘brother’ of the sisters, linked to them through the North Eastern Council since 2002. Sikkim has the smallest population of any state and became the first fully organic state in 2016. Andhra State (capital Kurnool ) came in 1953; in 1956 it joined the Telugu districts of Hyderabad State to form Andhra Pradesh , with Hyderabad as capital. In 2014 those Telangana districts became India’s 29th and youngest state ; Hyderabad stayed the shared capital until 2 June 2024, and Andhra Pradesh builds its capital at Amaravati . Kerala was formed in 1956 from Travancore-Cochin and Malabar — ‘God’s Own Country’, with the highest literacy and best sex ratio (Census 2011). Mysore State became Karnataka in 1973 (capital Bengaluru ), and Madras State became Tamil Nadu in 1969 (capital Chennai ). Asked every year: the number of UTs (8) , which ones have a legislature (Delhi, Puducherry, J&K), the largest (Ladakh) and smallest (Lakshadweep) , the capitals ( Kavaratti , Sri Vijaya Puram , Daman , Leh ), and the 2019 and 2020 changes. · Union Territories are run by the Centre through an Administrator or Lieutenant Governor (Article 239). Three of the eight also elect a legislature: Delhi (the National Capital Territory, by the 69th Amendment, 1991 , Article 239AA), Puducherry (Article 239A) and, since 31 October 2019 , Jammu and Kashmir , which uses Srinagar in summer and Jammu in winter. Ladakh (capital Leh ), split from J&K the same day, is the largest UT and has no legislature. The islands: Lakshadweep (capital Kavaratti ), the smallest UT , and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands , whose capital Port Blair was renamed Sri Vijaya Puram in 2024 and whose Indira Point is India’s southernmost tip. India has 25 high courts . The oldest three — Calcutta, Bombay and Madras — date from 1862 , Calcutta first. The newest are Meghalaya, Manipur and Tripura (2013) and the split of the Hyderabad court into Andhra Pradesh and Telangana high courts (1 January 2019). Konkani (Goa), Manipuri and Nepali entered the Eighth Schedule in 1992 . worldgeo.x: Asked again and again: largest and smallest continent and ocean, the highest peak of each continent , the deepest point (Mariana Trench) and the continent crossed by the Equator and both Tropics (Africa). · Earth has seven continents . Biggest to smallest: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe, Australia . Asia holds about 30% of the land and 60% of the people. Africa has the most countries (54) and is the only continent cut by the Equator, the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn. Antarctica is the coldest place — and the largest desert, because so little snow falls there. Water covers about 71% of the Earth. There are five oceans : Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, Arctic . The Pacific alone is bigger than all the land put together, and its Mariana Trench is the deepest point on Earth. The Indian Ocean is the only one named after a country. · Continents by area · Continent · By area · Note · Asia · the largest · About 30% of the world's land and about 60% of its people. · Africa · the 2nd largest · 54 countries — the most of any continent. · North America · the 3rd largest · South America · the 4th largest · Antarctica · the 5th largest · Coldest, windiest and highest on average; no permanent people. · Europe · the 6th largest · Australia (Oceania) · the smallest · The island continent. · Highest peak of each continent · Continent · Highest peak · Height and place · Asia · Mount Everest · 8,849 m — the highest point on Earth (Nepal–China border). · Africa · Mount Kilimanjaro · 5,895 m, in Tanzania; a dormant volcano. · North America · Denali (Mount McKinley) · 6,190 m, in Alaska (USA). · South America · Aconcagua · 6,961 m, in the Andes of Argentina. · Antarctica · Vinson Massif · 4,892 m. · Europe · Mount Elbrus · 5,642 m, in the Caucasus (Russia). · Australia (mainland) · Mount Kosciuszko · 2,228 m. Everest (8,849 m) sits on the Nepal–China border; K2 (8,611 m) is in the Karakoram ; Kangchenjunga (8,586 m) is on the India–Nepal border in Sikkim. worldgeo.x: Two question types: records (longest — Nile; largest by volume — Amazon; most countries — Danube) and “City X stands on which river?” — London–Thames, Paris–Seine, Rome–Tiber, Baghdad–Tigris, Vienna and Budapest–Danube. · The Nile is the longest river (about 6,650 km). It flows north into the Mediterranean; at Khartoum the Blue Nile and White Nile join, and at Cairo it nears its delta. The Amazon carries the most water of any river. The Yangtze is Asia's longest; the Huang He is the 'Sorrow of China' for its floods. In Europe the Volga is longest and empties into the Caspian Sea; the Danube passes through 10 countries and four capitals — Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest, Belgrade . Records again: largest lake (Caspian Sea), largest freshwater lake (Superior), deepest (Baikal), highest navigable (Titicaca), highest waterfall (Angel Falls) and where Victoria and Niagara Falls are. · The Caspian Sea is called a sea but is really the world's largest lake. Lake Superior is the largest freshwater lake by area, while Siberia's Lake Baikal is the deepest and oldest and holds about a fifth of the world's unfrozen fresh surface water. High in the Andes, Lake Titicaca (Peru–Bolivia) is the highest lake that boats can sail on. Lake Victoria , Africa's largest, feeds the White Nile. Water falls hardest in South America and Africa. Angel Falls in Venezuela drops 979 m — the highest. Victoria Falls on the Zambezi, between Zambia and Zimbabwe, is called Mosi-oa-Tunya , 'the smoke that thunders'. worldgeo.x: SSC asks the grassland names almost every year — Pampas (Argentina), Steppes (Eurasia), Prairies (North America), Veld (South Africa), Downs (Australia). Also: largest hot desert (Sahara), driest (Atacama) and the Roof of the World (Pamir). · The Sahara covers most of North Africa — the largest hot desert. In the south, the Kalahari (Botswana) and the coastal Namib (Namibia) are home to the San people. The Atacama in Chile is so dry that some weather stations have never recorded rain. Asia has the cold Gobi (Mongolia–China), the Taklamakan and India's Thar . Grasslands carry local names on every continent: Prairies in North America, Pampas in Argentina, Steppes across Eurasia, Veld in South Africa, Downs in Australia and Canterbury in New Zealand — all temperate. The tropical ones are the African Savanna , the Llanos of Venezuela and the Campos of Brazil. Above them all, the Tibetan Plateau is the highest and largest plateau, and the Pamir is the 'Roof of the World'. · Deserts · Desert · Where · Note · Sahara · North Africa · The largest hot desert. · Kalahari · Botswana (southern Africa) · Home of the San (Bushmen). · Namib · Namibia · A coastal desert; “Which strait separates X and Y?” and “Which canal joins X and Y?” are among the most-asked world-geography questions — Gibraltar, Bering, Palk, Malacca, Hormuz; Suez, Panama, Kiel. Also the largest island (Greenland). · A strait is a narrow sea passage between two pieces of land. Gibraltar separates Spain from Morocco and lets the Atlantic into the Mediterranean. The Bering Strait separates Russia from Alaska — Asia from North America. Palk Strait separates India from Sri Lanka. Oil tankers crowd Hormuz (Iran–Oman) and Malacca (Malaysia–Sumatra). A canal is dug by people. The Suez Canal (Egypt, 1869) joins the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, so ships from Europe need not sail round Africa. The Panama Canal (1914) joins the Atlantic and the Pacific. The Kiel Canal in Germany joins the North Sea and the Baltic. Three quick-fire favourites: boundary lines (Durand, McMahon, Radcliffe, 38th and 49th Parallel), nicknames (Land of the Rising Sun, Land of the Midnight Sun, Land of Thousand Lakes) and tribes (Bushmen, Masai, Eskimo, Bedouin, Pygmies). · Many borders were drawn by one man with a pen. Sir Mortimer Durand drew the Durand Line (1893) between British India and Afghanistan — today Pakistan–Afghanistan. Sir Henry McMahon drew the McMahon Line (1914) — India–China. Sir Cyril Radcliffe drew the Radcliffe Line (1947) — India–Pakistan. Lines of latitude became borders too: the 38th Parallel splits the two Koreas; the 49th Parallel runs between the USA and Canada. Places earn nicknames: Japan is the Land of the Rising Sun, Norway the Land of the Midnight Sun, Finland the Land of a Thousand Lakes, Bhutan the Land of the Thunder Dragon. And peoples are tied to places: the Bushmen of the Kalahari, the Masai of Kenya and Tanzania, the Inuit (Eskimo) of the Arctic and the Bedouin of the Arabian desert. · Boundary lines · Line · Between · Note · Durand Line · Pakistan and Afghanistan · Drawn in 1893 by Sir Mortimer Durand. · McMahon Line · India and China · Drawn at the Simla Convention, 1914; indgeo.x: Asked again and again: the Tropic of Cancer's 8 states , the Standard Meridian (82°30′E, Mirzapur) , the longest border (Bangladesh) and shortest (Afghanistan), and the Radcliffe, McMahon and Durand lines . · India lies wholly in the northern and eastern hemispheres , between latitudes 8°4′N and 37°6′N and longitudes 68°7′E and 97°25′E . The Tropic of Cancer (23°30′N) cuts it almost in half and crosses eight states. With 32.87 lakh km² it is the 7th largest country (2.4% of the world's land) — 3,214 km from north to south and 2,933 km from east to west. The sun rises in Arunachal about two hours before it does in Gujarat, so India keeps one time, set by the 82°30′E meridian through Mirzapur (UP) — 5½ hours ahead of GMT. Seven countries touch India by land; Bangladesh has the longest border and Afghanistan the shortest. indgeo.t: The Himalaya: ranges, peaks and passes
indgeo.x: Most asked: which state a pass is in (Zoji La, Rohtang, Shipki La, Nathu La, Bomdi La), the three parallel ranges (Himadri, Himachal, Shiwalik), and the highest peaks (K2, Kangchenjunga, Nanda Devi). · The Himalaya are young fold mountains , pushed up when the Indian plate ran into Asia. They curve for about 2,400 km from the Indus to the Brahmaputra. From north to south there are three parallel ranges: the Greater Himalaya (Himadri) with the highest snowy peaks; the Lesser Himalaya (Himachal) with ranges like Pir Panjal and Dhauladhar and hill towns like Shimla; and the low Shiwaliks , with flat valleys called duns behind them. North of the Himadri lie the Trans-Himalaya — Karakoram, Ladakh and Zaskar ranges — where K2 stands. In the east the mountains turn south as the Purvanchal : Patkai Bum, Naga hills and Mizo hills. The few gaps through the wall are the passes — Zoji La, Rohtang, Shipki La, Nathu La and Bomdi La. · Peaks · Peak · Where · Remember · Mount Everest · Nepal · 8,849 m — the world's highest; Sagarmatha in Nepal. · K2 (Godwin Austen) · Gilgit-Baltistan (PoK) · 8,611 m — India's highest peak as per India's map. · Kangchenjunga · Sikkim · 8,586 m — highest peak in Indian-administered territory; Favourites: Bhabar, Terai, Bhangar, Khadar ; the highest peaks of the south (Anamudi, Doddabetta, Guru Shikhar); Western vs Eastern Ghats ; and which state a plateau is in (Chotanagpur — Jharkhand). · The Northern Plains were built by the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra from silt. Coming down from the hills you cross four belts: Bhabar (pebbles, streams vanish), Terai (marshy, streams re-appear), then Bhangar (old alluvium with kankar) and Khadar (fresh alluvium of flood plains). South of the plains is the Peninsular Plateau , made of the oldest rocks. The Central Highlands (Malwa, Bundelkhand, Chotanagpur) lie north of the Narmada; the Deccan Plateau lies south. It is edged by the Western Ghats — high and unbroken, with Anamudi (2,695 m) the highest peak of the south — and the low, broken Eastern Ghats . The Aravallis , among the oldest fold mountains in the world, rise to Guru Shikhar at Mount Abu. · Words of the Northern Plains · Word · Meaning · Note · Bhabar · Belt of pebbles at the foot of the Shiwaliks where streams disappear · 8–16 km wide. · Terai · Wet, marshy belt south of the Bhabar where streams re-appear · Thick forest and wildlife. · Bhangar · Older alluvium, above flood level, with kankar · Khadar · Newer alluvium on the flood plains, renewed every year · Very fertile. · Doab · Land between two rivers · Ganga–Yamuna doab is the best known. · Dun · Long valley between the Lesser Himalaya and the Shiwaliks · Dehradun, Kotli Dun, Patli Dun. · Plateaus · Plateau · State · Note · Chotanagpur plateau · Jharkhand · India's 'mineral heartland'. · Malwa plateau · Madhya Pradesh · Black soil lava plateau. · Baghelkhand · Madhya Pradesh · Meghalaya (Shillong) plateau · Meghalaya · Cut off from the main plateau by the Garo–Rajmahal gap. · Karbi Anglong plateau · Assam · Deccan lava (trap) plateau · Maharashtra · Telangana plateau · Telangana · Mysore plateau · Karnataka · Dandakaranya · Chhattisgarh and Odisha · Marwar upland · Rajasthan · Peaks and hills of the peninsula and the north-east · Peak / hills · State · Remember · Anamudi · Kerala · 2,695 m — highest peak of South India (Anaimalai hills). · Doddabetta · Tamil Nadu · 2,637 m — highest peak of the Nilgiris. · Guru Shikhar · Rajasthan · 1,722 m — highest point of the Aravallis (Mount Abu). · Dhupgarh · Madhya Pradesh · Highest peak of the Satpuras (Pachmarhi). · Kalsubai · Maharashtra · Highest peak of Maharashtra. · Mullayanagiri · Karnataka · Highest peak of Karnataka. · Jindhagada (Arma Konda) · Andhra Pradesh · Highest peak of the Eastern Ghats. · Deomali · Odisha · Highest peak of Odisha. · Parasnath · Jharkhand · Highest peak of Jharkhand; Asked often: which coast is in which state (Konkan, Malabar, Coromandel, Northern Circars), Barren Island (only active volcano), Majuli (largest river island), and the channels — Ten Degree, Nine Degree, Eight Degree and Palk Strait. · The western coastal plain is narrow and lies between the Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea: Kachchh–Kathiawar (Gujarat), Konkan (Maharashtra–Goa), Kanara (Karnataka) and Malabar (Kerala, with its backwaters). The eastern coastal plain is wide, with big deltas: Utkal (Odisha), Northern Circars (Andhra) and Coromandel (Tamil Nadu). India has two island groups. The Andaman and Nicobar Islands in the Bay of Bengal are the tops of drowned mountains; Barren Island is India's only active volcano, and the Ten Degree Channel separates the Andamans from the Nicobars. Lakshadweep in the Arabian Sea is made of coral ; its capital is Kavaratti . Most asked: where a river rises (Gangotri, Yamunotri, Mansarovar), which river a tributary joins (Chambal → Yamuna, Son → Ganga, Beas → Sutlej), the Panch Prayag and the Indus Waters Treaty (1960) . · Three great rivers rise behind the Himalaya near Lake Mansarovar in Tibet: the Indus , the Sutlej and the Brahmaputra (Tsangpo) . The Indus flows west through Ladakh to Pakistan, picking up the five rivers of Punjab — Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej . Under the Indus Waters Treaty (1960) India got the eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) and Pakistan the western ones (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab); India put the treaty in abeyance in April 2025. The Ganga begins as the Bhagirathi at Gangotri (Gaumukh). The Alaknanda collects four rivers at four prayags and meets the Bhagirathi at Devprayag , where the Ganga is born. The Yamuna joins at Prayagraj ; Ghaghara, Gandak and Kosi join from the north; Son from the south. In Bangladesh the Ganga is the Padma and meets the Brahmaputra; together they form the world's largest delta, the Sundarbans . · Where Himalayan rivers rise · River · Source · Note · Indus · Bokhar Chu glacier, near Mansarovar (Tibet) · Enters India in Ladakh; Asked every year: the source of Narmada (Amarkantak), Godavari (Trimbakeshwar), Krishna (Mahabaleshwar), Kaveri (Talakaveri); west-flowing Narmada and Tapi; Godavari = longest peninsular river ; and the Vedic names of the Punjab rivers. · Peninsular rivers are older and fed by rain, so many shrink in summer. Most rise in the Western Ghats and flow east to the Bay of Bengal, building deltas : the Mahanadi , Godavari (the longest, about 1,465 km — 'Dakshin Ganga'), Krishna and Kaveri . Two big rivers flow west through rift valleys into the Arabian Sea and form estuaries , not deltas: the Narmada (from Amarkantak, between the Vindhyas and Satpuras) and the Tapi (from Multai). indgeo.x: Two question types never stop: “City X stands on which river?” and “Dam X is on which river?” Also: Tehri (highest dam) , Hirakud (longest) , Bhakra Nangal , DVC (1948) and the Ken–Betwa link . · Old cities grew beside rivers: Srinagar on the Jhelum, Delhi and Agra on the Yamuna, Varanasi and Patna on the Ganga, Lucknow on the Gomti, Ayodhya on the Sarayu, Jabalpur on the Narmada, Surat on the Tapi, Hyderabad on the Musi. After independence, Nehru called the big dams the “temples of modern India” . The Damodar Valley Corporation (1948) was the first multipurpose project. Bhakra on the Sutlej holds back the Gobind Sagar ; Hirakud on the Mahanadi is the longest dam; Tehri on the Bhagirathi is the highest . Most asked: Mawsynram (highest rainfall), the local winds — Loo, Mango showers, Kalbaisakhi — western disturbances , the retreating monsoon that waters Tamil Nadu, and El Niño . · India has a tropical monsoon climate. In summer the land heats up and a low-pressure belt (the ITCZ ) moves north; moist winds from the south-west rush in. The south-west monsoon reaches Kerala around 1 June and covers the whole country by about 8 July . Its Arabian Sea branch soaks the Western Ghats; its Bay of Bengal branch is funnelled into the Khasi hills, where Mawsynram gets the most rain on Earth. From mid-September the monsoon retreats . Winds now blow from the north-east and pick up moisture over the Bay of Bengal, so the Tamil Nadu coast gets its main rain in October–December . In winter, western disturbances from the Mediterranean bring rain to Punjab and Haryana — a gift for wheat. Asked every year: black soil = regur = cotton , alluvial = most widespread , laterite = leached , the forest types and their trees, and the ISFR numbers — forest cover %, MP largest, Mizoram highest share. · India's most widespread soil is alluvial , laid down by rivers across the Northern Plains. On the Deccan lava lies sticky black soil (regur) , which cracks in summer and 'ploughs itself' — perfect for cotton . Red soil gets its colour from iron oxide. Where heavy rain washes out the minerals, laterite forms — good for cashew and tea. The Thar has arid soil, and dry irrigated land can turn saline (reh, kallar, usar). Forests follow rainfall. Over 200 cm gives tropical evergreen forest (ebony, mahogany, rosewood) in the Western Ghats, the north-east and the Andamans. The most common type is tropical deciduous (monsoon) forest of teak and sal . Below 70 cm come thorn forests of babool and khejri. Asked often: which state a power plant is in — Tarapur, Kudankulam, Narora, Kaiga, Rawatbhata (nuclear); Vindhyachal, Korba (thermal); Bhadla, Pavagada, Rewa (solar); Muppandal (wind). · Coal still gives India most of its electricity, from giant plants like Vindhyachal (MP), the country's largest. Water came first, though: India's first hydro station ran at Sidrapong near Darjeeling in 1897 , and Shivanasamudra on the Kaveri followed in 1902. India's nuclear story began at Tarapur (Maharashtra) in 1969 ; today there are plants at Rawatbhata, Kalpakkam, Narora, Kakrapar, Kaiga and Kudankulam — the largest. The new power is the sun and wind: Bhadla in Rajasthan, Pavagada in Karnataka and Rewa in MP are huge solar parks, Khavda in Kutch is the world's largest renewable park, and Muppandal in Tamil Nadu is a giant wind farm. rivers.x: Asked again and again: where each river rises (Gangotri, Yamunotri, Trimbakeshwar, Mahabaleshwar, Talakaveri, Amarkantak), the longest rivers (Ganga in India, Godavari in the peninsula, Narmada flowing west), and the difference between Himalayan and peninsular rivers. · India's rivers come from two very different homes. The Himalayan rivers — the Indus, the Ganga and the Brahmaputra with their tributaries — are fed by snow and rain, so they flow all year. They are young: they cut deep gorges, carry huge loads of silt and keep changing course on the plains. The peninsular rivers are far older and are fed only by the monsoon. Most rise in the Western Ghats and run east to the Bay of Bengal — the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri build big deltas. Two big ones, the Narmada and the Tapi , run west through rift valleys and end in estuaries. About three-quarters of India drains into the Bay of Bengal. · Where the rivers rise · River · Source · Note · Ganga · Gangotri glacier (Gaumukh), Uttarakhand · It rises as the Bhagirathi and takes the name Ganga at Devprayag. · Yamuna · Yamunotri glacier, Uttarakhand · On the Bandarpunch range; Most asked: the Vedic names (Vitasta, Asikni, Parushni, Vipasha, Shutudri), the Indus Waters Treaty (1960) and who got which rivers, the Wular Lake on the Jhelum, and Harike , where the Beas meets the Sutlej. · The Indus rises near Lake Mansarovar in Tibet, flows north-west through Ladakh (past Leh), cuts a deep gorge round the Nanga Parbat massif and then turns south through Pakistan to the Arabian Sea near Karachi. In Ladakh the Zanskar and the Shyok join it. Five rivers give Punjab ('five waters') its name: the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej . In 1960 the Indus Waters Treaty , brokered by the World Bank , gave India the three eastern rivers and Pakistan the three western ones. rivers.t: The Ganga's source and the Yamuna
rivers.x: Most asked: the Bhagirathi and Alaknanda meet at Devprayag , the Panch Prayag , the Triveni Sangam at Prayagraj, the Chambal (ravines, gharials) and which city stands on which river. · The Ganga is born as the Bhagirathi at Gaumukh , the snout of the Gangotri glacier. The Alaknanda comes down from near Badrinath, collecting four rivers at four 'prayags' (confluences). At the fifth, Devprayag , the Bhagirathi joins it and the river becomes the Ganga . It enters the plains at Haridwar . The Yamuna rises at Yamunotri , flows past Delhi, Mathura and Agra, and joins the Ganga at the Triveni Sangam in Prayagraj. From the south it collects rivers of the Malwa plateau and Bundelkhand: the Chambal , Sindh , Betwa and Ken . · The Panch Prayag · Prayag · River that joins the Alaknanda · Note · Vishnuprayag · Dhauliganga · The first prayag downstream from Badrinath. · Nandprayag · Nandakini · Karnaprayag · Pindar · The Pindar comes from the Pindari glacier. · Rudraprayag · Mandakini · The Mandakini comes down from Kedarnath. · Devprayag · Bhagirathi · From here the river is called the Ganga. · Tributaries of the Yamuna · Tributary · Rises in · Note · Tons · Bandarpunch range (Uttarakhand) · The largest tributary of the Yamuna. · Hindon · Upper Shivaliks near Saharanpur (Uttar Pradesh) · Chambal · Janapav, near Mhow (Madhya Pradesh) · Famous for its ravines and gharials. · Sindh · Malwa plateau, Vidisha (Madhya Pradesh) · Betwa · Vindhyas, Raisen (Madhya Pradesh) · Ancient Vetravati; Orchha stands on it. · Ken · Kaimur hills (Madhya Pradesh) · It flows past Panna; the Ken–Betwa link starts here. · Cities on the Ganga and Yamuna · City · River · Note · Rishikesh and Haridwar · Ganga · At Haridwar the Ganga leaves the hills for the plains. · Kanpur · Ganga · Varanasi · Ganga · Patna · Ganga · The Gandak and the Son join nearby. · Bhagalpur · Ganga · The Vikramshila Gangetic Dolphin Sanctuary is here. · Delhi · Yamuna · Mathura and Agra · Yamuna · Prayagraj · Ganga and Yamuna (Sangam) · The Triveni Sangam — with the unseen Saraswati. · Kota · Chambal · Orchha · Betwa · The Chambal · Known for · Deep ravines (badlands) cut by gully erosion · Wildlife · National Chambal Sanctuary (Rajasthan, MP, UP) — gharials, Ganges river dolphins · Dams · Gandhi Sagar (MP), Rana Pratap Sagar (Rawatbhata), Jawahar Sagar, Kota Barrage (Rajasthan) · Panch Prayag downstream — “Vishnu Nand Karna Rudra Dev” : V ishnu-, N and-, K arna-, R udra-, D evprayag. rivers.x: Most asked: left- and right-bank tributaries (Gomti, Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi vs Yamuna, Son), the 'sorrow' rivers (Kosi — Bihar, Damodar — Bengal), Farakka and the Hooghly, and the Ganga as the National River . · On the plains, rivers from the Himalaya join the Ganga from the left (north) : the Ramganga, Gomti , Ghaghara , Gandak , Kosi and Mahananda. From the right (south) come the Yamuna and the Son from the old plateau. At Farakka (West Bengal) a barrage sends part of the water into the Bhagirathi–Hooghly , which flows past Kolkata to the sea and is joined by the Damodar . The main stream enters Bangladesh as the Padma , meets the Brahmaputra (Jamuna) and then the Meghna, building the Ganga–Brahmaputra (Sundarbans) delta — the largest delta in the world. · Where the tributaries join the Ganga · Tributary · Joins the Ganga · Note · Ramganga · Near Kannauj · A left-bank tributary from the Kumaon hills; Corbett National Park is on it. · Gomti · Near Ghazipur · Left bank; Lucknow and Jaunpur stand on it. · Ghaghara · Near Chhapra · Left bank; the Karnali in Nepal. Most asked: the names along the way (Tsangpo → Siang/Dihang → Brahmaputra → Jamuna), Majuli (largest river island), its tributaries (Subansiri, Manas, Teesta), and the Bogibeel and Dhola–Sadiya bridges. · The Brahmaputra rises near Mansarovar as the Yarlung Tsangpo and flows east across Tibet. Near Namcha Barwa it takes a sharp U-turn and plunges through one of the world's deepest gorges into Arunachal Pradesh as the Siang (Dihang) . Near Sadiya the Dibang and Lohit join it and it becomes the Brahmaputra . In the Assam valley it is wide and braided , full of sandbars and islands like Majuli . It floods every monsoon. It enters Bangladesh as the Jamuna , joins the Padma and the Meghna, and reaches the Bay of Bengal. Further south, the Barak rises in the Manipur hills, flows past Silchar and also ends in the Meghna. · One river, many names · Where · Name · Note · Tibet · Yarlung Tsangpo · It flows east for about 1,600 km, then turns round Namcha Barwa. · Arunachal Pradesh · Siang (Dihang) · It cuts a deep gorge into India. · Assam, after the Dibang and Lohit join near Sadiya · Brahmaputra · Bangladesh · Jamuna · Bangladesh, after it meets the Ganga (Padma) at Goalundo · Padma · The last stretch to the Bay of Bengal · Meghna · Tributaries of the Brahmaputra · Tributary · Comes from · Note · Subansiri · Arunachal Pradesh · The largest tributary; the Lower Subansiri project is on it. · Kameng (Jia Bhareli) · Arunachal Pradesh · Manas · Bhutan · Manas National Park is on it. · Sankosh · Bhutan · Teesta · Sikkim · It joins the Brahmaputra in Bangladesh. · Dhansiri · Nagaland · A south-bank tributary. · Kopili · Meghalaya · A south-bank tributary. · On the Brahmaputra · Place · River · Note · Majuli · Brahmaputra · The world's largest river island; a district since 2016. · Umananda · Brahmaputra · Among the smallest inhabited river islands, at Guwahati. · Guwahati, Tezpur and Dibrugarh · Brahmaputra · Bogibeel Bridge · Brahmaputra · India's longest rail-cum-road bridge (2018), near Dibrugarh. · Bhupen Hazarika Setu (Dhola–Sadiya) · Lohit · A long road bridge (2017) in Assam. · Silchar · Barak · Kaziranga National Park · Brahmaputra · On the south bank. · Brahmaputra facts · A 'male' river · Named as the son of Brahma · Channel in Assam · Braided — many channels and sandbars · National Waterway 2 · Brahmaputra, Dhubri to Sadiya · Barak · Rises in the Manipur hills; flows past Silchar; in Bangladesh it splits into the Surma and Kushiyara and joins the Meghna · The name chain — “Tsang-Siang-Brahma-Jamuna-Padma-Meghna” : Tibet, Arunachal, Assam, then three names in Bangladesh. · Teesta joins the Brahmaputra in Bangladesh , not in India. The Dhola–Sadiya (Bhupen Hazarika) bridge is over the Lohit ; Bogibeel is over the Brahmaputra. In Bangladesh the Brahmaputra is the Jamuna — not the Yamuna of India. · Yarlung Tsangpo (Tibet) → Siang/Dihang (Arunachal) → Brahmaputra (Assam) → Jamuna (Bangladesh). · It turns round Namcha Barwa; the Dibang and Lohit join near Sadiya. · Majuli is the world's largest river island (district since 2016). · Tributaries: Subansiri (largest), Kameng, Manas, Sankosh, Teesta; Dhansiri and Kopili from the south. · Bogibeel (2018) — longest rail-cum-road bridge; Dhola–Sadiya over the Lohit (2017).
