rivers.x: Most asked: Narmada and Tapi in rift valleys , estuaries not deltas , Mahi crosses the Tropic of Cancer twice , the Luni ending in the Rann of Kutch, Jog Falls on the Sharavathi and Periyar , Kerala's longest river. · The Narmada and the Tapi do not follow the tilt of the Deccan. They flow west along rift valleys — long troughs where the land sank between faults: the Narmada between the Vindhyas and Satpuras , the Tapi south of the Satpuras. They carry little silt and meet the sea in tidal estuaries at Bharuch and Surat instead of deltas. From Gujarat come the Sabarmati and Mahi ; from the Aravallis the Luni , which dies in the Rann of Kutch . The many short, swift rivers of the Western Ghats — the Mandovi, Sharavathi, Netravati, Periyar — race down to the Arabian Sea in a few dozen kilometres, making waterfalls like Jog and Dudhsagar . · Where the west-flowing rivers end · River · Ends in · Note · Narmada · Gulf of Khambhat, at Bharuch · An estuary, not a delta. · Tapi · Gulf of Khambhat, near Surat · Sabarmati · Gulf of Khambhat · Ahmedabad and the Gandhi Ashram stand on it. · Mahi · Gulf of Khambhat · It crosses the Tropic of Cancer twice. · Luni · Rann of Kutch · It never reaches the sea; salty after Balotra. · Mandovi · Arabian Sea at Panaji · Dudhsagar Falls is on it. · Zuari · Arabian Sea near Mormugao · Sharavathi · Arabian Sea at Honnavar · Jog Falls is on it. · Netravati · Arabian Sea at Mangaluru · Periyar · Arabian Sea near Kochi · The longest river of Kerala. · Bharathapuzha · Arabian Sea at Ponnani · Also called the Nila — Kerala's second-longest river. · Narmada, Tapi and the west coast · Feature · River · Note · Flows through a rift valley between the Vindhyas and the Satpuras · Narmada · Flows through a rift valley between the Satpuras and the Satmala–Ajanta hills · Tapi · Dhuandhar Falls and the Marble Rocks of Bhedaghat (Jabalpur) · Narmada · Omkareshwar and Maheshwar · Narmada · Sardar Sarovar Dam and the Statue of Unity (Kevadia) · Narmada · Surat and the Ukai Dam · Tapi · Ahmedabad · Sabarmati · Crosses the Tropic of Cancer twice · Mahi · Jog Falls · Sharavathi · Idukki Arch Dam · Periyar · Narmada in short · Length · About 1,312 km — the longest west-flowing river · Source → mouth · Amarkantak (MP) → Gulf of Khambhat at Bharuch (Gujarat) · Through · Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra (border), Gujarat · Big dams · Indira Sagar (MP), Sardar Sarovar (Gujarat) · Movement · Narmada Bachao Andolan (Medha Patkar) against Sardar Sarovar's displacement · West-flowers into the Gulf of Khambhat — “NT SaM” : N armada, T api, Sa barmati, M ahi. Most asked: dam → river (Tehri–Bhagirathi, Bhakra–Sutlej, Hirakud–Mahanadi, Nagarjuna Sagar–Krishna, Sardar Sarovar–Narmada) and waterfall → river (Jog–Sharavathi, Chitrakote–Indravati, Hundru–Subarnarekha, Dudhsagar–Mandovi). · After independence Nehru called the big dams the 'temples of modern India' . Bhakra on the Sutlej, Hirakud on the Mahanadi and Nagarjuna Sagar on the Krishna brought irrigation and power; the Damodar Valley Corporation (1948) tamed the 'Sorrow of Bengal'. Later dams like Tehri and Sardar Sarovar sparked protests over the people and forests they flooded. Most asked: which landform belongs to which stage (V-valley and gorge — upper; meander and oxbow lake — middle; delta — mouth), delta vs estuary , and drainage patterns (dendritic, radial, centripetal, trellis). · A river does three jobs: it erodes , it carries and it deposits . In its upper course , steep and fast, it cuts down — making V-shaped valleys, gorges, waterfalls and potholes . In the middle course it swings from side to side in meanders ; when the neck of a loop is cut through in a flood, the old loop is left as an oxbow lake . In the lower course , slow and heavy with silt, it builds floodplains and levees , splits into braided channels and, at the sea, piles silt into a delta — unless strong tides wash it away and leave an rivers.x: Most asked: which states share a dispute (Kaveri, Krishna, Narmada, Mahadayi), Article 262 , the Ken–Betwa link , National Waterways 1, 2 and 3 , and Namami Gange . · Rivers cross state borders, and in a dry year every state wants more water. Article 262 of the Constitution lets Parliament make laws for inter-state river disputes and keep them away from the courts; under the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 the Centre sets up tribunals . The Kaveri fight between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu is the most famous. To move water from surplus rivers to dry ones, India plans to link rivers (National Water Development Agency, 1982). The first, the Ken–Betwa link in Bundelkhand, began in December 2024. Rivers are also highways: National Waterway 1 on the Ganga is the longest. · River disputes · River · States · Note · Kaveri · Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Puducherry · Tribunal 1990, award 2007, Supreme Court 2018; natparks.x: Most asked: the first national park (Hailey, now Corbett, 1936), the largest (Hemis) and smallest (South Button Island), the state with the most (Madhya Pradesh), the floating park (Keibul Lamjao), and the difference between a national park and a sanctuary . · A national park is the strictest kind of protected area under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 . No grazing, no private rights, no human activity except tourism and research is allowed inside. A wildlife sanctuary is gentler: some local use goes on. A state government declares both; only the state legislature (with the National Board for Wildlife's advice) can change a national park's boundary. India's first national park was Hailey National Park (1936), in the Kumaon hills — today's Jim Corbett . India now has about 106 national parks, covering a little over 1% of its land. Madhya Pradesh has the most. · Records · Record · Park · Note · The first national park · Jim Corbett (Uttarakhand) · Set up in 1936 as Hailey National Park; renamed Ramganga, then Corbett (1957). · The largest national park · Hemis (Ladakh) · About 4,400 sq km — home of the snow leopard. · The smallest national park · South Button Island (Andaman and Nicobar) · Less than 1 sq km. · The state with the most national parks · Madhya Pradesh · Eleven — with the Andaman and Nicobar Islands (nine) close behind. · The only floating national park · Keibul Lamjao (Manipur) · On the phumdis of Loktak Lake — home of the sangai deer. · Where cheetahs came back to India · Kuno (Madhya Pradesh) · Project Cheetah, 17 September 2022 — cheetahs from Namibia. · The only home of the wild Asiatic lion · Gir (Gujarat) · The largest mangrove national park · Sundarban (West Bengal) · Also a tiger reserve and World Heritage site. · National park, sanctuary, tiger reserve · National park · Wildlife sanctuary · Law · Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 (Section 35) · Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 (Section 18) · Human activity · None allowed — no grazing, no private rights · Some allowed if it does not harm wildlife · Boundaries · Changed only by the state legislature · Changed by the state government · About how many · About 106 · About 570 · Tiger reserve? · A tiger reserve is a separate label (NTCA) — its core is often a national park · Same · Records in one breath — “First Corbett, Big Hemis, Tiny Button, Most MP, Floating Manipur” . · The largest national park is Hemis , but the largest tiger reserve is Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam and the largest biosphere reserve is the Great Rann of Kutch. clozerc.t: How SSC sets cloze and RC — and the method
clozerc.h: SSC क्लोज़ टेस्ट और अपठित गद्यांश कैसे पूछता है — हल करने की विधि
clozerc.x: In most Tier 1 shifts of SSC CGL and CHSL, the English section (25 questions) carries one cloze passage with 5 blanks and one reading passage with 5 questions — about ten questions, or 20 marks, between them. They are the slowest questions of the section, so a fixed method saves the most time. · A cloze test is a short paragraph — usually 120 to 180 words — with five words taken out. For each gap you get four words, and only one fits the grammar and the meaning of the passage. The examiner tests the same small set of skills again and again: words that go together ( heavy rain ), the right preposition ( depend on ), the right linking word ( however , therefore ), the right tense, the right word among near-synonyms, and articles. A reading comprehension (RC) passage is a little longer, often 250 to 400 words, on a neutral topic: the environment, health, technology, society or the history of an idea. The five questions nearly always come from the same five families: the main idea or title , a fact stated in the passage, an inference , the meaning of a word as used, and the tone of the author. Neither test needs outside knowledge. Every answer is decided by the passage itself. · The two tests at a glance · Cloze test · Reading comprehension · How many questions · 5 blanks, one passage · 5 questions on one passage · Length (typical) · 120–180 words · 250–400 words · What it checks · Grammar, collocation, linking words, word choice · Understanding: main idea, facts, inference, vocabulary, tone · Where the answer is · In the words around the blank and the flow of the passage · In particular lines of the passage — never in your general knowledge · Marks (Tier 1) · 2 each, −0.5 for a wrong answer · 2 each, −0.5 for a wrong answer · Time to aim for · 3–4 minutes for the whole passage · 5–7 minutes for the whole passage · Question stems and their type · The question says… · Type · Where to look · Which is the most suitable title for the passage? · Main idea / title · The whole passage — often the first and last lines · What is the central theme of the passage? · Main idea / title · The point every paragraph supports · According to the passage, … · Fact / detail · The line that holds the key word of the question · Which of these is NOT mentioned in the passage? · Fact / detail · Check each option against the text · Which of the following can be inferred? · Inference · What the lines suggest without saying it outright · The author would most likely agree that … · Inference · The author's stated views, taken one small step further · The word ‘…’ as used in the passage means · Vocabulary in context · The sentence the word sits in · Choose the word opposite in meaning to ‘…’ · Vocabulary in context · The sentence the word sits in · The tone of the passage is · Tone / attitude · The author's choice of words: praise, blame, worry, irony · The author's attitude towards … is · Tone / attitude · How the author describes that thing · The cloze method in five steps · Step · What you do · Why · 1. Name the slot · For each blank, ask: what part of speech fits here — noun, verb, preposition, linking word, article? · Often two options are the wrong part of speech and go at once · 3. Look both sides · Read the words just before and just after the blank · Collocations ( pay ___ attention ) and prepositions ( ___ of ) are decided by the neighbours · 4. Check the logic · Does the sentence agree with, contrast with, or follow from the one before? · This decides linking words: however (contrast), therefore (result), moreover (addition) · 5. Read it back · Put your five answers in and read the passage once more · A wrong choice usually sounds wrong when the passage is read as a whole · The RC method in five steps · Step · What you do · Why · 1. Skim the passage · Read it once at a steady speed; note what each paragraph is about in two or three words · You build a map, so you can find any line again in seconds · 2. Read the question · Find its type (title, fact, inference, word, tone) and its key word · The type tells you where to look and what a right answer looks like · 3. Go back to the lines · Find the key word in the passage and read the sentence before and after it · Answers are taken from the text, not from memory of it · 4. Strike out · Remove options that are too narrow, too broad, extreme ( always , never ) or not in the passage · Wrong options are usually wrong for one of these four reasons · 5. Prove it · Before you mark, point to the words that support your answer · If you cannot point to them, think again — or leave it (negative marking) · undefined · Worked cloze 1: answers and reasoning · Blank · Answer · Why, and why not the others · 1 · cooler · than follows the blank, so a comparative is needed; cool , coolest and coldly cannot go with than . · 2 · into · Water sinks into the soil (movement inside). Onto is movement on to a surface; at and over do not show going in. · 3 · Yet · The sentence goes against what came before (trees help, yet they were cut): contrast. Therefore is result; Moreover and Besides add a point. · 4 · rarely · Planners have realised the road is not worth the loss of trees — rarely worth says that. Always and mostly say the opposite; highly worth is not English. · 5 · take · The fixed pair is take care of . We do not make , do or give care of . · undefined · Worked RC 1: the five questions · Question · Answer · How to find it · Best title? · How the germ theory changed medicine · It covers the old belief, the new idea, the resistance and today's practice. ‘Bad air in history’ is only the first line — too narrow. · According to the passage, what did some doctors refuse to do? · Wash their hands between patients · Stated in line 3 — find the key word refused . · What can be inferred about hospitals before cleanliness was adopted? · More patients died in them · ‘Hospitals that adopted cleanliness saw far fewer deaths’ implies higher deaths before. Not stated outright — inferred. · ‘Adopted’ as used in the passage means · Took up and began to use · A hospital cannot ‘take a child as its own’ — the other dictionary sense does not fit here. · The tone of the passage? · Informative · It explains facts without praise, blame or irony. · Cloze: “Whole – Slot – Sides – Sense – Sound.” Read the whole, name the slot, look at both sides, check the sense, sound it out. RC: “Type – Key word – Lines – Prove.” · In RC, an option can be true in real life and still be wrong, because the passage does not say it. Options with always, never, all, only usually go further than the passage. In a cloze test, do not fill each blank by its own sentence alone — the tense and tone of the whole passage decide many blanks. · Tier 1 English usually has one cloze passage (5 blanks) and one RC passage (5 questions) — about 20 marks. · Cloze method: read the whole passage, name the slot, look at both sides of the blank, check the logic, read it back. · RC method: skim, find the question type and key word, go back to the lines, strike out bad options, prove your answer. · RC question families: main idea or title, fact, inference, vocabulary in context, tone. · Answer only from the passage; true-in-life but unstated options are wrong. · Extreme options (always, never, only, all) are usually traps.

Nearly every cloze passage has one blank decided by a collocation — a word that habitually goes with another: heavy rain , make a decision , pay attention , raise awareness . The wrong options are often near-synonyms that mean the same but are simply not said. · Why do we say heavy rain and not strong rain , or strong tea and not powerful tea ? There is no rule of logic — English speakers have just always put these words together. Such habitual partners are called collocations . The commonest kind in a cloze test is a verb with a noun : we make a mistake but do homework, take a break but pay attention. The second kind is an adjective with a noun ( heavy traffic , high temperature ). The third is a fixed pair joined by and ( safe and sound , pros and cons ), whose order never changes. You cannot work these out — you learn them as whole phrases, the way you learn a phone number. · Verb + noun: which verb goes with it? · Words · Verb · Example · ___ a mistake · make · Everyone makes a mistake now and then. · ___ an effort · make · She made an effort to speak slowly. · ___ a wish · make · Close your eyes and make a wish. · ___ progress · make · The patient is making good progress. · ___ the bed · make · He makes the bed every morning. · ___ a noise · make · Please do not make a noise in the library. · ___ homework · do · The children do their homework after tea. · ___ the dishes · do · I will do the dishes tonight. · ___ (someone) a favour · do · Could you do me a favour? · ___ a diary · keep · He kept a diary during the trip. · ___ calm · keep · Keep calm and leave the building. · ___ track of · keep · Keep track of your expenses. · ___ awareness · raise · The campaign raised awareness about clean water. · ___ funds · raise · Students raised funds for the flood victims. · ___ the alarm · raise · The guard raised the alarm when he saw smoke. · Fixed pairs: the order never changes · Begins · Ends with · Meaning · bread and … · butter · one’s means of living · safe and … · sound · unharmed · null and … · void · having no legal force · odds and … · ends · small things of little value · pros and … · cons · arguments for and against · ups and … · downs · good and bad times · law and … · order · the keeping of public peace · wear and … · tear · damage from ordinary use · by and … · large · on the whole · now and … · then · sometimes · hale and … · hearty · healthy and strong · kith and … · kin · friends and relatives · part and … · parcel · an essential part · first and … · foremost · most importantly · spick and … · span · neat and clean · hue and … · cry · a loud public protest · Adjective + noun: the natural partner · Say · Not · Note · heavy rain, heavy traffic · strong rain, big traffic · heavy for a large amount · strong tea, strong coffee · powerful tea · strong for a lot of flavour · high temperature, high price · tall temperature, big price · high for levels and amounts · dense fog, dense forest · crowded fog · thick fog is also right · deep sleep, sound sleep · strong sleep · — · sharp memory, sharp rise · pointed memory · sharp for quick or clear · hard work · heavy work (for effort) · hard for effort · bitter truth · sour truth · — · narrow escape · thin escape · only just escaped · golden opportunity · silver opportunity · a very good chance · open secret · public secret · something everyone knows · undefined · MAKE creates something new (a cake, a plan, a noise, a profit). DO is for work, tasks and duties (homework, the dishes, one’s duty, a favour). When in doubt: make = produce, do = perform. · Commit goes with crime , murder and suicide , but we make a mistake. We raise funds and awareness (the verb takes an object) — things rise by themselves (prices rise). Lodge or file a complaint, not put one. · A collocation is a word pair English speakers habitually use: heavy rain, strong tea, make a decision. · make — a mistake, an effort, a profit, progress, a noise; do — homework, the dishes, a favour, one’s best, research. · take — a photograph, a break, place; pay — attention, tribute, a fine, the price; catch — a cold, fire, a glimpse. · keep — a secret, a diary, calm, track of; raise — awareness, funds, the alarm; give — birth to, rise to. · Fixed pairs never change order: safe and sound, null and void, pros and cons, law and order, wear and tear. · Commit a crime but make a mistake; raise funds but prices rise.

About one blank in three of a cloze passage is a preposition . Most are decided by the word just before it — depend on , accused of , prefer X to Y — and the rest by time and place ( at 6 o’clock, on Monday, in June). · A preposition is a small word that links a noun to the rest of the sentence: in , on , at , of , for , with , from , to . It is the hardest blank to guess, because the meaning seldom helps — we are interested in music but fond of it, and both mean almost the same. The way through is to learn each word with its preposition, as one unit: not accuse but accuse … of ; not prefer but prefer … to . For time and place, three words do most of the work: at for a point, on for a day or a surface, in for a longer period or an enclosed space. · Words and the preposition they take · Word · Preposition clozerc.h: संयोजक शब्द — however, therefore, despite, although
clozerc.x: One or two blanks in almost every cloze passage need a linking word . The test is about logic — does the next idea go against, follow from, or add to the last one? — and then about grammar : despite takes a noun, although takes a clause. · Linking words are the road signs of a passage. However says ‘turn: the next idea goes against the last’. Therefore says ‘this follows from what came before’. Moreover says ‘one more point in the same direction’. So the method is simple. Read the sentence before the blank and the sentence after it, and ask what the second does to the first. Does it contrast with it? Is it a result ? An addition ? A reason , a condition , an example ? Once you know the job, only one or two options remain, and the grammar picks between them. Example: ‘It rained heavily. ___, the match went ahead.’ A match going ahead in heavy rain is unexpected — a contrast — so Nevertheless or However , not Therefore . · Connectors and their jobs · Connector · Job · Example · however · Contrast · The plan was cheap; however, it failed. · although · Contrast · Although it rained, the match went ahead. · despite · Contrast · Despite the rain, the match went ahead. · in spite of · Contrast · In spite of his injury, he finished the race. · nevertheless · Contrast · He was tired; nevertheless, he kept working. · whereas · Contrast · Cities are crowded, whereas villages are quiet. · on the other hand · Contrast · City life is fast; village life, on the other hand, is slow. · therefore · Result · The roads were flooded; therefore, schools were shut. · consequently · Result · The factory polluted the river; consequently, the fish died. · hence · Result · The shop was crowded; hence, we left. · as a result · Result · Prices rose; clozerc.t: Tense and verb form from the context
clozerc.x: When the options are four forms of one verb ( has been working / is working / was working / works ), the blank is about tense . The passage gives the answer through signal words ( since , by the time , yesterday ) and through the tense of the sentences around it. · A passage keeps to one time frame. A story about the freedom movement is told in the past; an article on climate change speaks of the present and the future. So the first clue to a tense blank is the tense of the whole passage — which you noticed on your first reading. The second clue is a signal word . Since 2018 or for three years joined to ‘now’ calls for the present perfect ( has worked , has been working ). By the time + a past event calls for the past perfect ( had left ). Yesterday , ago , last year call for the simple past. The third clue is a fixed verb pattern : look forward to takes -ing ; used to takes the plain verb; make someone takes the plain verb without to . · Signal words and the tense they call for · Signal · Tense or form · Example · every day, usually, always (a habit) · Simple present · She walks for an hour every morning. · a universal truth · Simple present · Water boils at 100 °C. · now, at the moment, Look! · Present continuous · Look! The children are playing. · since 2018 / for three years (up to now) · Present perfect · She has worked here since 2018. · just, already, yet · Present perfect · The train has just left. · yesterday, ago, last year, in 2010 · Simple past · He visited Agra last year. · while + an action going on in the past · Past continuous · While I was cooking, the lights went out. · by the time / before + a past event · Past perfect · The train had left before we arrived. · tomorrow, next week · Simple future · We will meet tomorrow. · at this time tomorrow · Future continuous · At this time tomorrow I will be flying to Chennai. · by next year / by the time + a future event · Future perfect · By next year she will have finished the course. · If + simple past (unreal now) · would + V1 · If I were rich, I would build a school. · If + had + V3 (unreal past) · would have + V3 · If he had studied, he would have passed. · It is high time … · Past form · It is high time we left. · The verb form after certain words · Word or pattern · Form that follows · Example · look forward to · -ing · I look forward to meeting you. · be used to (be familiar with) · -ing · He is used to getting up early. · avoid · -ing · She avoided answering. · enjoy · -ing · They enjoy reading. · mind · -ing · Would you mind closing the door? · finish · -ing · He finished writing the report. · used to (past habit) · V1 (bare) · He used to walk to school. · let (someone) · V1 (bare) · Let him speak. · make (someone) · V1 (bare) · The teacher made us repeat the poem. · had better · V1 (bare) · You had better leave now. · would rather · V1 (bare) · I would rather stay home. · decide · to + V1 · She decided to join the course. · want · to + V1 · They want to win. · refuse · to + V1 · He refused to sign. · hope · to + V1 · We hope to see you soon. · have (something) … · V3 (past participle) · I had my watch repaired. · get (something) … · V3 (past participle) · She got her eyes tested. · undefined · “Used TO + V1, used to + ING” : I used to walk (I no longer do) but I am used to walking (it is normal for me). The little word am / is / are before used to changes everything. · Since needs the present perfect, not the simple present: I have lived here since 2015 , not I live here since 2015 . In an if -clause about the future, use the simple present: If it rains tomorrow , not If it will rain . After wish about the past, use the past perfect: I wish I had known . · Keep to the tense of the passage unless a signal word changes it. · since / for + up to now → present perfect; by the time + past → past perfect; yesterday, ago → simple past. · If + present → will; if + past → would + V1; if + had + V3 → would have + V3. · look forward to, be used to, avoid, enjoy, mind, finish → -ing. · used to, let, make, had better, would rather → V1; decide, want, refuse, hope → to + V1; have/get something → V3. · It is high time and wish (present) take the past form.

clozerc.t: Near-synonyms: the right word by meaning and tone
clozerc.h: समान-अर्थी शब्दों में सही शब्द — अर्थ और भाव
clozerc.x: Some blanks offer four words of about the same meaning — famous, renowned, notorious, celebrated . Only one fits the shade of the sentence (good or bad), or the exact meaning ( economic vs economical ). Look-alike pairs ( affect/effect , principal/principle ) are also tested this way. · Words that look alike in a dictionary can feel very different in a sentence. A thrifty man and a miserly man both spend little — but the first is praised and the second is blamed. Childlike wonder is charming; childish behaviour is silly. Famous and notorious both mean ‘well known’, but only a criminal is notorious. So when the options look like synonyms, ask two questions. First, is the sentence approving or disapproving? Words such as finally arrested , shameful or praised tell you. Second, what exactly is meant? clozerc.h: आर्टिकल और निर्धारक (a, an, the, few, little)
clozerc.x: Article blanks appear now and then: a or an (decided by the sound , not the letter), the for something particular or unique, or no article . Determiners such as few / a few , little / a little , much / many are tested in the same slot. · A and an mean ‘one, any one’. Which you use depends on the first sound of the next word: an before a vowel sound ( an hour , an MBA ), a before a consonant sound ( a university , a one-rupee coin ). The spelling can mislead you; say the word aloud. The points to something particular — one the reader already knows, or one of a kind: the sun , the Ganga , the Ramayana , the best student .
