clozerc.t: RC: the main idea and the title
clozerc.h: अपठित गद्यांश: मुख्य विचार और शीर्षक
clozerc.x: Almost every SSC passage has one question on the main idea , the central theme or the most suitable title . The right option covers the whole passage; the wrong ones are a single detail, something far too wide, or a twist of what was said. · Imagine telling a friend in one breath what a passage was about. That sentence is its main idea . A title is the same idea squeezed into a few words. The main idea is usually stated or shaped in the first sentence and rounded off in the last . The middle gives reasons and examples. So read the first and last lines again, and ask: which option would every sentence of the passage agree to support? Then test each option. Is it too narrow — only one example? Too broad — about the whole world when the passage is about one town? Distorted — the passage’s words, but a claim it never made? Extreme — always , never , all ? What survives is the answer. · Testing a main-idea option · The option is… · What it looks like · Verdict · Too narrow · One example or one sentence of the passage · Wrong — it is a detail · Too broad · A claim about everything (all cities, the whole world) · Wrong — the passage is more limited · Distorted · Uses the passage’s words but changes the claim · Wrong — check it against the lines · Extreme · Always, never, all, only, completely · Usually wrong · Outside · True in life but not discussed in the passage · Wrong · Just right · Covers the beginning, the middle and the end · Right · Where the main idea hides · Passage shape · Where to look · Example · Problem → solution · The solution, often in the last line · ‘Unless shoppers carry their own bags, rules will change little.’ · Old belief → new view · The new view · ‘Zero is a number, not merely an empty place.’ · Gains and losses · Both sides together · ‘The change has given privacy … at the same time, the elderly live alone.’ · Praise of one thing · The thing and why it matters · ‘A brisk walk … its benefits are remarkable.’ · undefined · “First line + last line = main idea.” Then use the umbrella test : the right option is an umbrella under which every sentence of the passage can stand. · A title that repeats a striking word from the passage is not automatically right. ‘Water Tankers’ appears in a passage on rainwater harvesting, but it is only a detail. And a title should name the topic , not a moral the passage never draws. · The main idea is the one claim every sentence supports; a title says it in a few words. · Look at the first and last lines first. · Reject options that are too narrow (one detail), too broad, distorted, extreme or outside the passage. · For a ‘gains and losses’ passage, the main idea mentions both sides. · A striking word from the passage does not make an option right.

clozerc.h: अपठित गद्यांश: तथ्य और विवरण के प्रश्न
clozerc.x: Two of the five RC questions are usually fact questions — ‘According to the passage…’, ‘Which is NOT mentioned…’, ‘Why did…’. They are the surest marks in the section, because the answer is written in the passage, though usually in different words . · A fact question is a treasure hunt with a map. The key word of the question — a name, a number, an unusual word — is the map. Find it in the passage, read the sentence it is in and the one around it, and the answer is there. The examiner rarely copies the passage word for word into the right option. He rephrases it: ‘buy far fewer water tankers’ may become ‘need less water from outside’. Meanwhile a wrong option often copies the passage’s words exactly but gets the fact wrong. So match the meaning , not the words. For a NOT mentioned question, turn it round: tick off each option you can find in the passage; the one left over is the answer. · Fact question stems and the move to make · Stem · Move · According to the passage, … · Find the key word; read one sentence before and after · Which of the following is true? · Check each option against the passage; one contradiction kills it · Which is NOT mentioned / NOT true? · Tick off the options you find; the leftover is the answer · Why did …? · Look for because, since, so, as a result near the key word · What happened when / after …? · Follow the order of events in the passage · How wrong fact options are made · Trick · Example from a passage on electric buses · Opposite of the text · ‘Fares are higher than on the old buses’ (the passage says they are the same) · Right words, wrong link · ‘The buses are charged at stops during the day’ (they are charged overnight at the depot) · Not in the passage · ‘The buses were made in India’ (never stated) · Wrong number or name · ‘Each bus can run 100 km on a charge’ (the passage says 200) · undefined · “Key word → line → meaning.” Never answer a fact question from memory of the passage; go back to the line every time — it takes ten seconds and saves two and a half marks. · An option that copies a whole phrase from the passage can still be wrong if it joins it to the wrong subject or time . And in a NOT question, an option that is true in real life but absent from the passage is the answer, not a wrong option. · Fact questions: According to the passage, which is true, which is NOT mentioned, why did. · Find the key word, read its sentence and the one around it. · Right options usually rephrase the passage; wrong ones often copy its words with a changed fact. · For NOT mentioned, tick off what you find; the leftover is the answer. · Watch for opposites, wrong links, wrong numbers and outside facts.

‘It can be inferred…’, ‘The passage suggests…’, ‘The author would most likely agree…’. One RC question in many shifts asks for what the passage implies but does not say. The right answer is one small, safe step beyond the text — never a leap. · If a friend comes in with a wet umbrella, you infer that it is raining outside. You did not see the rain, but the umbrella makes it almost certain. That is an inference : a conclusion the facts force on you. Notice what you did not infer: that it will rain all week, or that your friend hates rain. Those may be true, but the umbrella does not prove them. Inference questions work the same way. The right option is something the passage makes almost certain . A wrong option either just repeats a stated fact (that is a fact question, not an inference), or goes much further than the passage allows. · Is it a sound inference? · The option… · Verdict · Why · Must be true if the passage is true · Right · This is what an inference is · Could be true, but the passage does not show it · Wrong · A guess, not an inference · Goes against something the passage says · Wrong · A contradiction · Uses extreme words (all, never, only) · Usually wrong · Too big a step · Brings in outside knowledge · Wrong · The passage must support it · Clues that point to an inference · The passage says… · You may infer… · ‘X can raise the level of water in wells’ · The level was lower before · ‘less need to keep change’ · They needed to keep change before · ‘If batteries become cheaper too …’ · Batteries are costly now · ‘not wicked; they simply believe …’ · They mean well · ‘Truly, technology has made our lives simpler’ after describing a long process · The author means the opposite (irony) · undefined · The “must be true” test : read each option and ask, ‘If everything in the passage is true, must this be true as well?’ Only one option passes. · An option that is stated in so many words is not an inference, though it is true — prefer the option that follows from the text. And do not choose a statement just because you agree with it. · An inference is what the passage makes almost certain without saying it. · The right option is one small step from the text; wrong ones are leaps, guesses or contradictions. · Use the must-be-true test on every option. · ‘The author would most likely agree’ asks for a view in line with the author’s stated views. · Irony: when praise does not match the facts, the author means the opposite.

One or two RC questions ask the meaning (or the opposite) of a word ‘ as used in the passage ’. The trap is a true dictionary meaning that does not fit this sentence — modest as ‘humble in manner’ when the passage means ‘a modest budget’ (a small one). · Many English words have several meanings. Recall can mean ‘remember’ or ‘call back a faulty product’. Common can mean ‘widespread’ or ‘vulgar’. Struck can mean ‘hit’ or ‘went on strike’. In a passage, only one meaning is alive. So never answer a vocabulary question from the word alone. Go to its sentence and replace the word with each option . The right option keeps the sentence’s meaning; a wrong one makes it odd or changes it. For an antonym question, first find the word’s meaning in the sentence, then pick its opposite in that same sense. · Words whose meaning changes with the sentence · Word · In this sentence… · …it means · modest · The mission was run on a modest budget. · small, limited · modest · Despite his fame, he remained modest. · humble · recall · Many people recall their first library visit. · remember · recall · The company will recall the faulty phones. · call back · common · Mobile payments have become common. · widespread · common · The two villages share a common well. · shared · struck · When floods struck the district … · hit suddenly · struck · The workers struck for higher wages. · went on strike · sharp · Prices showed a sharp rise. · sudden and large · sharp · She gave him a sharp reply. · harsh · sound · It is a sound plan. · sensible, reliable · sound · The child slept a sound sleep. · deep · table · They will table the proposal at the meeting. · present for discussion · humble · These humble grains are back on the plate. · simple, ordinary · The four-step method · Step · What you do · 1 · Find the word in the passage and read its whole sentence · 2 · Guess the meaning in your own words before looking at the options · 3 · Replace the word with each option and read the sentence again · 4 · Reject the option that is a real meaning of the word but not the one used here · undefined · “Swap and read.” Swap the word for each option and read the sentence aloud in your head. The right one sounds like the passage; the trap sounds like a dictionary. · The most familiar meaning is often the trap. And in an antonym question, one option is usually a synonym — read the question twice so you do not pick the same meaning when the opposite is asked. · Answer ‘as used in the passage’ — the meaning in that sentence, not the commonest one. · Guess the meaning first, then swap each option into the sentence. · Familiar dictionary meanings that do not fit are the usual traps (modest, recall, common, struck). · For an antonym, fix the sense first, then find its opposite; watch for a synonym among the options.

clozerc.t: RC: tone and the author’s attitude
clozerc.h: अपठित गद्यांश: लेखक का भाव और दृष्टिकोण
clozerc.x: ‘The tone of the passage is…’ or ‘The author’s attitude towards X is…’ comes up in many shifts. The options are tone words — critical, appreciative, objective, ironic, nostalgic, optimistic — so you need to know what each means and which signal words reveal it. · The same fact can be told in many voices. ‘The new road was finished in two years.’ — that is objective . ‘At last, after two long years of dust and delay, the road is finished!’ — that is relieved , even critical of the delay. ‘A mere two years for one kilometre — what speed!’ — that is ironic : the words praise, but the facts mock. Tone lives in the author’s choice of words . Praise words ( remarkable , gift , pride ) give an appreciative tone. Blame words ( ignored , careless , fails ) give a critical one. Worry words ( harm , danger , may be lost ) give a concerned one. Plain facts with no such words give an objective one. SSC passages are usually moderate . Extreme tones such as furious , hysterical or despairing are rarely right. · Tone words and what they mean · Tone word · Meaning · Signal in the text · objective · Without personal feeling · Facts and figures; no praise or blame · critical · Finding fault · ‘ignored’, ‘fails’, ‘left untouched’ · appreciative · Valuing, praising · ‘remarkable’, ‘gift’, ‘pride’ · ironic · Saying the opposite of what is meant · Praise that the facts contradict · sarcastic · Mocking, meant to wound · ‘Oh, brilliant work!’ for a failure · satirical · Using humour to attack foolishness · Exaggeration of a public folly · nostalgic · Longing for the past · ‘in those days’, ‘once upon a time’ · optimistic · Hopeful about the future · ‘could’, ‘promising’, ‘may save many lives’ · pessimistic · Expecting the worst · ‘nothing will change’, ‘doomed’ · didactic · Teaching a moral lesson · ‘we must’, ‘one should always’ · cynical · Believing people act only for themselves · ‘as usual’, ‘of course they did’ · sympathetic · Sharing others’ hardship · ‘struggle’, ‘hardship’, ‘fair price’ · indifferent · Showing no interest · Flat, uncaring language · laudatory · Full of high praise · ‘heroic’, ‘outstanding’ · condescending · Looking down on others · ‘simple folk who cannot understand’ · humorous · Meant to amuse · Jokes, light exaggeration · undefined · “Count the feeling words.” No feeling words → objective. Praise → appreciative. Blame → critical. Worry → concerned. Hope → optimistic. Praise that the facts mock → ironic. · Ironic and sarcastic are close: irony says the opposite of what is meant; sarcasm is irony meant to hurt someone. Indifferent (not caring) is not the same as objective (fair, without bias). Avoid extreme tones unless the passage is extreme. · Tone is shown by the author’s choice of words. · Objective = no feeling words; critical = blame; appreciative = praise; concerned = worry; optimistic = hope. · Ironic = the words say the opposite of what the facts show; sarcastic = irony meant to wound. · Nostalgic = longing for the past; didactic = teaching a lesson; cynical = doubting people’s motives. · SSC passages are usually moderate; extreme tones are rarely right. · Objective is not indifferent.

clozerc.t: Full mixed practice: cloze and RC together
clozerc.h: मिश्रित अभ्यास: क्लोज़ टेस्ट और गद्यांश एक साथ
clozerc.x: In the exam the skills come mixed: one cloze blank is a collocation, the next a connector, the next a tense. This lesson puts them together — two full cloze passages and two full RC passages worked out step by step, then practice in the exam’s own format. · On exam day the cloze and RC passages are usually the last English questions, and many candidates reach them in a hurry. A plan helps. Give the cloze passage about three or four minutes and the RC passage about six . Read each passage once before you answer anything. For each cloze blank, name the skill it tests — collocation, preposition, connector, tense, word choice or article — and use that lesson’s rule. For each RC question, name its family — main idea, fact, inference, vocabulary or tone — and go back to the lines. If a blank or question still has two good options after a proper look, it is fine to leave it: a wrong answer costs half a mark. · Exam-day plan for the two passages · Minute · Cloze passage · RC passage · 0–1 · Read the whole passage once · Skim the passage; note each paragraph’s topic · 1–3 · Fill the easy blanks: collocations, prepositions, articles · Answer the fact and vocabulary questions first · 3–4 · Fill the logic blanks: connectors, tense, word choice · Answer the main idea, inference and tone questions · Last · Read the passage back with your answers · Check that each answer can be pointed to in the text · undefined · Worked cloze 2: answers and the skill tested · Blank · Answer · Skill and reasoning · 1 · repairs · Tense: the passage is in the simple present ( sorts ), and the subject the body is singular. · 2 · yet · Connector: people need eight hours, yet they get less — contrast. So and because give a false link; unless makes no sense. · 3 · lack · Part of speech: after a regular we need a noun; the others are verb forms. · 4 · difference · Collocation: make a difference to . We do not make a variety or a distance to something. · 5 · during · Preposition of time: during the day . Since the day needs a starting point; among and beside are not time words. · undefined · Worked cloze 3: answers and the skill tested · Blank · Answer · Skill and reasoning · 1 · to · Preposition: we send something to someone. · 2 · fade · Phrasal verb: fade away = slowly disappear. Break away means to separate; give away and put away need an object. · 3 · collect · Verb form: help someone + V1 (or to + V1). Collecting , collected and collects do not follow help someone . · 4 · Although · Connector and grammar: letters vanished, yet it is busier — contrast; a full clause follows, so Although , not Despite . · 5 · has · Tense: is busier than it has been for years — present perfect with for years , matching is . · undefined · Worked RC 2: the five questions · Question · Answer · Family and reasoning · Main idea? · E-waste is handled dangerously, though safe recycling exists; families need an easy way to hand it over · Main idea: it covers the problem, the safe option and the missing link. ‘Workers burn plastic’ alone is too narrow. · Why do workers burn the plastic? · To recover copper and gold · Fact: sentence 2, key word burn . · What can be inferred about most families today? · They lack a simple way to send old gadgets for proper recycling · Inference: ‘what is missing is … a simple, trusted way’ implies families do not have one now. · ‘Yield’ as used in the passage means · Produce, give · Vocabulary: devices yield metals — produce them. ‘Give way, surrender’ is another sense that does not fit. · Tone? · Concerned but constructive · Tone: worry about poisons, then a practical way forward. · undefined · Worked RC 3: the five questions · Question · Answer · Family and reasoning · Best title? · From Privilege to Right: Schooling for All · Title: it covers the old privilege, the new right and today’s challenge. · For which ages did the 2009 Act make schooling a right? · Six to fourteen · Fact: sentence 4. · What can be inferred? · Many children who attend school are not learning enough · Inference: the struggle is now ‘making sure they actually learn’, which implies many do not. · ‘Privilege’ as used in the passage means · A special advantage open to only a few · Vocabulary: reading belonged to priests, scholars and the wealthy — a few. · Tone? · Informative and reflective · Tone: it traces history calmly and ends with a thoughtful point. · “Name it, then solve it.” Every cloze blank and every RC question belongs to one of eleven families you have studied. Saying the family’s name in your head — ‘connector’, ‘inference’ — calls up its rule. · Do not let one hard blank eat your time: fill the others first, then come back — the filled passage often makes the hard one clear. In RC, do not answer the main idea question first if you are unsure; the fact questions you answer first will show you what the passage is about. · Give the cloze passage about three or four minutes and the RC passage about six. · Read each passage once before answering anything. · Name the skill of each cloze blank: collocation, preposition, connector, tense, word choice or article. · Name the family of each RC question: main idea, fact, inference, vocabulary or tone. · Do the easy blanks and fact questions first; come back to the hard ones. · Leave a question only after a proper look leaves two equally good options.

parajumble.h: SSC में वाक्य पुनर्व्यवस्था के प्रश्न कैसे आते हैं
parajumble.x: Sentence rearrangement is a regular part of the English section of SSC CGL and CHSL Tier 1 — usually one or two questions a shift, sometimes none. Each is worth the same marks as any other question and takes under a minute once you know the clues. · A para jumble is a short paragraph whose sentences have been shuffled. Your job is to put them back. Most of the time SSC gives four sentences marked P, Q, R and S and four orders such as QPSR to choose from. Sometimes the first sentence is printed separately (marked S1) and you arrange the rest; sometimes both the first (S1) and the last (S6) are fixed and you arrange the four in the middle. Two other forms appear: a single long sentence cut into four parts , and a question that asks only which sentence should come first (or last). The skill is the same in every case: a well-written paragraph is a chain, and every sentence after the first holds on to the one before it. · The formats SSC uses · Format · What you see · What you choose · Four sentences · P, Q, R and S, all jumbled · An order such as QPSR · First sentence fixed · S1 printed first, then P, Q, R and S · The order of P, Q, R and S after S1 · First and last fixed · S1 and S6 printed; P, Q, R and S in between · The order of the middle four · Parts of one sentence · One sentence cut into four parts (sometimes the opening words are given) · The order of the parts · Opening sentence · Four sentences · The one that should start the paragraph · Closing sentence (less common) · Four sentences · The one that should end the paragraph · What makes a paragraph hang together · One topic · Every sentence is about the same subject. · An opener · The first sentence introduces the subject with a full noun — it does not lean on anything earlier. · Links · Pronouns (he, it, they), articles (a → the), pointing words (this, such) and connectors (however, therefore) tie each sentence to the one before. · A natural flow · Time order, cause before effect, general before specific, problem before solution. · An ending · A result, a summary, advice or a look ahead. · You never have to build the order from nothing. There are 24 possible orders of four sentences, but SSC shows you only four . Find one or two sure clues, strike out the options that break them, and check the one that is left. · An order can sound fine at a quick glance and still be wrong. Read your chosen order once from start to end: a sentence that begins with He , This or However cannot come before the sentence it refers to. · SSC sets four sentences P, Q, R, S; or S1 fixed; or S1 and S6 fixed; or four parts of one sentence; or ‘which sentence comes first’. · There are 24 possible orders, but only four options — test them. · A paragraph is a chain: one topic, an opener, links, a natural flow and an ending. · Links are pronouns, articles, pointing words and connectors. · Always read the chosen order once from start to end.

A fixed routine saves time and stops guesswork: topic → opener → one sure pair → strike options → read once . With practice it takes 40–50 seconds a question. · Think of the four sentences as four railway coaches that have come uncoupled. Each coach has a hook at the front (the word that points back — he, this, however, then ) and a ring at the back (the new thing it introduces — a farmer, a plan, a problem ). The engine is the one coach with no hook at the front: the opener. Find the engine first. Then find one hook that clearly fits one ring — a pair . Usually the opener and one pair are enough to strike out three options. Read the last option through once to be sure. · The five steps · Step · Do this · Ask yourself · 1 · Read · Read all four sentences quickly · What is this paragraph about? · 2 · Opener · Find the sentence that introduces the topic with a full noun and leans on nothing · Could I say this sentence to someone who knows nothing yet? · 3 · Pair · Find two sentences that must sit together: a noun and its pronoun, ‘a’ and ‘the’, a cause and its ‘so’ · Which sentence must come right after which? · 4 · Strike · Cross out every option that starts wrongly or breaks the pair · Which options are still standing? · 5 · Check · Read the surviving order from start to end · Does it read like one smooth paragraph? · A paragraph is a chain · The opener has nothing to point back to. Every later sentence holds on to the one before it, and the last one rounds the paragraph off. · The clues to look for · Pronouns · he, she, it, they, his, its, their — need a noun before them · Articles and pointers · a → the; this, these, such, the same — point back · Connectors · however, but (contrast); also, moreover (addition); so, therefore (result); for example (example) · Time and order · first, then, finally; dates in order; cause before effect · Shape · general → specific; problem → solution; question → answer · undefined · Write the four letters on your rough sheet and draw arrows for the pairs you are sure of (Q → P). An option that does not contain your arrow is out. · Do not judge an option by its first two letters only. Two options often start the same way (QPRS and QPSR); the last two letters decide it, so check the second pair too. · Step 1: read all four and find the topic. · Step 2: find the opener — full noun, no pronoun or connector at the start. · Step 3: find one sure pair that must sit together. · Step 4: strike the options that start wrongly or break the pair. · Step 5: read the surviving order once from start to end.

Finding the opener is the single most useful step: it strikes out half the options in seconds. SSC also asks it directly — “Which sentence should come first?” · Imagine walking up to a stranger and saying, “However, it closes early on Sundays.” They would ask: what closes? However what ? That sentence leans on something you never said. Now try: “Our town opened a public library last year.” It makes sense on its own. That is the stranger test . The opening sentence introduces the topic with a full noun — often with a or an , or as a general statement — and it does not begin with a pronoun ( he, it, they ), a pointing word ( this, such ) or a connector ( however, therefore, also ). · Can this sentence open a paragraph? · The sentence begins … · Can it open? · Why · A young farmer named Gopal … · Can open · Introduces a new person with ‘a’. · Water is essential for all life. · Can open · A general statement about the topic. · Photosynthesis is the process by which … · Can open · A definition of the topic. · In 1947, … · Can open · Sets the time and leans on nothing. · Once upon a time, … · Can open · The classic opening of a story. · There are many ways to save water. · Can open · Announces the topic. · Have you ever wondered why …? · Can open · A question that the paragraph goes on to answer. · Many people believe that … · Can open · Sets up a common view, often corrected later. · When Meena moved to a new school, she … · Can open · The time clause is complete inside the sentence. · Although the road was new, it … · Can open · ‘Although’ joins two halves of the same sentence. · He / She / They … · Cannot open · A pronoun needs a noun before it. · It was later sold … · Cannot open · ‘It’ and ‘later’ both point back. · This / These / Such … · Cannot open · Pointing words refer to something already said. · However, … · Cannot open · Contrasts with an earlier sentence. · But … / Yet … · Cannot open · A contrast needs something to contrast with. · Therefore, … / As a result, … · Cannot open · A result of something already said. · Moreover, … / Also, … · Cannot open · Adds to an earlier point. · For example, … · Cannot open · An example of an idea already stated. · Then … / After that, … · Cannot open · The next step after an earlier one. · Finally, … · Cannot open · The last of several steps or points. · Another reason is … · Cannot open · ‘Another’ means one was given before. · Similarly, … · Cannot open · Compares with something already said. · On the other hand, … · Cannot open · The second side of an argument. · In other words, … · Cannot open · Restates an earlier sentence. · The former … · Cannot open · Needs two things named just before. · What a good opener usually looks like · New noun · A full name or ‘a / an + noun’: “A small boat was seen …” · General truth · “Exercise is good for both the body and the mind.” · Definition · “A volcano is an opening in the Earth’s crust …” · Scene-setter · A time or place: “Last Sunday, we visited an old fort.” · Question · “What makes a good leader?” — the next sentences answer it. · Common belief · “Many people think that …” — often followed by ‘In fact’ or ‘But’. · Scan only the first two or three words of each sentence. Strike every sentence that starts with a pronoun, a pointing word or a connector. Whatever is left is your opener — often there is only one. · A sentence with a name is not always the opener: “Penicillin, for example , was found …” is an example of an idea stated earlier. And ‘The’ is not always a sign of a later sentence — “The Sun is a star” or “The Constitution of India came into force …” can open, because everyone already knows the thing named. · The opener makes sense on its own: the stranger test. · It introduces the topic with a full noun, ‘a/an + noun’, a general statement, a definition, a scene-setter or a question. · It does not begin with he/she/it/they, this/these/such, or a connector such as however, therefore, also, for example, then. · ‘Although’ and ‘When’ can begin an opener because the whole idea is inside the sentence. · A name alone does not make an opener — check for ‘for example’, ‘too’, ‘later’.

The commonest clue in SSC para jumbles: a sentence with he, she, it, they, his, its or their must come after the sentence that names the person or thing. · Writers name a person or thing once, in full, and then save words: Dr Rao opened a clinic. She examines fifty patients a day. Her clinic is always full. The pronoun is a hook that must catch on a noun that came before it. So when you see a pronoun, ask: who or what is this? Find the sentence that names it, and you have a pair. Check that the two agree — they needs a plural, she a woman or girl, it a single thing or idea. · What each pronoun needs before it · Word · Needs before it · Example · he / him / his · a man or boy already named · Mr Sharma retired. He now teaches hockey. · she / her · a woman or girl already named · Asha practised daily. She won the prize. · it / its · one thing, animal or idea already named · The bridge is old. Its pillars are cracked. · they / them / their · a plural noun, or two or more people · The students planted saplings. They water them daily. · this / that · one thing or idea just mentioned · Prices rose sharply. This hurt the poor. · these / those · several things just mentioned · Pepper and cardamom grow in Kerala. These spices … · such · a kind of thing just described · Some birds copy human words. Such skills … · the former / the latter · two things named together just before · LPG and firewood … The former is clean. · one … the other · two things announced earlier · There are two roads. One is short; the other is safe. · both · two people or things already named · Maya and Dev … Both became doctors. · there (a place) · a place already named · We reached the fort. From there we saw the city. · the same · something already mentioned · Last year a cyclone hit the village. This year the same village was ready. · How a reference chain runs · Full name · “Dr Meera Rao opened a free eye clinic.” · Pronoun · “She examines fifty patients a day.” · Describing noun · “The doctor also visits nearby villages.” · Possessive · “Her clinic is a blessing for the poor.” · Underline every pronoun and draw an arrow back to its noun. Each arrow is a pair: the noun’s sentence comes first, the pronoun’s sentence after — usually right after. · Check number and gender : they cannot point to one boy, and she cannot point to Ravi. When two people appear, decide which one the he means. And it or this may point to a whole idea (“Prices rose. This hurt the poor.”), not just a noun. · A pronoun’s sentence comes after the sentence that names its noun. · he/him/his: a man or boy; she/her: a woman or girl; it/its: one thing or idea; they/them/their: a plural. · this/that, these/those and such point back to something just said. · The former / the latter need two things named together just before. · Check number and gender; ‘it’ or ‘this’ can point to a whole idea.

parajumble.t: Articles and pointing words: a → the
parajumble.h: आर्टिकल और संकेतक शब्द: a → the
parajumble.x: A quiet but reliable clue: “a boat” comes before “the boat” ; “a scheme” before “this scheme” or “such a scheme” . One glance at the articles often gives you a pair. · When something appears for the first time, English gives it a or an : A small boat was seen near the shore. From then on it is a known thing, so it takes the : The boat had no one on board. The same goes for this , that , such and the same — they all mean ‘the one you already know about’. Another and the other work the same way: you can only speak of another storm if one storm has already been mentioned. · What the article or pointing word tells you · Word · Signals · Example · a / an + noun · first mention: something new · A stranger knocked on our door. · the + the same noun · second mention: already known · The stranger asked for water. · this / that + noun · the one just mentioned · Under this scheme, every school … · such a / such + noun · a kind just described · Such a facility was badly needed. · the same + noun · exactly the one named before · This year, the same village was ready. · another + noun · a second one of a kind already named · Another storm hit the coast. · the other + noun · the remaining one of two · The other road is longer. · the + something unique · known to everyone; can open · The Sun is a star. · the + superlative · unique by meaning; can open · The largest mangrove forest is … · some / many + plural noun · new; can open · Some birds can copy sounds. · Look for the same noun twice — once with a/an , once with the or this . The ‘a’ sentence goes first. If you also see such or these , that sentence usually sums up and comes late. · The does not always mean ‘second mention’. Unique things ( the Sun, the Taj Mahal, the government ) and superlatives ( the largest, the first ) can appear in an opener. Use the article clue together with the pronoun and connector clues. · a/an + noun = first mention; the + the same noun = second mention. · this, that, such and the same point back to something already named. · another = one more of a kind already mentioned; the other = the remaining one of two. · The + a unique thing or a superlative can open a paragraph. · Use the article clue with the pronoun and connector clues.

Connectors are the loudest clue in a para jumble. A sentence that begins However, Therefore, Moreover, For example or Also can never open, and each one tells you exactly what the sentence before it must say. · A connector is a road sign between two sentences. However says “the road turns — the next idea goes against the last one.” Therefore says “because of what you just read, this follows.” Moreover says “one more point in the same direction.” For example says “here is a case of what I just claimed.” So every connector is a pair clue. Read it, then look for the sentence it answers: the opposite idea for however , the cause for therefore , a similar point for moreover , the general claim for for example . · Connectors and their jobs · Connector · Job · Example · However · Contrast · The car is cheap to run. However, it costs a lot to buy. · But · Contrast · He wanted to come. But he had no ticket. · Yet · Contrast · Most cats avoid water. Yet tigers love to swim. · Nevertheless · Contrast · Fast food is tasty. Nevertheless, it should not be eaten daily. · On the other hand · Contrast · Paper books are easy on the eyes. Screens, on the other hand, are easy to carry. · Instead · Contrast · We did not cancel the picnic. Instead, we held it indoors. · Moreover · Addition · The scheme is cheap. Moreover, it is easy to run. · Furthermore · Addition · The road is narrow. Furthermore, it floods in the rains. · Also · Addition · Trees give shade. They also clean the air. · Besides · Addition · Besides honey, bees give us wax. · In addition · Addition · In addition, the number of vehicles is rising. · Therefore · Result · It rained all night. Therefore, the match was put off. · Thus · Result · Water expands as it freezes; ice thus floats. · Hence · Result · The bridge was weak. Hence, it was closed. · As a result · Result · The factory closed. As a result, many lost their jobs. · Consequently · Result · He missed the bus. Consequently, he was late. · That is why · Result · Light travels faster than sound. That is why we see lightning first. · For example · Example · Some birds copy sounds. Parrots, for example, repeat words. · For instance · Example · Many jobs are new. App developers, for instance, did not exist before. · Such as · Example · Spices such as pepper and cardamom grow in Kerala. · First / Firstly · Sequence · First, boil the water. · Then / Next · Sequence · Then add the tea leaves. · Finally · Sequence · Finally, strain the tea and serve it. · Similarly · Comparison · Parrots copy words. Similarly, mynahs copy sounds. · Likewise · Comparison · The first team trained hard; likewise, the second. · In short · Conclusion · In short, weather changes daily, but climate does not. · To sum up · Conclusion · To sum up, both have their uses. · Because · Reason · The match was put off because it rained. · In fact · Emphasis or correction · Many think the hump stores water. In fact, it is fat. · What the sentence before must say · Contrast word · The opposite idea: a good point before ‘however’ brings a bad one, and the other way round. · Addition word · A point in the same direction: a benefit before ‘moreover’ brings another benefit. · Result word · The cause: ‘It rained all night’ before ‘Therefore, the match was put off’. · Example word · The general claim the example illustrates. · Comparison word · A similar case: ‘Parrots copy words’ before ‘Similarly, mynahs …’. · Conclusion word · Everything else — it comes last. · Group the sentences by direction. Benefits go together, joined by also / moreover ; then however / but turns to the drawbacks; therefore or in short closes. A ‘moreover’ right after a ‘however’ sentence must add to the drawback, not to the benefit. · Connectors can sit in the middle of a sentence: “Their most important job, however , is …”, “It also helps …”. They still point back. But Although , Because and When at the very start join two halves of one sentence, so such a sentence can still open. · Contrast: however, but, yet, nevertheless, on the other hand, instead. · Addition: moreover, furthermore, also, besides, in addition. · Result: therefore, thus, hence, so, as a result, consequently, that is why. · Example: for example, for instance, such as. Comparison: similarly, likewise. · Conclusion: in short, to sum up — they come last. Connectors in mid-sentence still point back.

parajumble.t: Time and sequence order; cause → effect
parajumble.x: Stories, life histories and how-to paragraphs are common in SSC sets. Their order is fixed by time : first → then → finally, dates in order, cause before effect. · Some paragraphs have a built-in clock. A recipe goes boil → add → pour → serve . A life story goes born → studied → worked → honoured . A flood story goes rain → river rises → floods → people move . The sentences can only go one way, because each event needs the one before it. Watch for order words (first, then, next, after that, finally), dates and ages , and words of time (by then, soon, later, today). And remember that a cause always comes before its effect . · Order words and where they sit · Word · Stage · Note · First / Firstly · Beginning · The first step; may follow a scene-setting opener. · At first · Beginning · How things were early on, before a change. · Initially · Beginning · Same as ‘at first’. · To begin with · Beginning · The first of several points or steps. · Originally · Beginning · How something started. · Then · Middle · The next step after one already given. · Next · Middle · The following step. · After that · Middle · Follows a step just described. · Soon after · Middle · A short time after an earlier event. · Second / Secondly · Middle · The second of several points. · Later · Middle · Some time after an earlier event. · Meanwhile · Middle · At the same time as an event just told. · Finally · End · The last step or point. · Lastly · End · The last of a list. · At last · End · After a long wait or effort. · In the end · End · How things finally turned out. · Eventually · End · After a long time or many steps. · Ultimately · End · The final result. · Orders that never change · Pattern · Order · Cause and effect · cause → effect → further effect · A process · first step → middle steps → last step → result · Dates · earlier year → later year → today · A life story · birth → education → work → achievement → later life · A day or journey · morning → noon → evening; departure → journey → arrival · Then and now · the past → the change → the present · When you see dates or years, simply sort them. When you see At first … Then … Now or First … Next … Finally , the order words do the work for you. · Later , by then and since then point back to a time already mentioned, so they cannot open. Before that sends you back in time: the sentence it refers to comes just before it, even though its event happened later. · Order words: first/at first/initially → then/next/after that/later → finally/at last/eventually. · Sort dates and ages from earlier to later. · A cause comes before its effect; a process runs step by step. · Later, by then and since then point back, so they cannot open. · Then and now: past → change → present.

When there is no pronoun or connector to help, the shape of the paragraph decides the order: broad claim first, details and examples after; problem first, solution and result after; advice or summary at the end. · Most short paragraphs follow one of a few shapes. A general-to-specific paragraph opens with a broad statement (“India is a land of many festivals”) and narrows down to cases (“In Kerala, Onam …”). A problem-solution paragraph describes a trouble, its cause, the fix and the result. An old-view-new-view paragraph begins with what people once believed and ends with what we now know. Knowing the shape also tells you the last sentence : a result, a summary, a piece of advice (“We should therefore …”) or a look ahead (“If more people …”). · Common paragraph shapes · Shape · Order · Signals · General → specific · claim → detail → example · for example, in Kerala, one such · Problem → solution · problem → cause → solution → result · to solve this, one way, as a result · Question → answer · question → answer → explanation · the answer, the reason is · Claim → reasons · claim → reason 1 → reason 2 → conclusion · first, also, moreover, therefore · Old view → new view · what people believed → the change → what we know now · for centuries, in fact, today · Story · setting → event → reaction → outcome · one day, then, in the end · Two sides · side 1 → side 2 → balanced view · on the one hand, on the other hand · What a closing sentence looks like · Kind · Example · Advice · We should therefore carry our own bags. · Summary · In short, each has its own advantages. · Result · Within a year, reading levels improved sharply. · A look ahead · If more people joined them, hunger could be reduced. · A lesson · Such accidents remind us to keep our eyes open. · The final event · When she finished, the hall rang with applause. · Ask of each sentence: is it bigger or smaller than the others? The biggest, most general idea opens; the examples go in the middle; the sentence that tells you what to do or what it all means closes. · Do not end on an example or on a question. A sentence that asks something, or that begins For example , First or One reason , needs a follower, so it cannot be the last. · General → specific: the broad claim first, then details and examples. · Problem → solution: problem, cause, solution, result. · Old view → new view: past belief, the change, today’s knowledge. · The last sentence is advice, a summary, a result, a lesson or a look ahead. · A question, an example or ‘First …’ cannot be the last sentence.

A mandatory pair is two sentences that must sit side by side, in a fixed order. Find one and you can strike every option that splits it or turns it round — often three at once. · Some sentences cannot live apart. A question needs its answer right after it. “One reason is …” calls for “Another reason is …”. “Some people say …” calls for “Others believe …”. A sentence that names two things is followed by one that says “the former … the latter”. When you spot such a pair, write it down as two letters, say RP . Now look at the options: any option without RP side by side is out. · Pairs that must sit together · One sentence … · … so the next one · Example · introduces ‘a boat’ · refers to ‘the boat’ · A boat drifted in. / The boat was empty. · names a person · uses he, she, his or her · Dr Rao opened a clinic. / She treats the poor. · asks a question · gives the answer · Why do we see lightning first? / The reason is … · makes a general claim · gives a case: ‘for example’ · Some inventions were accidents. / Penicillin, for example, … · names two things · takes them in turn: ‘the former … the latter’ · LPG and firewood are used. / The former is clean. · says ‘One reason is …’ · says ‘Another reason is …’ · One reason is jobs. / Another is schools. · says ‘Some people …’ · says ‘Others …’ · Some say speed matters. / Others value patience. · says ‘On the one hand …’ · says ‘On the other hand …’ · On the one hand, jobs came. / On the other hand, shops closed. · gives a cause · gives the result: ‘so’, ‘therefore’ · It rained for days. / So the river rose. · states a common belief · corrects it: ‘In fact …’ · Many think the hump holds water. / In fact, it is fat. · reports what someone said · gives the reply · The doctor said, ‘Walk daily.’ / Anil said he had no time. · gives the first step · gives the next: ‘Then …’ · First, boil the water. / Then add the leaves. · Look for a pair before you look for the opener if one jumps out — a question and its answer, or ‘the former / the latter’. A pair often settles the question even when the opener is hard to spot. · A pair fixes order as well as nearness. If Q introduces ‘a scheme’ and S says ‘this scheme’, the pair is QS , not SQ. An option with SQ side by side is still wrong. · A mandatory pair is two sentences that must be side by side, in a fixed order. · Common pairs: a X → the X; name → he/she; question → answer; claim → for example; one reason → another. · Two things named → the former / the latter; some → others; on the one hand → on the other hand. · Write the pair as two letters and strike every option that splits it or reverses it. · Belief → ‘In fact’ correction; cause → ‘so’ or ‘therefore’.

In the exam you do not need to build the order — you need to pick it from four. A few quick tests usually strike out three options in under thirty seconds. · Think of the four options as four suspects. You do not have to prove who is guilty; you only have to clear the innocent. The opener test clears every option that starts with a sentence that leans on something. The pair test clears every option that splits a mandatory pair or turns it round. The ending test clears options that stop on a question, an example or a ‘First …’. Often two options survive the opener test because they start the same way. Then look at where they differ — usually the last two letters — and ask which of those two sentences links to the one before it. · The quick tests · Test · Strike out options that … · Example · Opener · begin with a pronoun, a pointing word or a connector sentence · R begins ‘However’ → strike R… · Pair · split a mandatory pair · Q names Dr Rao, S says ‘She’ → keep only options with QS · Direction · have the pair the wrong way round · ‘a scheme’ in P, ‘this scheme’ in R → PR, never RP · Ending · end with a question, an example or a ‘First …’ sentence · an option ending on ‘For example …’ is out · Fixed sentences · do not link to S1 or to S6 · the sentence after S1 must follow from it · Difference · survive — compare only the letters where they differ · QPRS vs QPSR: does R or S follow P? · undefined · Count how many options start with each letter. If three options start with the same letter, that letter is very likely the opener — but still check it with the stranger test. · Do not stop as soon as one test leaves a single option — read it through once. A careless pair (say a ‘they’ that really points to a different noun) can mislead you. · Opener test: strike options that begin with a sentence that leans on something. · Pair test: strike options that split a mandatory pair or reverse it. · Ending test: an option cannot end on a question, an example or ‘First …’. · With S1/S6 fixed, the first and last of P, Q, R, S must link to them. · When two survive, compare only the letters where they differ, then read the winner once.

parajumble.t: Rearranging the parts of one sentence
parajumble.h: एक वाक्य के भागों को क्रम में लगाना
parajumble.x: Some SSC sets cut one sentence into four parts (sometimes the first words are given). Here grammar, not story, decides the order: subject → verb → object → extra details , with each clause in its proper place. · An English sentence has a backbone: who (the subject) does what (the verb) to what (the object), then how, where and when . “The old man / walks his dog / in the park every morning.” A clause beginning with who, which or that sits right after the noun it describes: “The old man who lives next door walks …”. Some words come in partners that fix the order for you: not only … but also , neither … nor , either … or , so … that , no sooner … than , hardly … when , the more … the more . Find the partners and you have the skeleton of the sentence. · Partner words that fix the order · The first word · Its partner · Example · Not only · but also · Not only did he finish, but he also helped others. · Neither · nor · Neither the manager nor his staff knew. · Either · or · Either you or your brother must come. · Both · and · Both Maya and Dev became doctors. · So (+ adjective) · that · So heavy was the rain that the river rose. · Such (+ noun) · that · It was such a hot day that we stayed in. · No sooner · than · No sooner did we arrive than it rained. · Hardly / Scarcely · when · Hardly had we sat down when the bell rang. · The more … · the more / the better · The more you read, the better you write. · Whether · or · Whether you win or lose, play fair. · Rather · than · She would rather walk than wait. · Although · (no ‘but’) main clause · Although he was tired, he kept working. · Where the building blocks go · Subject · Usually first: “The scientist …”, “Neither the manager …”. · Relative clause · Right after its noun: “The book that you lent me …”. · Verb · Right after the subject (and its clause): “… was given …”. · Object · After the verb: “… an award …”. · Place, then time · “… in the park every morning.” · A ‘because / although / if’ clause · Either at the very start (with a comma) or after the main clause. · Find the subject (a noun group that can start a sentence) and the main verb ; they are usually two of the four parts. Then fit the ‘who/which’ part right after the subject and send the place and time to the end. · A ‘who/which/that’ part placed at the end can change the meaning: “The scientist was given an award by the government who discovered the medicine ” now seems to say the government discovered it. Also, ‘Although … but’ is wrong — ‘although’ takes no ‘but’. · Subject → verb → object → place → time. · A who/which/that clause goes right after the noun it describes. · Partner words fix the order: not only … but also, neither … nor, either … or, so … that, no sooner … than, hardly … when. · A because/although/if clause opens the sentence with a comma or follows the main clause. · Although takes no ‘but’; a misplaced clause can change the meaning.

parajumble.h: मिश्रित अभ्यास: सभी प्रकार एक साथ
parajumble.x: The exam mixes the formats and the clues. This set does the same: four-sentence jumbles, S1 and S1–S6 sets, single-sentence parts, and ‘which comes first / last’. · Work each question with the same routine, against the clock: topic → opener → one pair → strike → read once . Aim for under a minute each. When you get one wrong, read the explanation and name the clue you missed — pronoun, article, connector, time, shape or pair. That clue is the one to revise. · Which clue to try first · You see … · Try first · Names and he/she/they · Pronoun links (J4) · ‘a …’ and ‘the / this / such …’ · Article links (J5) · However, therefore, also, for example · Connectors (J6) · Dates, first/then/finally, a story · Time order (J7) · A problem, a claim, advice · Paragraph shape (J8) · A question, ‘one … the other’, ‘former … latter’ · Mandatory pairs (J9) · Parts of one sentence · Grammar order (J11) · Time yourself: 45 seconds for a four-sentence set, 30 for a ‘which comes first’. If you are stuck after a minute, mark your best guess from the opener test and move on. · Under time pressure people pick the option whose first two letters are right. Always glance at the last two letters too. · Use the same five steps on every question. · Match the clue to what you see: names → pronouns; a/the → articles; however → connectors; dates → time; problem → shape; question → pair. · Single-sentence parts: subject, verb, object, then details. · Aim for about 45 seconds a set. · After a mistake, name the clue you missed and revise that lesson.

firsts.x: Most asked: the flag's adoption date (22 July 1947) , ratio (2:3) and 24 spokes ; the emblem's source ( Sarnath ) and motto ( Satyameva Jayate , from the Mundaka Upanishad ); the anthem's author, first singing (1911) , adoption (24 January 1950) and 52 seconds ; Vande Mataram and Anandamath ; the Saka calendar; and the ₹ designer . · A new country needs symbols everyone can recognise. India chose them in the months around freedom. On 22 July 1947 the Constituent Assembly adopted the tricolour — saffron, white and green, with the blue Ashoka Chakra of 24 spokes in place of the spinning wheel of the 1931 Swaraj flag. On 24 January 1950 , its last sitting, the Assembly adopted Jana Gana Mana as the national anthem and gave Vande Mataram equal honour as the national song. Two days later, on 26 January 1950 , the State Emblem — the lions of Ashoka's pillar at Sarnath — came into use with the motto Satyameva Jayate . Later came the Saka calendar (1957), drawn up after Meghnad Saha's committee, and the ₹ sign (2010), designed by D. Udaya Kumar. In 2025–26 the national song was in the news again: its 150th year was marked from 7 November 2025, and in January 2026 the Home Ministry set the full six-stanza version (about 3 minutes 10 seconds) for official use. · The tricolour, drawn to scale · Width to length 2:3. Saffron on top, white in the middle with the navy-blue Ashoka Chakra (24 spokes), India green at the bottom. · The national flag · Adopted · 22 July 1947, by the Constituent Assembly · Colours · Saffron on top (courage and sacrifice), white in the middle (truth and peace), green at the bottom (faith, fertility and growth) · Wheel · The navy-blue Ashoka Chakra (Dharma Chakra) with 24 spokes, on the white band — taken from the Sarnath Lion Capital · Ratio · Width to length 2:3 · Based on · The flag designed by Pingali Venkayya; the 1931 Swaraj flag had a spinning wheel (charkha) where the Chakra now is · Rules · The Flag Code of India, 2002 (in force from 26 January 2002); amended in December 2021 (machine-made and polyester flags allowed) and July 2022 (flags in the open or on homes may fly day and night) · Law · The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971; the Emblems and Names (Prevention of Improper Use) Act, 1950 · Court · Union of India v. firsts.t: Living symbols: animal, bird, flower, tree, fruit, river and more
firsts.h: जीवित प्रतीक: पशु, पक्षी, पुष्प, वृक्ष, फल, नदी और अन्य
firsts.x: Most asked: the national animal (tiger) , bird (Indian peafowl) , flower (lotus) , tree (banyan) , fruit (mango) , river (Ganga) , aquatic animal (Ganges river dolphin) and heritage animal (elephant) — with their scientific names — and the trick question: India has no official national game . · Besides the symbols of the state, India has symbols from nature. The tiger replaced the lion as the national animal in the early 1970s, when tigers were vanishing and Project Tiger began (1973). The Indian peafowl became the national bird in 1963 ; the lotus , the banyan and the mango stand for the flower, tree and fruit. Newer ones followed. The Ganga was declared the national river in 2008 , and in 2009 the Ganges river dolphin — almost blind, finding its food by echo — became the national aquatic animal. In 2010 the elephant was named the national heritage animal. In 2012 schoolchildren voting on the Science Express train picked Lactobacillus , the bacterium that sets curd, as the national microbe. And some 'national' things were never declared at all — there is no national game , whatever many quiz books say about hockey. · National symbols from nature · Symbol · What it is · Note · National animal · Tiger ( Panthera tigris ) · Took the lion's place in the early 1970s; Project Tiger began in 1973. · National bird · Indian peafowl ( Pavo cristatus ) · Declared in 1963; protected under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. · National flower · Lotus ( Nelumbo nucifera ) · A sacred flower that rises clean from muddy water. · National tree · Banyan ( Ficus benghalensis ) · Its aerial roots grow into new trunks, so one tree can spread very wide. · National fruit · Mango ( Mangifera indica ) · India grows more mangoes than any other country. · National river · Ganga · Declared in November 2008, when the National Ganga River Basin Authority was set up. · National aquatic animal · Ganges river dolphin ( Platanista gangetica ) · Declared on 5 October 2009 — now National Dolphin Day; locally the 'susu'. · National heritage animal · Indian elephant · Named in 2010 to raise its protection; Project Elephant runs since 1992. · National microbe · Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus · Chosen by children in 2012; it turns milk into curd and yogurt. · Not declared — the trick questions · National game · None. The Sports Ministry said in RTI replies (2012, 2020) that no game has been declared; hockey is only linked with India through its eight Olympic golds · National reptile · Not officially notified; guide books often give the king cobra · Others you may see · 'National vegetable', 'national sweet' and the like have no official status · Laws that protect the living symbols · Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 · Tiger, peafowl, elephant and Ganges river dolphin are all in Schedule I — the highest protection · Project Tiger · 1973 — run by the National Tiger Conservation Authority since 2006 · Project Elephant · 1992 · National Dolphin Day · 5 October (from 2022) — the day the dolphin was declared in 2009 · In order — animal, bird, flower, tree, fruit: “The Peacock Likes Big Mangoes” = T iger, P eacock, L otus, B anyan, M ango. Then the 'water-and-heritage' trio in date order — Ganga 2008, Dolphin 2009, Elephant 2010 . · The lion was the national animal before the tiger. The aquatic animal is the dolphin , the heritage animal the elephant — don't swap them. Hockey is not the official national game : India has none. Ficus religiosa is the peepal — the national tree is Ficus benghalensis , the banyan. · Animal tiger (Panthera tigris); bird Indian peafowl (Pavo cristatus, 1963); flower lotus (Nelumbo nucifera). · Tree banyan (Ficus benghalensis); fruit mango (Mangifera indica). · River Ganga (2008); aquatic animal Ganges river dolphin (5 October 2009); heritage animal elephant (2010). · Microbe Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus (2012, chosen by children). · No official national game, and no notified national reptile.

Most asked: the first President, Vice-President, Prime Minister and Governor-General ; the first Speaker, Chief Justice, Chief Election Commissioner ; the first Muslim, Sikh, Dalit and tribal Presidents; and the first Indian in space , on the ISS and to win a Nobel . · When the Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950 , India filled its new posts for the first time. Rajendra Prasad became the first President, and in 1952 Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan became the first Vice-President. Jawaharlal Nehru had been Prime Minister since 1947, with Vallabhbhai Patel as his deputy. The Governor-General's chair passed from Lord Mountbatten to C. Rajagopalachari , the first and last Indian to hold it. H. J. Kania became the first Chief Justice, and Sukumar Sen , the first Chief Election Commissioner, ran the first general elections of 1951–52. Other 'firsts' came later: Morarji Desai led the first non-Congress government (1977); Rakesh Sharma went into space (1984); and in 2025 Shubhanshu Shukla became the first Indian to visit the International Space Station. · First holders of India's posts · First · Who · Note · The first President of India · Rajendra Prasad · Rajendra Prasad was President from 1950 to 1962 — the only one elected twice. · The first Vice-President of India · Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan · Radhakrishnan was Vice-President from 1952 to 1962 and then the second President. · The first Prime Minister of India · Jawaharlal Nehru · Nehru was Prime Minister from 1947 until his death in 1964. · The first Deputy Prime Minister of India · Vallabhbhai Patel · Patel was also the first Home Minister and joined the princely states to India. · The first Governor-General of independent India · Lord Mountbatten · Mountbatten stayed on as Governor-General from August 1947 to June 1948. · The first (and last) Indian Governor-General · C. Rajagopalachari · Rajaji held the post from 1948 until it ended on 26 January 1950. · The first Speaker of the Lok Sabha · G. V. R. Ambedkar · Ambedkar also chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constitution. · The first Indian Governor of the Reserve Bank · C. D. Deshmukh · C. D. Deshmukh led the RBI from 1943 to 1949 and later became Finance Minister. · The first non-Congress Prime Minister · Morarji Desai · Morarji Desai led the Janata Party government of 1977–79. · The first Muslim President of India · Zakir Husain · Zakir Husain (1967–69) was also the first President to die in office. · The first Sikh President of India · Giani Zail Singh · Zail Singh was President from 1982 to 1987. · The first Dalit President of India · K. C. D. V. V. Giri was the first acting President, but M. Hidayatullah was the first Chief Justice to act as President. Rakesh Sharma was the first Indian in space; Shubhanshu Shukla the first on the ISS . · President Rajendra Prasad; Vice-President S. The most asked 'firsts' of all: the first woman Prime Minister, President, Governor, Chief Minister, Union minister, Speaker ; the first woman Supreme Court and High Court judges ; the first woman IAS and IPS officers; and the first women to climb Everest , go into space and win Olympic medals . · Indian women broke one barrier after another. In 1947 Sarojini Naidu became the first woman Governor and Rajkumari Amrit Kaur the first woman in the Union Cabinet. Anna Rajam Malhotra joined the IAS in 1951; Kiran Bedi the IPS in 1972. In 1963 Sucheta Kripalani became Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh, and in 1966 Indira Gandhi became Prime Minister. The courts followed: Anna Chandy (High Court, 1959), Fathima Beevi (Supreme Court, 1989) and Leila Seth (High Court Chief Justice, 1991). Beyond the office: Bachendri Pal stood on Everest in 1984; Kalpana Chawla flew in space in 1997; Karnam Malleswari won India's first Olympic medal by a woman in 2000. In 2007 Pratibha Patil became the first woman President. · First women · First · Who · Note · The first woman Prime Minister of India · Indira Gandhi · Indira Gandhi became Prime Minister in January 1966. · The first woman President of India · Pratibha Patil · Pratibha Patil was President from 2007 to 2012. · The first woman Governor of an Indian state · Sarojini Naidu · Sarojini Naidu became Governor of the United Provinces (now Uttar Pradesh) in 1947. · The first woman Chief Minister in India · Sucheta Kripalani · Sucheta Kripalani became Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh in 1963. · The first woman Union Cabinet minister · Rajkumari Amrit Kaur · Rajkumari Amrit Kaur was Health Minister from 1947 to 1957 and founded AIIMS. · The first woman President of the UN General Assembly · Vijaya Lakshmi Pandit · Vijaya Lakshmi Pandit presided over the General Assembly in 1953 — the first woman anywhere to do so. · The first woman Speaker of the Lok Sabha · Meira Kumar · Meira Kumar was Speaker from 2009 to 2014. · The first woman judge of the Supreme Court · M. V. Sindhu · P. V. Sindhu won badminton silver at Rio in 2016. · The first Indian woman to fly an aircraft · Sarla Thakral · Sarla Thakral earned her flying licence in 1936, at the age of 21. · The first woman Chief Election Commissioner · V. S. Ramadevi · V. S. Ramadevi held the post briefly in 1990. · The first Indian woman to win Miss World · Reita Faria · Reita Faria won the title in 1966. · The first woman to win the Jnanpith Award · Ashapurna Devi · The Bengali writer Ashapurna Devi received it in 1976. · The first woman to win the Sahitya Akademi Award · Amrita Pritam · The Punjabi poet Amrita Pritam won it in 1956 for Sunehe. · The first winner of the Dadasaheb Phalke Award · Devika Rani · The actress Devika Rani received the first award in 1969. · The first Indian woman to win the Booker Prize · Arundhati Roy · Arundhati Roy won in 1997 for The God of Small Things. · More first women · First women graduates (1883) · Kadambini Ganguly and Chandramukhi Basu, University of Calcutta · First Indian woman with a degree in Western medicine · Anandibai Joshi — MD from Pennsylvania, 1886 · First woman to practise law in India · Cornelia Sorabji · First woman teacher of modern India · Savitribai Phule — opened a girls' school in Pune in 1848 · First woman Bharat Ratna · Indira Gandhi (1971) · First Indian woman Nobel laureate · Mother Teresa — Peace, 1979 · First Asian woman to swim the English Channel · Arati Saha (1959) · First woman Chief Minister of Delhi · Sushma Swaraj (1998) · First (and only) woman ruler of the Delhi Sultanate · Razia Sultan (1236–40) · First woman to head the State Bank of India · Arundhati Bhattacharya (2013) · First woman to present a full Union Budget as Finance Minister · Nirmala Sitharaman (2019) · First Indian winner of the International Booker Prize · Geetanjali Shree, Tomb of Sand (2022); Banu Mushtaq's Heart Lamp (2025) was the first Kannada winner · The first women fighter pilots , the first woman Lieutenant General and the first woman Rafale pilot are in Defence . Women leaders of the freedom struggle are in Modern History (L32). · The 1947 pair — “Sarojini Governs, Amrit Ministers” . The 'ladder' of the courts — “Anna climbs, Fathima reaches the top, Leila leads” : Anna Chandy (HC judge 1959) → Fathima Beevi (SC judge 1989) → Leila Seth (HC Chief Justice 1991). · Anna Rajam Malhotra = IAS; Kiran Bedi = IPS — don't swap. The first woman Governor is Sarojini Naidu, but the first woman Chief Minister is Sucheta Kripalani — both in Uttar Pradesh. firsts.x: Most asked: the first newspaper (Hicky's Bengal Gazette, 1780), the first film and talkie , the first universities (1857), IIT and AIIMS , the first nuclear reactor (Apsara) and power plant (Tarapur), the first Antarctic station , the first test-tube baby and the first general elections . · Modern India's 'firsts' tell its story. Printing brought Hicky's Bengal Gazette (1780), and in 1857 the British opened universities at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras . In 1913 Dadasaheb Phalke made the first Indian feature film, Raja Harishchandra ; in 1931 Alam Ara brought sound. After 1947 the young republic built: the first IIT at Kharagpur (1951), the first AIIMS (1956), and Apsara at Trombay (1956) — the first nuclear reactor in Asia. Doordarshan began in 1959; Tarapur became the first nuclear power station (1969); Pokhran saw the first nuclear test (1974); and in 1983–84 India set up its first base in Antarctica, Dakshin Gangotri . · Print, film and broadcasting · First newspaper · Hicky's Bengal Gazette, Calcutta, 1780 — started by James Augustus Hicky · First Hindi newspaper · Udant Martand, Calcutta, 1826 — its first day, 30 May, is Hindi Journalism Day · First feature film · Raja Harishchandra (1913), by Dadasaheb Phalke · First talkie · Alam Ara (1931), by Ardeshir Irani · First colour film made in India · Kisan Kanya (1937) · First radio broadcasts · The Radio Club of Bombay, 1923; the name All India Radio from 1936 · First television · Doordarshan, Delhi, 15 September 1959; colour TV in 1982, for the Asian Games · Education, science and health · First modern universities · Calcutta, Bombay and Madras, 1857 · First IIT · Kharagpur, 1951 · First IIM · Calcutta, 1961 (Ahmedabad followed weeks later) · First AIIMS · New Delhi, 1956 · First nuclear reactor · Apsara, Trombay, 1956 — also Asia's first · First nuclear power station · Tarapur, Maharashtra, 1969 · First nuclear test · 'Smiling Buddha', Pokhran (Rajasthan), 18 May 1974 · First satellite · Aryabhata, 19 April 1975, on a Soviet rocket · First expedition to Antarctica · 1981–82, led by S. Z. Qasim · First station in Antarctica · Dakshin Gangotri (1983–84); then Maitri and Bharati · First station in the Arctic · Himadri, Svalbard (Norway), 2008 · First test-tube baby · Durga (Kanupriya Agarwal), Kolkata, 3 October 1978 — Dr Subhas Mukhopadhyay's team · First heart transplant · AIIMS, 1994 — Dr P. Venugopal · Democracy, money and the map · First general elections · 1951–52; the first Lok Sabha met in 1952 · First Five-Year Plan · 1951–56 · First Lok Adalat · Junagadh, Gujarat, 1982 · Asia's oldest stock exchange · Bombay Stock Exchange, 1875 · Asia's first postage stamp · The 'Scinde Dawk', Karachi (Sind), 1852 · First telegraph line · Calcutta to Diamond Harbour, 1851 · One of Asia's first hydro plants · Sidrapong, near Darjeeling, 1897 · First Asian Games · New Delhi, 1951 · First World Heritage sites · Ajanta, Ellora, Agra Fort and the Taj Mahal (1983) · First Ramsar sites · Chilika and Keoladeo (1981) · First biosphere reserve · Nilgiri (1986) · The first railway (1853), metro (1984), Vande Bharat and India's first airline flight are in Industries & Transport , with the first cotton and jute mills and the first steel plant . Dakshin Gangotri is in Antarctica , Himadri in the Arctic . The first universities (1857) were Calcutta, Bombay and Madras — not Delhi or Banaras. · Hicky's Bengal Gazette (1780); Udant Martand (1826, first Hindi paper). · Raja Harishchandra (1913), Alam Ara (1931), Kisan Kanya (1937); Doordarshan 1959. · Universities 1857 (Calcutta, Bombay, Madras); IIT Kharagpur 1951; AIIMS 1956; IIM Calcutta 1961. · Apsara reactor (1956), Tarapur power station (1969), Pokhran test (1974), Aryabhata (1975). · Dakshin Gangotri (Antarctica, 1983–84); Himadri (Arctic, 2008); first test-tube baby Durga (1978). · General elections 1951–52; first Lok Adalat Junagadh (1982); Asian Games New Delhi (1951).

Asked now and then: the world's first woman Prime Minister (Sirimavo Bandaranaike), the first woman Nobel laureate (Marie Curie), the first to climb Everest and reach the South Pole , the first Nobel winners of 1901, and the first Olympics and World Cups . · The world's firsts are a story of explorers and pioneers. Vasco da Gama reached India by sea in 1498, and Magellan 's ships sailed right round the world (1519–22). Roald Amundsen reached the South Pole in 1911; Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary stood on Everest on 29 May 1953; and in 1975 Japan's Junko Tabei became the first woman there. Politics had its pioneers too. Sirimavo Bandaranaike of Sri Lanka became the world's first woman Prime Minister in 1960 — six years before Indira Gandhi — and Iceland's Vigdís Finnbogadóttir the first woman elected President (1980). The first Nobel Prizes were given in 1901 ; Marie Curie was the first woman to win one, and the only person to win in two sciences. · World firsts: people · First · Who · Note · The first woman Prime Minister in the world · Sirimavo Bandaranaike · Sirimavo Bandaranaike became Prime Minister of Ceylon (Sri Lanka) in 1960. · The first woman elected President of a country · Vigdís Finnbogadóttir · sailed in 1519; he was killed on the way and Juan Sebastián Elcano finished the voyage in 1522. · The first person to run a mile in under four minutes · Roger Bannister · Roger Bannister ran 3 minutes 59.4 seconds at Oxford in 1954. · The first person to sail alone round the world · Joshua Slocum · Joshua Slocum sailed the sloop Spray round the world alone in 1895–98. · The first Nobel Prizes · shared by Henry Dunant, founder of the Red Cross, and Frédéric Passy. · Economic Sciences · Ragnar Frisch and Jan Tinbergen · The Economics prize was first given in 1969, to Ragnar Frisch and Jan Tinbergen. · World firsts: events · First modern Olympics · Athens, 1896 · First Winter Olympics · Chamonix (France), 1924 · First Paralympics · Rome, 1960 · First FIFA World Cup · Uruguay, 1930 — the hosts won · First Cricket World Cup · England, 1975 — won by the West Indies · First Commonwealth Games · Hamilton (Canada), 1930, as the British Empire Games · First country where all women could vote · New Zealand, 1893 · First postage stamp · The Penny Black, Britain, 1840 · First atomic bomb used in war · Hiroshima, 6 August 1945 · First to the top of Everest · Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary, 29 May 1953 · First ascent of Everest without bottled oxygen · Reinhold Messner and Peter Habeler, 1978 · Space firsts in one line · First human in space · Yuri Gagarin, Vostok 1, 12 April 1961 · First woman in space · Valentina Tereshkova, 1963 · First people on the Moon · Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin, Apollo 11, 20 July 1969 · The full list · See Space , lesson 14 (World space firsts) · Women at the top, in order — “Sri Lanka 60, India 66, Iceland 80, Britain 79” : Bandaranaike (1960, PM), Indira Gandhi (1966), Thatcher (1979), Vigdís (1980, first elected President). · The world's first woman Prime Minister was Sirimavo Bandaranaike , not Indira Gandhi or Golda Meir. Amundsen reached the South Pole (1911); Peary claimed the North Pole (1909), a claim still doubted. firsts.x: Most asked: India's longest sea bridge (Atal Setu), river bridge (Bhupen Hazarika Setu), road and rail tunnels (Chenani–Nashri, T-50), longest national highway (NH-44), the Statue of Unity , the largest stadium , the largest and smallest districts (Kachchh, Mahe) and the highest waterfall (Kunchikal). · India's record book keeps changing because India keeps building. In January 2024 Atal Setu — about 21.8 km across Mumbai's harbour — became the longest sea bridge. In February 2024 the 12.77-km T-50 opened on the Kashmir rail line as the longest railway tunnel in use, and in June 2025 the Chenab Bridge , the world's highest railway arch, carried the first trains to the valley alongside Anji Khad , India's first cable-stayed rail bridge. Bigger records are on the way. The 14.57-km Tunnel 8 on the Rishikesh–Karnaprayag line broke through in April 2025; the 13-km Zojila road tunnel was dug through in June 2026; and the Delhi–Mumbai Expressway , about 1,386 km, is mostly open. Until they open in full, the older record-holders keep their titles — so in an exam, look for the words 'in use' or 'being built' . · Bridges, tunnels and roads (as of October 2026) · Record · Holder · Note · India's longest sea bridge · Atal Setu (Mumbai Trans Harbour Link) · About 21.8 km from Sewri to Nhava Sheva, over Thane Creek; opened January 2024. · India's longest river bridge open end to end · Bhupen Hazarika Setu (Dhola–Sadiya), Assam · About 9.15 km over the Lohit, opened 2017. The 9.76-km Kacchi Dargah–Bidupur bridge on the Ganga (Bihar), partly opened in June 2025, will pass it when finished. · India's longest rail-cum-road bridge · Bogibeel Bridge, Assam · About 4.94 km over the Brahmaputra, 2018. · India's longest rail-only bridge · Vembanad Rail Bridge, Kochi · About 4.62 km, across the backwaters to the Vallarpadam terminal. · The world's highest railway arch bridge · Chenab Bridge, Jammu and Kashmir · About 359 m above the Chenab; Asked now and then: the world's tallest building (Burj Khalifa), longest bridge (Danyang–Kunshan), highest bridge (Huajiang Grand Canyon, 2025), longest rail and road tunnels (Gotthard, Lærdal), longest railway (Trans-Siberian), the most populous country (India) and the record animals and plants. · People keep building higher and longer. Dubai's Burj Khalifa (828 m) has been the tallest building since 2010; Saudi Arabia's Jeddah Tower , planned to pass one kilometre, is due around 2028. China holds the bridge records: the 164.8-km Danyang–Kunshan Grand Bridge is the longest, and in September 2025 the Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge opened about 625 m above the Beipan river — the highest in the world. Under the Alps, the 57-km Gotthard Base Tunnel is the longest railway tunnel; Norway's Lærdal (24.5 km) is the longest road tunnel. Nature has its own champions. The blue whale is the largest animal that has ever lived; the cheetah is the fastest on land, the peregrine falcon the fastest of all in a dive. Among countries, Russia is the largest, Vatican City the smallest, and since 2023 India has the most people. · Built by people (as of October 2026) · Record · Holder · Note · the world's tallest building · Burj Khalifa, Dubai · 828 m, since 2010; Asked now and then: Pink City (Jaipur), Blue City and Sun City (Jodhpur), Golden City (Jaisalmer), City of Lakes (Udaipur), City of Joy (Kolkata), City of Nawabs (Lucknow), Queen of the Arabian Sea (Kochi), God's Own Country (Kerala) — and a few world nicknames. · A nickname usually hides a reason. Jaipur was painted pink to welcome the Prince of Wales in 1876. Jodhpur 's old town is washed in blue below Mehrangarh Fort, and the sun shines there almost all year. Jaisalmer rises in yellow sandstone from the Thar, so it glows like gold. Udaipur grew around the lakes Pichola and Fateh Sagar. Elsewhere: Kolkata became the 'City of Joy' after a 1985 novel; Lucknow is the 'City of Nawabs'; Hyderabad traded pearls; Kochi 's harbour made it the 'Queen of the Arabian Sea'; and Bhubaneswar 's hundreds of temples made it the 'Temple City of India'. · Nicknames of Indian cities · Nickname · City · Why · Pink City · Jaipur · Painted pink for the Prince of Wales's visit in 1876. · Blue City ·
