firsts.x: Exams mix these topics in 'which pair is correctly matched' and 'arrange in order' questions. This lesson puts the dates in order and sets the look-alike pairs side by side. · Revise this app in four sweeps. Symbols : say the dates aloud in order — 1947 flag, 1950 anthem, song and emblem, 1957 calendar, 1963 bird, 2008 river, 2009 dolphin, 2010 elephant and ₹, 2012 microbe. Firsts : picture each post with its first holder, then the first woman beside him. Records : remember that India's newest bridges and tunnels win only once they are open. Nicknames : tie each name to its reason. Then work through the look-alike pairs below — almost every wrong answer in this topic comes from mixing two of them. · Symbols in order of adoption · 1947 · 22 July — the national flag · 1950 · 24 January — the anthem and the song; 26 January — the State Emblem · 1957 · 22 March — the Saka calendar · 1963 · The Indian peafowl as national bird · 1973 · Project Tiger, for the national animal · 2008 · The Ganga as national river · 2009 · 5 October — the Ganges river dolphin as national aquatic animal · 2010 · The elephant as national heritage animal; the ₹ sign (15 July) · 2012 · Lactobacillus as national microbe · 2026 · Six-stanza Vande Mataram order (January); bill to protect the song passed (July) · Look-alike pairs · This · is not this · Remember · Atal Setu — Mumbai sea bridge · Atal Tunnel — Himachal road tunnel · Both opened 2020–24, both named after Atal Bihari Vajpayee. · Anna Rajam Malhotra — first woman IAS · Kiran Bedi — first woman IPS · Administrative 1951; China 2025. · Gotthard Base — longest rail tunnel · Lærdal — longest road tunnel · Switzerland and Norway. · Golden City — Jaisalmer · Golden Temple — Amritsar · Sandstone versus a shrine. · Before you answer a 'first' question, ask three words : first in India or the world? first woman or first person? first, or first in use? Most traps hide in one of these. · Tagore wrote the anthem but sang the song (1896). Pratibha Patil was the first woman President; Droupadi Murmu the first from a Scheduled Tribe. The lion was the national animal before the tiger. heritage.t: UNESCO and the World Heritage list
heritage.x: Most asked: India's total and the split (cultural, natural, mixed), the latest site , the first four (1983), the year of the Convention (1972) , the bodies that judge sites ( ICOMOS , IUCN ) and World Heritage Day (18 April) . · In the 1960s Egypt began the Aswan High Dam, and the rising Nile threatened the temples of Abu Simbel. UNESCO raised money from many countries, and the temples were cut into blocks and moved uphill. The lesson was clear: some places are too precious to be left to one country alone. So in 1972 UNESCO's General Conference in Paris adopted the World Heritage Convention . A country that signs it promises to protect its great places, and may put them forward for the World Heritage List . A committee of 21 member countries meets once a year and decides, after experts have checked each site: ICOMOS for cultural sites and IUCN for natural ones. India signed in 1977 , and its first four sites — Ajanta, Ellora, Agra Fort and the Taj Mahal — were listed in 1983 . As of October 2026 India has 45 sites : 37 cultural, 7 natural and 1 mixed. The latest is Sarnath (July 2026). · The World Heritage system in one look · UNESCO · United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization — founded 1945, headquarters in Paris · The Convention · Convention concerning the Protection of the World Cultural and Natural Heritage — adopted 16 November 1972 in Paris; in force from 1975 · India joins · Ratified in 1977 ; first Indian sites inscribed in 1983 · First World Heritage list · 1978 — 12 sites worldwide (the Galápagos Islands among them) · World Heritage Committee · 21 member countries, elected from those that have signed; meets once a year and decides which sites are inscribed · Advisory bodies · ICOMOS (cultural sites), IUCN (natural sites), ICCROM (conservation and training) · In India · The Archaeological Survey of India (Ministry of Culture) prepares and looks after cultural sites; natural sites go through the Environment Ministry and the Wildlife Institute of India · World Heritage in Danger · A separate list of sites under threat — Manas (1992–2011) and Hampi (1999–2006) were once on it; no Indian site is on it now · World Heritage Day · 18 April — the International Day for Monuments and Sites · The ten selection criteria · Criterion · What it recognises · Type · (i) · A masterpiece of human creative genius — the Taj Mahal is listed on this criterion alone · Cultural · (ii) · An exchange of ideas over time in architecture, technology, town planning or art · Cultural · (iii) · A unique or rare testimony to a culture or civilisation, living or lost · Cultural · (iv) · An outstanding example of a type of building, ensemble or landscape from a stage of history · Cultural · (v) · A traditional human settlement or use of land or sea · Cultural · (vi) · A direct link with events, living traditions, ideas, beliefs or great works of art and literature · Cultural · (vii) · Superlative natural phenomena or exceptional natural beauty · Natural · (viii) · Major stages of the Earth's history — rocks, fossils, landforms · Natural · (ix) · Ongoing ecological and biological processes in ecosystems · Natural · (x) · The most important habitats for conserving biological diversity and threatened species · Natural · A site must also show Outstanding Universal Value , be authentic and whole (integrity), and have legal protection and a management plan. A cultural site meets at least one of (i)–(vi), a natural site at least one of (vii)–(x), and a mixed site at least one of each. · India's additions, year by year from 2014 · Year · Added · Committee session · India's total · 2014 · Rani ki Vav (Patan, Gujarat); A site must be on it before it can be nominated; being on it is not World Heritage status · India's list · About 80 entries (October 2026) — the number grows as new places are added · Waited longest · Sarnath was on the Tentative List from 1998 until it was inscribed in 2026 · Added in 2026 · Bagh Caves (MP), Udaigiri Caves (MP), Group of Temples of the Chambal Valley, Painted Haveli Towns of Shekhawati (Rajasthan); in October, the Sirpur landscape (Chhattisgarh) and two volcanic sites of the Andaman Islands · Added in 2025 · Seven natural sites, among them the Deccan Traps at Panchgani, St Mary's Island (Udupi), the Varkala cliffs and the Meghalayan Age caves · Count the split as “37–7–1” : 37 cultural, 7 natural, 1 mixed = 45. The years since 2014 run 2-0-3-1-1-1, gap, 2, gap, 2-1-1-1 — 2014 two sites, 2015 none, 2016 three, then one a year to 2019, no meeting in 2020, two in 2021, no session in 2022, two in 2023, then one each in 2024, 2025 and 2026. · The Convention is of 1972 , but India's first sites came in 1983 ; the first world list was in 1978 . ICOMOS judges cultural sites and IUCN natural ones — not UNEP or WWF. A place on the Tentative List (Sirpur, Shekhawati) is not yet a World Heritage site. Maratha Military Landscapes (2025) was the 44th; Sarnath (2026) is the 45th. · For the full table of all sites with their states, see the UNESCO lesson in Art & Culture . The next five lessons here go through every site group by group, in more depth. · The World Heritage Convention was adopted in Paris on 16 November 1972; India ratified it in 1977. · India's first four sites (1983): Ajanta, Ellora, Agra Fort and the Taj Mahal. · As of October 2026 India has 45 sites: 37 cultural, 7 natural and 1 mixed (Khangchendzonga). · Latest: Sarnath, the 45th, at the 48th session in Busan (July 2026); before it Maratha Military Landscapes (2025) and Moidams (2024). · Ten criteria: (i)–(vi) cultural, (vii)–(x) natural. ICOMOS checks cultural sites, IUCN natural ones. · The Committee has 21 members; India hosted its 46th session in New Delhi in July 2024. · World Heritage Day is 18 April. A Tentative List place is not yet a World Heritage site.

heritage.t: Cultural sites I: Buddhist and ancient sites
heritage.h: सांस्कृतिक स्थल I: बौद्ध और प्राचीन स्थल
heritage.x: Most asked: Ajanta vs Ellora vs Elephanta (which faith, which king, which feature), Bhimbetka (rock paintings), Dholavira (the Harappan site, 2021), Sanchi and Ashoka , Bodh Gaya and Nalanda in Bihar, and the newest site, Sarnath (2026). · Walk through Indian time in nine stops. First, the rock shelters of Bhimbetka , where Stone Age people painted hunters and animals on the walls more than ten thousand years ago. Then Dholavira , a Harappan city on an island in the Rann of Kutch, which stored rainwater in huge stone reservoirs. Next come the places of the Buddha : Bodh Gaya , where he became enlightened under the Bodhi tree; Sarnath , where he gave his first sermon; and the stupas of Sanchi , begun by Ashoka. Later, Nalanda became a great university where students came from as far as China. Last, the cave sites of Maharashtra: Ajanta with its paintings, Ellora where three faiths carved side by side, and Elephanta with its giant Shiva. · Ancient and Buddhist World Heritage sites · Site · State · Year · Remember · Rock Shelters of Bhimbetka · Madhya Pradesh · 2003 · Raisen district, in the Vindhya hills; Stone Age paintings; found in 1957 by V. S. Wakankar. · Dholavira: a Harappan City · Gujarat · 2021 · On Khadir Bet in the Rann of Kutch; great water reservoirs and a 'signboard' of Indus signs. · Buddhist Monuments at Sanchi · Madhya Pradesh · 1989 · Raisen district; the Great Stupa begun by Ashoka, with four carved gateways. · Mahabodhi Temple Complex, Bodh Gaya · Bihar · 2002 · Where the Buddha attained enlightenment; one of the earliest brick temples, of the Gupta age. · Nalanda Mahavihara · Bihar · 2016 · A monastic university founded under Kumaragupta I in the 5th century. · Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath · Uttar Pradesh · 2026 · Near Varanasi, where the Buddha gave his first sermon; Dhamek and Chaukhandi stupas, the Ashokan pillar. · Ajanta Caves · Maharashtra · 1983 · Buddhist only; famous for wall paintings; cut into a horseshoe bend of the Waghora. · Ellora Caves · Maharashtra · 1983 · Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves side by side; the Kailasa temple (Cave 16). · Elephanta Caves · Maharashtra · 1987 · On Gharapuri island in Mumbai harbour; the great three-headed Shiva (Sadashiva). · Ajanta, Ellora and Elephanta compared · Ajanta · Ellora · Elephanta · Faith · Buddhist only · Buddhist (Caves 1–12), Hindu (13–29), Jain (30–34) · Mainly Hindu (Shaiva), with two Buddhist caves · Number of caves · About 30 · 34 main caves · 7 · Age · 2nd–1st century BCE, and a second phase in the 5th–6th century CE (under the Vakatakas) · About 600–1000 CE · About 5th–6th century CE · Famous for · Paintings — the Padmapani, Jataka stories · Kailasa temple (Cave 16), cut from one rock under the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I · The Sadashiva — a 6-metre three-headed Shiva · Where · Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (Aurangabad) district, on the Waghora · Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar district · Gharapuri island, Mumbai harbour · Note · Rediscovered in 1819 by a British officer, John Smith · Cave 10 (Vishvakarma) is a Buddhist chaitya hall · Named Elephanta by the Portuguese after a stone elephant there · The Buddhist sites in detail · Sanchi · The Great Stupa (Stupa 1) was begun by Ashoka in brick; the Shungas enlarged it in stone, and its four carved gateways ( toranas ) came in the Satavahana period · Bodh Gaya · The Mahabodhi temple stands beside the Bodhi tree and the Vajrasana (diamond throne); Ashoka built the first shrine, and the present brick temple dates from the 5th–6th century · Nalanda · Founded under Kumaragupta I ; the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang studied here in Harsha's time; destroyed by Bakhtiyar Khalji about 1193. A new Nalanda University opened at Rajgir in 2014 · Sarnath · The Deer Park (Rishipatana) of the first sermon ; the site includes the Dhamek Stupa , the Chaukhandi Stupa , the Dharmarajika Stupa, the Mulagandhakuti Vihara and the Ashokan pillar. Its Lion Capital is India's National Emblem · Four great places · Lumbini (birth, in Nepal — a World Heritage site of Nepal), Bodh Gaya (enlightenment), Sarnath (first sermon), Kushinagar (death — not a World Heritage site) · The two oldest sites · Bhimbetka · More than 700 rock shelters, about 400 of them painted, from the Stone Age onward; in the Vindhya hills south of Bhopal; the name is linked to Bhima of the Mahabharata · Dholavira · One of the five largest Harappan cities; a city of three parts (citadel, middle town, lower town), built of stone; found by J. P. Joshi (1967–68) and excavated by R. S. Bisht from 1990 · Not on the list · Lothal (the Harappan dockyard), Rakhigarhi and Kalibangan are not World Heritage sites — Dholavira is India's only Harappan site on the list · Ajanta = Art (paintings, Buddhist only); Ellora = Everyone (three faiths, and the enormous Kailasa); Elephanta = Eshwara (Shiva on an island). And “Raisen holds two” : Bhimbetka and Sanchi are both in Raisen district of Madhya Pradesh. · Sarnath is the first sermon, Bodh Gaya is enlightenment — do not swap them. Sarnath is in Uttar Pradesh , Bodh Gaya and Nalanda in Bihar . Lothal is not a World Heritage site; Dholavira is. The Ellora Kailasa is rock-cut ; Elephanta's great image is the Sadashiva , often called the Trimurti. · Stupa parts, chaityas and the other cave sites (Karla, Bhaja, Barabar, Udayagiri) are in the architecture lesson of Art & Culture . · Bhimbetka (2003) and Sanchi (1989) are both in Raisen district, Madhya Pradesh. · Dholavira (2021), on Khadir Bet in Kutch, is India's only Harappan World Heritage site. · Bodh Gaya (2002) and Nalanda (2016) are in Bihar; Sarnath (2026) is in Uttar Pradesh. · Ajanta: Buddhist, paintings. Ellora: Buddhist, Hindu and Jain; Kailasa temple of Krishna I. Elephanta: Shiva, on Gharapuri island. · Sanchi's Great Stupa was begun by Ashoka; its gateways are toranas. · Sarnath's Lion Capital is the National Emblem; the Dhamek Stupa marks the first sermon.

Most asked: which dynasty built each temple site (Pallava, Chola, Chandela, Chalukya, Hoysala, Kakatiya), Konark as Surya's chariot, Hampi as the Vijayanagara capital, Rani ki Vav (₹100 note) and the recent pair — Ramappa (2021) and the Hoysala temples (2023). · Picture a road trip down the east coast and across the Deccan. At Mahabalipuram the Pallavas cut whole temples out of boulders and built the Shore Temple facing the Bay of Bengal. Up north in Odisha, the Eastern Ganga king Narasimhadeva I turned the Sun Temple at Konark into a giant stone chariot with 24 wheels and seven horses. In the Tamil country the Cholas raised the towering Brihadisvara of Thanjavur. In Karnataka, the Chalukyas tried out northern and southern styles side by side at Pattadakal ; centuries later the Hoysalas carved star-shaped soapstone temples at Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura , and the Vijayanagara kings built their capital at Hampi . In central India the Chandelas built Khajuraho ; in Telangana the Kakatiyas built the Ramappa temple; and in Gujarat Queen Udayamati built Rani ki Vav , a stepwell carved like an upside-down temple. · The temple sites · Site · State · Year · Dynasty · Remember · Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram · Tamil Nadu · 1984 · Pallavas · Rathas, Arjuna's Penance and the Shore Temple, by the sea south of Chennai. · Sun Temple, Konark · Odisha · 1984 · Eastern Gangas · Surya's chariot in stone, built by Narasimhadeva I in the 13th century. · Khajuraho Group of Monuments · Madhya Pradesh · 1986 · Chandelas · Hindu and Jain temples of about 950–1050; the Virupaksha temple. · Great Living Chola Temples · Tamil Nadu · 1987 · Cholas · Brihadisvara at Thanjavur (1987); Gangaikondacholapuram and Darasuram added in 2004. · Rani ki Vav, Patan · Gujarat · 2014 · Chaulukyas (Solankis) · A stepwell built in memory of Bhima I by Queen Udayamati, on the Saraswati. · Kakatiya Rudreshwara (Ramappa) Temple · Telangana · 2021 · Kakatiyas · Built in 1213 at Palampet; named after its sculptor Ramappa. · Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas · Karnataka · 2023 · Hoysalas · Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura — star-shaped temples of soapstone. · Inside each site · Mahabalipuram (Mamallapuram) · Pancha Rathas — five monolithic shrines named after the Pandavas and Draupadi — and the open-air relief of Arjuna's Penance (Descent of the Ganga), from the time of Narasimhavarman I Mamalla (7th century); the Shore Temple is of Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha) , about 700 CE · Konark · Called the Black Pagoda by sailors; about 1250 CE; Kalinga style; the stone wheel is on the ₹10 note · Khajuraho · Chhatarpur district; of about 85 temples, some 25 survive in western, eastern and southern groups; Hindu (Kandariya Mahadeva, Lakshmana) and Jain (Parsvanatha); the Khajuraho Dance Festival is held each February · Hampi · Founded about 1336 by Harihara and Bukka; the living Virupaksha temple, the Vitthala temple with its stone chariot (₹50 note) and musical pillars, the Lotus Mahal; sacked after the Battle of Talikota (1565) · Pattadakal · Bagalkot district; the Chalukya coronation town; the Virupaksha temple was built by Queen Lokamahadevi to mark Vikramaditya II's victory over the Pallavas of Kanchi · Great Living Chola Temples · Brihadisvara, Thanjavur — Rajaraja I, completed about 1010; Gangaikondacholapuram — Rajendra I; Airavatesvara, Darasuram — Rajaraja II. 'Living' because worship still goes on · Rani ki Vav · Seven levels, hundreds of sculptures, mostly of Vishnu's avatars; silted up for centuries and dug out by the ASI; on the ₹100 note · Ramappa · Palampet, Mulugu district; built by Recharla Rudra, general of the Kakatiya king Ganapati Deva; light 'floating' bricks in its tower and a sand-box foundation against earthquakes · Hoysala temples · Chennakeshava, Belur (Vishnuvardhana, 1117); Hoysaleswara, Halebidu (12th century, at the old capital Dwarasamudra); Keshava, Somanathapura (1268); star-shaped plans on a raised platform ( jagati ), of soapstone · Two by sea in '84 — Mahabalipuram and Konark, both on the east coast, both 1984. Karnataka's three temple sites, oldest listed first — H ampi '86, P attadakal '87, H oysala '23: “Hampi, Pattadakal, Hoysala — HPH”. · Konark is the Black Pagoda; the White Pagoda is the Jagannath temple at Puri, which is not a World Heritage site. Brihadisvara of Thanjavur was built by Rajaraja I ; Gangaikondacholapuram by his son Rajendra I . Aihole , Badami and the Modhera Sun Temple are on the Tentative List only. Ramappa is in Telangana , not Andhra Pradesh. · The temple styles (Nagara, Dravida, Vesara) and famous temples that are not World Heritage sites come in lesson H8. · Mahabalipuram (Pallavas) and Konark (Eastern Gangas) were inscribed in 1984. · Khajuraho (Chandelas, MP) and Hampi (Vijayanagara, Karnataka) in 1986; Pattadakal (Chalukyas) and the Chola temples in 1987. · Brihadisvara, Thanjavur — Rajaraja I; Gangaikondacholapuram — Rajendra I; Darasuram — Rajaraja II (added 2004). · Rani ki Vav (Patan, 2014) is a stepwell built by Queen Udayamati; it is on the ₹100 note. · Ramappa (Telangana, 2021) is named after its sculptor; Hoysala temples of Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura (2023). · Konark is the Black Pagoda; Hampi's stone chariot is on the ₹50 note, Konark's wheel on the ₹10 note.

heritage.t: Cultural sites III: Mughal, Sultanate and forts
heritage.h: सांस्कृतिक स्थल III: मुगल, सल्तनत और किले
heritage.x: Most asked: the Taj Mahal (builder, architect, marble), Agra Fort vs Red Fort , Fatehpur Sikri and the Buland Darwaza , Qutb Minar (Aibak → Iltutmish), Humayun's Tomb (first garden-tomb), the six Hill Forts of Rajasthan , and the newer sites — Moidams (2024) and the Maratha Military Landscapes (2025). · Delhi's story is told in stone. Qutb-ud-din Aibak began the Qutb Minar as a tower of victory; Iltutmish finished it. Three centuries later Humayun's widow raised the first great Mughal garden-tomb, Humayun's Tomb , which later inspired the Taj. Akbar rebuilt Agra Fort in red sandstone and founded a new city, Fatehpur Sikri , in honour of the Sufi saint Salim Chishti. His grandson Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, then moved the capital to Delhi and built the Red Fort . Away from the Mughals, Rajput kings crowned the Aravalli hills with forts, Mahmud Begada built his capital at Champaner , the Ahom kings of Assam buried their dead in great mounds at Charaideo , and Shivaji and his successors held the Sahyadri with a chain of hill and sea forts — the Maratha Military Landscapes . · Sultanate, Mughal and fort sites · Site · State / UT · Year · Remember · Agra Fort · Uttar Pradesh · 1983 · Akbar rebuilt it in red sandstone from 1565; Itimad-ud-Daulah , Akbar's tomb at Sikandra and Bibi ka Maqbara are not on the list. · Mughal architecture (pietra dura, charbagh, the true arch) is explained in Art & Culture ; the reigns behind these buildings are in Medieval India. heritage.t: Cultural sites IV: colonial, modern and city sites
heritage.h: सांस्कृतिक स्थल IV: औपनिवेशिक, आधुनिक और नगर स्थल
heritage.x: Most asked: Ahmedabad as India's first World Heritage city, Jaipur City (2019) and its founder, the Mountain Railways (three lines, three years), CST and its architect, Le Corbusier and Chandigarh, and Santiniketan (2023). · Not every World Heritage site is ancient. The Portuguese built the great churches of Old Goa in the 16th and 17th centuries. In the 19th century the British gave Bombay its Gothic railway station, Victoria Terminus — now Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus — and a row of Gothic courts and colleges along the Oval Maidan ; across the same ground, in the 1930s, came a row of Art Deco flats and cinemas. Meanwhile engineers pushed little railways up the hills to Darjeeling , Ooty and Shimla . After Independence, Nehru invited the Swiss-French architect Le Corbusier to design Punjab's new capital, Chandigarh. Whole cities are on the list too. Ahmedabad , founded in 1411, was the first Indian city inscribed (2017); Jaipur , laid out in 1727 by Sawai Jai Singh II, followed in 2019. And in 2023 came Santiniketan , where Rabindranath Tagore taught under the trees. · Colonial, modern and city sites · Site · State / UT · Year · Remember · Churches and Convents of Goa · Goa · 1986 · Old Goa, the Portuguese capital; the Basilica of Bom Jesus holds the body of St Francis Xavier. · Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus · Maharashtra · 2004 · Mumbai's Victorian Gothic railway station by F. Its Samrat Yantra is one of the largest stone sundials in the world · Santiniketan · Birbhum district; Debendranath Tagore set up an ashram here in 1863; Rabindranath began a school in 1901 and founded Visva-Bharati in 1921; it became a central university in 1951 · Railways in the order they joined — “ D-N-K , '99-'05-'08”: D arjeeling 1999, N ilgiri 2005, K alka–Shimla 2008. Ahmedabad , not Jaipur, was the first Indian city. · Churches and Convents of Goa (1986): Bom Jesus holds St Francis Xavier's remains. · CST (2004) by F. W. Most asked: the seven natural sites and their states, the only mixed site (Khangchendzonga), the Western Ghats (four states), and Manas on the danger list. · India's natural sites trace a line across the country: rhinos and wild buffalo in Assam (Kaziranga, Manas, both 1985), birds in a Rajasthan wetland ( Keoladeo , 1985), tigers in the mangroves of Bengal (Sundarbans, 1987), the high peaks and meadows of Uttarakhand (Nanda Devi 1988, Valley of Flowers 2005) and Himachal (Great Himalayan, 2014), and the long green wall of the Western Ghats (2012). One site is valued for both nature and culture: Khangchendzonga in Sikkim (2016), where the mountain is a god for the Lepcha people and its valleys are sacred hidden lands for Buddhists. · Natural sites and the mixed site · Site · State · Year · Remember · Kaziranga National Park · Assam · 1985 · Two-thirds of the world's one-horned rhinoceroses; on the Brahmaputra floodplain. · Manas Wildlife Sanctuary · Assam · 1985 · On the Bhutan border; pygmy hog and golden langur; on the danger list 1992–2011. · Keoladeo National Park · Rajasthan · 1985 · The Bharatpur wetland, once a maharaja's duck-shooting reserve; once the winter home of the Siberian crane. · Sundarbans National Park · West Bengal · 1987 · The largest mangrove forest; tigers that swim; Bangladesh's part is a separate site. · Nanda Devi and Valley of Flowers National Parks · Uttarakhand · 1988 · Chamoli district; Valley of Flowers added in 2005. · Great Himalayan National Park Conservation Area · Himachal Pradesh · 2014 · Kullu district; the western Himalaya's high forests and meadows. · Khangchendzonga National Park · Sikkim · 2016 · India's only mixed site; sacred to the Lepcha and to Buddhists. · Western Ghats · Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra · 2012 · 39 component parts — national parks, sanctuaries and reserve forests; a biodiversity hotspot. · Points the National Parks app does not stress · Western Ghats · Older than the Himalayas; Bangladesh's Sundarbans is a separate site (1997) · Khangchendzonga · Mixed site — natural (criteria vii and x) and cultural (iii and vi); the world's third-highest peak · Other UNESCO lists · India has 13 biosphere reserves in UNESCO's World Network of Biosphere Reserves (Man and the Biosphere); the latest is the Cold Desert reserve, Himachal Pradesh (September 2025). Ramsar wetlands come under a separate treaty, the Ramsar Convention · The 1985 trio is “K-M-K” — Kaziranga, Manas, Keoladeo. Everything natural ends with the Himalaya (Great Himalayan 2014) and the one mixed site in Sikkim (2016). · The only mixed site is Khangchendzonga , not Nanda Devi. Keoladeo is in Rajasthan , not Gujarat. The Valley of Flowers joined in 2005 , not 1988. A biosphere reserve on UNESCO's network is not a World Heritage site. · Each of these parks — its animals, its records and its map — is covered in the World Heritage lesson (N10) of National Parks of India . · Seven natural sites: Kaziranga, Manas, Keoladeo (1985); Sundarbans (1987); Nanda Devi and Valley of Flowers (1988, 2005); Western Ghats (2012); Great Himalayan NP (2014). · One mixed site: Khangchendzonga, Sikkim (2016). · The Western Ghats site has 39 parts in Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra. · Manas was on the danger list from 1992 to 2011. · India has 13 UNESCO biosphere reserves; the latest is the Cold Desert (2025).

The most repeated monument question of all: “Who built …?” — Charminar, Gol Gumbaz, Hawa Mahal, Buland Darwaza, Alai Darwaza, Jama Masjid, Itimad-ud-Daulah, Gateway of India, India Gate, Victoria Memorial. Most of these are not World Heritage sites, which is itself a common trap. · Think of the builders as a relay. The Delhi Sultans began it: Aibak's first mosque, Alauddin Khalji's gate, the Tughlaqs' forts. Sher Shah built the Purana Qila in the short gap of Humayun's exile. Then the Mughals took the baton — Akbar's Buland Darwaza , Nur Jahan's marble tomb for her father, Shah Jahan's Jama Masjid , Aurangzeb's small Moti Masjid . In the Deccan the sultans built their own wonders: the Qutb Shahis' Charminar in Hyderabad and the Adil Shahis' Gol Gumbaz in Bijapur. Rajput kings built forts and palaces — Mehrangarh, Amber, the Hawa Mahal . The British added the Gateway of India , India Gate and the Victoria Memorial , and independent India the Lotus Temple, the Statue of Unity and a new Parliament. · Sultanate, Mughal and Deccan monuments · Monument · Built by · Place, date and note · The Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque, Delhi's first mosque · Qutb-ud-din Aibak · Delhi, 1190s; heritage.x: Most asked: temple → state (Kamakhya, Jagannath, Meenakshi, Dilwara, Modhera, Somnath), the three styles — Nagara, Dravida, Vesara — with one example each, and the parts of a temple ( shikhara, vimana, gopuram, amalaka, garbhagriha ). · Every Hindu temple begins with a small dark room, the garbhagriha (womb-house), where the deity sits. Over it rises a tower, and in front of it a hall ( mandapa ) for the worshippers. How that tower is shaped tells you the style. In the north, the Nagara tower — the shikhara — curves gently inward like a mountain peak and carries a ribbed stone disc, the amalaka , and a pot-shaped finial, the kalasha . In the south, the Dravida tower — the vimana — rises in stepped storeys like a pyramid, and the temple sits inside walls entered by huge gateway towers, gopurams . In the Deccan between them grew Vesara , which mixes the two; the Hoysalas gave it star-shaped plans. · The three temple styles · Style · Region · Marks of the style · Examples · Nagara · North and east India · Curvilinear shikhara over the sanctum, crowned by an amalaka and kalasha ; heritage.x: Most asked: the latest element (Deepavali, December 2025 — the 16th), which year Kumbh (2017), Yoga (2016), Durga Puja (2021) and Garba (2023) were inscribed, which state an element belongs to, and the Creative Cities (Lucknow 2025, Kozhikode and Gwalior 2023). · A temple can be measured and mapped, but a song, a festival or a craft lives only while people keep doing it. In 2003 UNESCO adopted a second convention for this intangible cultural heritage , and India joined in 2005. India's Sangeet Natak Akademi prepares the nominations. India's first three — Koodiyattam , Vedic chanting and Ramlila — had been proclaimed 'Masterpieces' between 2001 and 2005 and moved onto the new list in 2008. Since then India has added dances, chants, a craft, festivals and Yoga. In December 2025 India hosted the committee for the first time, at the Red Fort , and Deepavali became its 16th element. Two more UNESCO lists come up in exams: the Memory of the World Register of precious documents (the Rigveda manuscripts, and since 2025 the Bhagavad Gita and the Natyashastra) and the Creative Cities Network , where nine Indian cities are listed for music, crafts, film, food or literature. · India's intangible cultural heritage (16 elements, as of October 2026) · Element · State / region · Year · What it is · Koodiyattam · Kerala · 2008 · Sanskrit theatre of Kerala's temples; tribes.t: Scheduled Tribes: the Constitution, the law and the numbers
tribes.h: अनुसूचित जनजातियाँ: संविधान, क़ानून और आँकड़े
tribes.x: Asked most: Article 342 (who notifies an ST), the Fifth vs Sixth Schedule and its four states, the number of PVTGs (75) and the state with the most ( Odisha, 13 ), the Census 2011 ST share ( 8.6% ), the state with the most tribal people ( Madhya Pradesh ) and the highest share ( Mizoram ), and the Forest Rights Act, 2006 . · The Constitution never says what a tribe is . Instead, Article 342 gives the job to the President : for each state, after talking to the Governor, the President issues a list — the first was the Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order, 1950 . Once the list is out, only Parliament , by a law, can add or drop a community. Officials judge a claim by the old Lokur Committee (1965) tests: primitive traits, a distinct culture, geographical isolation, shyness of contact and backwardness. Where tribal people are many, the Constitution gives two kinds of shield. In ten states of the mainland, the Fifth Schedule lets the President declare Scheduled Areas , guarded by the Governor and a Tribes Advisory Council . In four north-eastern states — Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram — the Sixth Schedule goes further: elected autonomous district councils make some of their own laws. The 2011 Census counted about 10.4 crore tribal people — 8.6% of India — in some 705 groups, nine in ten of them in villages. Among them, 75 of the most fragile groups are called PVTGs . And since 2006 a law, the Forest Rights Act , has let forest-dwellers claim the land and forests they have always used. · Articles about Scheduled Tribes · Article · What it does · Remember · Article 342 · How a community becomes a Scheduled Tribe · The President notifies the list for each state or UT (after consulting the Governor of a state); tribes.t: Tribes of the north, west and centre
tribes.h: उत्तर, पश्चिम और मध्य भारत की जनजातियाँ
tribes.x: Most asked: the Bhils and Gonds (largest tribes, their states, Gondi language, Gond art), Baigas (shifting cultivation), the Gaddis of Himachal, the Tharus of the Terai, the Bhotias and Jaunsaris of Uttarakhand, the Minas and Sahariyas of Rajasthan, the Warlis and their painting, and the Murias and the ghotul. · Walk south from the Himalaya. In the high valleys live herders and traders: the Gaddis drive sheep across the Dhauladhar, the Changpas of Ladakh raise pashmina goats, and the Bhotias of Uttarakhand once carried salt and wool over the passes to Tibet. Below them, in Jaunsar-Bawar , the Jaunsaris kept the old custom of one wife with several brothers as husbands. Along the Nepal border, in the Terai forests, live the Tharus . The heart of tribal India is the centre. The Bhils — the archers of old stories, India's largest tribe — spread across western Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Rajasthan and Maharashtra. The Gonds , the second largest, gave their name to Gondwana ; their queen Rani Durgavati fought the Mughals in 1564, and today their bright dot-and-line paintings carry a GI tag. In the Maikal hills the Baigas farm without a plough, and in Bastar the Murias send their young people to the ghotul to learn songs, work and life. · Tribes with one clear home · Tribe · State / UT · Remember · Gaddi · Himachal Pradesh · Shepherds of the Dhauladhar range; Bharmour in Chamba is their homeland. They move their flocks up to high pastures in summer and down in winter. · Kinnaura · Himachal Pradesh · The people of Kinnaur on the Sutlej, near the Tibet border. · Lahaula · Himachal Pradesh · The people of the Lahaul valley beyond the Rohtang Pass. · Bakarwal · Jammu and Kashmir · Nomadic goat and sheep herders (Gujjar-Bakarwal) who cross the Pir Panjal with the seasons. · Changpa · Ladakh · Nomads of the high Changthang plateau who rear the goats that give pashmina wool. · Brokpa · Ladakh · Of the Dah-Hanu villages on the Indus; tribes.t: Tribes of the east: Jharkhand, Odisha, West Bengal, Bihar
tribes.x: Most asked: the Santhals (Santhal Parganas, Santhali, Ol Chiki), Mundas and Oraons (Kurukh), Hos of Kolhan, Odisha's PVTGs — Bonda , Dongria Kondh (Niyamgiri), Juang , Saora — and the Kondhs , Odisha's largest tribe. · The Chota Nagpur plateau is the oldest tribal homeland of the east. Three peoples fill it. The Santhals , India's third-largest tribe, live in the Santhal Parganas and far beyond. The Mundas of the Ranchi–Khunti plateau held their land jointly as the descendants of the clan founders, a system called khuntkatti ; its breakdown drove Birsa Munda's rising. The Oraons came later and speak Kurukh , a Dravidian language, unlike the Munda languages (Santhali, Mundari, Ho) around them. To the south, in Kolhan , live the Hos . Odisha has 62 tribes — more than any other state — and 13 PVTGs. The Kondhs are the largest; Kandhamal district is named after them. In the Niyamgiri hills, the Dongria Kondhs worship the mountain as their god Niyam Raja and, in 2013, their village councils turned away a bauxite mine. In Malkangiri live the Bondas , whose women wear heavy bead necklaces and metal neck rings. The Saoras paint spirit pictures, idital , on their walls. · Tribes of the east and their homelands · Tribe · Homeland · Remember · Santhal · Santhal Parganas (Jharkhand) · India's third-largest tribe; The Dongria Kondh are of Niyamgiri (Rayagada–Kalahandi), the Bonda of Malkangiri . Most asked: the Naga tribes and their districts (Angami, Ao, Konyak, Sumi, Lotha), the matrilineal Khasis and Garos of Meghalaya, the Mizos , the Bodos of Assam, the Apatanis of Ziro, the Nyishis (largest in Arunachal), the Adis , the Monpas of Tawang, and the Bhutias and Lepchas of Sikkim. · The North-East holds more than a hundred tribes, and most of them speak Tibeto-Burman languages. In Nagaland each district is home to one major Naga tribe: the Angamis of Kohima, the Aos of Mokokchung, the tattooed Konyaks of Mon, the Sumis , the Lothas and many more. They meet every December at the Hornbill Festival . Meghalaya is different. Its three peoples — the Khasis , the Jaintias (Pnar) and the Garos — are matrilineal : children take the mother's clan name, and among the Khasis the youngest daughter keeps the family home. The Khasi tongue is Austro-Asiatic , a cousin of Santhali far to the west. In Arunachal Pradesh the Nyishis are the largest tribe; the Apatanis farm fish in their rice fields in the Ziro valley ; the Adis live along the Siang; and the Buddhist Monpas keep the great monastery of Tawang . Assam's largest plains tribe is the Bodo ; Mizoram's people are the Mizos ; and in Sikkim the Lepchas , the oldest settlers, live beside the Bhutias and Limbus . · Tribes of the North-East and their states · Tribe · State · Remember · Angami · Nagaland · Kohima district; tribes.x: Most asked: the Todas of the Nilgiris, the Irulas , Chenchus and Soligas , and above all the Andaman and Nicobar tribes — Jarawa, Onge, Sentinelese, Great Andamanese, Shompen and Nicobarese : where each lives, which are Negrito and which Mongoloid, and which are PVTGs. · The Nilgiri Hills are a tribal world in miniature. The Todas herd sacred buffaloes and live in barrel-roofed huts; the Kotas were their potters, smiths and musicians; the Kurumbas gathered from the forest; the Irulas are famous snake catchers. On the plains to the east, the Chenchus still hunt and gather in the Nallamala forest, and in Karnataka the Soligas of the BR Hills and the honey-gathering Jenu Kurubas live inside today's tiger reserves. Far out in the Bay of Bengal live India's most isolated people. On the Andaman Islands are four Negrito groups: the Great Andamanese (now a small group on Strait Island), the Jarawas , the Onges of Little Andaman and the Sentinelese , who allow no visitors at all. In the Nicobars live two Mongoloid peoples: the forest-dwelling Shompens of Great Nicobar and the Nicobarese , the largest island tribe. Five of these six — all but the Nicobarese — are PVTGs. · The island tribes · Tribe · Where they live · Remember · Great Andamanese · Strait Island · Once ten tribes across Great Andaman; now about 50 people, resettled on Strait Island. Most asked: the Santhal Hul (1855, Sidhu–Kanhu), Birsa Munda and the Ulgulan, Janjatiya Gaurav Divas (15 November), the Kol, Khasi and Rampa risings, Rani Gaidinliu , and festivals such as Hornbill , Sarhul , Wangala , Chapchar Kut , Bhagoria and Medaram . · Long before 1857, tribal India was rising. The British and the moneylenders, traders and landlords who came with them — the dikus — took forest and land that tribes had always held together. In the 1780s Tilka Manjhi fought in the Rajmahal hills; in 1831 the Kols of Chota Nagpur rose under Buddhu Bhagat ; and in the Khasi Hills U Tirot Sing fought a British road for four years. The biggest storm came on 30 June 1855 , when the brothers Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu called thousands of Santhals to Bhognadih: the Hul . It was crushed, but the British carved out the Santhal Parganas . Forty years later a young Munda, Birsa , preached a new faith and led the Ulgulan (great tumult) for Abua Raj , the people's own rule. He died in Ranchi jail in 1900, aged only twenty-four; his people call him Dharti Aaba , father of the earth. Since 2021 his birthday, 15 November , is Janjatiya Gaurav Divas . Tribal India also celebrates. Nagaland gathers its tribes at the Hornbill Festival each December; Jharkhand greets spring with Sarhul under the flowering sal trees; the Garos beat a hundred drums at Wangala ; and in Telangana millions come to the Koya goddesses at Medaram . · Revolts and their leaders · Revolt · Leader · Remember · Santhal Hul (1855–56) · Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu · Began on 30 June 1855 at Bhognadih, with their brothers Chand and Bhairav and sisters Phulo and Jhano; afterwards the British made the Santhal Parganas a separate district. · Munda Ulgulan (1899–1900) · Birsa Munda · ‘Dharti Aaba’ called for Abua Raj, the people's own rule; he died in Ranchi jail on 9 June 1900, and the Chota Nagpur Tenancy Act (1908) followed. · Kol rising (1831–32) · Buddhu Bhagat · In Chota Nagpur, against outsiders (dikus) taking tribal land; Two days to keep apart — “30 June Hul, 15 November Birsa” . · Ulgulan is Birsa's (Munda) rising; Hul is the Santhals'. Sidhu and Kanhu were Santhals — not Mundas. tribes.x: Asked almost every year: how many languages are in the Eighth Schedule ( 22 ), which amendment added which (21st, 71st, 92nd), the classical languages (11, Tamil first in 2004, five more in 2024), and the official-language Articles 343–351 (Part XVII), with Hindi Divas (14 September). · On 14 September 1949 the Constituent Assembly agreed on a compromise. Hindi in the Devanagari script would be the official language of the Union ( Article 343 ), but English would carry on beside it for fifteen years. When 1965 came and protests broke out in the south, Parliament had already passed the Official Languages Act, 1963 ; its 1967 amendment let English continue for as long as needed. Beside the official language stands a longer list: the Eighth Schedule . It began in 1950 with 14 languages. Sindhi , a language without a state, came in 1967 (21st Amendment); Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali in 1992 (71st); and Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali in 2003 (92nd), making 22 . Dozens more, from Bhojpuri to Tulu, are still asking to join. A third list honours age. In 2004 the government declared Tamil a classical language , for its 2,000-year-old literature. Sanskrit, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam and Odia followed, and on 3 October 2024 five more were added at once — Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali — making eleven . · The Eighth Schedule: how tribes.t: Scripts: from Brahmi to Ol Chiki
tribes.h: लिपियाँ: ब्राह्मी से ओल चिकी तक
tribes.x: Asked most: Brahmi (mother script, read by James Prinsep ), Kharosthi (right to left), Devanagari and its languages, Gurmukhi (Guru Angad Dev), Ol Chiki (Santhali, Raghunath Murmu, 1925), Meitei Mayek (Manipuri) and Grantha (Sanskrit in the south). · Almost every Indian script is a grandchild of Brahmi , the script of most of Ashoka's edicts. Brahmi was forgotten for centuries until James Prinsep read it again in 1837 . In the far north-west, Ashoka's scribes used another script, Kharosthi , which came from Aramaic and ran from right to left . Over a thousand years Brahmi branched. In the north it grew into the Gupta script, then Siddham , Sharada in Kashmir and Nagari , which became Devanagari — today the script of Hindi, Marathi, Nepali, Sanskrit, Konkani, Bodo, Dogri and Maithili. In the east it became the Bengali–Assamese and Odia scripts; in the Punjab, from Sharada and Landa, Guru Angad Dev shaped Gurmukhi . In the south came Tamil , the Telugu–Kannada script, and Grantha , made to write Sanskrit, from which Malayalam grew. The twentieth century added new scripts for tribal languages. Pandit Raghunath Murmu made Ol Chiki for Santhali in 1925 ; Lako Bodra made Warang Citi for Ho; Mangei Gomango made Sorang Sompeng for Sora; Dr Narayan Oraon made Tolong Siki for Kurukh. In Ol Chiki's centenary year the President released the Constitution in Santhali , on 25 December 2025. · Scripts and the languages they were made for · Script · Language · Remember · Ol Chiki · Santhali · Made by Pandit Raghunath Murmu in 1925; tribes.x: Asked most: Andhra State (1953) and Potti Sriramulu , the States Reorganisation Commission , Odisha (1936) as the first language province, the movements behind Maharashtra, Gujarat and the Punjabi Suba, the four language families , and the language days — Hindi Divas, World Hindi Day, Mother Language Day . · Long before independence, the Congress had promised provinces drawn by language; Odisha became the first such province in 1936 . After 1947, Nehru feared that language states would split the new nation. The Dhar Commission (1948) and the JVP Committee — Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel and Pattabhi Sitaramayya — both advised waiting. The Telugu speakers of Madras State would not wait. On 19 October 1952 the Gandhian Potti Sriramulu began a fast for a Telugu state. He died on 15 December 1952 , after 58 days; riots followed, and on 19 December Nehru gave in. Andhra State was born on 1 October 1953 , with Kurnool as its capital. Sriramulu is remembered as Amarajeevi , the immortal one. Within weeks the government set up the States Reorganisation Commission under Fazl Ali , with K. M. Panikkar and H. N. Kunzru. Its report led to the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 , and the map was redrawn on 1 November 1956 . Language movements kept going: Samyukta Maharashtra and Mahagujarat split Bombay State in 1960, and the Punjabi Suba movement split Punjab in 1966. · Language movements and what they won · Movement · Result · Remember · Utkal movement of Madhusudan Das · Odisha province (1936) · The first province drawn on the basis of language, on 1 April 1936 — Utkal Divas. · Andhra movement and Potti Sriramulu's fast · Andhra State (1953) · The first state formed on language after independence, on 1 October 1953, with Kurnool as its capital. · Aikya Kerala movement · Kerala (1956) · Travancore-Cochin joined with Malabar on 1 November 1956. · Karnataka Ekikarana (unification) movement · Mysore State (1956), renamed Karnataka in 1973 · The Kannada areas of Bombay, Madras and Hyderabad joined Mysore. · Samyukta Maharashtra movement · Maharashtra (1960) · Bombay State was split on 1 May 1960; tribes.x: Exam questions often join two facts: a tribe and its language, a language and its script, a state and its Schedule, a revolt and its date. This lesson mixes them, and puts the key numbers on one screen. · Take one people and follow every thread. The Santhals live in the Santhal Parganas of Jharkhand, a Fifth Schedule state. Their rising, the Hul , began on 30 June 1855 . Their language, Santhali , is Austro-Asiatic ; it entered the Eighth Schedule in 2003 by the 92nd Amendment , and it is written in Ol Chiki , made by Raghunath Murmu in 1925 . Now the Bodos of Assam: a Sixth Schedule council (the Bodoland Territorial Council), a Tibeto-Burman language added to the Eighth Schedule with Santhali in 2003 , and written in Devanagari since 1975. Or the Khasis : matrilineal, in a Sixth Schedule state, speaking an Austro-Asiatic language written in the Roman script, with U Tirot Sing as their hero. When you can tell each people's story this way, the mixed questions answer themselves. · Five threads for each people · People · State · Schedule · Language · family · script · Revolt or festival · Santhal · Jharkhand · Fifth · Santhali · Austro-Asiatic · Ol Chiki · Hul, 1855 · Baha, Sohrai · Munda · Jharkhand · Fifth · Mundari · Austro-Asiatic · Ulgulan, 1899–1900 · Sarhul · Oraon · Jharkhand · Fifth · Kurukh · Dravidian · Tolong Siki · Tana Bhagat, 1914 · Sarhul, Karma · Ho · Jharkhand · Fifth · Ho · Austro-Asiatic · Warang Citi · Kol rising, 1831–32 · Gond · Madhya Pradesh and others · Fifth · Gondi · Dravidian · Masaram Gondi · Komaram Bheem · Nagoba Jatara · Bodo · Assam · Sixth · Bodo · Tibeto-Burman · Devanagari · Bwisagu · Khasi · Meghalaya · Sixth · Khasi · Austro-Asiatic · Roman · U Tirot Sing · Shad Suk Mynsiem · Garo · Meghalaya · Sixth · Garo · Tibeto-Burman · Roman · Wangala · Mizo · Mizoram · Sixth · Mizo · Tibeto-Burman · Roman · Chapchar Kut · Meitei (not ST) · Manipur · Manipuri · Tibeto-Burman · Meitei Mayek · — · Numbers to carry into the exam · 8.6% · ST share of India's people (Census 2011) — about 10.43 crore · 705 · ST groups counted in 2011 · 75 · PVTGs, in 18 states and 1 UT — Odisha has the most (13) · 10 and 4 · Fifth Schedule states and Sixth Schedule states · 10 · Autonomous district councils under the Sixth Schedule · 47 · Lok Sabha seats reserved for STs · 22 · Eighth Schedule languages (14 in 1950) · 11 · Classical languages (since October 2024) · 343–351 · The official-language Articles (Part XVII) · 121 · Languages in Census 2011 (22 scheduled and 99 others) · Three numbers in one breath — “22-11-75” : 22 scheduled languages, 11 classical languages, 75 PVTGs. · Do not mix a tribe's Schedule with a language's Schedule : the Fifth and Sixth Schedules are about tribal areas ; the Eighth is about languages . persons.t: Freedom fighters' titles and who gave them
persons.h: स्वतंत्रता सेनानियों की उपाधियाँ और उन्हें देने वाले
persons.x: Most asked: who gave Gandhi 'Mahatma' (Tagore) and 'Father of the Nation' (Bose), who called Tagore 'Gurudev' (Gandhi), who made Patel 'Sardar' (the women of Bardoli), and one-word titles — Lokmanya, Deshbandhu, Mahamana, Loknayak, Shaheed-e-Azam, Masterda . · Indians rarely called their leaders by their names. A title said what the people felt. Tilak was Lokmanya — the man the people accepted. C. R. Das was Deshbandhu , friend of the country. Patel was Sardar , the chief: the farmers' wives of Bardoli gave him the name after he won their tax fight in 1928. Leaders gave titles to each other too. Tagore called Gandhi Mahatma , the great soul; Gandhi answered by calling Tagore Gurudev . In 1944, though the two had quarrelled, Subhas Chandra Bose spoke on the radio and called Gandhi the Father of our Nation . Even enemies gave names: to Valentine Chirol, Tilak was the Father of Indian Unrest ; to Churchill, Gandhi was a half-naked fakir . · Title → leader · Title · Leader · Note · Bapu · Mahatma Gandhi · 'Father' in Gujarati and Hindi — the name millions used for him. · Netaji · Subhas Chandra Bose · 'Respected leader' — first used for him in Germany in 1942. · Sardar · Vallabhbhai Patel · Given by the women of Bardoli after the Bardoli Satyagraha of 1928. · Iron Man of India · Vallabhbhai Patel · For joining more than 560 princely states to India after 1947. · Bismarck of India · Vallabhbhai Patel · Compared with Otto von Bismarck, who united Germany. · Lokmanya · Bal Gangadhar Tilak · 'Accepted by the people as their leader'. · Father of Indian Unrest · Bal Gangadhar Tilak · A label from the British journalist Valentine Chirol (Indian Unrest, 1910). · Deshbandhu · Chittaranjan Das · 'Friend of the country'; founded the Swaraj Party with Motilal Nehru (1923). · Grand Old Man of India · Dadabhai Naoroji · Gave the 'drain theory'; three times Congress President. · Chacha · Jawaharlal Nehru · Children's name for him; his birthday, 14 November, is Children's Day. · Gurudev · Rabindranath Tagore · Gandhi's name for him. · Mahamana · Madan Mohan Malaviya · 'Great-minded'; founded the Banaras Hindu University (1916). · Deshratna · Rajendra Prasad · 'Jewel of the country'; India's first President. · Loknayak · Jayaprakash Narayan · 'People's leader'; led the 1974 movement for Total Revolution. · Shaheed-e-Azam · Bhagat Singh · 'The greatest martyr'; hanged at Lahore on 23 March 1931. · Masterda · Surya Sen · He was a schoolteacher; led the Chittagong Armoury Raid (1930). · Frontier Gandhi · Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan · Also Badshah Khan; led the Khudai Khidmatgars ('Red Shirts'). · Rajaji · C. persons.h: केसरी, क्षेत्रीय उपाधियाँ और स्वतंत्रता के बाद की उपाधियाँ
persons.x: Asked now and then: the Kesaris (Punjab, Andhra, Bihar), the Shers (Kashmir, Bangla), Kerala Gandhi , Utkal Gourab / Utkalmani , and the popular names of modern achievers — Waterman, Forest Man, Mountain Man, Padman, Iron Lady of Manipur . · Every region had its own lion. Kesari and Sher both mean lion, so Punjab's lion was Lala Lajpat Rai, Andhra's was T. Prakasam, Bihar's was Sri Krishna Sinha, Kashmir's was Sheikh Abdullah and Bengal's was Fazlul Huq. Odisha called Madhusudan Das its pride ( Utkal Gourab ) and Gopabandhu Das its jewel ( Utkalmani ). After 1947 the titles changed with the times. Newspapers named people for one great deed: Rajendra Singh brought dry rivers back to life — the Waterman of India ; Jadav Payeng planted a forest on a sandbar — the Forest Man ; Dashrath Manjhi cut a road through a hill — the Mountain Man . Learn the deed and the title follows. · Kesaris and regional titles · Title · Leader · Note · Punjab Kesari · Lala Lajpat Rai · 'Lion of Punjab'; died after the lathi charge at Lahore (1928). · Andhra Kesari · Tanguturi Prakasam · First Chief Minister of Andhra State (1953). · Bihar Kesari · Sri Krishna Sinha · 'Shri Babu', first Chief Minister of Bihar. · Assam Kesari · Ambikagiri Raichoudhury · Assamese poet and freedom fighter. · Sher-e-Kashmir · Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah · Founder of the National Conference. · Sher-e-Bangla · A. persons.t: Titles of reformers and women leaders
persons.h: समाज सुधारकों और महिला नेताओं की उपाधियाँ
persons.x: Asked: Nightingale of India (Sarojini Naidu), Father of the Indian Renaissance (Ram Mohan Roy), Mother of the Indian Revolution (Bhikaji Cama), Grand Old Lady (Aruna Asaf Ali), who gave Ram Mohan Roy his 'Raja', and who called Jyotiba Phule 'Mahatma'. · Reformers earned their titles by breaking old walls. Ram Mohan Roy fought sati and is called the Father of the Indian Renaissance ; the title 'Raja' came from the Mughal emperor Akbar II, who sent him to England. Jyotiba Phule was called Mahatma in 1888 — thirty years before Gandhi — and his wife Savitribai , India's first woman teacher, is remembered as Krantijyoti . Women leaders have titles too: Sarojini Naidu , the poet, is the Nightingale of India ; Bhikaji Cama , who raised an Indian flag in Germany in 1907, is the Mother of the Indian Revolution ; Aruna Asaf Ali , who raised the flag at Gowalia Tank in 1942, is the Grand Old Lady of the Independence Movement . · Reformers and women: title → person · Title · Person · Note · Father of the Indian Renaissance · Raja Ram Mohan Roy · Founded the Brahmo Samaj (1828); campaigned against sati. · Krantijyoti · Savitribai Phule · 'Flame of revolution'; India's first woman teacher (Pune, 1848). · Cyclonic Monk of India · Swami Vivekananda · American newspapers' name after his Chicago speech (1893). · Periyar · E. R. Rahman), and the poets' titles — Upanyas Samrat, Modern Meera, Rashtrakavi . · Film fans name their stars after the roles they play. Dilip Kumar died on screen so often, and so movingly, that he became the Tragedy King ; Meena Kumari was his Tragedy Queen . Raj Kapoor made big, colourful films full of songs — the Showman . Amitabh Bachchan's roles in Zanjeer and Deewaar made him the Angry Young Man , and Hema Malini kept the name of her film Dream Girl . Writers and musicians are crowned too. Premchand, who wrote of farmers and clerks, is the Upanyas Samrat (emperor of novels); Mahadevi Varma, who wrote of longing for the divine, is the Modern Meera ; Lata Mangeshkar's voice made her Swar Kokila , the cuckoo of melody. · Film stars · Title · Star · Note · Tragedy King · Dilip Kumar · For sad, intense roles such as Devdas (1955). · Tragedy Queen · Meena Kumari · For roles such as Sahib Bibi Aur Ghulam and Pakeezah. · The Showman · Raj Kapoor · Called the greatest showman of Indian cinema (Awara, Shree 420). · Dream Girl · Hema Malini · From her 1977 film Dream Girl. · Evergreen Hero · Dev Anand · Starred for six decades. · First Superstar · Rajesh Khanna · Gave a long run of hits from 1969 to 1971. · Angry Young Man · Amitabh Bachchan · From Zanjeer (1973) and Deewaar (1975). · King Khan · Shah Rukh Khan · Also 'King of Romance'. · Mr Perfectionist · Aamir Khan · For his careful choice and preparation of roles. · He-Man · Dharmendra · Action star of Sholay (1975). · Bharat Kumar · Manoj Kumar · For patriotic films such as Upkar and Purab Aur Paschim. · Jumping Jack · Jeetendra · For his energetic dancing. · Dadamoni · Ashok Kumar · 'Elder brother' in Bengali; an early hero of Hindi films. · Venus of Indian Cinema · Madhubala · Star of Mughal-e-Azam (1960). · Thalaivar · Rajinikanth · 'Leader' in Tamil; Dadasaheb Phalke Award 2019 (given 2021). · Ulaganayagan · Kamal Haasan · 'Universal hero' in Tamil. · Puratchi Thalaivar · M. persons.t: Nicknames of world leaders and figures
persons.h: विश्व नेताओं और हस्तियों के उपनाम
persons.x: Most asked: Iron Lady (Thatcher), Lady with the Lamp (Florence Nightingale), Maid of Orleans (Joan of Arc), Desert Fox (Rommel), Man of Destiny (Napoleon), Iron Chancellor (Bismarck), and the Father of the Nation of Pakistan, Bangladesh, Turkey and the USA. · Nicknames travel faster than history books. A Soviet army newspaper mocked Margaret Thatcher as the Iron Lady in 1976, and she wore the name with pride. Florence Nightingale walked the hospital wards of the Crimean War at night with a lamp — the Lady with the Lamp . Joan of Arc, a farm girl, led France to victory at Orléans — the Maid of Orleans . Generals got names from their enemies and their soldiers: the British called Rommel the Desert Fox ; Napoleon's men called him the Little Corporal . And almost every free nation has a father : Jinnah for Pakistan, Mujib for Bangladesh, Atatürk for Turkey, Washington for the United States, Mandela for South Africa. · World figures: nickname → person · Nickname · Person · Note · Iron Lady · Margaret Thatcher · Britain's first woman Prime Minister (1979–90). · Lady with the Lamp · Florence Nightingale · Nursed soldiers at night in the Crimean War (1850s). · Maid of Orleans · Joan of Arc · Led the French at Orléans (1429); Most asked: who gave Swaraj is my birthright , Do or Die , Give me blood… , Jai Jawan Jai Kisan (and who added Jai Vigyan and Jai Anusandhan ), Garibi Hatao , Total Revolution ; who coined Inquilab Zindabad, Jai Hind and Quit India; and who wrote Saare Jahan Se Achha . · A slogan is a whole speech in four words. Tilak said Swaraj was a birthright ; Gandhi, in August 1942, told the country to do or die ; Bose asked for blood in return for freedom. After independence the slogans changed: Shastri saluted the soldier and the farmer — Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan — and later Prime Ministers added the scientist ( Jai Vigyan , Vajpayee, 1998) and the researcher ( Jai Anusandhan , Modi, 2019). Many slogans were coined by one person and made famous by another. The poet Hasrat Mohani coined Inquilab Zindabad ; Bhagat Singh made the courtroom ring with it. Yusuf Meherally coined Quit India ; Gandhi made it a movement. It begins at Raj Ghat , where Gandhi was cremated in 1948. Nehru's Shanti Van (forest of peace), Shastri's Vijay Ghat (victory), Indira's Shakti Sthal (strength) and Rajiv's Veer Bhumi (the brave) follow. Each name says something about the leader: Kisan Ghat for the farmers' leader Charan Singh, Samata Sthal (equality) for Jagjivan Ram, Sangharsh Sthal (struggle) for Devi Lal. Land by the river ran short, so in 2013 the government decided that future leaders would share one complex, the Rashtriya Smriti Sthal . Vajpayee's Sadaiv Atal (2018) stands there. Exams mix this whole topic into 'which pair is correctly matched' and 'which is NOT' questions. Most wrong answers come from look-alikes — Lokmanya and Loknayak, the two Nightingales, Chaitya Bhoomi and Deekshabhoomi. This lesson sets them side by side and adds the real names behind famous names. · Revise this app in three sweeps. First the titles : say each leader's title and who gave it — Tagore's 'Mahatma', Bose's 'Father of the Nation', Gandhi's 'Gurudev', Bardoli's 'Sardar'. Then the words : each slogan with its speaker, and each coined slogan with the person who made it famous. Last the places : walk along the Yamuna from Raj Ghat to Sadaiv Atal, then out to Porbandar, Cuttack, Mhow and Mumbai. Many famous people were born with other names. Narendranath Datta became Swami Vivekananda , Mool Shankar became Dayananda Saraswati , Margaret Noble became Sister Nivedita , and Yusuf Khan became Dilip Kumar . scitech.x: Asked often: the year each body began ( CSIR 1942, DAE 1954, DRDO 1958, DST 1971, DBT 1986, MoES 2006 ), which bodies sit directly under the Prime Minister (atomic energy and space), the old names of ICMR (1911) and ICAR (1929), and who heads CSIR . · Think of Indian science as a house with many rooms. The Ministry of Science and Technology holds three of them: the Department of Science and Technology (1971), which pays for research in universities and runs the big missions; the Department of Biotechnology (1986); and the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (1985), under which the giant CSIR and its national labs work. CSIR is older than independent India — it began in 1942, and its first Director-General was Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar . scitech.x: Asked: Bhabha's three-stage programme and why it ends with thorium , what PHWR and FBR mean, the PFBR at Kalpakkam, which body does what ( BARC, NPCIL, BHAVINI, AERB, UCIL ), and the research reactors Apsara, CIRUS, Dhruva, KAMINI . · India has little uranium but some of the world's largest reserves of thorium , in the monazite sands of the Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Odisha coasts. Thorium cannot run a reactor by itself, so in 1954 Homi J. Bhabha drew up a plan in three steps. Stage 1 : burn natural uranium in pressurised heavy water reactors (PHWRs). They give power and leave behind plutonium-239 . Stage 2 : burn that plutonium in fast breeder reactors , which 'breed' more fuel than they use and, with a thorium blanket, turn thorium into uranium-233 . Stage 3 : run reactors on thorium and uranium-233 — power for centuries. Stage 1 has run since the 1970s. Stage 2 began on 6 April 2026 , when the 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor at Kalpakkam reached first criticality — about sixteen years late. Stage 3 is still on the drawing board, in designs such as BARC's Advanced Heavy Water Reactor. · The nuclear family: who does what · Body · Job · Where and when · Atomic Energy Commission (AEC) · Sets India's atomic energy policy · 1948; Homi J. The world answered by forming the Nuclear Suppliers Group and cutting off help. Twenty-four years later, on 11 and 13 May 1998 , came five more tests — Operation Shakti — led by A. P. J. Abdul Kalam and R. Chidambaram under Prime Minister Vajpayee, and India declared itself a nuclear-weapon state. In 2003 it set out a doctrine of no first use . The door reopened in 2008 with the India–US civil nuclear agreement and a waiver from the NSG. Russia's reactors rose at Kudankulam , while India built its own 700 MWe reactors at Kakrapar and Rawatbhata. In December 2025 Parliament passed the SHANTI Act , which replaced the Atomic Energy Act of 1962 and the nuclear liability law of 2010 and, for the first time, let private Indian companies build and run nuclear plants. · Nuclear power plants at work · Plant · State · Remember · Tarapur · Maharashtra · India's first nuclear power station (1969); Asked: Bt cotton (the only GM crop grown), GM mustard DMH-11 and the GEAC , the Genome India project, which company made which vaccine (Covaxin, ZyCoV-D, Cervavac), and India's firsts in gene and cell therapy — NexCAR19, BIRSA 101 — and genome-edited rice . · In 2002 India allowed its first genetically modified crop: Bt cotton , carrying a gene from the soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis that kills the bollworm. It is still the only GM crop farmers may grow. Bt brinjal was cleared by the regulator, the GEAC , in 2009 but put on hold in 2010; GM mustard DMH-11 , bred at Delhi University, was cleared in 2022 and is stuck in the Supreme Court. The pandemic turned India into a vaccine lab. Bharat Biotech made Covaxin , Zydus made ZyCoV-D — the world's first DNA vaccine for people — and Gennova made India's first mRNA vaccine. Then came the cures: the first home-grown CAR-T cancer therapy (2023), a haemophilia gene-therapy trial at CMC Vellore (2024), and BIRSA 101 , a CRISPR therapy for sickle cell disease (2025). scitech.x: Asked: the year each platform began ( Aadhaar 2010, DigiLocker 2015, UPI 2016, CoWIN 2021, ONDC and Bhashini 2022 ), who runs it, the DPDP Act, 2023 (Data Protection Board, ₹250 crore), the IT Rules, 2021 , CERT-In (2004, six-hour rule), and the latest UPI numbers. · Most countries let private companies build their digital roads. India built public ones that anyone may use, now called digital public infrastructure or the India Stack . The first layer is identity: Aadhaar , whose first number was given on 29 September 2010 to Ranjana Sonawane of Tembhli village in Nandurbar, Maharashtra. Then payments: UPI (2016) lets any bank app pay any other. Then data: DigiLocker (2015) keeps your certificates, and consent tools let you share them. On top came platforms for health ( CoWIN for COVID vaccines, ABHA health IDs), trade ( ONDC , an open network rather than one big shop) and language ( Bhashini , AI translation). With so much data online, India passed the Digital Personal Data Protection Act in 2023; its rules were notified in November 2025. · Platforms and when they began · Platform · Began · What it does · Aadhaar · 2010 · A 12-digit identity number linked to fingerprints, iris and face; issued by UIDAI. · DigiLocker · 2015 · A cloud locker for official documents; papers kept in it are legally valid. · UPI · 2016 · Instant bank-to-bank payments from a phone; built by NPCI. · UMANG · 2017 · One app for central, state and local government services. · ABHA (Ayushman Bharat Health Account) · 2021 · A 14-digit health ID under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission. · CoWIN · 2021 · Booked and recorded COVID-19 vaccinations and gave certificates with a QR code. · ONDC · 2022 · Open Network for Digital Commerce — any buyer app can reach any seller on the network. · Bhashini · 2022 · AI tools to translate and speak in Indian languages. · U-WIN · 2024 · A digital record of routine vaccinations for children and pregnant women. · Aadhaar and UPI in numbers · UIDAI · Set up in 2009 (first chairman Nandan Nilekani); a statutory body under MeitY since the Aadhaar Act, 2016 · First Aadhaar · 29 September 2010, Tembhli village, Nandurbar district, Maharashtra · Aadhaar numbers issued · More than 138 crore (end of 2024) · Supreme Court, 2018 · Upheld Aadhaar (Puttaswamy case) but limited its use by private companies; the 2017 ruling had made privacy a fundamental right · UPI, September 2026 · 24.07 billion transactions worth ₹29.37 lakh crore; record month August 2026 (24.51 billion) · UPI abroad · Live in 11 foreign countries (August 2026), including Bhutan, Nepal, Singapore, the UAE, France, Sri Lanka, Mauritius, Qatar, Cambodia, Greece and the Maldives · Laws and watchdogs · Law or body · Year · What it does · Information Technology Act · 2000 · Made e-records and digital signatures legal and defined cyber crimes (see Computer Knowledge). · CERT-In · 2004 · National agency that handles cyber attacks; under Section 70B of the IT Act; incidents must be reported within 6 hours. · NCIIPC · 2014 · Protects critical information infrastructure such as power grids and banks; part of NTRO (Section 70A). · IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules · 2021 · Duties of social media, digital news and OTT platforms; an amendment of February 2026 covers AI-made 'synthetic' content. · Digital Personal Data Protection Act · 2023 · India's personal data law; a Data Protection Board; penalties up to ₹250 crore. · Telecommunications Act · 2023 · Replaced the Indian Telegraph Act of 1885. · DPDP Rules · 2025 · Notified on 14 November 2025; fully in force after 18 months (by May 2027). · Words of the DPDP Act, 2023 · Data Principal · The person the data is about · Data Fiduciary · The company or body that decides why and how the data is used · Consent Manager · A registered platform through which a person gives, manages or withdraws consent · Significant Data Fiduciary · A large data handler with extra duties, such as a data protection officer and audits · Children · Anyone under 18; first pilot in five cities, April 2022 · Bhashini · MeitY's National Language Translation Mission; launched 4 July 2022 at Gandhinagar · CoWIN and U-WIN · Ministry of Health and Family Welfare · JAM trinity · Jan Dhan accounts, Aadhaar and Mobile phones — the base for direct benefit transfers · Launch years as a ladder — “10 Aadhaar, 15 Locker, 16 UPI, 17 UMANG, 21 CoWIN, 22 ONDC-Bhashini, 23 DPDP” . Asked: India's stations — Dakshin Gangotri (1983), Maitri (1989), Bharati (2012) in Antarctica and Himadri (2008) in the Arctic — the first expedition (1981–82), NCPOR Goa, the Indian Antarctic Act, 2022 , IMD 's colour warnings, and INCOIS ' tsunami warning centre. · In December 1981 a team led by S. Z. Qasim sailed from Goa and landed in Antarctica on 9 January 1982 — India's first expedition . Two years later India built Dakshin Gangotri on the ice shelf; snow slowly buried it, and in 1990 it was closed. Its successor, Maitri (1989), stands on rock in the Schirmacher Oasis , and Bharati (2012), made of shipping containers, sits in the Larsemann Hills . In the far north, Himadri (2008) is India's Arctic station at Ny-Ålesund on Norway's Svalbard islands. All of them are run by the National Centre for Polar and Ocean Research in Goa, under the Ministry of Earth Sciences. In 2022 Parliament passed the Indian Antarctic Act , so Indian law now applies to Indian expeditions there. Closer to home, IMD gives colour-coded warnings and INCOIS in Hyderabad runs the tsunami warning centre set up after the 2004 tsunami. · India's research stations · Station · Where · Remember · Dakshin Gangotri · An ice shelf in Queen Maud Land, Antarctica · India's first Antarctic station (1983–84); buried in ice and closed in 1990; now a supply base. · Maitri · Schirmacher Oasis, Antarctica · Built in 1989; Maitri II, a greener replacement, is planned for about 2029. · Bharati · Larsemann Hills, Antarctica · Opened in 2012; built from 134 shipping containers. · Himadri · Ny-Ålesund, Svalbard (Norway), in the Arctic · India's first Arctic research station (2008). · IndARC (underwater observatory) · Kongsfjorden, Svalbard · India's first underwater observatory in the Arctic (2014). · Himansh · Chandra basin, Spiti (Himachal Pradesh) · A high-altitude station for studying Himalayan glaciers (2016). · Antarctica and the Arctic · First expedition · Left Goa in December 1981, led by S. scitech.x: Asked: the four Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar awards and their limits, the first Vigyan Ratna (G. Padmanabhan, 2024) and the 2025 one (Jayant Narlikar), the team awards , the Infosys Prize , the Kalinga Prize , and Indian-origin winners of the Fields, Abel and Turing awards. · For decades the prize every young Indian scientist wanted was the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize , given by CSIR since 1958 . In 2023 the government cut down hundreds of science awards and put one national award in their place: the Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar . It has four parts, like the Padma awards: Vigyan Ratna for a lifetime, Vigyan Shri for distinguished work, Vigyan Yuva–Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar for scientists up to 45, and Vigyan Team for groups. The first awards were presented by President Droupadi Murmu on 22 August 2024 — 33 in all, with the first Vigyan Ratna to the biochemist G. Padmanabhan and the team award to Chandrayaan-3 . In 2025 the Vigyan Ratna went, after his death, to the astrophysicist Jayant Narlikar , and the team award to CSIR's Aroma Mission . The same year India lost several giants: Narlikar, K. Kasturirangan , R. Chidambaram and M. R. Srinivasan . · Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar: the four awards · Award · For · Remember · Vigyan Ratna · Lifetime achievement in science · Up to 3 a year; 2024 — G. Asked: full forms ( LED, LASER, LiDAR, RADAR, SONAR, GPS, NavIC, RFID ), one-line meanings ( nanotechnology, 3D printing, graphene, qubit ), 5G (October 2022) and the Bharat 6G Vision (2023), and biofuels — E20, 2G ethanol, SAF. · Most technology words are short forms that tell you how the thing works. RADAR finds things with radio waves, SONAR with sound under water and LiDAR with light from a laser. GPS is America's navigation system; NavIC is India's own, covering India and about 1,500 km around it. An LED is a tiny semiconductor that glows; India's UJALA scheme put crores of LED bulbs in homes. Mobile networks came in generations. India switched on 5G on 1 October 2022 , one of the fastest roll-outs anywhere, and in March 2023 released the Bharat 6G Vision . In September 2025 BSNL launched a 4G network built entirely on Indian equipment. On the road, petrol now carries 20% ethanol (E20) — a target India reached in 2025, five years before the original 2030 date. · Full forms · Short form · Full form · Remember · LED · Light-Emitting Diode · A semiconductor that glows when current flows; the UJALA scheme (2015) spread LED bulbs. · OLED · Organic Light-Emitting Diode · Each pixel makes its own light — thin, bendable screens. · LASER · Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation · A narrow, single-colour, powerful beam of light. · LiDAR · Light Detection and Ranging · Measures distance with laser pulses — 3D maps, self-driving cars, Moon landers. · RADAR · Radio Detection and Ranging · Uses radio waves to find aircraft, ships and storms. · SONAR · Sound Navigation and Ranging · Uses sound waves under water. · GPS · Global Positioning System · The United States' satellite navigation system. · NavIC · Navigation with Indian Constellation · India's own regional navigation satellites (IRNSS); see the Space app. · GAGAN · GPS Aided GEO Augmented Navigation · Makes GPS accurate enough for aircraft landings — ISRO with the Airports Authority. · RFID · Radio-Frequency Identification · Tags read by radio waves — FASTag on cars. · NFC · Near-Field Communication · Tap-to-pay over a few centimetres. · Li-Fi · Light Fidelity · Sends data with flickering LED light instead of radio waves. · IoT · Internet of Things · Everyday devices with sensors linked to the internet. · UAV · Unmanned Aerial Vehicle · A drone — an aircraft with no pilot on board. · CCUS · Carbon Capture, Utilisation and Storage · Catching carbon dioxide from chimneys to use or bury it. · SAF · Sustainable Aviation Fuel · Jet fuel made from waste oils, crop waste or other non-fossil sources. · CBG · Compressed Biogas scitech.x: Exam papers mix these topics in one question: 'which pair is wrongly matched', 'which came first', 'which is NOT under ministry X'. This lesson trains exactly that, across all ten lessons. · Before the exam, hang every fact on one of three pegs. Who runs it — a ministry, a department or a council. When it began — a year. Where it is — a city, a state or a continent. Most science-and-technology questions in SSC are one of those three, dressed up as 'which pair is correct'. Read the years below as a single story: CSIR in 1942 before independence, atomic energy in the 1950s, space in the 1960s and 70s, biotechnology in the 1980s, Digital India in 2015, and a rush of missions after 2020 — semiconductors, hydrogen, quantum, AI — ending with the SHANTI Act and the fast breeder of 2025–26. · Years in one place · 1942 · CSIR · 1948 · 1954 · Atomic Energy Commission · Department of Atomic Energy · 1958 · DRDO;
